N- 23.

The Examination of Richard Carter, Esquire, Receiver of the Deductions of One Shilling in the Pound upon Offices and Pensionsj taken upon Oath the 15th of December 1780.

This Examinant'faith. That tin's Duty is collected by vi rtue of the 31st of Geo. I hi, Chapter 22d; and such Parts of it as are stopt in the Offices in,

out of the Salaries and Pensions there issued or paid, are received by himself, some Quarterly, some Half Yearly, some Annually, according as the Smallness of the Sum, or Circumstances of the Payment, render it necessary or convenient.

The only Persons in the Country from whom he receives this Duty, are the Collectors of the Customsat the Out Ports; these Collectors return every Year, to his Requisition, an Account, signed by themselves, of their yearly Salaries and Fees, made up to the 5th of April, with a Bill for the Amount of the Duty upon them.

The Money received for this Duty is usually paid into the Exchequer, by Quarterly Payments, soon after

*53

it is received; he himself has paid it in oftener, and has reserved in his Hands about Two thousand Pounds.

The Account of the Year's Receipts and Payments has been, as he believes, usually made up once a Year, to the 5th of April, and the whole Balance remaining in the Receiver's Hands then paid into the Exchequer, and the Accounts are passed in the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest.

The only Deductions out of this Duty are the Three Pence in the Pound upon the Gross Receipt allowed to the Receiver (who pays out of that Poundage all the Expences of collecting the Duty) and Fifty Pounds paid to the Auditor of the Imprest towards passing the

Accounts. RichdCarter.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Thomas Wooldridge., Esquire; and also the Petition of William Prentice, Richard John Lewis, William Coiding, and John Elec-

tors of the Borough of Abingdon, in the County of Berks, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker; and One hundred and Twenty fix Members being found to be prefen t;

The Petitioner Thomas Wooldridge, Esquire, (who appeared for himself) and the Agent for the Petitioners William Prentice, Richard Blake, John Lewis, William Couting, and John Harper, Electors of the said Borough of Abingdon, and also the Counsel and Agents for the Sitting Member, were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the.House.

And the Names of Forty-nine Members then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Five Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who wereabfent from the House; Four, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions wore depending; and One, on Account of his having already in this hellion of Parliament, served on a Select Committee.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete;

Tire Petitioner Thomas Wooldridge, Esquire, was called upon by Mr. Speaker, to nominate One from among the Members then present, whose Names had not been draw'll, to be added to those chosen by Lot to serve on the said Select Committee.

Whereupon Mr. Wooldridge acquainted the House, that he declined to nominate any Member for that Purpose.

And thereupon the Name of the Honourable James Murray was drawn, and added to the Lift of the Forty-nine Names before drawn.

And then the Counsel for the Sitting Member nominated George Onjloiv, Esquire, to serve on the said Select Committee.

And One of the said Lifts was delivered by the Clerk to the said Petitioner Thomas Wooldridge, Esquire, and another to the Counsel for the Sitting Member.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Petitioner, and the Agent for the said other Pe-Voi» 38.

titioners, and the Counsel and Agents for the Sitting Member, withdrew.

In the Dead of the Night preceding the Day of Election, an immenle Number of People look Possession of the large Market Place, and the Booth erected in Front thereof for taking the Poll, when the Petitioners came to it, was wholly inclosed dole up to the Bread of it, by a Crowd as thick as they couid Hand, which continued there without moving so much as to have the Appearance of any one changing his Place even at the very Bread of the Booth, from the Time the Election opened, at Ten o'Clock, till Three in the Afternoon, when the Poll adjourned. In the faccceding Night, the Marketplace was again taken Possession of in the same Manner, a large Fire was lighted in the Market Place, round which the Crowd kept, and a Quantity of Straw was brought into the Poll Booth, where as many lay as it would hold, as the Petitioners were informed. In this Manner, Matters continued to go on without Variation for the First Two Days and Nights of the Election:

The Consequence was; that it was not possible for any one Person to approach the Poll Booth but at the Will; and by the Permidion, of the People who inclosed it a* above, and of whom certain Persons well known and distinguished, always kept the same Stations arid Places quite at or near the Bread of the Booth: There was clear Evidence, not only from the Persons who thus kept Pofiession, but from their open and avowed Language, that they were there for the Purpose of hindering any from coming to poll, but whom they chose should:

These People were impressed to believe that Voters had a Right to keep Pofiession of the Place of Election in that Manner, and could not be removed till they h-'d given their Votes; and the Petitioners were told, by the Persons themselves, and by those who spoke in their Behalf in Answer to any thing that dropt from the Petitioners and their Assessor, that this was the Law of Election: They were told, that all the People standing in Front of the Booth, were Freemen and Voters, and that the Petitioners would be guilty of a Breach of their Duty if they attempted to remove them: The Effect was, that during the First Days of the Poll, a very small Number of the Voters for one Set of the Candidates could by any Means whatever get up to the Booth to poll; and Notices signed by Numbers of Voters were conveyed to the Petitioners in the Booth, complaining that they could procure no Access, and demanding that a Way should be opened and made free for that Purpose, which the Petitioners were fendble it was not in their Power to effect without using a Force which they had not attheir Command; they were fendble of the Dan-ger of using any Means of Force if they had had them/ or, if the Occaiioirdiad admitted of using Force, seeing plainly that Blooddied would be the Consequence: The First Day the Petitioners were alarmed with a Scuffle, which plainly pointed out the Consequence of violent Measures; there were a very few of the ot-dinary Con-ftnbles attending at the back Entrance to the Hall of Justice, adjoining to which the Poll Booth is CrCfled, when the Petitioners came there the Morning of the Election, but the Petitioners did not order them to any Duty, or to go to the Election Booth, not having been called, for no particular Instructions were given them:

The Petitioners, before the Poll had begun, were fur* prized with a Noise and Disturbance from under the Axchway by one End of the Booth where the Pump stands, and in a Moment there came a Shower of Constables long Staves, and some of a diort Make (which the Petitioners never hadfeen, and which they and their Affeilor expressed their Disapprobation of in theftrongeft Terms when they appeared) thrown into the Poll Booth, which had been wrested out of the Hands of the Constables, it was said, in a Struggle between them and Part of the Crowd l'urrounding the Booth; the Petitioners do not know how the Scuffle began, otherwise than that it was said the Condables, by Directions of some Person the Petitioners do not know, and could by no Enquiry they made learn whom, were attempting to make a Pafifage to the Booth by that particular Approach where the Scuffle took Place, for Voters who wanted to come and poll; after this, there was not a Constable or Condables Staff appeared during the whole Election, except the High Constable's, who flood within the Booth; during the First Days of the Poll, the Peti- t ioners saw from the Booth divers Acts of Violence at different Times, but at such a Distance from the Booth, that they could make no Interposition in Time to prevent the Mischief; they saw within their View

and that the Candidates, the Voters for whom were prevented from Access in the Manner above-mentioned, having, during these First Days of the Poll complained in a very urgent Manner, to the Petitioners, demanding the Interposition of Authority to procure equal and indifferent Access to Voters of all Sides, the Petitioners, by the Mouth of their Assessor did declare, in the moll public and serious Manner, that the Obstructions complained of, were absolutely dellructive of the Freedom of Election, and that an Election, carried under the Influence of such a forcible Obstruction |o Voters, was not free, and would be void: It was represented, that the Law, for the Sake of the Freedom of Election, had re-ftrgined from such Measures of legal Force as might, on other Occasions, be resorted to; that it was plain the Use of Constables in this same would only produce such Violence and Riot as might be very dangerous, without dist who was guilty; and that the Notions of the Law of Election, which the People seemed to have learned, were erroneous: That if the Voice of the Law, and the Commands of the Magistrates, were not of Efficacy to maintain Order, Peace, and Access to vote, violent Measures would only lead to great Mischief and Bloodffied; but that if free Access was not permitted, it would be doing an Injury to the Law, and sacrificing the Freedom of Election, to permit a Poll to proceed in such a Manner. The Petitioners afterwards published through the City a Proclamation, in the strongest Terms, exhorting to and commanding the Peace and Freedom of Election to be preserved inviolate. After Two Days of the Poll, an Agreement was entered into, and signed by the Candidates, and some of their Friends, in Consequenceofa Proposal made by the one Party, and acceeded to by the other, that, upon Sir Thomas Hdll\fax and Mr. Rogers contenting that there should be polled 150 Votes for Colonel Holroyd and Mr. Yeo, above the Number polled for the other Gentlemen, the Friends of both Parties should concur to procure a Lane to be opened in Front of the Booth, for the Voters to come up to poll freely and without Interruption; and this Agreement the Petitioners and their Assessor were called upon by all the Candidates to countenance; but the Petitioners were advised, that the Law and Authority which was in their Hands were too sacred to be exposed to Contempt; that as it was their Warrant, lb it ought to be »h°ir otjly Support and Protection to which they were

to trust; that it tto way* belonged to them to take any Part in a Compromise that, bore the Aspert of compounding for the Peace and Freedom of Election: flic Petitioners only expressed their Satisfaction if any Measure had the EflVCt to redeem them from the difitgree-alde Dilemma they were in; and to prevent Tumult and Riots; and the Agreement was publicly intimated to the furreunding Croud, who had for so many Days kept the Booth under their Power and in their Possession; the Notification was made by lVrloni) in whom they bad Confidence; it had an Effect which the Law anil Authority had not produced; a Lane was formed for the Voters to come up; and this Lane was kept by Gentlemen, some of them of great Rank and figure, among whom were a noble Lord ami an honourable Gentleman, both Members of this House, who condescended, upon the Occasion, to act the Part of Constables for a Day or two. Tired out at length in the disagreeable Service, it was proposed that a Wav should be raised in for the Voters to come up; and;accordingly a Rail was permitted to be erected, though the Petitioners had not been able to get any Bar, or Convenience of the Kind, made before, as they had desired and ordered, by Reason of the constant Possession held of the Booth by the Multitude, and their Opposition to the Attempt, which defeated the Endeavours of the Tradesmen employed to do the Work. For some Weeks after this Agreement, the Poll went on, without any considerable Interruption: At different Times there were Instances to be seen from the Booth, of the Practice above-mentioned of hufiling, as it is called, Persons through the Crowd, and forcing them away in the Manner before described; but they were generally at some Distance from the Booth, and the Persons not prel'enting themselves to complain of the Mai treatment, the Petitioners, rather than give Occasion to retard the Poll, or create more Confuflon, chose to take no Notice of the Acts; the Entrance to the Rail-way was alf'o frequently stopped up, and Voters who were not to the Liking of the Crowd were not fufftred to come forward, which obliged the Petitioners and the Under Sheriff, with their Officers, to go in Person to remove the Obstruction, which, after Efforts that were fruitless by reason of Violence and Opposition, at length succeeded, by the Aid and Interposition of the Candidates of one Side, and their Friends, who had undertaken for the Performance of the Agreement. On Monday the 18 th of a Question occurred, wholly unforeseen to the Petitioners, and the Occasion of which was entirely unknown to them, or their Assessor: Considerable Number of Freemen having been admitted and enrolled by the Council, which, by the Constitution of the City of Coventry, is the Body competent to the Admission of Freemen, upon their antecedent 'Title of Servitude (which constitutes the Right of Election in the City of Coventry) one of them presented himself to vole, which produced an Objection to all under that Description; the Objection was argued, at great Length, by the CounlcI on both Sides; and the Petitioners Assessor, after having, at some Length, and in pretty strong Terms, expressed his Sentiments, as no ways partial or favourable to the Circumstances of that occasiona! Kind of Admission, though clearly excepted in the Acts against oecasional Freemen, upon the Ground of the Nature of 1 lie Title, took Time to give his Decision, and particularly to consider the same of Bristol, determined in the last Parliament, the Facts of which were not agreed upon by the Counsel. said, that all possible Pains had been used to make them quiet, but that one might as well speak to the Pavement as to them; adding, that they were afraid to seem to inler-pose with them, led it might be thought they had the Direction of them: In the Course of One whole Day only a very few Voters were polled, which those Guards of the -Approach to the Booth permitted to come up, because they did not dispute their Title; and the Petitioners patiently waited, enduring all the Insult and Abuse, and declaring against varying the Mode of taking the Votes, though thereto repeatedly pressed by Voters who could not get Access in the usual Way till Fonr o'Clock, the usual Hour for adjourning the Poll: The next Day was spent in the same Manner, with an Increase of Outrage; the Candidates of the one Side demanded, of the Friends of the other, the Performance of the Agreement, to which Answers were made verbally, and read in Writing, refusing that the Agreement applied to the New Freemen, and some of them saying, not very prudently, that instead of affiding to procure them Access, they would rather prevent it: A Freeman, in the Uniform of the Militia, who by some Means or other had got within the Railway, and come up to the Front of the Booth w as immediately dragged from the Place with great Force and Violence, and was introduced within the Booth by the Communication through the Public Hall, called the Mayor's Parlour, with the Marks of the Violence be had differed upon him; whereupon the Assessor of the Petitioners, after Yol. 38.

very fully explaining, in the Hearing of all present, the Mischief and dangerous Consequences of fitch a Contempt and Defiance of all Law and Authority, advised to attempt taking the Poll of the Person \Vlio had been so abided within the Booth; lipdrt this, those without the Booth, in great Numbers and by Force, broke into the Booth; intimriting, by their Words and Actions, their Purpose to put their Threatienings into Execution; they qitite enclosed and surrounded the Petitioners and their Aflelfor within the Booth, and with the utmost Difficulty vVere kept; by the Entreaties and by the Exertions of some df thieir own Friends, from proceeding to farther Extremities; in that Situation they continued till Four o'Cloek, when they retired, to let the Adjournment of the Poll be proclaimed. The next Day the same Scene was renewed in every Part; the Poll was not allowed to proceed, but just as these Rioters and disorderly Persons, who were the fame, from Day to Day, plealed: They were Matters of every Thing; the Assessor of the Petitioners again represented, in the warmest and most inoffensive Manner, not only the Danger but the Folly of such Conduct, and the ill Consequences they exposed themselves to; but the Booth was again broke into, in the same Mariner as the Day before, in Spite of a very firong Refinance made by some of their own Party who did all they could, by main Force, and the utmost Exertions of bodily Strength, to oppose and keep down with their Hands, and in every possible Way, the Persons who were leaping over the Breast of the Booth; thofd who made that Resistance seemed to be very much afraid of the Consequences, for they not only opposed the Attempt to their utmost, but swore they would themselves knock down the first Man that attempted, to touch any Person in the Booth, particularly the Assessor of the Petitioners, whom they mentioned by Name: To those Persons who made the Resistance, ii was probably owing, that no further Mischief was done; for when the Assessor of the Petitioners was quite enclosed and surrounded, they exerted themselves to the utmost, by streteking out their Arms, and pushing, with all their Strength, to keep the Crowd off', and preserv a Space clear in a very small Circle, till at last they prevailed upon the People to go out of the Booth, when Four o'Clock came, and the Poll was adjourned: In this State the Poll was adjourned over to Tuesday, Sunday and Chrijhnas Day intervening, on

which Day the Assessor to the Petitioners was called to in the Streets to take Care, he would be polled Tomorrow (alluding to an El eft ion Phrase in which signifies the Practice of forcing off and abusing Voters, in the Manner before described ;) a large Stone was also thrown at him and the Under Sheriff in the Streets, which only touched the Under Sheriff's Leg, without Hurt. On Tuesday Morning the Booth was surrounded in the same Manner, and by the same People, as the preceding Days: Before attempting to proceed in the Business of the Poll, the Assessor to the Petitioners, having the justest Reason from Appearances to apprehend a Renewal of the former Scenes, began with representing, in their proper Colours, the Proceedings of the pall Days, and the Necessity there was for doing every Thing that the Law would do by such Means as could be used eonfiftently with the Cir-cumstances peculiar to an Election, for the Protection and Security of those employed in the Execution of their Duty under legal Authority, and for attaining the Ends of His Majesty's Writ of Election: He observed, that it was then morally certain, from the Voices of the Persons. and the State of the Poll, that there was not One of those surrounding the Booth who had the Pretence (insufficient as it was) that had been adopted in the Beginning of the Election, it being wellknou-n, that all of them who were Freemen had voted; he said, he would not wish rashly to change their Situation, and to put them into one of greater Danger,

and he knew the tender and delicate Ground he was going to enter upon; but he thought it his Duty to the Laws of his Country and to them, to warn them of the Hazard they might run by persisting in such Jawless and riotous Acts* and therefore, though he did not meanito read the Proclamation of the Riot Act, unless absolutely drawn to it as the lad Remedy, and although, if it were read, it was impossible in the present same to carry into Effect the most dreadful Part of that Statute, as there neither was, or could be, a necessary Force present when an Election was going on, yet they ought to be informed, that if they refitted the Commands of the Proclamation, when made according to the Statute, and continued together for no other Purpose but to persevere in so flagrant a Violation of the Freedom and Peace of Election ,they might incur a Capital Felony; and to apprize them of their Risk, he would only read the Act, hoping that foine of the Friends of these deluded People would explain the Consequences to them. The Act was accordingly read over at length; and the Observation made upon it by one who was acting as an Assistant Agent for one Side of the Candidates, was, that he supposed the Gentlemen knew that a Sheriff had once been sent to Newgate for reading the Riot Act at an Election, not considering the Difference between prostituting Office and the Law for base Purposes, and using them for protesting and promoting the Ends of both: This Information had probably some Effect to give Weight to the Influence which had been used by the Friends of these People, and fortunately their Attention was divided by another Question, respecting the Right of a large Number of Freemen" who belong loan Hospital in the Nature of The Charter Hous, the Hearing of which Question, and Evidence upon it, took up all that Day, and ended in a Decision to their Willi; but to whatever the Effect was owing, the Poll was allowed to proceed, without Interruption, till the Election was finished. The Petitioners thought it their Duty to lay these Matters before this honourable House, conceiving the y justly merit the Attention thereof, that by a seasonable Interpofnion of their Authority, some Check may be put to the like in future, and the Peace and Freedom of Election secured in Coventry, and such Proceedings not drawn into evil Example elsewhere: The Petitioners only further say, that among the principal Actors in the aforesaid Violences and riotous Acts, so far as they could be marked and distinguished in the Confusion, were , a Soldier in the

A Petition of Wibliam Smith, Doctor of Physic, being offered to be preferred to the House;

The Lord Norths by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner did, in Consequence of an Application to him. by order of a Committee then iubfifting in Westminster, visit several of the Gaols and Prisonsin London, Westminster, and Southwark, and administered Relief to many of the sick Prisoners confined therein, from the 25th Day of March 1776 to the 10th of November 1779, and continued the same occasionally, upon Application, to May 1780; and that the Number of Prisoners relieved by the Petitioner with Medicines and other Assistance, amounts to 1051, by Means whereof an Expence of £.566. -\s. gd. was incurred by him for Medicines only, exclusive of other Assistance given by the Petitioner to Prisoners, many of whom lie also attended at their own Habitations, and suppli^d them with Medicines, when they were discharged out of Gaol, before their Cure was completed, which Attendance, together with the writing and publishing several Treatises relative to Prisons and Prisoners, which he considered as Part of his Duty, caused an Expence and Loss of Time, from his own Concerns and Business, that very considerably reduced his annual Income, and has, in a very great Degree, injured his private Fortune, for all which he has received no Satisfaction whatever, except the Sum of £. 50 by Order of the said Committee, which was applied in Discharge of Part of the Apothecary's Bill, due for Medicines sent to Prisoners, and for which the Petitioner was to be accountable; and that the Petitioner did, in the last Session of Parliament, apply to the House for Relief, and upon a State of Fa&s being reported to the House, the House did, on the 20th of December 1780, come to a Resolution, that a Sum, not exceeding £. 1,200, be granted to His Majesty, to be paid to the Petitioner, in Recompence for his unwearied and humane Attendance upon the sick and diseased Prisoners, and for repaying him the several Sums of Money expended in purchasing proper Medicines for them; and that the Petitioner has hitherto been deprived of the Benefit intended him by the said Resolution, in Consequence of Petitions preferred to the House, which were referred to a Committee, but from that Committee no Report was ever made to the House, and the Petitioner is Hill unpaid, having also suffered by Loss of Time, and Expences incurred , by a long Attendance on the above Committee: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief to the Petitioner as shall be thought proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Herbert Mackworth, Mr. Townshend, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, 24

and Records; and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

Stepney A Petition of Amt King, of Low Layton, in the County

and of E/fex, Widow, was presented to the House, and read;

IkAa'T. Setting forth. That the Petitioner held, by letters

Record0 Patent, of the Nineteenth Year of King Charles the Second, a Court of Record, within the Manors of Stepney and Hackney, in the County of the

Hamlets and Liberties of the fame, for the Trial of Personal Actions under Five Pounds, and was entitled to, and did receive, divers Fees arising from Writs and other Processes issued out of the said Court; and Vol. 38.

that the Petitioner was left a Widow, dependent on, and deriving her chief Subsistence from, her legal Fees arising out of the said Court, which the Petitioner's Husband having quietly enjoyed as his Freehold, left the same to her, who continued to enjoy the fame, without having ever entertained a Doubt but that die had a permanent Estate, sufficient for her Maintenance, not less secure than any other Freehold; and alledging, that the Act passed in the Twentieth Year of His present Majesty, to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests, hath operated to the almost total Annihilation of all legal Proceedings in the Petitioner's Court, as the Suitors are discouraged, by a great and certain Expence, before they can bring the Defendants into Court (without mentioning the Length of Time which mull necessarily elapse) to obtain a Satisfaction, always uncertain in the Event; and that these Difficulties, attending the Recovery of Small Debts, fall very heavy upon the lower Order of Tradesmen, and poorer Sort of Credit tors, and, unless some Remedy is provided, they must continue to submit to lose the greater Part of t heir final! Book-debts; and that, if the Petitioner was empowered to exercise her Chartered Rights, in regard to her pecuniary and within her local Jurisdiction, at a less Expence, and in a Way less burthensome to the Suitors, if would prove highly beneficial to both Creditor and Debtor, and be the Means of indemnifying the Petitioner for the Injury (he has sustained by the said Act:

And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for enabling the Petitioner's Court, held for the Manors of Stepney and Hackney, in the County of Middlesex, the Hamlets and Liberties of the fame, to proceed by Summons, and to determine, in a summary Way, within her local Jurisdiction, all Suits or Actions for Sums from Forty Shillings to Five Pounds, her pecuniary Jurisdiction, under her Steward of the said Court, and under such Regulations as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of John William Anderson, John Verdi£*«»fe

and William Bartlett, Merchants, and Proprietors of the Manufactory. Works established at Newnham, in Gloucestershire, for the Manufacture of Verdigrcafe, was presented to the House, and read. Setting forth, That the Petitioners and others, having observed, from the Entries made at

the

11 Geo. III. 6° Febr. 183

the Customs, that very large Quantities of Verdigrease were annually imported into this Kingdom from France, free of all Duties and Customs, and conceiving that it might be a National Benefit, as well as private Advantage, if a Manufacture of Verdigrease could be established in England, the Petitioners Manufacture was set on Foot, and a considerable Sum of Money employed in that Undertaking; and that, after many Years Application and Labour, and the Expence of several thousand Pounds, the Petitioners succeeded so far as not only to be enabled to supply the different Trades with Verdigrease of a Quality equal, if not superior to that which had been imported from France, but even to furnish it at a Price at lead Fifteen per Centum cheaper than the French were accustomed to fell it; and that, having arrived at this Degree of Perfection, it has excited a Rivalship in the French, who, Availing themselves of the Advantage of importing Verdigrease into this Kingdom Duty-free, have of late imported such Quantities as, with the Produce of the Petitioners Works, have reduced the Article to so low Price, that the Petitioners cannot proceed in their Adventure, and, instead of being able to undersell the French, are now themselves undersold, their Works, which they are desirous of extending, are suspended, and thteir Capital of many thousand Pounds, already employed, in Danger of being annihilated, and the Advantages arising from the said Manufactory in Danger of being loll to this Kingdom; and that the Success of the Petitioners Works would render this Kingdom independent of a Foreign Market for the said Article, hut such Success cannot be attained without fonie Encouragement is given them by the Legislature; And therefore ('.raying for such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Were severally p relented to the House* and read;

Setting forth, That by the Act lately puffed, for more effectually preventing the pernicious Practice of Smuggling; the Ship or Vessel in which shall be imported Foreign Brandy, or other Foreign Spirituous Liquors, in any Calk not containing Sixty Gallons at the lead (except only For the Use of the Seamen, not exceeding.

Two Gallons each Man) with her Tackle and Apparel, is forfeited; and when Tea, Coffee, or any Goods whatsoever, are liable to Forfeiture, for being found on board any Ships or Vessels coming from Foreign Parts, at. Anchor, or hovering within the Limits of any Port of this Kingdom, or within Two Leagues of the Coast thereof. Sec* the Ship or Vessel, if corning from any Part of Europe, on board which l'ucll -Goods shall be so found, together with her Guns*

Stores, and Materials, shall be forfeited, provided each Ship or Vessel do not exceed the Burthen of Two Hundred Tons; and that the said Law (by making no Distinction between such Ships as are usually employed in a fair and open Trade, and such as are employed for the sole Purpose of Smuggling) doth subject the Ship Owner to the Loss of his Property, although he is no Ways concerned in, or privy to, any Offence committed against the Laws made to prevent Smuggling; and that the Mailers and Seamen, employed by Owners of Ships, being Persons of little or no Property, no Recompence can be had against them, in case of Forefeiture of the Ships by the said Law; and that the said Forfeiture greatly discourages the building and fitting out Ships for the Foreign and Coailing Trade in general, and may, in Time, occasion a total Decrease in the Number of Ships so employed* and of course in His Majesty's Revenue arising from those extensive Trades; and the Petitioners conceive* that if the Legislaturewere, by a new Law, to declare, that the said Act shall not extend to the Forfeiture of any Ship or Vessel belonging to* and usually failing out of, a British Port, and constantly employed in a fair and open Trade, and where the Owner thereof can make it clearly appear, that he has no Concern in, or privy to, the illicit Transaction, the same would be agreeable to Justice and Equity; and that if the Mailers and Seamen, belonging to Ships or Vessels on board which any prohibited Goods shall be found, were thereby made liable to serve in the Royal Navy, or to some personal and exemplary Punishment, the same would greatly tend to discourage the pernicious Practice of Smuggling, and more effectually obtain the Objects of the present Act: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners J*

such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A PETITION of the Owners of Ships belonging to the Port of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, residing on Shore, w'as presented to the House, and read; Reciting an Act made in the Nineteenth Yrear of His present Majesty\s Reign, for more effectually preventing the pernicious Practice of Smuggling; And felting forth, That the said Act (by making no Distinction between such Ships as are usually employed in a fair open Trade, and such as are employed for the sole Purpose of Smuggling) subjects the Ship Owner to the Loss of his Property, although he be no Way concerned in, or privy to, any Offence committed against the Laws made to prevent Smuggling; and that, the Mailers and Seamen employed by the Petitioners in their Ships, being Persons of little or no Property, the Petitioners can have no Recompence against them in same of Forfeiture of their Ships by the aforesaid Law, which Forfeiture is a Discouragement to the building and fitting out Ships, especially for the Holland and CoastingTrade, and may occasion a great Decrease in the Number of

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Letters Patent, granted in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for dstablishing a Court of Jtecord within the Manors of Stepney and Hackney, in the County of Middlesex, the Hamlets and Liberties of the fame, for the Trial of Personal Actions under Five Pounds, weFe produced: And,

Mr. Richard Farmer being examined, said,. That the Right of holding the said Court passed by Way of Sale; through divers Hands, into the Posselhon of the late Jjufband of the Petitioner Mrs. King, who left it t8 her as a principal Source for her Maintenance after his Death — That the said Court hath been regularly kept, agreeably to the Rules and Orders contained in the said Letters Patent, much to the Benefit of the trading Part of the Inhabitants within its Jurisdiction — That the present Method of proceeding to an Execution in the said Court, under the said Letters Patent, is so tedious, and the Expences attending it so high, that in all Cases it mull exceed the Debt to be recovered, and in many Instances may be Four Times as much, though no Defence should be made- -That if proper Powers were granted by Parliament, for shortening the Proceedings of the said Court, in order for a Creditor to obtain an Execution in a more summary Way, the Expences thereof would be so much reduced, that Numbers of Tradesmen, resident within the said District, who mull now submit to the Loss of their small Debts, would have the fair Means of recovering the m.

That it is proposed to confine the Jurisdiction of the said Court to Sums from Forty Shillingsfo^ive Pounds, and to limit the Term of Confinement of a Debtor taken in Execution, which at present is left wholly to the tn-.clination of the Creditor.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for. diminishing the Fees payable, and altering the Mode of proceeding, in the Court of Record, within the Manors of Stepney and Hackney, in the County of Middlesex, the Hamfets and Liberties of the fame; And that Mv.Byng,

Mr- Solicitor General, and Mr. Alderman Wilkes, dd prepare, and bripg in, the fame.

Sir Robert Smyth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for cleansing and making navigable the Channel from The Hythe at Colchester, in the County of Fff'ex, to Wivenhoe, in the said County, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Borough and Towns adjacent, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relating to Navigation Bills, it not being proposed to extend the Navigation, or to raise any further Sum of Money for that Purpose 5 and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read: and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, several Acts, passed in the Ninth and Tenth Years of William the Third, the Fifth of George the First, and the Thirteenth and Twenty-third Years of his late Majesty King George the Second, for cleansing and making navigable the Channel from The Hythe at Colchester to Wivenhoe, in the Coouty of Essex; and for repairing the Streets of Colchester, and cleansing the fame, were read; whereby it appeared, that a Duty of Six Pence the Chaldron upon Sea Coals, was laid for a Term which will expire at the End of the present Session of Parliament, and that the Monies to arise therefrom were to be from Time to Time applied for the above mentioned Purposes.

Mr. William Phillips being examined, said, That unless the Term of the said Acts be further continued, the said Navigation must be ruined, as Shoals are continually forming the rein, which cannot be removed vithout a very considerable Expence.

That the Streets and Lanes of the said Town of Colchester cannot be kept in Repair, unless some further Powers be given for that Purpose.

That it would be a great Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and to the Public, if Provision was made for lighting and regulating the Streets, Lanes, and other Places therein, altering the Spouts, and removing Annoyances.

Mr. William Mason being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing and making more effectual several Acts of Parliament, passed for cleansing and making navigable the Channel from The Hythe at Colchester, to Wivenhoe, in the County of Essex; and for repairing and cleansing the Streets of the Town of Colchester, and also for lighting the Streets and Lanes, and for preventing Annoyances, in the said Town: And that Sir and

Mr. Rebow Martin, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other principal Inhabitants, refuting in or near the Town of Wantage, in the County of Berks, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill to enlarge the Term and Powers of Two Acts, passed in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of His present Majesty, for amending and widening the Road from Beffcl-Jleigh, through Wantage, to Hungerford, in the County of Berks, ami from Wantage to Marlborough in the County of Wilts, and from the Turnpike Road between Reading and Wallingford, through Halfpenny Lane, to The Old Red House upon Wantage Downs, and from thence to Lambotirn, in the said County of Berks; and for amending the Road through Fidgeon Lane, instead of the said Road through Halfpenny Lane;and setting forth. That in the said Bill Power is given to the Trustees to amend and widen a certain Lane called Fidgeon Lane, in the Parish of Wantage, and close adjoining upon the Town of Wantage and representing to the House, that Fidgeon Lane is in as good Condition as any Turnpike Road in that Neighbourhood, and the Statute Work is sufficient to keep it in proper and complete Repair; and that by including the said Lane under the Power of the Trustees for executing the said Acts, the Inhabitants of Wantage will be obliged to pay Toll, though they only pass along the said Lane for a final! Distance, and the Lane itself is, in its present Situation, sufficiently convenient for the Passage of Cattle and Carriages to and from tage; and that as the Petitioners will receive no Benefit' by the intended Bill, they trust they ilia.ll not be burthened with a Toll for repairing and widening a Road lor which the Statute Work is fully sufficient: And therefore praying. That they may be heard by them-lelves or Counsel, against such Parts of the Bill as affect the Petitioners, and that they may have such Relief in the Premises as to the Houselhall seem meet.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Nine Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glafies, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Forty Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Lord Sheffield being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, and his Name was set aside.

' And the Names of Nineother Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said , Names, the Names of Thirty-one other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Three, on Account of their being Sixty years of Age, or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Ten, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; One, on Account of his being a Petitioner to this House, complaining of an undue Election and Return; Eleven, \ on Account of their then serving on Select Committees; Four, on Account of their having already in this Session of Parliament served on Select Committees; and Two, on Account of their halving voted at the said Election.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete, the Counsel for the Petitioner named George Onslow,. Esquire, to serve on the said Select Committee.

And Lists of the said Forty-nine Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides, withdrew.

Gf Norfolk, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Complaining of an Act, made in the Nineteenth Year of His present Majesty's Reign, for more effectually preventing thepernicious Practice of Smuggling, and which subjects to Forfeiture the Ship or Vessel and Furniture bringing any Foreign Brandy, or other Foreign Spirituous Liquors, excepting only Two Gallons for the Use of each Seaman, then belonging to and on board such Ship or Vessel; and Hating, That the said Law will tend greatly to discourage the Building and Fitting out of Freight Ships, and thereby deprive the Nation of its most valuable Nursery for Seamen: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consuleration* and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the Hoilfe shall seem meet.

dtmcrf}(T Sir William Gtnfe reported from the Committee, to Gaol, &c. whom the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the City of Gloucester, in Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said City, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same waS read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr; John Wilkins Jepfon being examined, said. That The Upper North Gate, or Common Gaol, of the City of Gloucester, is both incommodious and inconvenient — That there are not separate Apartments for theMen and the W omen — That the G aoler has often been obliged to put the Prisoners in his own House4 for Want of proper Accommodation in the Gaol; and in Cafes where it may be necessary to keep the Prisoners apart, there is no _ Convenience in the Gaol lor that Purpose — That the Vox.. 38.

Gaol is situate across the Street which leads from London to the City of Gloucester; and that Part thereof is over the City Wall, of which the Gate is a Part — That the Gate-Way is very narrow, inso much that Two Carriages cannot pftfs each other, nor even a Horse pass a Carriage, without Danger — That the Gaol is an ancient Building, and greatly decayed — That there are many Defc6ts in the Walls, in the Floors, and in the Roof, by Means whereof Prisoners have escaped from the Gaol; and that it is necessary that a new and more commodious Gaol should be built.

That fhere are Two other Gate-Ways, called The Lower North Gate and The South Gate, within the said City, both which are across principal Streets, abd are as narrow and incommodious as The Upper North Gate —

That if the Gates are taken down, it will be necessary to purchase Three or FoUr Houses, of the Value of about £. 470, in order to lay Part of the Ground on which they stand into the Street.

Then the several Acts of Parliament passed relating to the Maintenance and Support Of the Poor, and for lighting the Streets, and also for enforcing the proper paving and cleansing the several Streets within the said City, and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances, were read.

And the Witness being further examined, said, That the Powers of the said Acts are very defe6tive — That in the Paving Act the Power to raise the Vagrant Money. is defective — That a Power is wanting to pave The Loxoer North Gate Street (which is much desired by the Inhabitants) and also some other Parts of the City; and also for making Spouts from the Roofs of the Houses —

That the Act for lighting the Town is defective, particularly with respect to lighting the Lamps at unnecessary Times; and that no Power is thereby given for lighting the Streets between Lady Day and Michaelmas.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for erecting a new Gaol and House of Correction, and for removing certain Gateways, in the City of Gloucester; and for amending the several Acts passed for the Maintenance and Support of the Poor of the said City, and lighting, paving, and regulating the Streets there: And that Sir William Guise, the Earl of Surrey, and Sir George Yonge, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Third Report of Coir.milT\oners of Public Accounts.

To the honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled.

the Third Report of the Commissioners, appointed to examine, take, and state, the Publie Accounts of the Kingdom.

- Having fini/lied our Examination of all those Public Accountants that came to our Knowledge in the Firli Class, as far as relates to the Balances of Public Money in their Hands, we in the next Place, directed our Attention to those Accoutants who receive Public Money out of the Exchequer, by way of impreft, and upon Account.

The Certificate of the Accounts depending in the Office of the Auditors of the Impreil, transmitted to us pursuant to our Precept, furnished us with a List of these Accountants: As much of this Certificate as relates to the ifuhjed Matter of this present Report, is inserted N° 1. in the Appendix. We took them into our Consideration in the Order in which they stand upon tliat Certificate; a Rule we pursuein regard to all Lists of Accountants, unless there is some special Reason for departing from it.

The Set of Accountants therein first mentioned, are the Treasurers of the Navy; and of these, the Names that stand first are the Executors of Anthony Viscount Falkland., whole final Account is dated the 4th of April 1689, and from whom a Balance of Twenty-seven thou-fami Six hundred and Eleven Pounds Six Shillings and Five Pence Farthing is de dared to be then due. We did not mispend our Time in a Pursuit where there was so little Probability of Benefit to the Public: A Debt that hasfubfifted for near a Century, may be presumed desperate. Palling over therefore this Article, we ittued our precepts to Earl Temple, as Representative of the late George Grenville, Esquire; to Lord Viscount Barring! on, Lord Viscount Howe, and to Sir Gilbert Elliot, Baronet, as Representative of the late Sir Gilbert Elliot, for an Account of the Public Money in their Hands, Custody, or Power, as late Treasurers of the Navy. The Returns made to our Precepts are set forth in the N° 2. Appendix*, from which it appears that the Balances of Public Money remaining in their respective Hands, upon the Days therein mentioned, amounted together to the Sum of Seventy-six lhoufand Seven hundred Ninety-three Pounds Eighteen Shillings andOne Penny Farthing.

That we might learn for what Reasons, Services, or Purposes, These Sums are permitted to remain in the Hands of Treasurers of the Navy, so long after they are out of Office, we examined several of the Officers in Tsjo this Department: namely. George Swqffield, Esquire, 4* Caftiier of the Victualling; Andrew Douglas, Esquire, N° 6 Pay matter; Mr. Adam Jellicoe, Chief Clerk to the 7 8 Pay matter, and Mr. Francis Cook, Ledger Writer.

By them we are supplied with the following Informa-J tion:

The Office of the Treasurer of the Navy is divided into Three Branches, the Paymaster's, the Caftiier's and the Victualling Branch. All the Money he receives is for the Navy Services, and placed under, or carried #ver to one of these Branches; the Money in each ^Branch is subdivided, arranged, and kept under various different Heads of Services; the whole Balance, at the Time he leaves the Office, continues to be liable, whether it be iu his Hands, or in the Hands of his Representatives, in case of his Death, to the same Services Tor which itsfeveral Parts were originally destined; and the Commissioners of the Navy, Victualling, and Sick and Hurt Offices, each in their several Departments, continue to assign Bills upon him for Payment, until they have reduced his Balance to such a Sum as, in their Opinions,;will not be more than sufficient to answer Purposes for which it has been usual to leave Money with him, until his final Account is patted. These purposes are, first; to carry on the Recalls upon those

Ships Books which were open in his Treasurership, and the Payment of the Half Pay Lifts and Bounties to Chaplains. The Ships Books are usually kept open for Recalls, for Seven or Eight Years after the Expiration of the Treasurership, in order to give those Seamen who, by being either turned over to other Ships, or employed in other Places, could not attend at the 'Time their Ship was paid, an Opportunity of receiving their Wages when it is in t.heir Power to apply for them. The only Fund applicable to this Service is the Money in the Pav Branch, placed under the Head of" To pay " Ships, and carry on Recalls:" This Service is at an End when the Ships Books are made up. They are made up as they come in course in order of Time; and after the last is closed, the Half Pay Lifts are also closed, and the Payment of the Bounty to Chaplaius ceases.

The other Purpose is to pay the Fees and Expences of carrying on, making up, and patting his Accounts. Upon patting every Animal Account, Fees are paid to the Auditors of the impreft, out of the Money in his Hands, under the Head of " To pay Exchequer Fees,

<c and other Contingent Expences of the Pay Office but upon patting his final Account, there is a Gratuity also paid in the following Manner: — The Officers and Clerks who transact the Bufniefs of the Treasurer in Office, carry on also at the same Time, and finally make up, the Accounts of the Treasurers out of Office; for which extra Work they have no Salary or Recoin-pence whatever, until the final Account is ready to be patted, at which Time it has been usual for them, by Petition to the Lords of the Treasury, to obtain a reasonable Allowance for their Trouble, which has been paid them, by virtue of a Treasury Warrant, out of any Money remaining in the Hands of that Treasurer under whatever Heads of Service it may be placed. This Gratuity, together with the Fee of passing the Annual Accounts, and for the Quietus, it is imagined, will exhaust the whole Balance now remaining in the 1 lands of I ord Temple.

The Right Honourable Welbore Ellis, the present Treasurer of the Navy, returned to our Ryquilition, a Balance in his Flands, upon the 31st of August last, of Three hundred Forty-eight thousand Niue hundred Forty-one Pounds Eleven Shillings and Nine Pence. The Act directs us to examine into all Balances in the Hands of Public Accountants, for the Purpose of considering what Sum may be taken out of their Flands, to be applied to the Public Service. It is obvious, we could not examine the Balance in the Hands of the Treasurer in.Office with this View; it could not be in our Power to say, t hat any Part of it ought to be paid back into the Exchequer, because, in an Office ofloconstant and large an Expenditure, this Sum rauft probably be exhaulled, even while it was under our Consideration; but it was competent to us, and we thought it our Duty, to examine whether this was a larger Sum than the current Business of the Office required should at that Time be entrusted to the Treasurer of the Navy. irxA Companion between the Quantum of the Sum, and . Commissioner of the Victualling, and John Bell, EC- ]sj«22* quire, Commissioner of the Sick and Hurt; from whom ft* we coileft the following Information.

All the Money received by the Treasurer, for the Services of the Navy, is either issued to him out of the Exchequer, or paid to him by sundry Persons, in pursuance of the Directions of the Navy, Victualling, or Sick and Hurt Boards. The Money from the Exchequer is issued to him, and arranged in his Accounts under various Heads of Services; these Heads are kept distinct; and he cannot place or transfer a Sum issued to him under one Head, to any other Head of Service.

All Bills assigned upon him for Payment by these Boards, specify the correspondent Head of Service out of which that Bill is to be paid, and he must not pay it out of Money placed under any other Head of Service than that so specified on the Bill

When Money is wanted; the Application for it never originally moves from the Treasurer, except in the Tingle Instance of Money to pay Fees, and other contingent Expences: this he craves of himself, when that Fund is nearly exhaulled; in all other Cafes, the Board in whose Department it is, by Letter, desire him to present a Memorial to the Lords of the Treasury, specifying the Sum wanted, and for what particular Service; the Memorial pursues the Letter, and thelflueis directed from the Exchequer in the Terms of the Memorial. The Treasurer immediately certifies to the Navy Board the whole Sum he receives, and to the other Boards, so much of that Sum as concerns them; he also transmits to the Navy Board an Account of all his Receipts and Payments in the Cashier's and Victualling Branch every Fortnight, and in the Pay Branch every Month; by these Means they have an exact Knowledge of the State of his Balance under each Head of Service. Each of these Boards enter in their Books all the Assignments they make upon him for Payment; of which they transmit to him a List; hence they know what the actual Demands upon him amount to; and, from their Experience in the Course of the Navy Business, they can form some Conjecture relative to the probable approaching Demands that may be made upon him in the various Branches of the Service. By such Knowledge and Conjecture these Boards are guided in their Directions to the Treasurer, as to the Time when, the Quantum of the Sum, and the Service for which every Application for a Supply is to be made to the Treasury.

At the End of every Month the Navy Board transmit to the Treasury a Certificate, containing an exact State ©fall the Receipts and Payments made by the Treasurer during that Month, as they appear from their Books; hence the Lords of the Treasury have full Knowledge of the State of his Balance every Month: This Certificate for the Month of August last we procured from the Navy Office, on which the Balance in the Hands 2^ of the Treasurer appears to be Two hundred Sixty thousand Seven hundred Sixteen Pounds One Shilling and Eight Pence Farthing.

Being made acquainted thus far with the Course of Business in this Office, our next Step was to resolve this Balance of Three hundred Forty-eight Thousand Nine hundred Forty-one Pounds Eleven Shillings and Nine Pence into its constituent Parts, and compare the Quantum of each Part, as far as we could, with the actual and probable Demands of Service upon it on the 31st of August, the Date of his Return.

To search into the actual and probable Demands, at that Time, upon each of these Sums, was hardly practicable; one Circumdance alone might enable us to judge with suffi-cieut Accuracy, whether the Sum Total was too large or not; that is, in what Time this Balance was in Fatt paid away by the Treasurer. As the Public Money should pass without Delay from the Pocket of the Subject into the Exchequer, so it ought not to issue out of the Exchequer, either before it is wanted, or in larger Sums than the Service for which it is issued requires. By this lad Account, a very large Sum has been conftaiitly in his Hands, during the Period therein mentioned, exclusive of the Amount of Bills assigned upon him, but not presented to him for Payment. The principal Cause of the Magnitude of this Balance, is, the Practice, in this Office, of not applying Money issued under one Head, towards satisfying a Demand upon any other Head of Service; the Consequence of which is, when the Money upon the Account of any Head of Service is nearly exhausted, a Supply mud be procured for that Service, how abundant l'oever the Sums upon other Heads of Accounts, or the Sum Total of his Calli, may be. Were all the Sums he receives to conditute and be considered as one common general Calli, and be applied indiferi-minately to every Service, a much less Sum than the lowed of the Balances in the Account Jad-mentioned would, in our Opinion, fufiice to carry on the current Services of the Navy, even various and extendve as they now are. It would create no Confudon in the Accounts; for the Receipts and Payments under each Head of Service might dill be kept didinct; and though the Payments might frequently exceed the Receipts on some Heads of Accounts, yet the Treasurer would not be without sufficient Cadi, and the next Issue from the Exchequer would restore the Balances. What the Sum necessary for carrying on the Service should be, mud depend upon Circomdances; it will be different at different Times, and mnd be left principally to the Discretion of those Commissioners from whom the Direction for Supplies move, who, being conversant in the Business, can bed determine. But, to enable the Lords of the Treasury likewise to judge of the Propriety of, and be a Check and Contro'ul upon, the Requid-tion, we are of Opinion, that, besides the Certificate sent every Month from the Navy Board, an Accouat of the Sum Total of the Balance in the Hands of the Treasurer of the Navy should be inserted in every Application for a Supply to the Treasury.

We have not been inattentive to Defeats we have observed in this Office during the Course of our Inquiries;

DefeCls which concern the Officer, the.Office, and the Public.

The Treasurer finds his Business does not end with his Office; his Accounts are dill open: He goes on, receiving and paying, until he feels himself, his Family, and his Fortune, subject to all the Evils of long Public Accounts far in Arrear, and the Difficulties of rendering an Account increasing daily: He continues responsible for Millions, without an Expectation of obtaining his final Discharge during his Life.

The Office is perplexed with the Multiplicity of these Accounts. — There are Four didinct Accounts, of Four Treasurers of the Navy, at this Time open at the Pay Office, and Business is carried on upon every one of them at the same Time, by the same Officers, when the current Business of the present Treasurer > alone would find Employment enough for them all*

There have been idued to Three of these Treasurers, for the Navy Service, upwards of Thirty-three Millions, the Accounts of which are not paffid; exclusive J of above Twenty-five Millions to the late Mr. Grenville, whose final Account is not yet settled; and of

The Navy Accounts in July last, when the Imprest Certificate was transmitted to us, were in Arrear in the Otlice of the Auditor of the Imprest Twenty-two Years. This Delay7 is occasioned by the Accounts of the subsequent Years net being made up at the Pay Otlice of the Navy, where there is a Want of Officers and Clerks for this Department. A sufficient Number of Persons, intelligent in this Branch, should forthwith be provided by tire proper Authority with adequate Salaries, for the sole Purpose of proceeding upon, bringing forward, and making up these Accounts, with as much Dispatch as the Nature of the Business will admit.

By this Delay in making up the Accounts, the Public loles the Use, at lead, of considerable Sums of their own Money; not that the Principal itself has always been safe. A Defaulter of above Twenty-seven thousand Pounds Hands at the Head of the Lift of Trea-iurers of the Navy upon the Imprest Certificate.

We inquired why a Treasurer, under the present Constitution of the Office, might not, upon his Resignation, immediately pay over his Balance to the Successor, or into the Exchequer, and all the subsequent Transactions of Office be carried on by the Treasurer for the Time being. — Two Reasons were assigned for the Necessity of keeping open his Accounts, though out of Office.

ift That sufficient Time may be given to his Sub-Accountants to clear theirlmprefts.

The Sub-Accountants are certainly very numerous; and as, according to the present Mode of puffing these Accounts, they mud all be set insuper upon the final Account, was that Account to be made up soon after the Expiration of the Treasurership, it would be very voluminous and troublesome to the Office. — But, since the Treasurer in Office does now clear the Imprefts of feme of his Predecessors, and can clear the Imprells of all, and the Three Boards can, at their Pleasure, call upon the Sub-Accountants to clear their Imprefts, we do not think this Reason conclusive.

2d. That the Payment of his Ships Books may be completed.

A Ship's Book is the Voucher for the Treasurer who pays it: Two cannot pay upon the same Book; it would create Confusion, as the Payments of the one could not, without great Trouble and Difficulty, be distinguished from those of the other; it could not therefore be made a Voucher for Two Treasurers. To enable a Treasurer in Office to carry on the Payment of a Ship's Book open in the Time of his Predecefior, 4he Names of all the Seamen not paid must be ab-liracted, and entered in a new Book; a Work of great Labour and Length of Time, where the Books are so numerous; and during all that Time no Payment of Wages could be made to the Seamen unpaid upon those Books.

Upon the Examination of a Ship's Book, there ap- Third pears a Foundation for this Objection, which opens a c:ommif?.ness Door for a possible Mischief, worthy Consideration. It of Public is in the Power of a Treasurer of the Navy, retiring Awiim* in Difgnft, to refuse carrying on any more Payments, and by that Means to put a Stop, for Eight Months or more, to the Payment of all the Seamen on the numerous Volumes of Ships Books open at the several Ports in his Treasurership. Mr. Grenville left open above Thirteen Hundred. This Evil does not rest in Speculation: We have an Inilance of it in Evidence. N*6.

The Office that does hot gurird against the Possibility of such an Evil, is fundamentally7 defective.

These Defers should be speedily corrected. To alter the Constitution of the Office; to abolish the fub-ordinate Treasury; to render the Treasurer a mere Accountant; and to vary the Mode of accounting, carry with them a strong Appearance of an effectual Remedy: But were we, in the present State of our Inquiries, to come to Decisions of such Moment, we should be premature, perhaps rath. It is easier to see the Defeats than to supply the Regulation. The Pay of the Navy is an important Object; and any Alteration in the Mode should be well weighed before it is adopted; it should be traced through all its Effects, and perfectly ascertained to be as feasible in Practice as it is specious in Theory. To disturb, to confound, or to delay (Effects not unfrequent, when Novelty of Form is introduced, and new Principles applied to an old Office) might be attended with very feripus Consequences.

The Defers, to which we have alluded, presented themselves in the Course of an Examination made, in Obedience to the Ad, for a more limited Purpose.

Coming, however, before us, they are, in our Opinion, too important to be passed over in Silence: We thought it our Duty to point them out, that, should they be deemed a proper Subject for the Exercise of the Wisdom of the Legislature, the solid Advantages, which would result to the Public from their Correction, might not be delayed. Had we protracted this Report until we were possessed of Materials for a well-grounded Opinion upon these Points, we must have disobeyed the Ad, that enjoins us to report, in the first Place, upon the Balances in the Hands of Accountants in this Session of Parliament, to the End that the Public Money, long ago issued, and still remaining in their Hands, may, with all convenient Speed, be restored to the Possession of the Public.

The Examination of George Swaffield, Esquire, Cashier of the Victualling, in the Pay Office of the Navy; taken upon Oath, the 18th and 19th of October 1780.

This Examinant faith. That he now is, and has been between Seven and Eight Years, Cashier of the Victualling, under the Treasurer of the Navy, and that he has been upwards of Thirty-three Years in the Pay Office of the Navy.

That his Business is to receive and pay all Money issued to the Treasurer of the Navy on the Head of Victualling.

That the Office of the Treasurer of the Navy con-fists of Three Branches, the Paymaster's, the Cashier's, and Victualling.

That he superintends and takes Care of the Accounts of the late George Grenville, Esquire, and of Lord Viscount Barrington, late Treasurers of the Navy.

That it is the Practice of the Office for the Pay-tn after to superintend the Accounts of the Treasurers of the Navy, after they are out of Office; and that, during Mr. Wallis's Time, who was Paymaster to Mr. Grenville and Lord Barrington, but very infirm, he transacted the Business for him, and on his Death the said Business devolved upon him.

That he thinks the Balance of One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-nine Pounds Five Shillings, returned by Lord Temple to be in his Hands as Representative of George Grenville, Esquire, under the Head of Wages, is not likely to be demanded on that Head, the Books being all made up for that Branch.

That in the Cashicr's Account, he thinks the Balance of Seven thousand Four hundred and Seventy-five Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Four Pence Halfpenny, will be exhausted ih Fees and Gratuities to be paid on passing the Accounts; for larger Sums passed through Mr. Grenville's Hands, in the Four last Years of his Treasurership, and the Auditor's Fees increase in proportion.

That in the Victualling Branch he thinks there may be some few Bills, but to no great Amount, still to be paid out of the Balance of Three thousand One hundred and Fifteen Pounds Four Shillings, remaining on that Head, and that the Residue will be exhausted in Fees and Gratuities.

He believes that some Sections of Mr. Grenville's Accounts for the Year 1757 and 1758, were delivered into the Auditor's Office soon after the Expiration of those Years, and that the voluntary Charge, the Account of Payments of Wages to Seamen for the Years 1759 and 1760, are not yet delivered in to the Auditor, but are ligned by the Commissioners of the Navy, and wiH be iddivered in a few Days, which will complete the Accounts for these Two Years; that all Payments by Bills, for both the Navy and Victualling Branches, for the Year 1761, have been delivered into the Audffor's Office near Eighteen Years. It es . a Rule in the Office, to fend in these Parts of t he Treasurer's Accounts as foeedily as possible after the Year Expires.

That none of the Accounts for the Year are as yet sent into the Auditor's Office, that being Mr. Grenville's final Account, which is the most troublesome, and the Office wishes to have the former Accounts cleared, before any Part of the final Account is delivered in, as the Persons who have received Money on Account, and have not cleared their Accounts, are returned insuper in the final Account, and the Treasurer then, and not before* takes Credit for the Sums he has advanced them, and all the Tran factions of his Treasurership are then finally doled.

_ That he believes all Mr. Grenville s Accounts, as far as relates to the Treasurer of the Navy's Office, will

be in the Auditor's Office before the End of the Year 1782, and finished there by the End of the following Year.

That the Reason why the Ships Books, for the Payment of Seamen's Wages, cannot be delivered in along with those of the Payment of Bills, is, because they must be kept open to give the Seamen an Opportunity to receive their Wages; which they often cannot do, when the Ships are ordered to be paid, being turned over to other Ships, and dispersed in different Parts of the World.

The Ships Books are generally kept open for Recalls about Seven or Eight Years, and are then made up as they come in Course in Order of Time. When a Ship's Book is onceclosed, no further Payment can be made upon it, but the Seaman entitled to his Wages must apply by Petition to the Navy Board, who order the Wages to be entered on the Lift of Arrears, and paid out of the Money received on the Head of Wages; the Treasurer's Accounts for any Year cannot be made up until all the Ships Books of that Year are doled; the same Reason holds as to the voluntary Charge, that Account cannot be completed until the Ships Books are closed.

When a Treasurer's final Account is passed, he pays the Balance remaining in his Hands into the Exchequer.

That a Treasurer's Account must necessarily be kept open after he is out of Office, to give Time to those who have received Money from him upon Account, to clear their Accounts; and that a Treasurer's Account cannot be made up, and the Balance paid over to hi.* Successor, soon after he goes out of Office, because of the Trouble it would create to the Office, and the Delay of paying the Seamen's Wages; as all the Sums not paid by him must be extracted, and carried over to new Books, to be paid by the succeeding Treasurer; for different Treasurers cannot pay on the same Book* as one Voucher cannot be admitted for Two Persons.

That this Examinant believes Mr. Grenville paid in his Treasurership between Thirteen and Fourteen hundred Ships Books, which were left open when he went out of Office.

That the Treasurer for the Time being has no Power to call upon any Persons, to whom Bills have been issued by Way of Imprest, to clear their Accounts; that is the Business of the Navy, Victualling, and Srck and Hurt Boards.

This Examinant further faith. That as to Lord Barrington's Account, none of his Paymaster's Accounts are yet in the Auditor's Office; they cannot be sent in until Mr. Grenville's Accounts are settled in the Treasurer's Office, as the Clerks must finish one before they begin another.

That he thinks there may be some small Demands still made upon Lord Barrington for Wages, but to no great Amount; and the Navy and Victualling Boards may still assign Bills upon him for 'Payment, so asJLo reduce his Balance to such Sum only as shall be fufti-cient to pay the Expencek of passing his Accounts; and they do exercise that Power.

That he believes all Lord Barrington's Accounts will be complete in the Auditor's Office within Three Y'ears after Mr. Grenville's are finished; and that there are no other Services to be carried on with these Balances, except such as are above-mentioned.

The further Examination of George Swaffield, Esquire; taken upon Oath, the t6th February f 1781.

This Examinant faith. That after a Person has received Money, by way of Imprest, from either the Navy, Victualling, or Sick and Hurt Boards, he delivers in an Account of his Disbursements to the same Board. They settle his Account; and if a Balance is due from him to Government, in the Navy and Sick and Hurt Offices, an Entry is generally made at the Foot of his clearing Bill, that such Balance is to be paid in to clear the Account. This Bill goes to the Treasurer; who receives that Balance, either to clear the Imprest, or, if the Imprest was in a former Treasurer-ship, to become a Part of his voluntary Charge. In the Victualling Office, they write to the Treasurer, desiring him to receive the Balance, in order to clear the Imprest.

In the Navy Branch, alone, the Number of Imprefts is always great, and if a Treasurers Account was to be made up soon after his Resignation, ail those Persons whose Imprefts were not cleared must be returned in-super, and every Imprest Bill described upon his final Account. The Practice of the Auditor's Office makes this necessary, and is one Cause of the Delay in passing a Treasurer's final Account.

The Sum under the Head of Fees and Contingencies, is applied by the Treasurer in Office to the Payment Fees at the Treasury and Exchequer, upon his Application for and Receipt of Money, and to the Payment of other small incidental Expences. After he is out of Office, this Sum is applied solely to the Payment of the Fees of passing his Accounts.

When the voluqtary Charge of any Year's Account is carried into the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest, the Fees for passing that Year's Account are then settled, and paid out of Money remaining in his Hands under the Head of Exchequer Fees, Sic.; which Sum they allow in his Account. The Expence of procuring the Quietus is paid by him in pursuance of a Bill made out by the Navy Board, and assigned upon him for Payment, out of the same Fund.

When the final Account is ready to be passed, the Officers and Clerks who have carried oq the Accounts of a Treasurer ever finqe he was out of Office, and who have no other Reward or Emolument for, that Business, petition the Lords of the Treasury for an Allowance for this extra Trouble, in proportion to the Length of the Treasurership, the Sum. accounted, for* and the Extent of the Account. The Treasury refer the Memorial to the Auditors ofi the Imprest, to examine and certify whether the Sum applied for be reasonable $ and upon Their Report' the Lords of the Treasury issue a; Warrant to the Auditors, to allow that Sum out of any , Money reqiaining in the Hands of that Treasurer; who pays, it to the Officers and Clerks in pursuance of that Warrant

The Examination of Andrew Douglas, Esquire, Paymaster to the Treasurer of the Navy; taken upon Oath, 25th of October 1780.

This Examinant faith, That he now is, and has been for upwards of Ten Years, Paymaster to the Treasurer of the Navy.

Vol. 38.

That he superintends the Accounts of Sir Gilbert Elliot, late Treasurer of the Navy.

That, according to the Report of the Clerks of the Office, from their Books, the last Se&ions of his Victualling Ledgers, to the Year 1778, were delivered in to the Auditor's Office on the 17th June 1779.

That he cannot form any Judgment when Sir Gilbert Elliots Accounts will be finally passed.

That he is informed, and believes, all the Open Accounts of the Treasurers of the Navy are proceeded upon at the same Time; but a subsequent Treasurer's Account is never finished until his Predecessor's is finally closed.

That the Balance that was in the Hands of Sir Gilbert Elliot, when his Treasurership expired, has been red uced by Pay men ts made on the Head of W ages. Navy, Victualling, and Sick and Hurt Bills, assigned by these Boards upon him for Payment.

That the Balance remaining is applicable to the several Services for which the Money was granted, and the Payment of the Expence of passing his Accounts.

That he believes the Expence of passing the late Sir Gilbert Elliots Accounts will amount to Five thousand Seven hundred Pounds and upwards, besides the usual Allowance granted to the Officers and Clerks employed in the Treasurer's Office in settling the Accounts, which he thinks may, according to former Instances, amount to Four thousand Pounds more, and upwards.

That he knows of no Rule which governs the Navy Board, as to the Amount of the Balance they permit to remain in the Hands of a Treasurer of the Navy, after he is out of Office.

Andrew Douglas.
