The Exam illation of the Right honourable

Ellis, Treasurer of tine Navy; taken upon Oath, the 8th and 10th of November 1780*

This Examinant faith* That all Sums of Money received by the Treasurer of the Navy from the Exchequer, are issued to him under distinct Heads of Services, and that he is strictly forbid, by his Iofirudions, to transfer Stuns issued on one Head of Service to any other Head of Service; if the Sum granted for one Service be nearly exhausted, a Supply for that Service must be procured, though he has large Sums in his Hands under other Heads of Services.

That »o Demand on the Treasury moves originally from the Treasurer of the Navy, independent of the Navy, Victualling, and Sick and Hurt Boards, except the Sums roquisite for the Payment of Exchequer Fees, and other Contingencies at the Pay Office.

When the Sum received for any other particular Head of Service is nearly exhausted, a Letter comes from the Navy, Victualling, or Sick and Hurt Boards, each for their respective Departments, to the Treasurer, requiring him to present a Memorial to the Lords of the Treasury.specify ing the Sums required, distinguished under particular Heads of Services; that thereupon a Memorial is drawn up, according to the exact Words of the Letter, and, together with the Letter, is presented by the Paymaster to the Treasury; who direct the Issue exactly in the Form of the Memorial.

That the Paymaster, on the Receipt of the Money immediately certifies the Whole to the Navy Board: and the respective Parts which regard the Victualling and Sick and Hurt Boards, to them also.

That the Navy Board has full Knowledge of the Receipt and Expenditure of the Money in the Hands of the Treasurer; of the Receipt, by these Certificates; of the Expenditure, by their own Books, in which are entered every Bill, Order, or Assignment, given on the Treasurer for Payment, under the respective Heads of Service; and by the Accounts which the Treasurer transinits to the Navy Board once a Fortnight, on the Head of Victualling and Cashier's Branch, and once a Month on the Pay Branch. Thcle Accounts are compared with, and must agree exactly with their own Books; and from thence must appear the Balances on each respective Head of Service.

That he does not know of any Rule which governs the Navy Board in their Direction to him to apply to the Treasury for Mon^y, except their Knowledge of the actual or approaching Services, and of the exact State of the Balance in his Hands under each Head.

That, upon Application to the Lords of the Treasury for a Supply of Money, they do not, to his Knowledge, examine into the State of the Balance in the Hands of the Treasurer; but he is informed, and believes, that they have an exact Account of it, by the Means of a Paper transmitted Monthly from the Navy Board, containing an Account of the Cash received by the Treasurer, and the Assignmenta made upon him by the several Boards for I*ayruent.

That, to the belt of his Knowledge and Belief, the several Sums of One hundred and Sixteen thousand Five hundred and Twenty-four Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Nine Pence Halfpenny, in the Paymaster's Branch; of One hundred and Fifty-two thousand Nine hundred and Seventy-two Pounds and Four Pence Three Farthings, in the Cashier's Brandi; and of Seventy-nine thousand Four hundred and Forty-four Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Six Pence Three Farthings, in the Victualling Branch; making together Three hundred and Forty-eight thousand Nine hundred and Forty-one Pounds Eleven Shillings and Nine Pence, men-20

tioned in the Returns made by his Order to this Board on the 31st of August last, was the whole Balance for which he was then accountable to the Public as Trca-surer of the Navy.

That of this Balance, the Sum of Twenty thousand Two hundred and Two Pound Seventeen Shillings and Eleven Pence Farthing was in the Ilauds of Mr. Taylor, Pay Clerk at Por/Jinoiith; the Sum of Thirty-seven thousand and Sixty-one Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Seven Pence, in the Hands of Mr. lynch. Pay Clerk at Plymouth-, and the Sum of Three thousand Eight hundred and Five Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence Halfpenny, in the Hands of Nr. Pay

Clerk at Chatham-, which Suras were, at that Time, Balances remaining in their Hands of sundry Payments ordered by the Navy Board for the Use of those Ports: That there was in the Hands of Mr. Six thousand One hundred and Twenty-four Pounds Six Shillings and Seven Pence Three Farthings, for the Purpose of paying Wages, Ships, and Recalls; in the Hands of Mr. Slade, Twenty-five thousand Seven hundred and Thirty-eight Pounds Seven Shillings and Six Pence Three Farthings, and Four thousand and Seventy-seven Pounds Five Shillings and Two Pence, in Money and Premiums, making together Twenty-nine thousand Eight hundred and Fifteen Pounds Twelve Shillings and Eight Pence Three Farthings, for the Puprofe of carrying on the Payments of Three Months Course of the Navy and other Bills; in the Hands of Mr. Swaffield, Twenty-nine thousand Eight hundred and Ninety-five Pounds Two Shillings and Three Pence Three Farthings, for the Purpose of carrying on the Payments of Three Months Course of the Victualling and other Bills; which were the Rea-fons why such large Sums were permitted at that Time to be in their Hands: And in the Hands of Mr. Douglas, Five thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-six Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Three Pence, for carrying on the Payments of Exchequer Fees and Contingencies: Which Sums, amounting together to the Sum of One hundred and Thirty-two thousand Six hundred and Thirty-two Pounds Four Shillings and Ten Pence, reduced the above Balance to Two hundred and Sixteen thoustmd Three hundred and Nine Pounds Six Shillings and Eleven Pence.

That this Balance is only applicable, in his Hands, to the respective Services for which it was issued.

That, in his Issues of Money to the Chief Clerks in the different Branches, to carry on the current Services, he is guided by their Requisition; which, in the Cashier and Victualling Branches, is formed upon the Amount of the Daily assigned Lifts, transmitted from the different. Boards to the respective Departments in the Treasurer's Office; which Lifts contain a particular Account of all Bills assigned on that Day for Payment; and in the Pay Branch, by a Conjecture formed of the Demands which may probably be made for paying of Ships, carrying on Recalls, Payment of the Yards, and of Half Pay.

That Bills assigned by the several Boards, in their respective Departments, upon the Treasurer of the Navy for Payment, are not always presented to him immediately after such Assignment; on the Contrary, they are frequently, by the various Accidents of Death, Litigation, Trusts, and Executorships, the Absence or Convenience of the Proprietors, not presented for Payment until a considerable Length of Time afterwards.

That he does not know what Part of the above Balance of Two hundred and Sixteen thousand Three hundred and Nine Pounds Six Shillings and Eleven Pence had been assigned by the several Boards for Payment on the 31st o[ August last; but that, by the Monthly Certificate sent by the Navy Board to the Treasury for that Month, it will appear what Alignments

Geo. III. 70 Martii. 26$

ments had been made, and of what Parts that Balance is compounded.

W. Ellis.

Guy Carleton>

N° 22.

The "Examination of Timothy. Brett, Esquire, One of the Commissioners of the Navy, and Comptroller of the Treasurer of the Navy's Ac-coi|nts; taken upon Oath, the 29th and 30th of November 1780.

This Examinant faith, That he is Comptroller of the Treasurer of the Navy's Accounts.

That the Navy Board transmit every Month to the Treasury a Certificate of the Receipts and Payments by the Treasurer of the Navy, under the respective Heads of Services.

That the Victualling and Sick and Hurt Boards fend the like Accounts to the Navy Board, which they include in their Certificate, to the Intent the Treasury may have full Knowledge of the Sums, under their several Heads, in the Hands of the Treasurer of the Navy. The Navy Board has the same Knowledge, from the Certificate sent them by the Treasurer every Fortnight.

That the Navy Board desire the Treasurer to apply to the Treasury for suchSums, and for such Services, and at such Times, as they, from their Knowledge of the Demands for those Services, judge will be wanted.

That the Difference between the Treasurer's Balance and the Navy Board Balance, in the Hands of the Treasurer, on the 31st August last, in the Cashier's Branch, arises from Bills assigned by the Navy Board upon him for Payment, and not presented to him.

That upon the Back of every Bill assigned upon the Treasurer for Payment, is indorsed out of what Fund it is to be paid.

That in the Cashier's Branch, Assignments are continually making by the Navy and Sick and Hurt Boards, for Payments out of the several Funds which constitute the Balance appearing to be in the Treasurer's Hands in that Branch; and in the Pay Branch, the Navy Board are continually making Assignments of Tickets for Payments, and directing Payments of Ships, for which there were open, on the 31st of August, Eight hundred Books and upwards.

That Part of the Fund of Old Stores is appropriated for certain Payments, and the Navy Board reduces the Remainder, from Time to Time, by their Assignments, as they in their Discretion think proper.

That as to the Sum of Thirty-six thousand Pounds, which appears to be received in the Cashier's Branch on the 10th of August, and no Part of it to be paid away in that Month, the Treasury was applied to for that Sum on the 8th, and issued it upon the 10th; whereas it frequently happens that the Sum is not issued until Eight or Ten Days after it is applied for; and it appears that in the next Month this whole Sum, and Seventeen thousand Eight hundred Pounds and upwards of another Sum of Thirty-six thousand Pounds, was paid away for the same Service.

T. Brett.

Guy Carleioiiy T. Anguifhy A. Piggotty

Sam1 Beachcrofty Geo. Drummond.

N 23k Third

The Examination of John Slade, Esquire, One of ComXiwrs the Commissioners of ths Victualling Office 5 of Public taken upon Oath, the 5th of December 1780. Accounts.

This Examinant faith. That the Difference between the Treasurer's Balance and the Victualling Board Balance, in the Hands of the Treasurer, on the 31st August last, in the Vi6tualling Branch, arises from Bills assigned by the Vi6tualling Board upor* him for Payment, and not presented to him; they are outstanding Bills, payable at Sight, remaining in the Hands of the Proprietors.

The Treasurer never asks for Money, in the Visual-ling Branch, but by Direction of the Victualling Board: when the Comptroller of the Treasurer's Accounts finds a Fund nearly exhausted, he informs the Board of it, and, in Consequence of that Information, they direct the Treasurer to solicit a Supply for that Fund.

The Sums received by the Treasurer, are kept under a Variety of Heads of Service; the Bills assigned under these Heads of Service are kept quite distinct, and Bills under one Head of Service are never assigned upon a,

Fund under another Head of Service, except in the same of old Stores, upon which Fund Bills under any other Head are assigned, according as they may be wanted*. The Fund of old Stores arises from the Sale of decayed Stores in the Vi6tualling Branch, andt the Board directs the Treasurer to receive from the Purchasfers the Sums those Stores are fold for.

As to the Sum of Seventeen thousand Pounds to pay Imprest and Bills of Exchange, appearing in the Navy Certificate to have been obtained on the 4U1 of August, and no Part of it exhausted at the End of the Month, it appears from the Account of the Chief Clerk of the Comptroller, that this Sum was applied for on the 31st o{July and received so soon after as the 4th of August, whereas the Treasury frequently do not issue the Sum applied for until Ten Days or a Fortnight afterwards*

When that Sum was applied for, Bills of Exchange to that Amount, or thereabouts, had been presented to and accepted by the Board; and it appears that a great Part of them were paid the Beginning of September.

Bills of Exchange are presented to the Board every Day for Acceptance.

J. Slade.

Guy Carleton.

T. Anguifhy A. Piggotty Geo. Drummond.

N° 24.

The Examination of John Bell, Esquire, One of the Commissioners of the Sick and Hurt Office; taken upon Oath, ift December 1780.

This Examinant faith, That when a Supply of Money is wanted for the Service of the Sick and Hurt Office, the Board, by Letter, desire the Treasurer of the Navy to apply to the Treasury for such a Sum, as they, to the best of their Judgments, think will be wanted under each particular Head of Service, which Sums they endeavour to render as small as possible: out of these Sums the Board assign Bills upon the Treasurer for Payment, which Bills are payable at Sight, and it is directed upon each Bill out of what Sum it is to be paid.

Each Head of Service is kept as distinct a,s possible, both as to the Bills assigned, and the Funds out of which they are to be paid.

The Board takes Care that the Treasurer has constantly in his Hands a Sum, in each Branch of Service, sufficient to answer the probable Demands upon him for that Branch.

JM

Guy Carleton,

T. Anguifhy A. Piggotty Rich* Neave,

Geo. Drummond.

Sir John Irwine, from the Select Committee, who were appointed to try and determine the Merits of the Petition of Sir John Paterson, of Eccles, Baronet, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County of Berwick, informed the House, That the said Select Committee have determined,

That Hugh Scott, Esquire, is not duly elected a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Berioick.

And also. That the said Select Committee have determined,

That Sir John Paterson, Baronet, the Petitioner, is not duly elected a Com mi (Boner to serve in this present Parliament for the said County of Berwick:

And also. That the said Select Committee have determined,

That the last Election of a Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the said County of Berwick, was a void Election.

And the said Determinations were ordered to be entered in the Journals of this House.

Sir John Irwine also reported from the said Select Committee, That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it jn at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolution of the Committee is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Agreement between Hugh Scott, Esquire, Younger, of Harden, for himself and his Friends in the County of

Berwick, on the one Part, and Alexander La-

merton, Esquire, and George Home, of Branxlon, for themselves, and as authorized by lundry other Gentlemen and Freeholders in that County, on the other Part, relative to the Election of a Commissioner for the said County at the last General Election, was a corrupt and illegal Agreement.

Prayers.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of John Saunders and Alexander Hume, Esquires; and also the Petition of certain Freeholders, of the Borough of Dozcnton, in the County of Wilts, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and other Freeholders of the said Borough, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Twenty fix Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration. And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Two Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of William Baker, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioners, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Forty-three other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Lord Kensington being drawn, he required to be excused from Serving on the said Select Committee on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age or upwards, and having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Four other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Thirty-one other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Two, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Four, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; Fourteen, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees; Ten, on Account of their having already, in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees; and One, on Account of his Return to serve in Parliament not having been brought in Fourteen Days.

" as well in India as in Europe11 the wholeCivil and Military Government of the Presidency of Fort William in Bengal, and the Ordering, Management, and Government of all the Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues in the Kingdoms of Bengal, Bahar, and Orijfa, are vested in the Governor General and Council of the said Presidency, in like Manner, to all Intents and Purposes whatsoever, as the same were at the Time of passing the Act, or at any Time before might have been exercised by the President and Council, or Select Com-T mittee, in the said Kingdoms, subject to the Orders received from the Court of Directors; and that by the said Act His Majesty was impowered to erect and constitute a Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William -aforesaid, with full Powers and Authority to exercise and perform aft Civil, Criminal, Admiralty, and Ecclesiastteal Jurisdiction over all British Subjects reficlent in the said Kingdoms or Provinces, under the Protection of the said United East India Company, and to hear and determine all Complaints against any of His,'

Majesty's Subjects, for any Crimes, Misdemeanors, or Oppressions, committed or to be committed, and also to entertain, hear, and determine any Suit, Action, or Complaint, against any Person who shall, at the Time^ when such Debt or Cause of Action or Complaint shall ' have arisen, have been employed by, or shall then have^ been directly or indirectly in the Service of the faiclUnited,

East India Company, or of any of His Majesty *s Subjects, and against any Inhabitant of the said Kingdoms, for a Debt arising on any Contract, or Agreement in Writing, with any of His Majesty's Subjects, where the Gause of Action shall exceed the Sum of Five *" hundred current Rupees, and where the said Inhabitant shall have agreed in the said Contract, that in same of Disputes, the Matter shall be heard and determined in the said Supreme Court of Judicature; which said Pbwer and Authority His Majesty hath been graciously pleased to carry into Execution by His Royal Charter, bearing date the 26th Day of March, in the Fourteenth Year of His Majesty's Reign; and that by the said Act and Charter, Two independent Powers have been erected, that of the Governor General and Council entrusted with the Supreme Authority of Government, and that of the Judges entrusted with the Su' preme Administration of Justice within the Provinces

1r>f Bengal, Bahdr, and Oriffa, between whom very alarms ing Contentions have arilen, which have proceeded to such Extremity, that a Military Force has been employed to refill the Process of the Court* and this extraordinary Interpofitiop, avowed and jtiftified upon the Plea of Necessity, finer* without this Interposition, the Governor General and Council affirm, that the lie-venues must have been loft, the Natives of high Rank disgraced, and the Provinces involved in Confiifion; and that your Petitioners apprehend these Contentions have principally arisen from Defeats in the Institution itself, which has eilabiithed Two Powers perfectly dif-tinct, and independent, without providing sufficient Means, to prevent their Collision; and this Opinion your Petitioners are more inclined to adopt, by observing, that the Governor General and Council on the one Hand, and the Judges on the other, were unanimous in every Measure taken throughout this unhappy Contest { That the express Reference in the said Act to the Powers exercised by former Presidents and Council, as well as the Nature of the Subject, decide on the Intention d( the Legislature, not to prefdribe any definite Limits to the Authority of the Governor General and Council in the Civil and Military Government of the Provinces and the Management of the Revenues: Probably, where a small Number of Strangers govern an extensive Terri*, tory, in which a despotic Power has ever before prevail* ed, and col left the Revenues of that Territory adapted to the Nature of their former Government, it will ever be impossible to prescribe any oevtnin known Rules of Conduct to Men entrusted with such an Authority; much less will it be possible to apply the Laws of this Country to so novel a Situation; neither do your Petitioners apprehend that the Court of Justice established by His Majesty's Charter can be rendered subordinate to the Governor General and Council, as the Inha-

bitants in their Petition to this honourable House, have requested, without totally defeating the Ends of Its In* stitution; since, therefore, both these Powers mull fub-iift independent of each other, some Limit seems necessary to prevent their Opposition, which can only be productive of Disgrace and Ruin; for this Purpose it» seems not sufficient that the Distinction between private, Acts of Individuals and public Acts of Government should be recognized as a Principle: This the Judges have already done, but Experience has demonstrated, that a rigid Adherence to Forms, and strict Interpretation of Law, unavoidable in Judges where private Rights are concerned, will greatly impede, if not in many Infiances wholly suspend, the Functions of Government: Indeed, if Men, exercising an undefined Authority, shall be bound to Rate t,heir Defence with technical Precision, to set forth former Practice as a Custom to prove the Act within the Power exercised by former Presidents and Council, and be entangled by all the strict Rules of Evidence, fuqli a legal Exemption must be merely nominal: Your Petitioners, therefore, biunhly fubyrut to the Wisdom of this honourable House, whether the Object may not be better attained, by permitting Persons to alledge generally, that the Act complained oti was done under an Authority derived from the Governor General and Council; making the ic Certificate, upon,a Reference to them, conclusive Evidence of this Fafc't, always permitting the Judgfs to proceed where Corruption was imputed as the Foundation of the Action entertained by the Court: By such a Provision, every Individual acting honestiy in any Department of Government, will enjoy; the Protection necessary in an unsettled State, where Do-, minion muR be uphold by the Sword, and the Country regulated, as the Occasion shall require, by a large dif-cret ionary Power; while the Attention of the Governor General and Council will be drawn to the moR questionable Conduct of Inferiors, who may be punished by Censure, Suspension, or Dismission; and every Act where Corruption is imputed, will be submitted to the piore ri-Vol,;8.

gorous Iuveftigationofan EnglishiZomt of Law: Your AdminifWma Petitioners find like wife, by Papers transmitted to of Justice them, that Men fitting in the Administration of Justice have been subjected to large Damages, where no un-i n' worthy Motive was even suggested, Men have Consequently been unwilling to act without an Indemnity from the Company, and had they not been protected by the Govemor.General and Council, at a great Expence to the Company, the Administration of Justice throughout the Country muR have been iufpended: The Decision may be consonant to the Rules of the Supreme Court of Judicature, and to the Laws by which the Judges are obliged to proceed, but is-certainly inconfrilent with the present State of the: Country: Where British Subjecta preside in Courts which administer Justice according to the ancient Laws and Customs-of the Country, a Dele* gation of Authority to those versed in the respective Laws of the Gentoos or Mahomedans, as the same may require, seems necessary,. and the Prgftice has long pre-< vailed: To examine the Conduct o/.these Delegates, to hear Objections to their Report, and finally to decree upon the Rights of Litigants thus ascertained, appear to be the whole Duty of a Judge under such Circumstances; yet Acts of this Nature have been deemed Trespasses in the Plaintiff) in the Delegates, and the Judges; should Ac s done in such, or the like Situations, be hereafter examined by the rigorous Maxims adapted to a more perfect J udicature, should the Parties be embarrassed in their Defence by technical Forms in alledging a*id proving the Authority of the Court, and the Regularity of their Proceeding, muchlnjusticefeems '

unavoidable: Your Petitioners, therefore, humbly fub-mit to the Wisdom of this'honourable House, whether it may not be just to leave the Officers, and other Per-lbns acting under the Authority of these Courts, wholly to the Cohtroul of the Judges of the said Courts, and to subject the Judges to the Supreme Court of J udicature, ohly where Corruption, or other criminal Motive, shall be proved in a Prosecution by Information or Indictment, leaving, their Errors or Irregularities to be re-dressed by Appeal to the Superior, Courts of the Country: And whether it may not be expedient to render the intended Prated!ion effectual, by making the necessary Allegations few and Ample, and at the same Time, to fa* cilitate the Proof of these Allegations by making the Certificate.of the Judges conclusive Evidence that the Act complained of was done under their Authority, and the Certificate of the Governor General and Council conclusive Evidence of the Appointment of the Persons claiming to act as the Judges of the Court ? And herb your Petitioners think themselves compelled, by Humanity and Justice, to entreat the Attention of this honourable House to the unhappy Situation of the Cauzee. and Mustees, who now languith in Confinement without, a Possibility of Relief, except from Parliament: Ydtir Petitioners are further alarmed by the Embarrassinent in the Management a,udCollection of the Revenues created by the Jurisdiction of the Supreme-Gourt* which have been represented to your Petitioners to be so great.and extensive, as to threaten the Loss of thoieS up plies which: can alone provide for the Government and Defence of the Provinces, or render the Possefljon of these beneficial to Great Britain: And yoiir Petitioners, in examining these Papers, discover abundant Proofs of the Truth of that Opinion which the Legislature, in the Act of the Thirteenth of His present Majesty, seem already to have adopted, that the Administration of Justice by an English Cour:t of Judicature is wholly incompatible,

not only -with the State of -Government in every Part of the Country, but likewise with the Laws, Custoros,

Religion, and Manners, of, the People, which,; amongst Hindoos who constitute the great Body of the Nation,

A Petition of Charles Roe and Company, concerned in a Manufactory of Copper and Brass carried on at a Place called The Havannah, in the County of was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, that the Petitioners carry on a very extensive and valuable Manufactory of Copper and Brass, which is of great public Utility, as well as of great local Advantage, to those Parts of the County of Chester which adjoin upon, or lie contiguous to, that Part of the Country where the said Manufactory is carried on; and that if the said Bill passes into a Law as it uow stands, the Petitioners will be aggrieved and heavily burthened by the Tolls to which they will be subject, in passing with their Goods and Manufacture from The Havannah to their Wharf near The Red Bull in Church Lawton, and returning back to The Havannah: And therefore praying. A Petition of Henry Cvuger, Esquire, was delivered Rriftol in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That on the Election. 31st Day of January now last pad, an Election of One Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the City and County of the City of Bristol, in the room of Sir Henry Lippincott, Baronet, deceased, was holden, by virtue of His Majesty's Writ for that Purpose, in the Guildhall of the said City, before Samuel Span,

Esquire, and Joseph Smith, Esquire, Sheriffs of the said City and Comity; and that, at the said Election, the Candidates were the Petitioner awd George Daubeny,

Esquire; and that, by polling great Numbers of Persons who received Parish Pa}r, Alms, and Charities, and others who had no Right to vote, and by many Acts of Bribery and Corruption, and other undue, partial, and illegal Practices and Proceedings, the said George Daubeny procured a colourable Majority of Votes; and though, on the Part of the Petitioner and his Electors, a Scrutiny was solemnly demanded, for the Sake of enquiring into the Legality of many V otes whose Circumstances were avowedly concealed, nevertheless the Sheriffs, in Violation of the Plights of the said Electors, refused to grant the Petitioner such Scrutiny; and by these, and the like Means, the said George Daubeny caused himself to be returned, by the Sheriffs aforesaid, as One of the Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City, whereas the Petitioner had a Majority of Legal and undoubted Votes upon the said Poll, and ought to have been returned as One of the Citizens to serve in this present Parliament for the said City. And therefore praying the House to take the several Matters aforesaid into their Consideration, and grant him such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet and competent.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 26th Day of June next, at Thfee of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration at the same Time that the last preceding Petition is ordered to be taken into Considera-tiofl.

Mr. Joshua Bryan, one of the Trustees under the said Acts, being examined, said, That after the said Order was made, and the Petition signed, but before it was presented, he remembered some Conversation parting with Mr. Sharland, at aTurnpike Meeting, held to consider whether any Alterations should be made by the Act that was to pass — The Trustees had been talking about Alterations, and had come to a Resolution not to have any, because they thought they might be expensive — That he could not recollect that they had any other Reason — They had talked of exempting Lime from the Payment of Toll, but thej' thought they could not do it without the Conient of the Creditors — That, neverrhe-less, it rtiould he the first Thing to be exempted; in which all the Trustees present agreed.

And being asked. Upon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it does not appear to this Committee, that the Repeal of the exempting Clause, prayed in the said Petition, is in the least Degree necessary.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Evidence hath been brought, which makes out the Charge alleged in the Petition of t he said Trustees, presented to this House on the 17th' Day of November bill, against the said John Sharland, their late Clerk.

Resolved, That it. doth not appear to this Committee, thst the said John Sharland, hath in any wise abused the Confidence the said Trustees had reposed in him, or imposed upon this House, as is alleged in their Petition, or that he attempted so to do; or that either the said John Sharland, or any other Person employed by him, or concerned in soliciting the said Act, was guilty of any Misconduct relative to that Business.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee that while the said Act wasdepending in this House, the Reverend Richard Bowden, Clerk, one of the Pet itioners, pernfed the Clause complained of in the said Petition; and, upon being informed that it would not be attended with any additional Expence, corrected and altered the same with his own Hand, and then expressed himself perfectly satisfied therewith.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petition of the said Trustees, which was presented to this House on the 17th Day of November last* is frivolous, vexatious, and highly injurious to the said John Sharland.

Resolved, that it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Richard Bawden hath been the Contriver,-Promoter, and Prosecutor of the said Petition; and that hisConduft in so doing hath been scandalous and Malicious.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Report be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

W*ys and Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the Mean*. Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred toconlider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and arc as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty or Charge of Five Pounds per Centum be laid upon the Produce and Amount of the several Duties and Revenues under the Management of the respective Commissioners of Excise in Britain (except on the Produce of the Duties on Malt, Beer, Soap, Candles, and Leather) the said additional Duty of Five Pounds per Centum to be charged, collected, paid, and drawn back, under the same Rules and Regulations, and in the same Manner and Form,

as the present Duties of Excise are now charged, collected, paid, and drawn back.

Refplved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Discounts or Abatements (which, by virtue of the seventeenth Rule annexed to the Book of Rates, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, or of any other Act of Parliament, are made in the Computation of the Subsidies, Impost?, and other Duties of Customs in Great Britain, or for Prompt Payment) shall cease, determine, and be no longer made or allowed out of the said Duties on Entries, except the Allowances to the Company,

for Charges of Sale and Prompt Payment, provided that the Duties on Unrated East India Goods, sold at their Sales, be paid within Three Months from the Termination of each Sale respectively; that is to say, that the Duties on the March Sale shall be paid on or before the First Day of December following, and the Duties on the September Sale on or before the First Day of June following such Sales; and except the usual Discount on Bonds for Tobacco warehoused, for the Time they have to run when they are paid off before they are due; and except the usual Allowances for Leakage on Wine.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Five Pounds per Centum additional Duty, or impost, granted by an Act of the Nineteenth of His

»5

present Majesty, or by any subsequent Act, shall b'b1 laid,' computed, and received, upon the Gross Duties which ilia.Il accrue, and become due and payable, when such Discounts or Abatements shall cease, determine, and be no longer allowed or made.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That so much of the several Acts of Parliament as relate to the Importer giving Bond, with One or more Securities, for the Duties on Tobacco, be repealed; and that, when the Duties on Tobacco are paid down at the Time of Entry, the Impost of Five Pounds per Centum, granted by an Act of the Nineteenth of His present Majesty, shall not be collected on such Duties io paid down; but if the Tobacco shall be warehoused, and Bond given for the Duties, pursuant to an Act of the Twelfth of Queen Anne, or any other Act of Parliament, then there shall be taken Ten Pounds per Centum instead of Five Pounds per Centum for the Impost, granted by the said Act of the Nineteenth of His present Majesty, on the Gross Duties.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,.

That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty of One Penny and Three Farthings per Pound Weight be laid upon all Tobacco imported into Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty of Four Shillings and Eight Pence per Hundred Weight, containing One hundred and Twelve Pounds, be laid upon all Sugars imported into Great Britain, and so in proportion for any greater or less Quantity.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the said additional Duties shall be subject and liable to the Payment of the Duty or Charge of Five Pounds per Centum laid upon the Produce and Amount of the several Duties under the Management of the respective Commissioners of the Customs and Excise, by an Act made in the Nineteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Dr. Smith produced to your Committee, a Copy of a Resolution made at a Committee, called The Charity, dated the 25th March 1776, and sent to him by Sir Charles Whitworth, Chairman of the said Committee, desiring him to visit the Sick in the respective Gaols and Prisons of London, , and tvark, in order to administer proper Relief; for which a Sum of Money was appropriated by the said Charity: Which Copy was proved to be in the Hand Writing of Sir Charles Whitworth, and was directed to the Keepers of the several Gaols, Sic. in the Cities of London and Westminster, and Borough of Southwark.

YourC'ommittee then examined John Summerville, a Coach Maker, William Read, a Surveyor, John a Miller, John Andretvs, a Coach Mailer, and Brackell, a Taylor, who had been confined for Debt in the Fleet Prison; — George. Haa Taylor, and

Broivn, a Jeweller and Stock Broker, and Joseph Pinckny, a Baker, who had been confined for Debt in —

William Fergujim, a Mariner, and a Cord-

wainer, who had been confined for Debt in the King's Bench: — together with Sampson Mockett, lateKeeper of the Poultry Compter, Thomas Grove, T urnkeyand Cham-

berlain of the Fleet, Daniel Brown, Turnkey to the Poultry Compter, Joshua Murray, a Meifengerto the Poultry Compter, John Newma Keeper of Ludgate, and Jeremiah Severs, Keeper of the Borough Compter: — by whole Evidence it appeared, That Dr. Smith, and an Apothecary appointed by him, had frequently attended the said Prisons, at ditferentTimes, from March 1776 till March 1780, and administered Relief to the Sick Prisoners; — That Dr. Smith sometimes attended Two or Three Times in a Day, and had seldom been a Day absent, at some of the Prisons, for several Months together; — That great Numbers were relieved by his Assistance, and supplied with Medicines from his Apothecary, by his Orders, without paying any Thing for them, which it appeared had been given in great Quantities, and whenever the Prisoners sent for them; — That he left Directions at all the Prisons, to be sent for whenever his A Alliance was wanted, and always attended, or sent Medicines, when applied to; — That none of the aforesaid Gaols, except t he Marshalsea, had, during that Time, any Medical Assistance, and there an Apothecary only attended; — That Dr. Smith had treated the Patients with great Tenderness and Humanity, giving pecuniary Assistance to many, as well as Medicines; and it was the Opinion of the Witnesses, that he had been the Means of saving the Lives of many People, who must have died but for his Assistance: — That several, in great Danger, had been cured under his Directions; and that Surgeons occasionally attended in consequence of his Orders, and at his Expence.

Then a Letter was produced, and proved to be the Hand Writing of J. Stracey, deceased, late Deputy Keeper of Ludgate, and sent to Dr. Smith — a Copy of which Letter is as follows;

"Sir,

" The bad State of Health I am at present in, renders me incapable of waiting upon you personally;

" and finding it necessary to be known, whether yon " attended this Prison, and ordered proper Medicines, Vot. 38.

" Sic. permit me to acquaint yon, that I do hereby " acknowledge that you attended, these Four \ ears " pall, whenever sent for; that the Medicines always " came, agreeable to your Directions, to the Prisoners " in general; and that both Self and Family received " your Advice and Medicines; — this I will authenticate to any Person whatever, as well as that all Persons here were attended with the greatest Tenderness " and Care. t

" I am. Sir,

* Ludgate, " Your obliged and

" April ;o, 1780. " obedient humble Servant,

" J. Stracey.'*

" Dr. Win. Smith."

Then Mr. John Cofens was examined; who said, He had attended the several Prisons before-mentioned as Apothecary, at the Request and under the Directions of Dr. Smith, from the Month of March 1776 till the Year 1780, and at different Times gave ana sent Medicines to the fiek Prisoners; — That lie regularly made a Report to Dr. Smith, of the State of the Health of the Prisoners, and kept regular Accounts of Medicines delivered, which were always examined by the Doctor.

And he produced to your Committee his Book of Accounts; by which it appeared, that from the 6th of April 1776 to the 14th of April 177q, the Charges for Medicines delivered to Sick Prisoners, at the different Prisons during that Period, amounted to £.521. 1 is.yd.

And being further examined, he said, That his Charges for Medicines delivered to Prisoners, were in general the same that he made to other People; but that he had made no.Charge for a very long and constant Attendance, which was of great Prejudice to his other Business; — That being employed by Dr. Smith, he considered him as answerable for the Payment; — That he has only received 50, paid by Sir Charles Whitworth from a Committee at Westminster, which Sum is to bededuCled from the before-mentioned Account; — That since that Account was made up, he had delivered Medicines, under the Prescriptions of Dr. Smith, to Sick Prisoners, to the Amount of near C-io.

And Dr. Smith informed your Committee, That he considered himself obliged, under the Directions he received from Sir Charles Whitworth, to examine, as far as lay in his Power, the State, Condition, and Management, of the several Gaols he attended; and did with great Labour, and at a considerable Expence, compile several Pamphlets, with such Observations and Remarks as he thought might tend not only to set "forth the true State and Condition of such Gaols, but also to point out such Alterations and Amendments as he apprehended might in some Degree improve the general Police relative to Prisons and Prisoners: And, as a Proof of the Truth of this Assertion, he produced the following printed Pamphlets:

" State of the Gaols in London, Westminster, and " Borough of Southwark."

" Observations on the Laws relative to Debtors " and Felons."

" Considerations on the Laws between Debtors " and Creditors."

" Observations on the Bill depending in Parliament for the Relief of Debtors,

" A Short View of the Modern Practice of " Physic."

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Charles Brett, Esquire, being examined, said, That the Road described in the Petition is out of Repair, narrow in some Places, and incommodious — That it is the direct and high Road from London to Maidstone, the County Town of Kent-r-ThaX it cannot be properly amended and kept in Repair by the Laws in being — That it is about Five Miles in Length; and that it would be a Convenience to tlfe Neighbourhood, and of public Utility, to have the same included in One of the Turnpike Acts, the Roads, of which communicate with it.

A Petition offeveral of the Commissionersforcleanfing and making navigable the Channel from The at

Colchester, to Wivenhoe, in the County of Essex, and of several Merchants, Tradesmen, and principal Inhabitants of the Town of Colchwhofe Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and others interested in the Navigation of the said Channel, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for continuing and making more effectual several Acts of Parliament, passed for cleansing and making navigable\he Channel from The Hythe at -

chester, to Wivenhoe, in the County of Essex; and for repairing and cleansing the Streets of the Town of chester, and also for 1 ighting the Streets and Lanes, and for preventing Annoyances in the said Town; and Setting forth. That there is a Clause contained in the said Bill . whereby the Commissioners are obliged to keep in Repair the Walls on each Side of the said Channel, which Walls have always been the Property of the Owners of Lands contiguous to the said Channel, and were made by the said Owners to proteCl their Lands from Inundations, and have always been supported and repaired by them *, which Clause, if passed into a Law, would, as the Petitioners apprehend, be of the greatest prejudice to the Navigation of the said Channel, aAd very inju-' rious to the Public; and that any absolute Limitation of the Time for keeping up the Lock Water, as pro-5

posed by the said Bill, will occasion the greatest Inconveniencies to all Persons concerned in the said Navigation, and will entirely defeat the End for which the said Lock was erected, which was to keep up a sufficient Head of Water at Neap Tides, by the Addition of the fresh Water, that the Vessels, when loading, might be removed from one Quay to another; and the Petitioners are well assured the Trade of the said Channel cannot possibly be carried on, unless the Commissioners are authorized to keep up the Lock Water for such Time as they shall think proper; and that the Clause in some former Acts relating to the said Navigation, for incapacitating such Persons as farm Quays or Wharfs upon the said Channel from being Commissioners, is now without any Foundation, as the Reasons upon which it was grounded do no longer exist; and the Petitioners therefore submit, whether the said incapacitating Clause ought to remain in Force, more especially as the Persons who farm Quays or Wharfs are, by their Situation and Employment, most particularly qualified to atlas Commissioners for the Care and Management of the said Navigation; and that the Boundaries of the Jurisdiction of the said Commissioners, as described in the said Bill, are different from those agreed upon at a General Meeting of the said Commissioners, and the fixingtlie same in theManner prescribed by the Bill will, be attended with considerable Inconvenience to the said Navigation; and the Petitioners further submit, whether some Qualification be not necessary for such Persons as shall act as Commissioners: And therefore praying.

That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill as may be injurious to them; and that they may have such Relief in the Premises as the House shall think just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard at the same Time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of Thomas Noxon and Thomas Butler, late Coventry Sheriffs of the City of Coventry, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners having been found guilty of a high Violation of the Law, and a gross Breach of the Privileges of this House, for not having made any Return of Members to serve in Parliament at the lall General Election for the said City, were, for the said Offence, committed to His Majesty's Gaol of Newgate, where they were confined until Friday Evening last; and that the Petitioners wer® then discharged by this House from the said Gaol, and committed to the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms, where they are now confined; and that the Petitioners are thoroughly sensible of the great Offence they have been guilty of, and humbly beg Pardon of the House for the fame: And therefore praying. That they may be discharged from their Confinement.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Sir , Baronet,

complaining of an undue Election and Return for the County of Ayr, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed by Mr. Speaker to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Sixteen Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration. And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which bad been

A Petition of John Paulin and John , the

priticipal Land Coal Meters of the City and Liberty of Wefihtinjlbr, Was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend the Clause in the Act of the Thirty-second of George the Second, which directs that none of the Provisions of that Act, or of the Acts of the Nineteenth Tear of the same Reign, respecting the Payment of ahy Money for the Metage of Coals, or the Punishmfent of the Perfofls therein named, shall take Place, unless the Buyer of such Coals shall, by Notice given in Writing, require the Attendance of the Coal Meter, has, in many Irtllances, tended to the Prejudice of the Public and the Fair Trader, and the Prevention of the Petitioners in the Execution of their Office, in as much as the Purchasers of Coals are, in a great measure, unacquainted With that Clause, and as many Dealers have there by been enabled to practise the Frauds, for the Prevention of which the Coal Meters Office Was erected, and in the conducting of Which the Petitioners are compelled, under a f&Vere Penalty, and at a very great Expence, Without the Certainty Of being repaid, location LabOUringCoal Meters at the established Wharfs in the City and Liberty of Westminster, where the Meters frequently observe the mofl Tcandalous Frauds ttanfafted irt the Measurement of Coals, yet, if they appear to take arty Notice of them, or attempt to prevent such Frauds, they are driven off the Craft, and threatened to be prosecuted as Trespasser, under the Pretence that the Petitioners are not authorized to inspect the Measurement of Coals, where the Buyer has not signified in Writing his Desire to have the Attendance of the Meter; and that the Petitioners apprehend t he abovementioned Evils might be remedied, and an Option Hill left with the Purchaser (and of which he may be fully appHfed) of having his Coals ttleted or hot, if, in liett Of that ClaUlfe it Wfere Cuafted, that all the Provisiotts contained in the same Acts, relating to the Metage of Coals, shall be in Force, unless the Seller offndi Coals flmll deliver to the Labouring Coal Meter Rationed at the Wharf, a Notice, signed or subscribed by the Buyer, signifying his Intention not to have the Coals irteted; and tire Petitioners also apprehend, that the following Regulations respecting the Coal Merchants, their Fillers, and Carmen, and the Sacks used by them, will be of still further Advantage to the Public; viz. That Penalties more adequate to the Offence, and more eafrly to be recovered, be inflicted on the Coal Merchant, in case of short Measure, whether the Coals have been meted or not; that the Fillers should be subject to Penalties as well as the Labouring Meters, in case of short Measure; that the Size of the Sacks beenlarged, and the Mouths properly secured by the Carmen, and so preferred till Delivery,

Vol. 38.

under proper Penalty; that the Carmen shall be obliged to attend the Re-admeasurement of Coals, if required, and to deliver their Tickets before the Shooting of the Coals: And the Petitioners suggest, that, if the following Regulations respecting the Execution of the Coal Meters Office, which the Petitioners! now voluntarily practise, were directed under the Authority of Parliament, they would give further Satisfaction to the Public, and be of Utility, as well to the Seller as to the Purchaser of Coals; viz. That there be a Meter appointed, at the Request of the Purchaser, to re-measure, without. Fee or Reward, any Coals which have been previously measured at the W harfs, or, tinder certain Regulations, to attend the Admeasurement of them at the Purchaser's House in the first Instance; and that the Meters shall keep proper Entries of all Coals that are measured tinder the Inspection of the Office, which Buyers and Sellers shall have Liberty to examine, and have Certificates of any Transaction delivered to them gratis; and further, that the principal Coal Meters for the Time being do deliver an Annual Account to the House of all the Transactions of the Office on Oath: And therefore praying the House to take these Matters into Coniidetation, and to do therein as to them ffiaj! seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

A Petition of the Goldsmiths, Toymen, Watchr makers, Cafemakers, Chainmakers, Small Workers in Gold, Chafers, and other Persons concerned in the manufacturing or vending of Gold Wares, rftiding within the Cities of London and Westminster, and the liberties thereof, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have, for many Years, pall, reflected with the deepest Concern on the depreflbd State of ' lie Manufactures of Gold Wares in this Kingdom, proceeding principally from the Necessity under which the fair Trader lies, of using and employing Gold of the Fineness and Standard ellablithed by the Laws now in being, which Gold is, in almost all Cafes, considerably too soft, and thereby not only exposed to be easily bruifcxl and injured, but will not admit of so high a Polish as Gold of an inferior Standard; rod that, by the Laws of many Foreign Countries, the Subjects of those Countries are permitted, in Manufactures that are made of Gold, to use and employ Gold of Two inferior Qualities and Standards, whereby they are enabled to underfell the Subjects of this Country at all Foreign Markets, and thereby to engross a very considerable Part of that Branch of Trade, which might be feeuied to the Subjects of this Kingdom, if they tvere by Law permitted to employ in such Manufactures Gold of the same Standards and Values as are generally employed by Foreign Goldsmiths, who, by Means of such Per;uiiIion, have gained a Preference iu Favour of their Manufactures all over the World, to the great Detriment of the Petitioners and the Eng-li/hNation; and that Foreigners have taken Advantage of such Impediments and Obstacles under which the Petitioners have been placed by Law in respect of the; Premises, whereby the fair and.honest Tradesmen and Artificers do suffer considerably, and are wholly deprived of the Advantages which might be secured to them, and to the Nation in general, if they were delivered from fneh disadvantageous Restraints, under which by Law they now labour; and that all such ruinous Obstacles and Impediments may be effectually removed by a Law establishing (beside the present Standard of this Kingdom) Two distinct new Standards for all Gold to be hereafter used and employed in all Manufactures of that Metal, the one of such Standards to contain ip each Pound Troy Twenty Carrats of fine Gold, and Four Carrats of Alloy; and the other of such Standards to be of an inferior Quality; and to contain in each Pound Troy Eighteen Carrats of fine Gold, and Six Carrats of Alloy, all which several Standards would be particularly advantageous to the Petitioners to have established, in as much as different Kiuds of Gold Wares respectively require to be made of Gold of different Degrees of Hardness, and of different Degree*

Then the said Petition was delivered in, and read; Setting forth. That at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Hellefon, in the Place of Jocelyn Dean, F.squire, deceased, the Right honourable Thomas Lord Hyde and Richard Harwell, Esquire, were proposed as Candidates to represent the said Borough in Parliament; and that the Sheriff of the said County of Cornwall delivered the Precept for the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament, in the Place of the said Jocelyn Dean, to Matthew Wilts, one of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and refused to deliver the same to the Petitioner John Rozve, the Mayor of the said Borough, to whom such Precept ought to have been directed, and who had the Right to preside at the said Election, and is the proper Returning Officer of the said Borough; and that the Poll was then taken before the said John Roxoe, the Mayor of the said Borough, and the Petitioners and others, being a great Majority of the Persons legally entitled to vote at the said Election, voted for the said Thomas Lord Hyde, who was duly elected, and rightfully returned by the said Mayor to the Sheriff of the said County of Cormcall, who refused to accept the said Return, or annex the same to his Writ of Election; and that the said Matthew Wills took upon himself to preiide at another pretended Election for the said Borough, at which he the said Matthew Wills, and also Richard Penhaleand William Rogers, took upon themselves to vote for the said Richard B; and the said Matthew Wills, without any lawful Authority, returned the said Richard Bancell as Member for the said Borough, although no other Persons, save the said Matthew Richard Penhale, and William Rogers, voted for the said

Richard Barwell-, and the said Sheriff accepted and-

annexed the said last mentioned Return to his Writ of Election, and transmitted the same to the Office of the Clerk of the Crown; and that the said Richard Penhale, and William Rogers, claimed to vote as Freemen of the said Borough, pretending to have been elected to such Franchise under a Charter granted to the said Borough in the Twenty-seventh Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, although in Truth the said Matthew Wills, Richard Penhale, and William Rogers, were not duly elected Freemen according to the Provisions of the said Charter, but were elected by the Mayor and Aldermen only, and in the same Manner as all the other pretended Freemen of the said Borough, who claimed their Franchises under the said Charter, and who were oitfted by the Judgment of His Majesty's Court of King's Bench, and although the Corporation created by the said Charter is dissolved: And therefore praying, That the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and give such Relief as the Circumstances of this same shall call for.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Friday the 29th Day of June next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Considera- pivm0uth tion the Petition of John Culme, Esquire, com- Election. plaining of thoundue Election and Return of George Darby, Esquire; and also the Petition of the Reverend John Julian, Clerk, John Crojfman, George Bough ton,

Thomas Woolcotnbe, and Thomas Squire, Gentlemen, all

4 Q legal

334

legal Voters of the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, on Behalf of themselves and many other Elec* tors of the same Borough, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Sir Frederick Leman Rogers, Baronet, and of the said George Darby, Esquire, for the said Borough, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms wasdirested by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Six Members being found to be present *,

The Counsel and Agents for the Petitioner, Mr. Culme, and the Counsel and Agents for the other Petitioners, the Voters of the said Borough, and the Counsel and Agents for the Sitting Members, were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House was locked.

And the Counsel for Mr. and the Voters, respectively acquainted the House, that they appeared on distinct Interests — That the said Petitioner Mr. Culme, Complained only of the undue Election and Return of Mr. Darby, and claimed, on the Part of the Freeholders within the said Borough, only a concurrent Right, with the Freemen, to vote at the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the other Petitioners, the Voters, complained of the undue Election and Return of both Sir Frederick Leman Rogers and of the said Mr. Darby, and claimed a Right to vote at such Elections by virtue of their Freeholds, exclusive of the Freemen of the said Borough.

And the said Petitions, and also the Act of the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to explain and amend an Act, made " in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act " to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament," were read.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Members making no Objection to the said Petitioners appearing as separate Parties on distinct Interests;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of the said Select Committee accordingly.

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Forty-nine Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Thirty-seven other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names ofthofe who were absent from ilte House; Four, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Seven, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions weredepending; Thirteen, on Account of their then fervingon Select Committees; and Thirteen, on Account of their having already, in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete. Lists of the said Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Cotinfel.

And the Door of the House being opened; .

The Counsel and Agents withdrew.

A Petition of the Prisoners confined for Debt in Execution in Wood Street Compter, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been confined in Wood Street Compter

above

Account of East India Military Charges.

Importation

of

Portugal

Goods.

Debtors.

340 4 Aprilis.A. 1781.

above Two Years, and flatter themselves that, upon the most minute Enquiry, their Misfortunes will be found to have proceeded from unforeseen and unavoidable Accidents in Trade, and wholly free from any Imputation of Fraud; and that the Petitioners, from their long Confinement, are not only entirely ruined in their Trade and Circumstances, but have beeft obliged to part with every Necessary they had, to support themselves and Families; and representing to the House, that, at the Time of the late Riots, the Petitioners were liberated from the Gaol of Street by the Mob, but, from a Consciousness of the Rectitude of their Conduct, their Hopes of Relief, by the Interposition of the Legislature, and their Unwillingness to any Infringement on, but to act in Conformity to, the Lavvs of their Country, chose rather to return to their Confinement then enjoy an illegal Liberty; and in this Resolution they were strengthened by the Sheriffs 1 Fright and Pugh, who pledged themselves to use their utmost Endeavours in Behalf of the Petitioners; and that, upon the puffing the late Act of Indemnity to Sheriffs, Gaolers, &c. the Petitioners found it was not possible for them to receive the same Benefit as other Prisoners enjoyed by surrendering in Discharge of their Bail, in conformity to the Limitations of the said Act, thereby obtaining their Liberty until called upon to surrender by public Advertisement; and the Petitioners are also deprived of the Benefit of through

their extreme Necessities, although they were advised they are equally entitled to the Benefit of the said Act with the Prisoners of The King's Bench and Fleet Prisons, but chuse wholly to rely on the Humanity of the House: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Holford and Mr. Bicknell:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for declaring certain Provisions of an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, relating to the Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called England, to extend to all Acts made, and to be made, for repairing Roads, subsequent to the passing of the said Act; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, passed in the Thirty-third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for amending, widening, and

keeping in Repair, the High Roads from the Borough of Tannvorth, to Ashby-de-la-Zouch, in the County of

Leicester, and from Saivley Feny, in the said County, to a Turnpike Gate at or near the End of Sioarclif Lane, leading to and in the Parish of Aftiby-de-la-Zouclt aforesaid; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

The House being informed that Mr. Tomkyns, from the Commissioners of the Customs, attended at the Door; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Order,

An Account of all British Plantation Tobacco which has been imported into the several Ports of that Part of Great Britain called England, from the British West India Islands which appears, by the Clearances, not to have been of the Growth or Produce of those Islands, nor Prize Tobacco, for the Four last Years ending the 5th January last.

And then he withdrew.

And the Title of the said Account was read.

Ordered, That the said Account do lie upon the' Table, to be perused by the Members of the House. The said Account is preferred amongst the other Papers of this Session.

Proceeding in our Inquiries into Balances in the Appendix Hands of those Accountants who appear upon the |^o j Certificate of Accounts depending in the Office of the Auditor of the imprest, we find therein, next to the Treasurers of the Navy, the Names of several Perilous whole Accounts have not been prosecuted for tip-wards of Seventy Years. We could have no Expectation of profiting by a Pursuit of Claims arising at so remote a Period; and therefore, paffiugon to the next Class, namely, the Paymasters of the Forces, wfe fee Handing first in that Class the Name of Henry Earl of Lincoln; whose final Account of the Forces for Six Months, to the 24th of June 1720, is therein defaulted " to have been delivered into Auditor s Office,

" but, being very imperfect, to have been long since " withdrawn, and not returned." We ifl'ued our Precept to his Grace the Duke of Neiccastle, for an Account of the Public Money in his Hands, Custody, or Power, as Representative of Henry Earl of , late

Paymaster General of the Forces. The Duke of castle, in a Letter dated the 24th of lad, in-

formed us, that " he never had in his Hands, Custod\-, or Power, any of the Public Money which " was possessed by his late Father as Paymaster of " the Forces, nor any of his Accounts or Vouchers " relative thereto; nor could he inform us what Balance, if any, was due from him on that Account; " that his late Father died inteilute, leaving him, and " several other Children, then Infants, and that " Countess of Lincoln, his Widow, administered to " him, and possessed what Effects he left, which the applied towards Dischacge of his DebtsAnd in a subsequent Letter, dated the 23d of November Lift, the Duke informed us, that he took out Adminifixation

bonis non to his late Father, in 1748. In confe-

quence of tliefc Letters from the Duke of we proceeded 110 further in this Enquiry.

Having thus obtained a Knowledge of the Balances, our next Step was to examine whether they were liable to any such Services, or subject to any such Payments, in the Hands of these Accountants, as rendered it ne-cellary to permit them, or auy Part of them, to remain longer in their Pollession. For this Purpose we examined John Poioell, Esquire, the Cashier, and Charles 3* Bernbridge, Esquire, the Accountant to the Payinalter General of the Forces; by whom we are informed, that the Money in the Hands of the Paymasters General of the Forces, after they are out of Office, continues, as long as their Accounts are kept open, liable to the Payment of any Claims of the Stall'or I lospital Officers, or of any Warrants for Contingencies and Extraordinaries, which were voted during the Time they were respectively in Office, and have not been claimed: After the final Accounts are cfofi-d, such. Mr. Fox and Mr. Powell object to the Payment into the Exchequer of so much of the Sum of Two hundred Fifty-six thousand Four hundred Fifty-six Pounds Eight Shillings and Two Pence (being the Balance in the Hands of Mr. Powell, as Executor of the iate Lord Holland) as may be affected by the Decision of certain Suits depending in the Court of Chancery: the Sum that may be so affected, according to Mn Powell's Account, amounts to Seventy-three thousand One hundred Forty-nine Pounds Ten Shillings and Seven Pence.

The State of the Proceedings in these Suits is set forth in Mr. Powell's Information to be as follows: — The Accounts of Mr. Robert Paris Taylor, one of the Deputy Paymasters to Lord Holland, in Germany, during the late War, were examined in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, where he is surcharged with the Sum of Twelve thousand Fifty-two Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Ten Pence Half Penny, which Surcharge he controverts. In the Beginning of lad Year, the Executors of Lord Holland commenced Two Actions in the Court of King's Bench against Mr. Taylor, and the Executors and Devisees of Peter Taylor, his Father, who was his Surety, to recover the Sum of Twenty-eight thousand One hundred Eighty-five Pounds Nine Shillings and Five Pence Three Farthings, being the Balance supposed to be due from him upon these Accounts, in which Sum the Surcharge is included. As the Question in these Causes appears to be, whether Mr. Taylor was indebted to the Executors of Lord Holland in this Sum, or any Part of it, the Balance of Public Money in Mr. Powell's Hands might be increased, but could not be diminifiied, by the Event of these Actions; and therefore Mr. Powell does not infill upon retaining any Part of this Balance to secure him against such Event; but Mr. Taylor, and the Devisees of Peter Taylor, soon after filed Two Bills in the Court of Chancery against the Executors of Lord Holland, suggesting Errors, and praying that these Accounts may be taken in that Court. These Causes have not yet come to a Hearing; but the Ground of Mr. PowelVs Claim to the Detention of this Sum of Seventy-three thousand One hundred Forty-nine PoundsTenShil-lingsand Seven Pence, as collected from his Information, and the Letter of his Solicitor, appears to be this: That should an Account be decreed, every Item in Mr. Taylors Accounts will be open to Litigation; and Mr. Taylor having charged himself before the Auditors of the Imprest, with the Sum of Seven hundred Eighty-six thousand Three hundred Fifty-fev^n Guilders Nine Stivers, which is Seventy-three thousand One hundred Forty-nine Pounds Ten Shillings and Seven Pence Sterling, as a Profit to the Public arising on Money Tran-factions in his Department, as Deputy Paymaster, may fnggeft, in the Progress of these Causes, that he has er-roneously charged himself with this Sum; and therefore Mr. Powell claims to retain it in his Hands, to guard against the Consequences of a possible Decision upon this Sum in Mr. Taylor's Favour.

Subjects under Litigation in a Court of Justice should not be examined elsewhere without an absoluteNeceffity, and not even then but with great Caution. This Point coming thus incidentally before us, in the Progressofan Inquiry within our Province, we may, without Impropriety, venture to say, that, in our Opinion, the bare Possibility that Mr. Taylor may, in the Court of Chancery, object to, and be discharged of, a Sum he has charged himself with before the Auditors of the Imprest, and which he was bound by his Instructions to charge himself with, as a Profit to the Public, and to which, for aught that appears to us, he has never yet objected, but has, on the contrary, in Part applied to the Use of the Yol. 38.

Lady Greenwich, Lord North, Mr.

Colonel Cooke, and Mr. Molloy, do not object to the Payment into the Exchequer of their Balances; nor do Mr.

Fox and Mr. Powell, os to the Residue of Lord Hollands Balance, upon severally receiving their Quietus, or a Security equivalent thereto.

Where Accounts must be passed by the Auditors of the Imprest, the Payments into the Exchequer, made by the Accountants, before the final Adjustment, are Payments upon Account only; but should these Accountants be directed to pay in their full Balances, they will be entitled to, and ought in Justice to receive, a Security and Indemnification against all Claims and Payments whatever, to which the Balances were in their Hands subject; the Fund possessed by the Paymaster in Office being substituted in the Place of these Balances, to answer such future Claims and Demands, the Accountant himself will Hand liable only to the Errorsand Oraiffions that may be discovered in the Examination of his Accounts, in the Office appointed for auditing the m:

Should there be Errors, he may either pay the Balance to, or receive it from, the Paymaster in Office, according as it may be determined; then, and not before, he will be entitled to his Quietus; which being the formal official Discharge of every public Accountant, cannot but be subsequent to the complete *Examination, and the Payment of the Balance, if any, according to the final Adjustment of his Accounts.

Having the refore not heard, either from the Accountants themselves, or from those who may be interested in our Decisions, any Reasons to alter ourOpinion, we conceive that the Balance of Public Money now remaining in the Hands of John Powell, Esquire, as the only acting Executor of Lord Holland, and in the Hands of Lady Greenwich, as Administratrix to Mr. Charles late Paymasters of the Forces; and in the Hands of Lord North, and of Mr. Thomas Townshend, as late Paymasters of the Forces, each jointly with Mr.

George Cooke, deceased, ought to be paid into the Exchequer, to be applied to the Public Service; and that such Payments should be without Prejudice, and a proper Security and Indemnification be given to each of them against any Loss or Detriment that may accrue to them in Consequence of such Payment.
