The Examination of John Powell, Esquire, Cashier to the Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 20th and 26th of gth,

nth, 15th, 19th, and 28th 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he is the only acting Executor of Henry Lord Holland, late. Paymaster General of the Forces: That the Sum of Two hundred Fifty-six thousand Four hundred Fifty-six Pounds Twd Shillings and Four Pence, mentioned in his Return to the Precept of this Board, upon the 2 7th of September last, was, to the heft of his Knowledge, the whole Balance then remaining upon the Account of the said Henry Lord Holland, as Paymaster General of the Forces.

When a Paymaster goes out of Office his Accounts of the Year's Establishment are generally carried on, either to the 24th of June, or to the 24th of December, preceding or subsequent to his Resignation or Death, as most convenient for the Public Service. If his Accounts end the 24th of June, he receives his Proportion of that Year's Supply if they end on the 24th of December, he receives the whole Year's Supply, out of the Exchequer as it is wanted in Order of Time. In Lord Hollands Time it was the Usage of the Office to afic of the Treasury, generally every Four Months, a Third Part of the whole Year's ordinary Supply; but since the Year 1759 the Practice has been not to apply for Money for any Service, until near the usual Time for Payment of that Service, at which Time the Paymaster, though out of Office, upon Application to the Treasury, receives it by their Direction from the Exchequer, and applies it to satisfy the Demands of those who have Claims upon that Service.

Lord Hollands Accounts ended on the 24th of June 1765, and his final Account was delivered into the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest on the 11th of January 1772. The Balance for which he is accountable to the Public, as Executor to the late Lord Holland, is at this Time subject to the following Services:

To Claims of the Staff and Hospital Officers and to Warrants for Contingencies and Extraordinaries voted by Parliament during the Time Lord Holland was in Office, and not yet claimed, if there be any such Claims or Warrants existing. If Lord Hollands Accounts were closed, he is inclined to think these Claimants must apply either to the Treasury or to the Secretary at War, to renew their Warrants for Payment. As all the Fees for passing the Accounts, and for the Quietus, are, as he believes, provided for, the only remaining Payment to which the present Balance is subject, is, the usual Gratuity to the Officers and Clerks of the Paymaster General for making up the Accounts of the Paymasters out of Office: The Officers and Clerks of the Paymasters in Office carry on and make up the Accounts of the Paymaster out of Office; for which extra Business they have no Salary or Reward, until the final Account is ready to be passed; at which Time they present a Memorial to the Treasury, praying them to obtain the King's Warrant to the Auditors of the Imprest, to allow them a certain Sum for this Business; which Sum, pursuant to this Warrant, is paid to them out of the Balance.

The Sums received by a Paymaster, after be is out of Office, are either Sums iflfced to him out of the Exchequer, which were due for the ordinary Service of the Army at the Time he went out of Office, and for which he had at that Time Credit at the Exchequer; or Sums received by him from the Paymaster iu Office, by virtue of Treasury Warrants, for Extraordinary Services advanced by him during the Time of his being in Office; or from the Treasury in Ireland, for the Pay of the Irish Regiments serving out of that Kingdom according to the Irish Establishment. Lord Holland has received, as

he believes all the Public Money due to him out of the Exchequer, and from the succeeding Paymasters, and from Ireland,

After a Paymaster has resigned his Office, he has continued to receive Money out of the Exchequer for the following Services:

The Pay of the General and Staff Officers at Home and Abroad; the Pay of the Officers of the Hospital at Home and Abroad; the Pay of the Staff of the Garrisons at Home and Abroad; for Contingencies of the Army at Home and Abroad; for House Pensioners, Servants, and Artificers of C Hospital; for Half Pay Officers, Widows Allowances, Offrreckonings, and the Clearings.

He farther faith, He was Accountant to the Paymaster General from June 176510 March 17 76, when he was appointed Cashier: That during the Time he was Accountant, and, as he believes, from the Year 1759, and since he was appointed Cashier, the Mode of Rating the Army Accounts, and of asking for Moneys was and has been as follows

The Sums voted to pay the General and Staff Officers, and the Officers of the Hospital, are generally asked of the Treasury at the customary Periods of Payment; these Sums, after they are directed by the Treasury, and received, remain in the Hands of the Paymaster until a Certificate comes to him from the Secretary at War, specifying the Names and Stations of the several Officers actually employed: Upon a Debenture, being made out pursuant to that Certificate, and a King's Warrant obtained, agreable to that Debenture, the Sums due to the several Officers are paid to them, or to their Agents, upon their Application.

The Sums to pay the Staff of the Garrisons atHome and Abroad, arealked in like Manner as the Sums to pay the General and Staff Officers; and when received, are paid, fometo the Governors of the Garrisons, or to their Agents; others, to the Officers themfe!ves, or their Agents.

He does not recoiled that the Sums for Contingencies are atked from the Treasury; they are paid, when applied for, pursuant to the Warrants of the Secretary at War, out of any Money in the Hands of the Paymaster; Warrants for this Service are almost every Day presented to the Pay Office for Payment.

The Sums to pay the House Pensioners, Servants, and Artificers of Chelsea Hospital, are asked every Six Months, when Twelve Months are due, and paid into the Hands of the Deputy Treasurer; who is appointed by the Paymaster, and accountable to him.

The Sums to pay Half Pay Officers are aflced every Six Months, when due, and paid to the several Officers entitled, or their Agents, on their Application.

The Sums to pay the Pensions to Officers Widows are not, as far as he can recoiled, afited of the Treasury; they are paid by the Paymaster General, out of any Money in his Hands, to the Paymaster of the Pensions (who is appointed by Patent) upon his Application, and paid by him to the Claimants every Four Months.

When Fifteen or Sixteen Months of the Off-reckon-ings are due, it is usual for the Paymaster to ask of the Treasury for Six Months; and when received Notice is given, and the Money is paid soon after to the Persons to whom the Colonels have assigned them.

As to the Clearings, a Debenture Warrant is sent to the Paymaster by the Secretary at War, signifying the King's Directions to him to make up the Accounts of Certain'Regiments; in consequence of which the Paymaster dates the Accounts of those Regiments, and cei^ tifies to the King the Amount of the full Pay of such Regiments, according to the Establishment (provided no Respite is directed) for the Time specified in the Warrant, upon which Certificate the King's Warrants are obtained for the full Pay of the Regiments, if there is no Respite; and the Paymaster applies to the Treasury >

for

for the Sums due for Clearings, and upon receiving the m. Notice is given, and they are paid to the Agents of the respective Regiments.

The Sums for these several Services are asked of the Treasury, received, and paid, in the same Manner, by the Paymaster, whilst he is in Office.

It is the Practice of the Office to introduce the Annual Receipts and Payments of the Deputy Paymaster, for Extraordinaries, into the Paymaster General's Account for that Year, which Account is font t o the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest: but Mr. Peter Taylor and Mr. Robert Paris Taylor, who were Two of Lord Holland's Deputies, did, as he is informed and believes, at Lord Holland's Request, make up their own Accounts themselves, and fend them to the Auditor's Office, for their immediate Examination; Lord Holland suggesting, that it would be for his own Advantage, as well as that of the Public, to have those Accounts, which were very voluminous, and contained a great Expenditure, settled and adjusted as speedily as possible, that in case any Articles weredifallovved or questioned by the Auditor, MeflYs. Taylors, and their Assistants, might have then an Opportunity of explaining the m; had they been inlertod into the Annual Accounts, in the usual Manner, these Persons might have been either dead or absentat the Time these Accounts came in course under the Examination of the Auditor.

The Deputy Paymasters are subject to the Contronl of the Paymaster General; they are inflruCled to fend their Accounts to the Office by every Opportunity that offers, and he may call upon them to account whenever he pleases.

N* 4.

The Examination of Charles Bembridge, Esquire, Accountant to the Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 20th and 22d of March 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he carries on and makes Up the Accounts of the Paymasters, after they are out of Office, as well as those of the Paymaster in Office.

The only Obstacle to the final Adjustment of the late Lord Holland's Account, is a Dispute relative to the Balance in the Hands of Mr. Paris Taylor, who was one of his Deputies.

The Accounts of the Paymaster General are sent from the Pay Office to the Office of the Auditor of the Im-prest, with near all the Payments inserted, which have at that Time come to the Knowledge of the Office, and the Vouchers for them; after the Auditor has examined them, if any Doubts arise, he fends to the Pay Office an Account of the Queries he makes; if any of these Queries are not answered to his Satisfaction, he fur-charges the Paymaster with the Amount of them, and returns the Account to the Pay Office, who add the Charge, and such Articles of the Discharge as were not before inserted; it is then sent again to the Auditor's Office for Examination, after which the Pay Office adds the Totals, and strikes the Balance.

The final Accounts of Mr. Charles Townshend, and of Lord North and Mr. Cooke, and of Mr. Cooke and Mr. Thomas Townshend, have been sent from the Pay Office to the Auditor's Office, with their several Vouchers; none of them have yet been returned back to the Pay Office, nor any Queries sent thither relative thereto.

The Balances in the Hands of these Three late Pay-mailers are still subject to some Claims upon several Heads of Services, and likewise to the Payment of Fees of divers Natures, and of passing their final Accounts, and of obtaining their Quietus, and to the Payment of the usual Gratuity to the Officers of the Pay Office for carrying on and making up these Accounts.

He knows of no Objection to making up and passing the Accounts of a subsequent Paymaster, though his Predecefior's are not finished,

Bembridge.

Guy Carleton,

T. Anguish,

Bichd Neave,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond.

N*5.

Half a Year, from the 25th of December 1764 to the 24th of June 1765, was delivered into the Office of Lord Sondes, on the nth of January 1772. The Reason why this Account is not yet doled, is, that it came from the Pay Office to the Auditor's Office imperfect, with Blanks: That since it came in Articles have at several Times been added, by the Pay Office, both to the Charge and Discharge: That the greatest Part of this Account has been examined and ingrossed; but there are still some Blanks left, which must be filled up before it can be completely closed: He has several Times applied to the Pay Office to complete this Account, but it is not yet done: Were they to fend it into the Office correct and complete, with the Balance ascertained, it would probably be ready for Declaration within Three Months afterwards. It is the usual and most regular Method in the Office, not to finish one Pay mailer's Account until those of his Predecessors are closed. This Mode is not absolutely necessary; for though the Annual Payments, by successivePaytnaliers, follow each other in Order of Time, and should regularly be examined in the Order in which they are made, yet they are not so connected with each other, as to prevent the passing of a subsequent Paymaster's Account before that of his Predecessor's.

The Balance declared, upon a final Account, to be due from the Paymaster, is usually directed by the King's Warrant to be paid to his Successor.

It appears, from the Books of the Office, that Mr: Charles Toxcnjhend's final Account, from the 25th of

December 1765 to the 24th of June 1766, was delivered into the Office of Lord Sondes on the 12th of 1777; and that the final Account of Lord North and Mr. Cooke, from the 25th of December 1766 to the 24th of December 1767, was delivered into the same Office on the 30th of October 1779.

These Two Accounts are not yet perfect, neither the Charges nor Discharges are completed; but Mr. -Jhend's Account is under Examination.

When an Account is ready for doling, he returns the Book of Accounts to the Pay Office, and desires them to complete it; upon receiving it back again, he examines the Articles that are added, and if both Offices agree in the Balance, the Account is closed- It is not in his Power to form any Judgment within what Time these Accounts will be ready for Declaration, as it does not depend upon the Office of the Auditor.

The Paymasters fend their Accounts to the Auditor's Office at such Times as they think proper; after they are delivered in, they lie open at the Office, for any Additions that may be made to them, at any Time, until they are closed.

The Auditor has no Power of compelling Accountants to deliver in their Accounts for Examination.

John Lloyd.

Guy Carleton,

T. Anguish,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond.

The Witness further said, That no Inconvenience Could arise by establ idling Three Standards by Law in this Country, asGoldis always fold pure by the Refiner, and never mixed; but that the Alloy is given separate and distinctto the Workmen by the Refiner.

And the Witness informed your Committee, That lie has often employed many Foreigners, who instructed his EnglijfiWorkmen in their Business; but thqt he has

known feme English Workmen as able as any of other

The Witness said, That he had been often under the Necessity of refilling many large Orders, because he was forbidden by Law, to make Work of the Standards that were fold'in Foreign Markets — That some of the said Orders came from France, some from Spain, and some from dilF.-rent Parts of America.

1 he Witness further informed your Committee, That different Persons in this Country had, notwithstanding the Laws now in being, made Work of Twenty Car-rats, and of'Eighteen Carrats fine; and that, in order to avoid t lie Penalties of the Statutes, they had fold the same as Metal, not daring to fell it as Gold; all which W< rk is always fold, without being either allayed or marked at Goldsmiths Hall.

That Work of Twenty Carrats fine had often been exported from this Country to France, under the Denomination of Metal, but had been fold in France, as being French Standard Gold.

And that different Kinds of Work made in this Country of Twenty Carrats fine (particularly Chains for Watches) had been preferred by the French to similar Kinds of Work made in their own Country, which shews the great Advantage the English would have, if they were allowed by Law to work Gold of a proper Standard.

The Witness added, That, if the Standard were lowered to that of -Geneva, the Exportation of Gold Wares to German})would be very considerable.

Mr. Thomas Jeffreys,

Mr. Mark Thome gay,

Mr. William Pickett, And

Mr. Andrew Hogg, being severally examined, confirmed all the principal Facts given in Evidence by Mr. Moriffet; and the said Witnesses agreed. That great Inconvenience arose to the Makers and Venders of Gold Wares in this Kingdom, from the great Multiplicity, as well as from the great Imperfection, of our Laws relative to this Branch of Business.

Mr. Thomas Jeffreys being further examined, said. That he was a Goldsmith and Shopkeeper in Cockfpnr Street; that his Customers had often objected to the English Gold Wares in respect to their Colour, Polish, Beauty in Point of Workmanship, and their extraordinary Price. That the great Weight of English Snuff Boxes, and other large Work, had been frequently objected to likewise. That it would be highly advantageous to the Persons concerned in vending, as well as to those concerned in manufacturing. Gold Wares, if the Prayer of the Goldsmiths Petition were complied with by Parliament.

Mr. Mark Thomegay, of Moor fields, being further examined, said, That he was a Working Goldsmith, and that some Years ago the Goldsmiths Company had relaxed in inflicting the Penalties incurred by making Gold Wares of an inferior Quality to the Standard of Twenty-two Carrats, at which Time his Father carried on a very considerable Trade in Gold Manufactures of Twenty Carrats fine to Foreign Parts; but, the Cora-20

pany having enforced the Laws against this Practice, his Father was obliged to decline a Branch of Business very profitable to himself as well as beneficial to this Kingdom.

The Witness informed your Committee, that Three Ounces of Eighteen Carrat Gold will go about as far, in manufacturing Gold Wares, as Four Ounces, or Four Ounces and One Quarter, of Gold of Twenty-two Carrats fine.

That the Manufacturers of Gold Wares in this Country with to have, not only a Standard of Eighteen Carrats fine, but also to have a Standard of Twenty Carrats fine; because Gold of Eighteen Carrats Standard, will not fell in France where the legal Standard is Twenty Carrats fine.

And that the Manufacturers of Gold Wares in this Country wish to have, besides the Standards of Eighteen Carrats and of Twenty Carrats, also, the present Standard of Twenty-two Carrats fine; inafmueh as Gold of Twenty-two Carrats fine is better adapted to enamelled Work and chafed Work, than Gold of any inferior Standard.

The Witness informed your Committee, That the Manufacturers are permitted by Law in this Kingdom, to work Gold in the Jewellers, and some other Branches of Business, of an inferior Quality to English Standard; and that in consequence, a very great Quantity of such Sort of Work is exported from this Country; but that in those Branches of the Goldsmith's Business, where the-English Workmen are obliged to make Use of Twenty-two Carrat Gold, there is little or no Work made for Exportation.

That he had been informed by his Correspondents in Holland, that they send to Paris instead of fending to England to purchase Gold Manufactures, on Account of the extraordinary Price of those made in England, which the Witness imputes entirely to the Difference between the Standards of this and of Foreign. Countries.

The Witness further said, That it was genera'ly reckoned that in making, polishing, and finishing of Gold Wares of Twenty-two Carrats fine, about Two Penny Weights of Gold were unavoidably wasted in -every Ounce; but that not more than One Penny Weight of Gold was wasted in every Ounce in the making, polishing, and finishing Gold of Eighteen Carrats fine.

That in many Cafes, the Labour of finishing and polishing Gold of the English Standard of Twenty-two Carrats was near Twice as great as the Labour of finishing and polishing Gold of the Geneva Standard.

Mr. William Pickett was then further examined, and said. That he was a Goldsmith and Shopkeeper upon. LudgateHill; that there are at present, in this Country, Two Standards, for Silver, the one of Eleven Ounces and Ten Penny Weights of fine Silver in the Pound Troy, which Silver is marked at the Hall with a Britannia; and the other Standard of Eleven Ounces and Two Penny Weights of fine Silver in the Pound Troy, which Silver is marked at the Hall with a Lion.

That little Silver, except of the inferior Standard, is manufactured in this Country; which proceeds from the Lion Silver being cheaper, harder, and more durable, than the Silver of an higher Standard; in like Manner as the Eighteen Carrat Gold is cheaper, harder, and more durable than Gold of a superior Standard.

And that the Lion Silver in this Country, is rather of an inferior Standard to the Silver manufactured in

France; that therefore, the Manufacturers of Silver in this Country, labouring under no Disadvantage in that Respect, have arrived to a greater Degree of Excellence, and have carried the Manufacture of Silver in this Kingdom to a greater Degree of Perfection than if is carried at Paris. And that English Silver Plate has a

great

a i Geo. III. 9 Aprilii397

great Preference in the Foreign Markets; which the Witness further fays, would also be the same with respect to the Gobi Manufactures of this Country, if the Goldsmiths were permitted here to manufacture Gold of Twenty and of Eighteen Carrats fine.

Mr . GedeonMacaire being examined, laid, That he

'was a Native of Geneva, and had been established in this Metropolis these Six Years last past, and that he was, by Prufellion, a Watch-case-maker.

That he was well acquainted with the Standards of France and Geneva; that the Standard of Geneva, for the Manufacture of Gold Wares, is Eighteen Carrats fine; but that the Standard for the Gold Coin of Geneva is Twenty-one Carrats fine — That the Standard of Paris, for the Manufacture of Gold Wares, is Twenty Carrats fine; but that the Standard for the Gold Coin in France, is Twenty-one Carrats and Three Quarters fine; but there being One Quarter of a Car-rat allowed in France to the Manufacturer of Gold Coin, for the Expence of Coinage, the Standard of the Gold Coin in France Hands nominally at Twenty-two Carrats fine.

This Witness further said, That he has been very conversant in working Gold of Eighteen Carrats fine; and that the Waste of Gold in iinishing and polishing of Work of Eighteen Carrats, is not above Half of what the Wade is in finishing and polishing of Gold of the EnglishStandard. And that in regard to the La-

bour in limilar Kinds of Work, it is not so great by One-third (and in some Cafes not so great by One-half) in the Eighteen Carrat Gold, as it is in thp Gold of the established Standard of this Kingdom.

Skppjy A Petition of the Commissioners acting under the and Hat kney Authority of an Act of Parliament, made and palfed Coun of in the Twenty-fourth Year of the Reign of his late Ed.©id. Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act 41 for the more ealy and fjpeedy Recovery of Small " Debts within The Totver Hamlets," and of several other Householders and luhabitants of the said Hamlets, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by the said Act, the said Commissioners are authorized to take Cognizance of any Debt under Forty Shillings, sued for in the Court of Requests for The Tower Hamlets; and that the Petitioners observe, by the Bill now depending, for diminishing the Fees payable, and altering the Mode of Proceeding, in the Court of Record within the Manors of Stepney and Hackney, in the County of Middlesex, the Hamlets and Liberties of the fame, the Powers thereby created are to extend to any Debt above Thirty-nine Shillings, not exceeding a certain Sum therein to be mentioned; and that the Jurisdiction of the said Court of Record is of the same Extent with the Jurisdiction of the said Court of Requests; and there are divers Clauses in the said Bill, which, if the same should pass into a Law, would not only interfere with the Powers of the said Court of Requests, but would be very prejudicial to the Inhabitants of the said Tozcer Hamlets in general; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that an extensive Credit to the lower Order of People would be attended with very mischievous Consequences, and particularly in the said Tower Hamlets, by reason of the numerous Manufacturers and labouring Poor residing in the fame, and that no Benefit can accrue to the Public, by extending the Powers of the said Court, held for the said Manors of Stepney and Hackney: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, or such Parts thereof as may be necessary; and that the same may not pass into a Law as it now (lands.

VOL. 38.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel; before the said Committee, upon their .'etition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time> in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Ordered, That all have Voices, who come to the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed.

Mr. Rolle reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for dividing, allotting, and inclosing, certain Moors, Commons, and Waste Lands, called Mark Moor, otherwise Thurll Moor, Mark Liberty Moor, otherwise Yonder Moor, and Foie Moors and Commons, situate within the Parish of Mark, in the County of Somerset, was committed; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Bills of Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true, and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee, and had also given their Consent to the adding of Two other Commissioners to the Bill (except the Owners of Common Rights, who consented, but would not sign the Bill; and also except the Owners of 6 Common Rights and an Half, who are under legal Disability; and also except the Owners of 143 Common Bights and Three Quarters, some of whom were not applied to, and others who, upon Application, could not be met with, or who were unknown; and also except the Owners of 39 Common Rights, who objected to the Inclosure; anil that the whole Number of Common Rights is 1,084, exclusive of the Lord of the Soil, and the Impropriator of the Tythes, and his Lessee, who have also signed their Consent; and thatno Person appeared before the Committee to oppose the Bill); and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

A Clause was ollered to be added to the Bill, declaring, that the Payments for Moor Metes shall not prejudice or asseft the Rights of any Person.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be m.ide Part of the Bill.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingross'ed.

Mr. Elzoes also reported from the said Select Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it being the Opinion of this Committee, That the Resolution of the 18 th 1661,

by which all the Inhabitants of the Borough of Preston are declared to have Voices in the Election, is a last Determination, within the meaning of the Act 2 Geo. II.: But, it being also the Opinion of the Committee, That such a Right of Election is too indefinite;

Resolved, That the Chairman be directed to move for Leave to bring in a Bill to ascertain the Description of Inhabitants who shall, for the future, have Voices in the Election; humbly recommending it to the House, that the Right be confined to all In-Burgesses resident, and to all other Inhabitants Householders, paying Scotland Lot.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon this Day Three Weeks, the First Day of May next.

Ordered, That the Minutes of the Proceedings, taken before the said Select Committee, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That the proper Officer or Officers do attend this House, upon this Day Three Weeks, the First Day of May next, with the Charters, Books, Polls, Returns, and other Papers, which were read in Evidence before the said Select Committee.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of One Million Nine hundred thousand Pounds be granted to His Majesty, for paying off and discharging the Exchequer Bills, made out by virtue of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for raising a further Sum of Money, by " Loans or Exchequer Bills for the Service of the Year - One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty," and charged upon the first Aids to be granted in this Session of Parliament

Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of an Act, made in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to " permit Goods, the Product or Manufacture of certain " Places within The Levant or Mediterranean Seas, to " be imported into Great Britain or Ireland in British " or Foreign Vessels, from any Place whatsoever; and " for laying a Duty on Cotton and Cotton Wool imported into this Kingdom in Foreign Ships or Vessels " for a limited Time," the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Goods the Product or Manufacture of certain Places within The Levant or Mediterranean Seas, be permitted to be imported into Great Britain or Ireland, in British ox Foreign Vessels, from any Place whatsoever, for a Time to be limiteJ.

Petitions A Petition of the Freeholders, Justices of Peace, resptding the and ConmnHioners of Supply, of the County of Forfar: Linen And also,

uu a urc. Petition of the Manufacturers and Dealers in Linen, in the Royal Burgh of Perth: And also,

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Dealers in Linen, in the Royal Borough of Dundee: And also,

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Linen Manufacturers in Dunfermline, in the County of Fife-,

Were severally preferred to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Linen Manufacture of Great Britain, upon which the Bread of many Thoul'ands of industrious Subjects depends, has been the coniiant Object of Parliamentary Pro-Vol. 38.

tection and Encouragement; and that His Majesty's Subjects in Ireland pay no Excile Duty upon Soap and Starch, Two Materials of Importance used in Bleaching; and that, by an Act, passed in the Parliament of Ireland, in the Third Year of His present Majesty, for the better Regulation of the Liuen and Hempen Manufactures, it is enacted, That no Duty whatsoever shall be paid upon the Importation of any Wood or Weed Allies, of any Kind, used in Bleaching, or any Blue called Smalts, pr any Oil of Vitriol, or any Black Soap; and that, by another Law* the Duty paid upon Importation of all Brimstone and Saltpetre used in making Oil of Vitriol, an essential Material in Bleaching, is, on the Oath of the Maker, to be drawn back; and that, by a Law passed in the last Irish Parliament, in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of His present Majesty's Reign, Bounties are granted on the Exportation of divers Species of Linen, the Fabric of Ireland, to Africa, America, Spain, Portugal, Gibraltar, and Minorca, in which Law, the Exception of Linen printed or stained, or made into Buckrams or Tilletings, whereby the same were excluded from the Bounty by the Act of the Twenty-ninth of George the Second, is entirely omitted; and that there is now no Market in the World in which the Manufacturers of Irish Linen will not be enabled by these several Encouragements, added to the natural Advantages of that Country, to undersell the British Manufacturer, and by these Means Ireland will in a short Time acquire the foie Benefit of this valuable Manufacture, unless it shall in both Countries be put upon an equal Footing: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Manufacturers of Britain into their most serious Consideration, and grant them such Relief as shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whoriC it is referred to consider of the State of the Linen Manufacture of Great Britain.

Sir,

Conscious that the most ardent Exertions of a British Subject to promote the Glory and Interest of his King and Country cannot obtain a more honourable Reward than the Thanks of a British House of Commons, I want Words to express how very fenlibly I feel the

distingnished Mark of Approbation with which that augull Assembly has been pleased to honour my Services.

W ere severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Linen Manufacture of Great Britain, upon which the Bread of many Thou lands of industrions Subjects depends, has been the constant Object of Parliamentary Protection and Encouragement; and that the Ex-fcife Duties upon Soap and Starch, Two Materials of Importance used in Bleaching, are now become a very considerable Charge on the British Bleacher, which His Majesty's Subjects in Ireland are not subjected to; and that, by an Act passed in the Parliament of in the

' Third Year of His present Majesty, for the better Regulation of the Linen and Hempen Manufactures, it is enacted, That no Duty whatsoever shall be paid on the Importation of any Wood or Weed Allies of any Kind, used in Bleaching, or any Blue called Smalts, or any Oil of Vitriol, or any Black Soap; and that, by other Laws puffed in the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, Seventeenth and Eighteenth Years of His present Majesty's Reign, the Duty paid upon Importation of all Brimftoneand Saltpetre used in making Oil of Vitriol, an essential Material in Bleaching, is, on the Oath of the Maker, to be drawn back; and that, by a Law palfed in the lall Irish Parliament, in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of His present Majesty's Reign, for granting Bounties on the Export of certain Species of Linen and Hempen Manufactures, Bounties are granted on the Exportation of divers Species of Linen, the Fabric of,

to Africa, America, Spain, Portugal, and Minorca, in which Law the Exception of Linens printed or stained, or made into Buckrams and Tilletings, whereby the same are excluded from a Bounty by the Act of the

Twenty-ninth of George the Second, is entirely omitted; and that, by Means of these several Encouragements granted by the Parliament, luperadded to the natural Advantages of that Kingdom in Point of Situation, and being subjected to fewer Taxes than His Majesty's British Subjects, it is evident that the Manufacturers of Irish Linens will be enabled to undersell the British Manufacturers in every Foreign Market, unless both Countries are put on an equal Footing; and the Petitioners, at the same Time that they feel the Propriety of praying for an Exemption from the Duties on Bleaching Materials, sincerely lament the disagreeable Necessity they are laid under of applying for a Bounty on Linens, printed or stained, or made into Buckrams and Tilletings, a Manufacture which, they apprehend, might have been supported without the Aid of a Bounty, but, whilst the Irish enjoy a Bounty on that Species of Linens, it is obvious the British Manufactures cannot compete with those of the Sifter Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take their same into the most lerious Consideration, and grant them l'uch Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of John Savage was prefeinted to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner, being a Native of Germany, and having served Forty Years in Military Service, was employed, about the latter End of the Year 1775, by the Right honourable Lord North and other British Ministers, to go over to Germany, to raile Recruits for the Serviceof His Majesty; and belkies pecuniary Recompense, was tojbe rewarded With aCommission of Major in the Army, and to have the foie Benefit that might arise from the said Recruiting Service in Germany; and that, in order to perform the said Service, the Petit ioner disposed of all his Eflefts, embarked for Germany, and entered upon the Lid Service, and, from his Connections and Interest at the Courts of several Princes, and great Industry, in the space of Two Months, raised near Fifteen hundred Recruits; and that the Petitioner, having passed into Hanover, to his great Surprize, found that General Fawe Hi and aColonel Sdieider were also employed by the

16

Ministers on the same Service, contrary to the express Agreement with the Petitioner; but, notwithstanding such Breach of Faith, the Petitioner, with unwearied Diligence, proceeded in the same Service, and obtained Leave to recruit in those Dominions, when the said General Fawcitt, and Colonel Scheider could not; and the Petitioner thereupon received the Approbation of General Fawcitt, and Leave was after-Wards given to the said General Fawcitt and Colonel Scheider to recruit also; and that the Petitioner having, at a great Expence, brought above Seven Hundred of his Recruits to The Rhine, and being utiable, without some Remittance, to transport them to England, applied to Sir Joseph Yorke, His Majesty's Ambafiadoc at The Hague, for Assistance, and also to the King's Ministers in and the said

Sir Joseph Yorke also informed His Majesty's Ministers of the fame, and sent proper Proofs of the Men being ready, but without Eflect; and that the Petitioner remained upwards of Two Months without kny Orders or Support, and, having so many Men to maintain, was reduced to the lowest Extremity; and that, during this Time, Colonel Scheider received the Recruits of the Petitioner, and fentmany of them over to England, with the Clothing the Petitioner had given them; and that the Petitioner at length, by the Advice of Sir Joseph Yorke, embarked for Harwich, with Twelve of the Men, and then applied to the King's Ministers to know the Cause of such Neglect and Treatment, and desired that proper Officers might be sent back with him to bring over the Seven Hundred Men then waiting; but the Petitioner was answered, that the Recruits were not wanted, Government having sent Orders to engage the Regular Forces of Hefje and Brunfunck; in this Situation the ‘Petitioner hoped that the Exigences he had been put to, on Account of the said Service, would have been repaid him, and that he should be promoted to the Rank of Major, agreeable to the Promise given to him before he entered on the same Service; but the Petitioner was put Off from 'Time to Time, and ‘fent'front Office to Office, without 'Effect; and that, on the 20th of March 1776, the Petitioner offered his Service, and was ordered by Lord North and Mr. Robinson to attend General Burgoyne, then going to America, to command a Van-Guard of the German Recruits raised by the Petitioner, and sent over by Colonel Scheider (and who were dissatisfied that the Petitioner was not with them, os the Petitioner had promised); and the Petitioner set out immediately for Porlfmoulh, and embarked in a few' Days by Order of General Burgoyne; and that, upon the Petitioner's Arrival at the Army in America, near Fort Saint John, without any previous Notice or Complaint, and for no Cause whatever, as he knows, or can imagine, the Petitioner was put under an Arrest by Order of General Carlelon, and kept a Prisoner at MontrealYYnee Weeks, and afterwards at Quebec aFortnight, and' sent for England without Supply of Provisions for Support in the Voyage; and that the Petitioner, upon his Arrival in England his Complaint

before Lord North and other Ministers, but without Redress, till at the Distance of Nine Months, when the Petitioner received^. 20 by Order of Lord North, with a Promise that he should be provided for; and that, having no Means of Support, and having contracted Debts during a long and fruitless Attendance upon Ministers, the Petitioner was arrested for a small Debt; and whilst he was under the said Arrest, Mr. White, Partner with the Solicitor of the Treasury, informed the Petitioner, that he had Orders from Lord to pay the Debt and Costs, and to furnish the Petitioner with Money, to enable him to go off for and when

there, that he should receive £. 100; and the Petitioner, not suspicious of any improper Dealing, and intending to obtain Certificates of his Services and Expences on the Recruiting Service, went accordingly to Rotterdam, where he was directed to wait upon Mr. Irvine the Agent, to receive the £. 100; but the Petitioner,

tioner, finding that the Agent was at The Hague, set out accordingly, and, on his Arrival, was flopped by one of his Recruiting Officers just before he entered the Hotel of Sir Joseph Yorke (where Mr. Irvine then was) upon a Debt of £.30 due to the said Officer for the said Recruiting Service, and which said Officer then waited with Process to arrest the Petitioner: and that the Petitioner prevailed on the said Officer to wait till hecduld go Into the House and receive the Money from Mr. Irvine; and tfiat, upon the Petitioner's applying to ‘ Mr. Irvine for the Money, to his great Astonishment he was informed by Mr. Irvine, that, before the Money was paid the Petitioner must sign a Paper agreeable to Instructions from Lord North, which Paper was shewn to the Petitioner, and is as followeth: "I underwritten,

" commonly called Captain John Savage, hereby acknowledge to have received of Robert Irvine, His 4( Bi'itannic Majesty's Agent residing here, One hundred Pounds Sterling; and the Conditions on which I have received said Sum expressly are, that I oblige myself not to return again to England, nor to make any fur-'* & ther Claim or Demands upon Government, or be any " wife troublesome thereto; which Conditions I hereby oblige myself to fulfil, as Witness my Hand to du- plicate Receipt of like Tenor and Date at Rotterdam this 5th Day of July 1777*" and that the Petitioner remonfirated to the said Mr. Irvine against the fame, as cruel and oppressive, and as a Fraud upon the Petitioner, and calculated to deprive him of his just Claims, but was answered, that the same was done by Orders from Lord North, and that, unless the Petitioner figued the fame, the£. 100 would not be paid to him, at the same Time expressing his Concern that he was obliged to exact the fame; and that the Petitioner, being so ffiftreffed, without Money in his Pocket, a Creditor and Bailiff at the Door to arrest him, the Prospect of a Gaol, and perishing through Want, all which the Petitioner ifold to the said Mr. Irvine, yet the Petitioner was compelled to sign the said Paper, and thereupon receiving the laid£. 100 paid the £. 30 to preserve his Liberty;

: and that the Petitioner, intending to lay his Grievances and Claims before this honourable House, set out for Germany to obtain proper Certificates thereof, and, being arrived at Coblenlz, was put under Arrest by Mandate from the Emperor, and was doomed to Imprisonment for Life, for having drawn the Subjects of those Dominions to become Recruits for the Army of Great Britain; and that the Petitioner was at the same Time informed he had been advertised to be apprehended on that account in the German and other Foreign Papers, many Months before (and whilst he was in America) which Papers are read in this Kingdom, and the same must have been known at the Court of London long before the Petitioner was directed by Mr. White to go into Hollands and that, whilst under the Horrors of a Sentence of close Imprisonment for Life, and about to be removed to the Castleof Coblentz, by the humane Stratagem of a Friend and Brother Officer, the Petitioner made his Escape, and by the generous Afirftance of that ' Friend was enabled to return to this Kingdom to seek i Redress: and that as soon as the Petitioner arrived he was arrested by his Creditors for small Debts contracted during his long Solicitations to the Treasury for the , Reward of his Services, and, being unable to pay them, was confined in the King's Bench Prison, until he took the Benefit of the last Insolvent A&, and obtained his 1 Discharge; and that the Petitioner hath presented several Petitions, Memorials, and Remonstrances to His Majesty and His Majesty's Ministers for Redress, but i without Effect, and is now in the greatest Distress, and l unable to support himself, having expended every Farthing of his own Property, and exposed himself to ! the Dangers, Difficulties, and Sufferings above-mention-1 ed, in performing the said Services for His Majesty the '<l King of Great Britain; and that the Petitioner presumes J the Right honourable the Earl of HilsborourL Lord \ VOL. 38.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the respective Bounties on Plain British and Irish Linen, granted by an Act, passed in the Twenty-ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, and continued by several subsequent Statutes, be extended to British and Irish Linen, printed or stained in Great Britain, and to Buckrams or Tilletings.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Wood and Weed-Allies, Pot and Pearl-Aihps,

thock :And also,

A Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and Dealers in Linen, in the Royal Borough of Brecbine;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Linen Manufacture of Great Britain lies under certain disad van tageous Circumstances, which, if not speedily remedied, cannot fail of producing fatal Consequences to it; and that the Petitioners saw with Pleasure that Spirit of Liberality and Humanity, which framed Lawsfofalutary to the Commerceof their Fellow Subjects in Ireland; but, while they expresstheirentire Approbation of these Measures, they cannot but observe, that they esteem it essential to the very Existence of the Linen Manufacture here, that it be put on no worse Terms than that of Ireland; and beg Leave to mention certain Particulars in which the Subjects of Ireland have the Advantage: First, That by

an Act, passed in the last Irish Parliament, in the Nineteenth and Twentieth Years of His present Majesty's Reign, Bounties are granted upon the Exportation of different Kinds of Linen, the Fabric of , to , America, Spain, Portugal, , and Minorca;

and, by the British Act of the Twenty-ninth of George the Second, Linens printed or iiained, or made into Buckrams or Tilletings, are ex* eluded from the Bounty; but this Exception from the Bounty is altogether omitted in the Irish Act: Secondly, The Subjects of Ireland pay no Excise Duty upon Soap and Starch, Two Materials of Importance ul'ed in Bleaching: Thirdly, That by an Act of the Parliament of Ireland, in the Third Year of His present Majesty, for the better Regulation of the Linen and Hempen Manufactures, it is enacted, That no Duty whatever be exacted upon the Importation of any Weed or Wood Allies, or Allies of any Kind, or any Blue called or any Oil

of \ itriol, or any Black Soap: And Fourthly, I. That by another Law', the Duty paid upon Importation of all Brimstone and Saltpetre used in making Oil of Vitriol, an effV-ntial Material in Bleaching, is, on the Oath of the Maker, to be drawn back; and that the Subjects of Ireland enjoy many natural Advantages over the tish Manufacturers, besides these immediately pointed out, and both joined together, mult infallibly enable them to undersell the in all Foreign Markets, the Consequence of which will be, that the Linen Manufacture of Britain will gradually decline, and go to Ruin, and the numerous induffrious Subjects, who were supported by it, will be thrown into Idleness and Misery: Aud therefore praying the House to take this important Matter into Consideration, and frame such Regulations as will most effectually tend to prevent the Evils dreaded by the Petitioners.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of Thomas De la Mayne, Esquire, and Preventing Thomas Greafer, Gentleman, Proprietors of Car life Profanations

House, was presented to the House, and read; Setting 0 Suufcy. forth. That, from a general Regret amongst the genteel Class of People, that there was not any Place of polite Resort within this Metropolis, where Conversation and Exercise might hje united in a general Society on Sunday Evenings after Divine Service, without subjecting Persons of a foperior Rank to mix with inferior Orders of the People in Tea Houses, and such other public Places as from want of such a Place of polite Resort, they were frequently tempted to employ their Evening's Leisure in private Assemblies, where Play, Music, and Drinking, were too frequently introduced; the Petitioners, at aii Expence of not let's than 4,00a, fitted up and opened a large Suite of Rooms at Car life House with the greatest Elegance, after the Plan of the Bath Rooms, and other Places of the Kingdom, as a Promenade for Sunday Evenings, or a Place of Exercise and Society, which was immediately, and continues 10 be visited and frequented by the first Nobility of both Sexes, the Clergy,

Justices of the Peace, and other respectable Characters>; and that, in framing the Plan thereof, the Petitioners were guided in every Part by the ftritieft Attention to the Rules of Decency and good Order; that they admitted no Singing or Music whatsoever, Dancing, or any Kind of Pkty or Gaming, nor any Drinking of Wines, Beer, or Spirituous Liquors, nor any Kind of Exhibitions, Tranl'parent or Moving Pictures, nor De-batings of any Kind whatsoever; that they never opened their Doors till after the Evening's Services and Lectures of the Church were over, and the Company always retired footo lifter Eleven o'Clock, and the Doors were font before Twelve; nevertheless the Petitioners have Reason to believe that several false Reports have been let forth, in Misrepresentation of the said Place, by Persons envious of the very succeseful Reception it met with in the Approbation of the Public; and that, if feme few Persons of light Behaviour foroetimes appeared in the Rooms, they have been font with a Design to throw a temporary Blemish on the Institution, and their final! Number, multiplied in Idea, being more conspii-cuous, as in Contrail to every other Part of the Aflerm-bly, yet, from the w&tcbful Attention the Proprietors have ever paid to their Duty, and Honour to the Public, every such improper Object has been with all possible Care refused Admittance; and from this EmbarralT- ‘ ment to improper Admifitons, and every other attentive Regard to Decency and good Order, the original In-ilitution has given Proof of its Merit, in becoming a Recreation useful to Society, where Innocence, Tftfte, and Politenefe, can engage Yifitors; and that, for the above Reason and ' .'onsideration, the Petitioners hope, the decent and virtuous Institlition of the Promenade may not be included nothin, the Bilbuow depending, for; 5 preventing

A Petition of the Sugar Refiners of the City of duties on Bi'iftol, was prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting nzc u*ar## forth, That the Petitioners have laboured, for some*

Years past, under the Disadvantage of a losing and ruinous Trade, on which Account many of them, who were concerned in large and extensive Manufactories rrt the said City, have been obliged to discontinue the fame, and some of the principal of them have shut up their Houses, which cost from Eight to Ten thousand Pounds each in erecting, whillt others have found themselves under the disagreeable Necessity of lessening their Business considerably; and that the Loss of the captured Islands, together with the late dreadful Hurricanes in The West Indies, and the great Rilque of Navigation in Times of War, mull necessarily lessen the ensuing Imports; and from these unavoidable Consequences the Petitioners labour under much greater Disadvantages than the Refiners of other Kingdoms, as all Sugars captured by the Enemy go in Aid to the Foreign Manufacturers, whilst all those captured by British Ships are obliged to be sold for Foreign Markets: And the Petitioners therefore hope, That the House will take into their Consideration a Petition lately presented by the Sugar Refiners of Ijondony praying for Leave to use Prize Sugars in their Manufactories, and, if it shall seem meet to the House, to grant this Liberty, subject to itich moderate Duties only as will enable them to work such Sugars, the Petitioners think it will greatly tend to relieve them from the great Disadvantages and Inconveniencies under which they at present Labour.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee to whom the Petition of the Sugar Refiners of London is referred.

A Petition of the Grocers of London was presented to Duties on the House, and read; Setting forth, That a principal *r,ze Sup*-Part of the Petitioners Trade consists in buying and selling of Raw and Refined Sugar; and that, during the Four last Years, the Quantity of Sugar annually imported hath fallen greatly lliort of what is necessary for the Consumption of this Kingdom, and, in Consequence thereof, the Trade of the Petitioners hath been diminished, at the same Time that a larger Capital became necessary to carry it on, and whilst its Extent and its fair Profits were exceedingly reduced, the unavoidable Risks to which they are exposed, were augmented in a con-fideiable Degree; and the Petitioners, therefore, have seen with Concern the several Prize Cargoes of the *

Sugars of the Enemy, which have from Time to Time been brought into this Kingdom, carried away from our Ports for the Use of Foreign Markets, whilst the Trade of the Petitioners hath been almost at a Stand for Want of a Supply;, and they are apprehensive that a large Proportion of the British Plantation Sugars will, during the ensuing Season, be consigned to Ireland in Consequence of the Privilege that Kingdom will, during several Months, enjoy of importing Sugar at a much lower Duty than must be paid here; and that the Scarcity of Refined Sugar has been such, at several Periods during the last Four Years, that much of the Petitioners Time hath been taken up, and often to no Purpose, in endeavouring to purchase such Sugars as were necessary for their Trade; and representing to the House, that the Sugars of Grenada, great Part of which are the Property of English Subjects residing here, are now sold at Foreign Markets on Behalf of such English Proprietors, and no Means have yet been devised to compensate to the Sugar Trade of this Kingdom that and the other heavy Losses it has sustained; and that British Plantation Sugar being allowed Drawbacks on Exportation equivalent to the Whole of the Duties which were paid on Importation, and, in Consequence of this Allowance, the Drawback now allowed on Mtfcovado Sugar being almost Twelve Shillings per Hundred Weight, and the Drawback on Refined Sugar being Twenty-six Shillings perHundredWeight, and the

Petitioners being well informed that, in Consequence of those Drawbacks, very large Contracts for Refined Sugar for Exportation have been offered at enormous Prices, they are exceedingly alarmed, and pray the House to take into Consideration the Danger which the Petitioners conceive does manifestly exist; and that, in the present State of the Sugar Trade of Europe, at a Time when the Dutch have loft a principal Part of their Supply, and as it is probable that the French cannot get Home the Produce of their Plantations, the Demand on this Market will be so extensive, that the Public will be much inconvenienced; and the Trade of the Petitioners greatly injured: And therefore praying for a Bill to . 6 A allow

458 11° M A, 1781.

allow the Prize Sugars to be entered for Home Gon-fumption under moderate Duties, or for such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table; until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Sugar Refiners of London is referred.

Mr. William Montague, principal Clerk in the Chamberlain's Office, being then examined, said. That the whole of the said Money was borrowed by virtue of the said Acts, and has been duly and regularly applied in the several Works and Purposes thereby directed to be done.

George Dance, Esquire, the Surveyor for the City of London, beingexamined, said, Thatin the Month of 1780, the Gaol of Neicgale was so nearly completed, that nothing was wanting in it but a few Locks and some Furniture; that in June following it was rendered totally unfit for the Purposes of a Prison, by a riotous and unlawful Assembly of People; that the Floors and Roofs were all burnt and destroyed, and the Walls very much damaged; that he bad examined the State of- the Building lately, and had taken an Account of what may be the probable Expence of repairing and rein-stating the Gaol; and that, in his Opinion, to do the same completely, and provide for all Expences, it will require the Sum of Thirty thousand Pounds; that in this he includes the Keeper's House, which is a Part of the said Gaol, and was damaged very greatly at-the same Time with the rest of the Building.

Mr. Richard Akerman, being then examined, said. He had been the Keeper of the Gaol of Twenty-

eight Years; that before it was rebuilt, and from thence to the Time when it was so much damaged, about a Thousand Prisoners were committed to it annually, on an Average; that the greater Part of them were from the County of Middlesex, probably Two-thirds at the least; and that Prisoners were lent there by both Houses of Parliament, and from all Parts of the Kingdom.

Mr. Dance being again examined, said, That the Gaol of Newgate is not in its present State fit for the ‘urposes for which it was intended; and that it will be /dangerous and prejudicial to the City of Iwndon aid the Public, if it is not immediately repaired and made secure for the Confinement of Prisoners.

Mr. Akerman being again examined, confirmed the last Evidence given by Mr.; and added, That

many Prisoners lately escaped from other Gaols, where they were kept, because Newgate was not in a State to receive them.

'.Mail 453

Mr. Dance being further examined, said, that since the said Gaol was demolished, the City of London have proceeded to refit the Apartments for the Reception of Prisoners, on which they have expended between Four and Five thonfund Pounds, although they have not, as he believes, any Fund applicable to that Purpose.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Philfips's Sir Gilbert Elliot reported from the Committee, to pomposition whom the Petition of Henry , of Knightsbridge,

*?:*Wng *n the County of Middlesex, was referred; That the Committeehad examined the Matter of the said Petition;and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Christopher Pinchbeck being examined, informed Your Committee, That Ive is a Member of the Society for Encouragement of Arts and Sciences, and attends con-flantly, particularly in Committees of Agriculture, in which he has seen repeated Experiments of Mr. Phillips's Powder upon Ants, but more particularly on the 8th of January 1776, when the Experiment gave entire Satisfaction. The Method pursued in this Experiment, was putting a Quantity of Ants alive upon a Sheet of Paper, and then throwing the Powder over them, when they immediately began to be convulsed, and in less than an Hour almost every one was dead. In Consequence of this Experiment, and many others, the Committee have made several Reports to the Society in Favour of Mr. Phillipss Powder.

Your Committee then called Mr. Samuel Moore, Secretary to the said Society; who produced a Book, containing the Proceedings of the Committees of Agriculture and Chemistry, from which it appeared, that those Committees, in Consequence of References from the Society, had examined at several different Times the Testimonies offered by Mr. Phillips in Favour of his Powder, and had likewise made several Experiments themselves, upon which they had made several Reports, and came to several Resolutions; Extracts whereof are hereunto annexed, by way of Appendix, N* 1.

Copy of a Petition offinrry Phillips to the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, dated zSth July 1777, together with the Minutes and Certificate of the Commissioners at , dated 9th anil 10th

September 1776, reflecting the Efficacy of the Powder, upon the Cane Ants, was laid before Your Committee; and is hereunto annexed in the Appendix, N* 2: And also,

Copy of Letter from Mr. Cumberland to Mr. Ro-binfon. Secretary to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, dated 8th August 17 77, is also annexed in the Appendix, N° 3.

Your Committee then proceeded to examine Daniel Grimwood; who informed them, That he is Nurseryman at Chelsea, and has made several Experiments of Mr.

Phillips's Powder; particularly in the Year 17 77, he had VoL. 38.

some Peas which were infectert by the Weevil, and by applying Mr. Phillips's Powder to them, he found in about the Space of a Week it entirely eradicated the Weevil, and the Peas were not infected again for the Space of Nine Mouths, at which Time he parted with them — >That he tried the Powder again, by way of Prevention; he put into an empty Sack about Two Handfuls of the Powder, he then put a Bnfiiel of Peas into the Sack, which forced the Powder upwards, and covered every Part of the Sack with it; he then filled the Sack with Peas, which remained in it for Six Months, and were not at all affected by the Weevils — others, that had not the Powder, and which were kept in the same Place, and in the same Manner, were infected- — That he has also tried the Powder upon some blighted Trees, where it has destroyed all the Infects on the blighted Parts, in the Space of a very few Hours; whenever he has any Trees that are particularly infected by Infects, he always uses the Powder, considering it a sovereign Remedy, and he never found it of any Prejudice to the Fruit upon which it has been applied — That lie has also tried it on various Sorts of Plants, which have been infected with divers Sorts of Infects, in which it has had the same Effect; and is found very efficacious in preventing the Snails and Slugs from eating the Fruit: And fays, that he had applied a little of the Powder on a Snail, and found it killed it almost instantaneously — That he knows of no Remedy against Blights or Infects, so effectual as Mr. Phillips's Powder. Some of the Experiments alluded. to were made last Year; he has had no blighted Trees this Season.

Mr. James Malcolm, being then examined, said, He is a Nurseryman at Kensington — That he has seen various Experiments made of Mr. s Powder; in the

Y-ear 1779, the Experiment was made upon a Quarter of young Cherry Trees, to the Amount of Three or Four Thousand, the much greater Part of which were blighted so bad, that all Hqpes were given over of recovering them, and by applying Mr. Powder to

them, in a very short Time the Blight was very considerably lessened, and the Trees began to grow, and by a Repetition of the Powder,'in the Space of Three Weeks Time, the whole Quarter were perfectly recovered — That he has found the Powder to be also effectual when applied to train Trees, on Walls or Paling, and very effectual in removing of Blights — That he never found any Remedy against Blights or Infects so efficacious as this Powder. Since the Beginning of April 1777, they have had Ninety Barrels of Mr.

Phillips'sPowder, of which Fifty-four were sold to Customers, and the rest used by themselves.

Mr. Thomas Allen, being then examined, said. He is a Gardener at Brompton — That he has tried Mr. Phillips's Powder for Four Years successively, and found it always answered in Cafes of Blights, particularly on Fruit Trees against Walls, and never knew of any Remedy so effectual against Blights — That he has lately tried the Powder on black Ants, which infect Houses, and are the hardest of all Ants to kill, and has found it totally destroyed them in the Course of Three or Four Hours; and has likewise tried it on Fleas and Bugs with the fante-Success.

Mr. William Cotes, being examined, said. He is a Gardener at Mr. Hewit'sNurfery at Brompton, and has tried Mr. Phillips's Powder for several Years together, on Fruit Trees, and found it of very great Service in Cafes of Blight, and in killing Pifmires and red Spiders in Hot-houses, and of great Use in destroying Caterpillars, Slugs, and such like Infects.

John Peachey, Esquire, a Member of the House, informed Your Committee, That Sir James Peachey, his Father, had found Mr. Phillips's Powder of great Service in his Garden and Hot-house.

The Right honourable the Earl of next in-

formed your Committee, That, from the Year 1777 to the present Time, he had used Mr. Phillips's Powder upon various Plants — That he applied it to a Quarter, Part of which was infected by the Grub and Part not; the Powder prevented the Grub from spreading to the Part uninfected, and stopt its Progress on the Part that had been attacked, which recovered — That he tried the Powder on Turnips in the following Manner: He mixed a Pound of Powder with each Bushel of Seed, and sowed it; the First Crop was eat by the Fly: The same Pvocefs was repeated, and the Crop was again eat by the Fly: But upon repeating it again, and powdering the Field as soon as the Turnips appeared, the Crop succeeded; and a small Part of the Field which had not been powdered was eat by the Fly. He took Notice, that the: Powder which he had mixed with the Turnip Seed of the Two first Crops, and which failed, was Part of a Barrel which had been in his Possession Three Years, and he believes had not been kept sufficiently tight. This Season, the first Part of a Crop of Turnip Cabbage, which had not been powdered, was destroyed; that which came up afterwords was immediately powdered, and escaped — That he tried the Powder on some Peach and Ne6tarine Trees against Walls, which were infilled by Ants, and the Trees were perfectly cured — That he likewise found; the Powder of great Service in destroying the Ants which infected the exotic Plants in his Stove; before he had done powdering. Numbers of the Ants fell; to the Ground, and upon tliaking the Stem of the Plant, after it was powdered, every Ant dropt, apparently dead: And being asked as to the Expence

ofpowdering the Turnip Field, he informed your Committee the Expence was very small, and forms no Objection to using that Remedy, and he never knew the Powder fail.

Your Committee proceeded tocall Mr. John Debmiere Junior4 who laid. He superintends the Brewery ofiMef-sieurs Hooper, Gordon, and Deboniere, at Bow — That he has-made several Experiments of Mr, s Powder

in one of the Malt Houses, particularly about Ten Days ago — Ttjat they first-cleared the Room of Malt, and on examining it, observed a great Number of Weevils; but wishing to make a.more complete Experiment, they had a Quantity of Weevils fifted from Malt in another Room, and brought into the Room where the Experiment was made — That the Powder brought the Weevils out from all the Crevioes in less than an Hour, and in the Course of Five or. Six Hours they had all fallen on the Floor — That the next Morning the Room was powdered again, and no more Weevils appeared, so. that he apprehends they all came oat on the first powdering; the greatest Proportion of the Weevils on the Floor were dead after the Second Day, and none of them, from the Beginning, had Power to quit the Floor, or get up the Wall — That, in order to try the Effect of the Powder, he took some of those which feetned the lead affected by it, and put them itv a-Box, with some fresh Malt off the Kiln, and after Two or Three Days he found they had not been able to perforate a single Grain — That after having powdered the Room, he took up some of those which seemed dead, and endeavoured, by Warmth, to recover them, but without Effect.

And being asked. Whether, from his Experience in Granaries, and the Experiments he has made of Mr. Phillips's Powder, he thinks, it will be of Service in Granaries? he answered. He certainly did; when the Granaries are empty the Powder will clear them of the Weevil, but it cannot be used when the Granary is full of Malt, on Account of the Impofiibility of reaching the Weevil, which is mixed with the Malt. And being »7

Mail. A, 1781*

also asked. If he considered the clearing of empty Granaries of the Weevil of material Service ? replied, He did. And being further asked. If they found the Weevil very detrimental in Malt Houses? he laid, They did, and in Brown Malt, particularly, there are very great Quantities of Weevils, which destroy the Hfeart of die Malt, and materially affect its Quality — That he never knew of any Means before of getting rid of the Weevil — They have sometimes in Granaries walked the Walls with Slack Lime, which had some Effect while die Lime was fresh, but afforded no material Relief.

Mr. Samuel Gordon, being next examined, informed your Committee, He is in Partnership in the above Brewery — That he has seen Two Experiments made of Mr. Phillips's Powder, at the Distance of Ten-Days from each other; the First Experiment was about Three Weeks ago, when they powdered a Corner of a Malt Loft, without clearing the Room of the Malt; and they found a Number of Weevils dead upon the Floor; but not thinking that a fair Experiment* on Account of the Malt that remained in the Loft, they some Days after repeated it in a small Loft, which was cleared of Malt; they brought Weevils out of another Loft, and laid1 them on the Floor, they then powdered the Walls and fifted the Powder over the Floor — That he left the Room immediately after it was powdered, and returned Two. Days after, when he examined it, and observed great-Numbers of Weevils upon the Floor, and the Walls perfectly clear; those on the Floor were all' either totally dead, or in a State of Stupefaction; some few. did not seem perfectly dead, but were incapable of; doing any further Mischief, and might be swept itito'a1 Shovel, and carried away. And being asked, Whether he thinks this Powder may be of material Service in Granaries? he answered. He is of Opinion it may. And being asked. If he found the Weevil' of material Detriment in his Trade? he said, They had received great Injury from the Weevil, by the Destruction of the Malt; that he knows of no other efficacious Method' of destroying or getting rid of the Weevil.

Your Committee then examined Lieutenant David Allen, regulating Lieutenant at who said. He

was on board His Majesty's Ship the Union, of Ninety Gnns, in Company with Mr. Phillips, when the Experiment of his Powder was made, about the Beginning of last Year, by Order of Sir The Ship's,

Bread Room was swept out, in order to try the Experiment; which being done, he assisted M r. Phillips in powdering it, according to his printed Directions. And being asked. What was the State of the Bread Room before the Experiment was made? he said. The Mailer - and Officers informed him, that the Ship was overrun with Vermin of all Kinds, Weevils, Cock Roaches, and Rats in Abundance; and that the Weevil had been of infinite Deflrudion to the Bread, ancffie thinks they . told him the Ship was obliged to leave her Cruize upon the said Account. The Bread Room appeared to him; before it was swept, to have been overrun with \\ eevils , and Infects, to the Damage of the Bread — That after lie and Mr. Phillips had powdered the Bread Room, and inflructed the Mailer and the Warrant Officer to

do the same on a future Day, he then retired about his Business; and came on board a Day or two after', to view the Ship again, when the Mailer and Carpenter, who had been powdering the Ship as before, informed him, that they apprehended the Powder would effectually answer the Purpose intended: The Carpenter informed him it would also kill Cock Roaches; having tried the Experiment in his own Cabin, he had intirely cleared it of Infects — That he requested him to come and fee the Trial made, which he did himself; he powdered the Back of the Galley, where there was a Number of Cock Roaches, which came out of their Holes, and fell to the Ground, and by Appearance to him dead; this happened in the Space of about an Hour — That he saw several of the Cock Roaches lying upon the Floor, which had been killed by the Carpenter's Experiment — That he did not go on board again himself, after the Bread Room had been powdered a Third Time; but he met the Mailer of the On Shore, a Week after, who informed him that they had swept off the Powder frojn the Bread Room, and that although there was no Appearance before of the Weevil, there were very great Numbers dead among the Powder — That the Ship went on a Cruize, and upon her Return some Months after, he met Mr. Osborn, the Purser, on Shore, who informed him that the Powder had had its defsred Effect, and that the Bread xyas as good as when first put into the Ship. Your Committee then called Captain King, late of His Majesty's Ship The Discovery, who being examined, said. He made the late Voyage on Discoveries with Captain Cook, and commanded the said Ship for the last Year of the Voyage — That Weevils and Cock Roaches are extremely prejudicial to dried Provisions; and, as an Example, said. That on the Voyage, in One Year, Two thousand out of Eleven thousand Weight of Bread was destroyed by them, and other Vermin — That when the Biscuits were first put on board. Three of them weighed a Pound; but in a Year after, it took Five to weigh a Pound; and this Loss is attributed to the Weevil only, which not only destroy great Quantities of Bread, but render what remains unwholesome and Unpalatable — That Captain Cook had felt very (Irongly the Mischief and Ravages of the Cock Roaches, and had made many Attempts to destroy them, or to lessen the Evil, but without Success — That he knows of no Method, unless it be this Powder, of getting rid of the Cock Roaches and Weevils — That he has' lately seen the Method of applying the Powder, on board the Ship Hawke East Indiaman, at Blackwall, and found it might be insinuated into the smallest Crevices; immediately upon its Application, the Infects, which were before concealed, ftiewed themselves; and after the Experiment Vol. 38.

was completed, he observed a Number of Cock Roaches Phillips'* which had fallen on the Ground, feme of which were dead, and others feebly creeping about — That the Experiment being made in a small Part of the Ship, he cannot judgewhat its general Effect might be, when applied to every Part of a Ship; but he apprehended, from what he saw, it would be effectual in keeping the Bread Room, or, Store Room, or any other particular Spot, clear of Weevils, and perhaps, by repeated Application, of Cock Roaches, which he is of Opinion will be of very important Advantage to the Navy

Your Committee then called Mr. the

Petitioner; who being asked, Whether he made use of the same Powder for all the Purposes to which it was applied ? he said. No; the Powder which is used for Shipping, Granaries, Storehouses, and Bale Goods, is made stronger than that which is used in Gardeus and Nnrferies. And being asked, Whether there was any thing in the Composition of the Powder noxious or unwholesome to Men ? he replied, No, nor to any do-meftic Animal. And being asked, At what Price he fold the Powder ? he said. He fold that which is used for Shipping and Granaries at Five Guineas per Hundred Weight, and the Laud and Garden Powder at Fifty Shillings per Hundred Weight — That One Hundred Weight will be sufficient to clear a First-rate Man of War of Infects — That Government, or the Public, may make the Powder much cheaper than the Prices he has mentioned. And being further examined, he, said,

That in consequence of Mr. Cumberland's Letter to the Treasury (before referred to in this Keporl) he received £. 200, on the 7th November 1777; ntvcr received any other Assistance from the Public — That he has pro-feented the Discovery Sixteen Years, in the Course of which he hasexhaufted upwards of 4,000, which was the Whole of his Fortune — That he is at present in very dillreffed Circumstances, and unable either to provide for the carrying on his Works, or for his Maintenance —

That he has contracted Debts to a considerable Amount, which he is unable to pay, and which threaten him w.th immediate Distress — And being asked. Whether he had any Proposition to make respecting his Terms for dif-closing his Discovery to the Public? he said, That having Hated the Sum expended by him in the Pursuit, and his present Circumstances, he submitted it to the Determination of this honourable House.
