APPENDIX, N* 2.

To the Right honourable Lords Commissioners of Trade and Plantations.

The humble Petition of Henry Phillips, of Knightf-bridge, in the County of Chymist,

Sheweth,

That your Petitioner, having been informed of the ruinous State of the several Sugar Colonies, from the Ravages and Devastation of the Cane Ant, applied himself for a long Course of Time, with great Assiduity, to discover some cheap and effectual Remedy, capable of destroying that pernicious Infect.

That, after considerable Expence and Labour, your Petitioner hath discovered a Composition, or Powder, of moderate Expence, easy in its Application, which instantaneously destroys the Ant, and every Species of Infects with which it comes in Contact.

That your Petitioner, at the Request of many respedable Merchants and Proprietors of Plantations in the West Indies, resident. in Lon, lately made a Voyage

to the Island of Grenada, to try Experiments ♦pon the Cane Ants, with which that Island is greatly iufefted; the Success of which evidently appears by the annexed Certificate your Petitioner humbly submits: And whereas your Petitioner could not perform an Experiment upon a more enlarged Plan, to contribute to the general Extermination of the said pernicious Infect, for Want of a sufficient Quantity of the necessary Ingredients, and being in a bad State of Health, your Petitioner thought it incumbent on him to disclose the Methods of preparing his Powder, which he accordingly did to the Commissioners of the said Island, appointed by a Law of the Legislature there, intituled, "An Act " for granting Rewards to such Persons as have discovered, or should discover, the cheapest and most " effectual Methods for destroying the Cane Ant, and " for appointing Commissioners to carry the same into " Execution;" which Ad is in your Petitioner's Possession.

That y/sur Petitioner humbly conceives the said Composition, whereof he is the foie Author and Inventor, howevefrffmple, and in all other Respects innocent, will not only completely answer the Willies and Purposes of the West India Planters, but, from the Extent of its Operation And Effects upon every Species of Infects, will be of <tntversal Benefit*

That your Petitioner bath greatly impaired his Health, ind exhausted his Fortune, in bringing this Discovery to Perfection, is thereby deprived of the Means of reaping such Benefits from it as, he humbly hopes, he will be entitled to firom the Legislature of Grenada and the Public, unless your Lordships condescend to encourage 15

Mr. Phillips, according to his Proposal at the last Board, attended the Meeting of the Commissioners this Day; and in their Presence mixed the Ingredients, and made up his Composition or Powder for destroying Ants; and different Experiments were made of the same on the Gane Ants, by which it appeared to the Board, that the said Composition or Powder dellroyed, in a very short Space of Time, all Ants upon which a very small Quantity of it was sprinkled: And although the Board are of Opinion, that the same has answered Mr. Phillips's Description of it, in the small Experiments made in their PrefenCe, yet they cannot from thence form a Judgment to what Extent the Destrudiou of the said pernicious In fed may be carried, or how far the said Powder may be made to contribute to their general Extermination, until Experiments can be made upon a more enlarged Plan; which cannot at present be done, for want of a sufficient Quantity of the uecef fary Ingredients.

APPENDIX, N* 4.

The Application of your Powder, by the Process you directed, has been duly attended to in His Majesty's Ship the Union; and the Success exceeded our Expectation, in the Destruction of the different Kinds of lufeds in her, and more particularly of the Weevils, which were in great Abundance, in all Parts of the Ship between the Decks, at the Time your Experiment for destroying them was put to Practice; and I have the Pleasure to assure you, that none of them are to be seen now; which evidently proves the Efficacy of your Method in removing that very great Evil, so injurious to Bread, and all other dry Provisions in Shipping.

There is not any of the Powder remaining, and it is desired of you to fend some more.

I am. Sir,

Your obedient humble Servant,

I was favoured with Two Letters touching the Success of your indefatigable, Industry to destroy the Vermin on board His Majesty's Ship under my Command. l declined answering either, till the Wonderful Effects should warrant ah Acknowledgment you are at Liberty to communicate to any Friend; which is, that before your Visit, thfe Ship was swarmitig with Weevils, Maggots; Spiders, Cock Roaches, Moths, Sc. so that the dry Provisions in Six Weeks were in great Part consumed by them, and what remained very unfit for life, by their Nests, Sc.: And 1 have the Pleasure to find, on Enquiry, there is not ft Weevil, and few other Vermin, to be seen.

I am. Sir,

Your moll humble Servant;

Sir,

As I never feel so much Pleasure and Satisfaction as when I am intlrumenlal to the Happiness and Welfare of others, I am particularly rejoiced in having an Opportunity of acquainting you with the Success of your Powder for destroying InfeOs.

It is with unfeigned Pleasure I can acquaint Mr; Phillips I have it in my Power to say, the Experiment^ made use of to destroy Infects on board His Majesty's Nich* Kelly, Surgeon. Ship the Union, by the Application of his Powder, have been so successful, as to exterminate a very great Abundance of Weevils, which had over-run the Ship in every Part of her, so totally and effectually, with their Nidus, or generative Power, that otherwise would have produced Successiions of them; none of such Species of IufcCt being now in the Ship. And as the Process pursued in using the said Powder fell under my immediate Inspection, it sufficiently proved the infallible Efficacy it pofl'efied, to me, and which, in Justice to your Invention, I cannot do less than inform you of it, and to assure you I shall be ever reqdy to attest the fame, at any Time hereafter, if it can in any ways lead to induce the Public in general, or Individuals, to encourage your Industry in this Business, by a Compensation given

By the Cqmraissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain and Ireland, SCc.

Having taken into Consideratkm your Report of the 8th Instant, upon MfT*Henry Phillips's new-invented Powder for destroying Weevils and other Vermin on board Ships, by which it appears, that, exclusive of the strong Testimonials which you had seen of the great Utility of the said Powder in the Destruction of Weevils, Maggots, Spiders, and Cock Roaches, One of the Members of your Board had examined the Power of the same, and had had ocular Demonstration that it kills Weevils; and you have proposed to us to fend a few Pounds of it on board each of His Majesty's Ships on foreign Voyages, and to acquaint the Pursers of all other Ships, that in case they find the Stores in Danger of Injury from Weevils, or other Infefts, that such a Powder will be sent to them on their Requisition, together with the Puffs used to insinuate the same into the Parts of the Store Rooms affected, so that the dry Provisions may be the better preserved: We do hereby signify to you our Approval of the said Proposition; and require and direct you to carry the same into immediate Execution. Given under onr Hands, the 23d December 1780.

G.

Commissioners for victualling His Majesty's Navy.

By Command of their Lordships,

Phf Stephens.

A Petition of the Merchants and Tradesmen of the Town and County of Texvcafile upon Tyne;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an Act passed in the Seventh Year of His present Majesty's Reign, for granting additional Duties on certain Foreign Lineins to be imported into this Kingdom, and enacting. That the said Duties should, from Time to Time, be paid into the Exchequer, distinct from all other Branches of the Public Revenue, and that a Sum, hot exceeding15,000per Annum, arising from the said Duties, should be kept apart as a Fund for the Encouragement of railing and dressing Hemp and Flax in this Kingdom, in such Manner as Parliament should direct; and that the Town of Newcastle upon Tyne hath heretofore carried on a very large Trade with Holland for Flax and Flax Seed, upon which many considerable Linen Manufactories established in the North of England depended; and that the late Rupture with the States of Holland put an immediate Stop to that Trade, which mult prove very detrimental to this Country in general, and to the Town and Neighbourhood of Neiocajile upon Tyne in particular, if some Means are not speedily found to procure a Supply of Flax and Flax Seed from some other Resource; and that the Petitioners, in the present Emergency, apprehend, that promoting and encouraging the Growth of Flax and Flax Seed in England, with all possible Affi-duity, would be of the greatest Importance, as it might in Time not only render the Linen Trade of Great Britain independent on Foreign Nations for those valuable Commodities, but would prove a great Encouragement to Agriculture in this Kingdom; and, to shew the Necessity of preventing an absolute Dependence upon the States of Hollander a Supply of Flax and Flax Seed, the Petitioners beg Leave to Hate the following Circumstances, viz. That Two Ships, laden in Holland with several Hundred Matts of Flax and Flax Seed for the Port of Nexocastle upon 7ywe, having been detained in Hollanduvon the Commencement of Hostilities, and 'afterwards released, were obliged, before they were suffered to depart thence, to re-deliver all their Flax and Flax Seed; and that the States have issued a Placart, obliging all Persons shipping Flax there for any Port at Peace with the States, to give Security, to the Amount of Ten Times the Value of such Flax, that it shall not be re-shipped to be sent to any Part of Great Britain or Ireland j and that the Petitioners presume there never was a Time when the aforesaid Fund given by Parliament, and still remaining in the Exchequer, could have been applied to the Purposes it was wifely intended for, with so much Propriety and solid Advantage to the Public as it may at present, when the Want of Flax is likely to occasion great Distress in the Country, and when Bn7i//rSubjects have no other Pro-speft of being supplied, than from an Increase of the Culture of it at Home: And therefore praying the House to take the Matter into Consideration, and to direct the said Fund to be applied to the lalutary Purposes it was intended for, in such Way and Manner as the House shall deem moll expedient.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered ' to lie upon the Table.

That the Sums of Fifty thousand Pounds and Forty thousand Pounds were to be borrowed according to the Directions of the said Acts for the Purposes of pulling down the Gaol of Newgate, and building a new one instead thereof; and towards purchasing such Houses and Lands as were judged necessary for the Purpose of rendering such new Gaol more airy, extensive, and commodious, and for making, widening, enlarging or improving, the Streets, Ways, and Passages adjoining or leading to the said new Gaol or Sessions House.

Mr. William Montagu, principal Clerk in the Chamberlain's Office, being then examined, said, That the whole of the said Money was borrowed by virtue of the said Acts, and has been duly and regularly applied in the several Works and Purposes thereby directed to be done.

George Dance, Fiquire, the Surveyor for the City of London, being examined, said, That in the Month of May 1780, the Gaol of Newgate was so nearly completed, that nothing was wanting in it jmt a fevy Locks, and some Furniture — That in June following it was rendered totally unfit for the Purpose of a Prison, by a riotous and unlawful Assembly of People — That the Floors and Roofs were all burnt and deftrpyed; and the Walls very much damaged. — That he had examined the State of the Building lately, and luid taken an Account of what, may be the probable Expence of repairing and re-instating the Gaol; and that in his Opinion, to do the same completely, and provide for all Expences, it will require the Sum of Thirty thousand Pounds — That in this he includes the Keeper's House, which is a Part of the said Gaol, and was damaged very greatly at the same Time with the rest of the Building.

Mr. Richard Akerman being then examined, said* lie bad been the Keeper of the Gaol of Newgate 2.8 Years: — That before it was rebuilt, and from thence to the Time wheu it was so much damaged, about a Thousand Prisoners were committed to it annually on an Average — That the greater Part of them were from the County of Middlesex, probably Two Thirds at the lead; and that Prisoners were font there by both Houses of Parliament, and from all Parts of the Kingdom.

Mr. Dance being again examined, said, That the Gaol of Newgale is not, in its present State, fit for the Purposes for which it was intended; and that it will be very dangerous and prejudicial to the City of London, and the Public, if it is not immediately repaired, and made secure for the Confinement of Prisoners.

Mr. Akerman being again examined, confirmed the last Evidence given by Mr. Dance, and added. That many Prisoners lately eleaped from other Gaols where they were kept, because Newgate was not in a State to receive them.

Mr. Dance being further examined, said, That force the said Gaol was dernolished, the City of Lyndon have proceeded to refit the Apartments for the Reception

A Petition of t he Mayor and Commonalty of the Growth of City of York, in Common Council assembled, was also on fen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of Mis present Majesty, a Sum not exceeding £. 15,000 per Annum, was directed to be kept apart as a Fund for encouraging the railing and dressing Hemp and Flax in this Kingdom; and that by another Act, passed in the Tenth Year of lits present Majesty's Reign,£. 8,000 per Annum, or Fight Fifteenth Parts of the said Fund, was appropriated and directed to be applied for encouraging the raising and dressing Hemp and Flax in England, and the remaining £. 7,000 per Annum, or Seven Fifteenth Parts of the said Fund, was appropriated for the like Purposes in Scotland; and the said last mentioned Sum being by the same Act directed to be paid Annually, and piit under the Direction of the Commissioners and Trustees for encouraging and promoting Fifilings Manufactures, and Improvements in Scotland, the Persons entitled to the said Sum of£. 7,000 per Annum so appropriated, have had the full Benefit thereof; but the Sum of£. 8,000 per Annum, or Fight Fifteenth Parts of the said Fund,

so appropriated for England, has been suffered to accumulate since the passing of the said first-mentioned Act, and the Petitioners are informed the accumulated Sum, to a very considerable Amount, is now in the Exchequer, unapplied to the Purposes for which it was intended; and that the County of York produces very large Quantities of Hemp and Flax, and the City of York is a considerable Market for vending the fame, and there are several very considerable Manufactures from those Materials carried on in the same County and City; and that the late Rupture with the States of the United Provinces, and the Placart ifl'ued by them to prevent the Flax and Flax Seed of that Country being imported into tilts Kingdom, has wholly flopped the very large Supply of those Articles which the Manufacturers of this Kingdom received from those States, infomuc h that such Manufacturers must be greatly diltreffed, the Quantity of Hemp and Flax grown in this Kingdom at present being very inadequate to the Demand; and representing to the House, that a very valuable Opportunity now presents itself, by a proper distribution of the said accumulated Fund, not only to enable the Subjects of this Kingdom to throw off their Dependence on Foreign Countries for a Supply of the Commodities above-mentioned, but to gain a Trade which has for several Years been pursued with the greatest Attention and Advantage by the Subjects of the States in Holland; and that the right Application of the Fund created by the said first-mentioned Act would, by a speedy Increase of the Culture of Flax and Flax Seed, produce the happiest Consequences to this Kingdom, by an Encouragement of Husbandry and the Linen Manufactures, and by saving the great National Expenditure of Money Annually paid to Foreigners for Flax and Flax Seed: An-1 therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to take such Measures as shall seem most expedient for preventing the said accumulated Fund from being applied to other Purposes than those so; which it was originally intended, and for applying the farm , a;id also the Fund annually accruing as aforesaid, to the effectual Advancement and Improvement of the same Trade.

That the Petitioners are greatly alarmed by observing in the Votes, that the Sugar Refiners of London have applied to Parliament for a Bill to- reduce the Duties on Foreign Prize Sugars for the Consumption Of Great Britain, an Equality with the Duties ort British Plantation Sugar; and alleging, that the

West India Islands have been settled and cultivated upon the Faith of the whole System of the Commercial Law! o f Great Britain, whereby the exclusive Privilege of supplying the British Consumption has hitherto been fe* cured to them without Interruption, and, if that Faith were forfeited by the fntroduftion of Foreign Sugar, so aS to deprive the Planters of that Increase of PriGe which forms their natural Relief under the Pressure of those enormous Duties, Expences, and Lodes, which have of late Years fallen upon them, the most fatal Consequences roust ensue to the Sugar Colonies, and to the Navigation, Commerce, Revenue, and Manufactures of Great Britain dependent thereon j and that, linless the Petitioners could have relied on such ex-dlufive Right, they would not have rilked such immense Sums as are invented for the Increafo of the Colonies; and if the En joyment thereof Humid be rendered precarious, by encouraging even an Idea that so great a System of Commercial Lawnnay be broke in upon for flight and temporary Causes, even if such could be proved to exist, the Consequences must be highly inju-

rious to the Credit of the Sugar Colonies, tend directly to prevent their further Extension, and thereby weaken the Source from which alone the very Manufactory in question can be permanently fed, and which can never flourish but in Proportion to the Encouragement given to the Cultivation of our own Colonies t and that, whilst the Principle of the Application is thus exceptionable, the Petitioners conceive it cannot be necessary to enter into a minute Consideration of the Allegations in Sop-'port of it, but trust, that the House will deem the Pro-Jiofition Wholly inadmiftible: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by their Counsel, and, if necessary, be allowed to examine Witnesses, to shew the pernicious Consequences that must arise from granting the Prayer of the said Petition, pjtto. A Petit ion of Stephen Fuller, Esquire, Agent for Jamaica, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Application mentioned in the preceding Petition; and representing to the House, That, at a Time when this Nation is involved in an unhappy Contest with its own Subjects, and at War With Three great Maritime Powers, when Freight, Tnfurnnce, I/imber, Provisions, Plantation Utensils, "and Goods of every Kind, bear a very advanced Price, when the Taxes of the Island are not adequate to the growing Expences, when it has pleased God to visit the Sugar Colonies with violent and destructive Hurricanes, when a heavy additional Duty has been laid upon the Importation of British Plantation Sugar, when so many united Circumstances contribute to in-

crease the Price of SugXf, and.without which Increase* the poor and middling Planters in the Island cannot go on; at this very Time, to trample under Foot the whole' System.. ,of our Commercial Laws, erected by the Wisdom of our Ancestors, and to set up i« the room of it, an arbitrary Innovation, avowedly calculated to lower the natural Price of that Commodity, when so many Causes conspire to raise it higher than it has Been in former Wars, is unreasonable-and unjust; and, as every Thing that tends to difeou-rage our own Sugar Colonies, at the same Time naturally tends to encourage those of our Enemies, it is evidently impolitic; and the Petitioner conceives; that the only true and permanent Method of lowering the Price of Sugars, is to give Encouragement to the Agriculture of the Colonies, the Strength and Sinews of our Maritime Power, and to increase by every pofli-ble Means, the Production of that Commodity; and that every other Method, particularly that in question, will turn out in the End ruinous to the desponding Planter, and productive of Kffecis totally different from those held out upon this Occasion, for the Contemplation of the Legislature: And therefore praying.

That the House will not give Leave to bring in the< said intended Bill.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,.

That the East India Company be permitted, during a Time to be limited, to remain in the Possession of thef Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues lately acquired in India; and that a distinct Account of the Ket Profits of the Company be made up, from the jft Day of March 1781 to the ift Day of March 1782; and that

the Net Surplus Profit thereof be divided in; the Man- ....

ner following; that is to say. That the Company ftiaTJ receive upon their Capital of^. 3,200,000, a Dividend ofj£.8 per Centum, if the Profits be equal thereto;

That the Public shall also receive a Proportion of the said Profits, equal to £. 8 per Centum per Annum, if the Profits shall amount to £. 16 per Centum per Annum;

That, in case such Profits shall be less than £. per Centum per Annum, the Public shall receive alt such Profits over and above the Dividend of 8 per Centujfi per Annum; That, in case such Profits shall exceed £. 16 per Centum per Annum, the Surplus shall be equally divided between the Public and the Company: That the M oiety of such Surplus above £. 16 per Centum per Annum, so appropriated to the Company, shall be applied to the Payment of an increased Dividend, as follows, that is to say, That the Proprietors shall be permitted, in Addition to the DK vidend of £. 8 per Centum per Annum, to take out of the Moiety of such Surplus, over and above the 16pet Centum per Annum, an increased Dividend, not exceeding £. 1 per Centum, if the Moiety of the said Surplus so appropriated to the Company be equal thereto; and that, after the Payment of such inereased Dividend, the Residue of such Surplus be applied to the Discharge of the Company's Bond Debt.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That in Cafes of Necessity, the East India Company, during a Term to be limited, be at Liberty, with the Approbation and Consent of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, to borrow upon Bond or otherwise, any Sum or Sums of Money, not exceeding £. 500,000, over and above the Amount of their present Bond Debt.

APetition of the Gentlemen, LandOwners, Farmers Growth of and Inhabitants of the Towns and Neighbourhood of Hemp and Selby, Snaith, Huivden, and Caivood, fife, in the County Fla*, of York, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, that the present Rupture with the States cf Holland having put a

6 N Stop

go6 7* fund. A. 1781.

Stop to the Importation of Flax from that Country, a great Demand has of consequence fallen on the County Of York for that Article, as well as other Places in England; and that the Quantity is by no Means equal to the Demand, nor likely to be lb for a considerable Time, unless some Means are fallen upon to increase the Culture of it more speedily than it would be in the ordinary Way, and the present Time affords a valuable Opportunity of gaining the Possession of the FlaxTrade, Which the Dutch have pursued with great Attention and Advantage to themselves for a long Period of Years; and that an Increase of the Culture of Flax in England will be of great Advantage to the I and Owners, to the Linen Manufactures of Great Britain, and to the Nation at large, by saving a great Sum of Money annually paid to Foreigners for that Article; and that in the Year 1767 a Fund was established by Parliament for encouraging the Growth of Flax in England, which has never been applied to the Purpose intended, and a right Application of it in the present Time would be productive of the happiest Consequences to the Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take the above into Consideration, and to appropriate the Flax Fund for England to the laudable Purpose for which it was intended, in such Way and Manner as the House flia.ll judge most effectual.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to consider the several Petitions which have been presented to this House in this Session of Parliament, respecting the Fund established for the Growth of Hemp and Flax in Great Britain; and to examine, and report to the House their Opinion relating to the Manner of distributing such Part of the said Fund as ought to be allowed to the Growers of Hemp and Flax in that Part of Great Britain called England.

Naval A Petition of the Merchants and Owners and Mailers

Volunteers, of Ships in the Port of Neiocaflle upon Tyne, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have maturely considered a Maritime Plan for Manning the Royal Navy voluntarily, and for the better Regulation of Seamen in the Merchants Service, which was printed and published by Order of the House last Session of Parliament, and are clearly of Opinion that it is well calculated to answer the great Purposes intended, and, with the Addition of a Clause for regulating the Wages of Seamen in the Merchants Service. practicable in every Part; and that the Petitioners, after having long felt and lamented those expensive and dangerous Delays which the Naval Operations 'and Commercial Concerns of the British Empire have often suffered, are extremly happy to find that a Plan so well calculated to prevent the like Evils in future, has so far obtained the Consideration and Sanction of the House: And therefore praying the House to resume the Consideration of the said Plan, and to order in a Bill upon the Principles thereof; and that it may, with such Alterations and Amendments as to the House shall seem meet, be passed into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to consider whether by any, and by what Means, more effectual Encouragement can be given to Volunteers to enter on board His Majesty's Ships of War, and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House.

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town Growth of of Kingston upon Hull, in Common Council assembled, Hemp and was presented to the House, and read Setting forth, flax* That by an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for granting additional Duties on certain Foreign Linens imported into this Kingdom, and for establishing a Fund for encouraging the railing and dressing of Hemp and Flax, the said Duties were directed to be paid into the Receipt of the Exchequer, distinct from all others, and a Sum, not exceeding £. 15,000 per Annum, arising from the fame, was to be kept apart as a Fund for the Encouragement of railing and dressing Hemp and Flax in this Kingdom, in such Manner as Parliamentffiould direct; and that, by another Act, passed in the Tenth Year of His Majesty's Reign, His Majesty was im powered to direct the Distribution of £. 8,000 per Annum, or of Eight Fifteenth Parts of the Money which had grown due and been kept apart, and which should afterwards grow duo and be kept apart, for the Encouragement of raising and dressing Hemp and Flax in England, pursuant to the First-mentioned Act, and £. 7,000 per Annum, or Seven Fifteenth Parts of the said Money, were to be applied for encouraging and promoting Fishings, Manufactures, and Improvements in Scotland-, and that the Petitioners are informed, that the said Sum off. 7,000

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, in Common Council a.Tembled,

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the betterSupport and Establishment of the Greenland And. Whale Fishery, the former Bounties granted by any Act of Parliament for the Encouragement of the G or Whale Fishery, were declared to cease, and be no longer paid1or allowed, except in such Cases only where special Provision wjas made for the same by the then present Act; and in lieu thereof, the respective Bounties thereinafter mentioned, were to be paid and allowable, that is to say, for every Ship, asdeferibed in the said Act, which should proceed on the said Fishery, from the 25th Day of December 1771 to the 25th Day of Dec 1776, the Sum of Forty Shillings per Ton; and for every such Ship as should proceed on the said Fishery, from the 25th Day of December 1776 to the 25th Day of December 1781, the Sum of Thirty Shillings Ton; and for every such Ship as should proceed on the said Fishery, from the 25th Day of December 17S1 to the 25th Day of December 1786, the Sum of Twenty Shillings Ton; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if the said Bounty of Thirty Shillings per Ton should be permitted to cease at the Time limited by the said Act, it would render ineffectual the Views of the Legislature in making those faluta'ry Provisions for the Encouragement of the Whale Fishery, and, as a necessary Consequence, would greatly prejudice so important and useful a Branch of Trade, the Petitioners having Cause to fear, that since the Rupture between Great Britain and the States of The United Pi evinces, the Navigation to the Greenland Seas, and Davis's Straights will be attended with more Peril than heretofore, and will consequently require a longer Continuance of the present Bounty of Thirty Shillings per Ton, than is provided for by the said Act: And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief, as the Nature of the same may require.

Junii. A. 1 781.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tliurfday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

A Petition of the Guild or Brotherhood of Mailers and Pilots, Seamen of the Trinity House of Kingston upon Hull, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That by an Act passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, cerlain Bounties were granted for the Support and Establishment of the Greenland and Whale Fishery, which were to decrease at limited Periods; and that the present Bounty of Thirty Shillings per Ton, will be reduced after the current Year; and, as the Owners of Ships employed in the said Fisheries, at this critical Juncture, labour under many Disadvantages from the present exorbitant Wages to Seamen, the high Premiums of Insurance, and other Discouragements, the Petitioners, from their Knowledge of Maritime Matters, are well convinced, that if a further Diminution of the present Bounty is permitted to take Place, it will tend to dellroy that Branch of useful Commerce, and greatly prejudice the Nursery for Seamen, which is the Object the Legislature had in View at the pading of the said Act, and which, in the Petitioners Opinion, the present Demand of the State absolutely requires to he encouraged: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to pass a Law for the Continuation of the Bounty as it now hands, during the present Hostilities, or to take such Measures as to the House shall appear expedient, for preventing the Annihilation of the said Trade.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the Port of Liverpool, in Behalf of themselves and others, especially of those who are immediately interested in the Whale Fishery, to Greenland, Davis's Streights, and the Seas adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton, granted by Parliament, upon the Shipping employed in the Whale Fishery, was the foie Means of bringing that Trade to a flourishing Stale; and that a Supply of Oil and Whalebone fully equal to the Consumption of these Kingdoms, besides great Quantities of Oil exported, have been furnished by Shipping,

navigated chiefly by British Seamen, through the Operation of this wife and salutary Law; and that in the Year 1776, which was the last Year of the Allowance of the Bounty above-mentioned. Twenty-two Ships of large Burthen were fitted out in the Port of Liverpool, for the Whale Fisheries in Greenland and Davis's

Streights; and that a Redtiblion of: he Bounty after the 25th of December 177 6, till the 27th of December 1781, to Thirty Shillings per Ion, which from that Time to the 25th of December 1786 will, by the Laws hitherto enacted, be no more than Twenty Shillings per I on, and then finally cease, has reduced the Number of Ships fitted out at the Port of lover pool for the Northern Whale Fishery this present Year, to Two Ships only; and that this Trade, which has been an excellent Nursery for great Numbers of able and healthy Seamen, is likely to lapse again into the Hands of Foreigners, without the Aid of a sufficient National Bounty, which, from the great Advance in Seamen's Wages and Insurance, is at this Time rendered still more particularly necessary: And therefore praying. That the former Bounty of Forty Shillings a Ton, may be again granted for a limited Time, upon Shipping employed in the Whale Fishery, to Greenland, Davis's and the Seas adjacent; or that such other adequate Relief may be granted, as the House shall judge meet.

And the said Petitions were (overall v ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the last preceding Petition is referred.

Mr. Ord, according to Order, reported from the Watuoi Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Proposal of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; both which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the Proposal and Resolution were read; and are as followeth; viz.

To the Honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

The Governor and Company of the Bank of England humbly propose.

That they advance the Sum of 2,000,000 for the Public Service, in the Manner following;

£. 1,000,000 on or before the 15th Day of November next, and £. 1,000,000 on or before the 15th Day of February 1782, on Exchequer Bills, to be made forth by virtue of an Act to be passed in this Session of Parliament, bearing Interest at the Rate or Premio of £. 3 per Cent, per Annum; the said Interest to be paid Quarterly; and the said Exchequer Bills to be charged and chargeable upon, and repaid by and out of, the First Aids or Supplies which shall be granted by Parliament for the Service of the Year 1784; and in case sufficient Aids or Supplies should not be granted for that Purpose before the 5th Day of April 1784, the same to be charged and chargeable upon, and be repaid out of, the Sinking Fund.

And they humbly further propose. That they be continued a Corporation, with the foie Power of Banking, for the Term of Twenty five Years from the lit August 1787, with all Abilities, Capacities, Powers, Authorities, Exemptions, and Privileges, they now enjoy, by virtue or in pursuance of their Charter, or of any Act or Acts of Parliament; redeemable afterwards on a Year's Notice, and the Repayment of all the Principal Money, and also the Payment of all the I nterest Money which shall be then due and owing to them upon all such Tallies, Exchequer Orders, Exchequer Bills, or Parliamentary Funds, which they shall have remaining in their Hands, or be entitled to, at the Time of such Notice to be given as aforesaid (such Funds, for the Redemption whereof Provision is already made in any Act or Acts of Parliament now in Force, always and only excepted) they continuing a Corporation, with an ,-exclusive Power of Banking, notwithstanding such Notice given, till all the Money due to the Bank as aforesaid shall be paid them.

Signed by Order of the Court of Directors,

Bobert Leioin, Secretary.

That the Petitioners have been arrested and taken in Execution since the Seventh of June last, for Debts due (and for which Writs were issued dut against them) prior to that Day, and are confined with Felons in Rooms, the Windows of which are all broken, and the Roof in such had Repair, that the Rain comes through in many Places, to the great Danger of the Petitioners Lives; and that the Petitioners are desirous of making all the Satlsfaction in . their Power, by delivering np their Effects for the Be*-nefit of such Creditors whose Debts accrued due before the Seventh of June last: And therefore praying.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Importers of Spirituous Liquors, Distillers, Rectifiers, Compounders, and Tea Dealers, in Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the H<»use, and read; Setting forth, That the Cocoa and Chocolate Bill, now before the House, contains a Clause, which declares that all Judgments of the Commissioners of Excise, or Justices of the Peace, within their respective Jurisdictions, for the Condemnation of any Commodities, Goods, or Effects, seized as forfeited under that, or any other Act of Parliament relating to the Duties of Excise, or other Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise, shall be, and shall be deemed and taken to be, as final and conclusive, to all Intents and Purposes whatsoever, as any J ndgment for the Condemnation of any Commodities, Goods, or Effects, given in His Majesty's Court of Exchequer; and that the Petitioners are much alarmed at the many threatening Evils which such Powers would be productiveof, as well to themselves as to every Trader and private Gentleman subject to an Excise Duty from the above Clause, which seems calculated to make the Judgments of summary Jurisdictions as final as the solemn Determinations of a Court of Record; and that, although it should be alleged that the said Clause is necessary for the better Management of the Public Revenues, the Petitioners submit, that the Court of Exchequer, being aCourt originally instituted, and now in Practice, for executing the Revenue Laws, all Questions relative to His Majesty's Revenue of Excise, and all Seizures made by virtue of the fame, may with as much Ease and Safety be determined in that Court, as the Questions relative to the Revenue of the Customs, or for Seizures under those Laws, now are, and have been Time immemorial; and that there are several other Clauses in the said Bill, which, if permitted to pass into a Law, must not only tend to the manifest Injury of the Petitioners, but will render several of them under the Necessity of totally leaving off their Trades: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and suffer the Petitioners to be heard, by their Counsel, against the passing of the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for repealing the Duties payable upon Chocolate made in Great Britain, and for granting certain Inland Duties upon Cocoa Nuts in lieu thereof; for the better and more effectual securing the Revenue of Excise, and of the Inland Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise, and for preventing Frauds therein; for the more punctual and ready Payment of the Allowances to be made to Brewers out of the additional Duties imposed on Matt; and for rectifying a Mistake in an Act, made in this present Session of Parliament, with respect to the exempting of Candles from the additional Duty of Five Pounds per Centum upon the Duties of Excise, imposed by the said Act, is committed; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the Order of die Day, for receiving the Report from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill was committed, be now read.

And the said Order being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Report be received upon ThtirJdayMorning next.

A Petition of the Common Brewers, Makers of Beer, Supply B2| and Ale, fife, was presented to the House, and read; Dutwos Setting forth, That the Cocoa and Chocolate Bill, now Chocobte. before the House, contains a Clause which declares, that all Judgments of the Commissioners of Excise, or Justices of the Peace, within their respective J urifdiftious, for the Condemnation of any Commodities, Goods, or Eflefts, seized as forfeited under that or any other Act of Parliament relating to the Duties of Excise, or other Duties under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise, shall be, and shall be deemed and taken to be, as final and conclusive to all Intents and Purposes what-foe ver as any Judgment for the Condemnation of any Commodities, Goods, or Effects, given in His Majesty's Court of Exchequer; and that the Petitioners are much alarmed at the many threatening Evils which the above Clause would occasion should the same pass into a Law, as it is calculated to make the Judgments of summary Jurisdictions as final as Trials by Jury: for the Petitioners submit, that, although a Judgment in the Court of Exchequer may be considered as final and conclusive against Actions to be brought after such Condemnation, yet, as that Court was originally instituted for the Determination by Jury of all Cafes respecting His Majesty's Revenues, the Petitioners apprehend that the Judgment of any summary Jurisdiction should not be deemed and taken to be as final and conclusive as such Judgment given in the Court of Exchequer, because the Petitioners conceive, that such summary Judgment would be repugnant to the Law and Confutation of this Country, and tend to the manifest Oppression of the Petitioners, and to injure their Fortunes and Properties; and that there are also Two Clauses in the said Bill, one relative to the Limitation of Time for Permits, the other requiring an Oath or Affirmation fur recovering the Drawback of the Malt Duty, both of which Clauses may tend to the Obstruction of Trade and Prejudice to the Revenue: And therefore praying

A State of the Matter of the said Complaint is as follows;

i ft. That a Letter, dated fronvou Board The Camel at Spit head, May 27th; 1781, from Captain John Taken* ham, and directed for the Honourable John Luttrell at Mr. Lecrafs's, Walbrook, one of the Places of his usual Residence, has been charged at the General Pott Office in London, with the Duty of Three Pence.

2d. That the Pottage of Three Pence has been taken at the General Pott Office in London, as the Duty on a Letter directed to the Honourable John Luttrell at Kimpfon, near Alresford, Hants, another of the Places of his usual Residence; and this notwithstanding the Pottage of the said Letter had been paid at the Time it was put into the Pott in London, and the Letter was stamped with the Letters " Pott paid" upon it.

3d. That the Pottage of Six Pence has been charged at the General Pott Office in London, for a Letter from Sir John Huffey Delaval, dated Hanover Square, June 8th, 1781, and directed to Captain Luttrell at Kimpfon.

4th. That the Pottage of Four Pence has been charged at Portsmouth on a single Letter, dated on Board His Majesty's Ship Jason at Saint Jago, and brought Home by the Oporto Sloop of War, which Letter was directed to the Honourable John Luttrell at Kimpfon, and put into the Poftat Portsmouth, for which a Penny and uo more had been paid by the Poll-matter there, at the Time of putting in the fame.

5th. That several of such Letters as have been charged with the Duty of Pottage since the 21st Day of September 1780, and directed for the Honourable John Luttrell at Kimpfon, have been refused by the Post-matter at Alresford to be delivered to the Servant . of the said Honourable John Luttrell, without Payment being firtt made; the said Post-matter informing the said Servant, that he had before written to the General Pott Office respecting Captain s Letters

being charged, but having received no Answer, be would not part from the Letters without the Money, which the Servant accordingly paid.

Your Committee then called Anthony Todd, Esquire, Secretary to the Postmaster General; who being examined with respect to the said Charges, said,

That the Letter directed to Mr. Luttrell at Mr. Lecrafs's, which was charged with the Duty of Pottage . at the General Pott Office, London, was apprehended not to be directed to his usual or actual Place of Residence, and as not being intended for himself: But Mr. Todd admitted that the same ought not to have been charged with Pottage, as it appeared to be intended for himself:

That the Letters directed for Mr. Luttrell at -fan, one of his Places of Residence, ought not to have been charged with Pottage, the Post-matter at Aire fori having mittook the Directions given to him; and that all such Charges have arisen from Mistakes, except as to that which came by the Oporto Sloop of War.

But that with respect to the Letter charged with Pottage from Portsmouth, brought from Jago by the Oporto Sloop, he thought it a proper Charge, as being a Ship Letter; that they look upon all Ship Letters as chargeable with Pottage, whether they come by the Packet, a Man of War, or private Ship; that a Ship Letter is a Letter brought from any Part beyond the Seas to any Port in the King's Dominions; but that they call every Letter a Ship Letter, for which a Penny is demanded at the Office — That inCafes where Letters are brought from Ships cruising or laying in Hart bour, the Pottage ought not to be taken: But,

Being asked, If a Captain of a Man of War (who is a Member of Parliament) ttiould be cruising in the Channel, arid fend his Letters ou Shore franked, and the Person carrying them should demand a Peony for each

Reign of His present Majesty; and that the Petitioners* are desirous to have the exclusive Trade in, to, andr from the East Indies, continued to them for a further Term of Years, and are willing that the Public should participate with them in the Profits arising from the Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues lately obtainedin. the East Indies, for the Time past, since the Petitioners Bopd Debt was reduced to or under £. 1,500,000, and for the Time to come, during the Continuance of the Petitioners said exclusive Trade; wherefore the Petitioners at several general Courts lately h Id, have taken into Consideration the Terms and Conditions of aa> Agreement to be made between the Public and the Petitioners, and at a General Court of Proprietors, held on the 25th Day of this Instant7«nc, the Petitioners agreed to the Propositions hereunto annexed for those Purposes, and for the Purpose of establishing certain Regulations for the better Management of the Petitioners Affairs:

And therefore the Petitioners beg Leave to submit the said Propositions to the Consideration of the House, as the Terms and Conditions for prolonging the Petitioners exclusive Trade in, to, and from the East Indies, and for making a further Agreement between the Public and the Company in respect of the Territorial Acquisitions and Revenues lately obtained in the East Indies, and for establishing certain Regulations for the better Management of the Petitioners Affairs.

farehoufinc A Petition of the Sugar Refiners of London, was pre->f Sugars, fented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed, That a Bill is depending, to allow Sugars of the Growth and Produce of the British Plantations, to be warehoused under the Care of the Officers of the Customs, upon Payment of a Part of the Duties, and upon the Importer's Bonds for the Payment

VoL 3

of the Remainder, and under certain other Restrictions and Regulations; and representing to the House, that it hath been the Usage in the Sugar Trade, from Time immemorial, for the Importers to pay the Duties on Sugars on or before the landing and housing of the fame; and they apprehend it would be a great Detriment to them, and to the Venders and Confutners of Sugar, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, as it would tend to promote and encourage Speculation in that Commodity, by better enabling the Importers to withhold their Sugars from the Market, and thereby increase the Price, which is already unreasonably high, causing great Injury to the Petitioners, and much public Discontent: And therefore praying the House to allow them to be heard, by Counsel or otherwise, against the said Bill.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lieupon the Table, until the Bill to permit Sugars, the Produce of thq British Islands in the West Indies, to be warehoused in this Kingdom, under certain Restrictions, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard,' by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill, upon, their Petition if they think fit.

A Petition of sundry Persons, being Owners or Oc-- Warehousing cupiers of Warehouses within the City of o{ Su6ar*-

Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That a Bill is depending before the House, to allow the warehousing of British Plantation Sugar under Bond, in which the Petitioners are informed there is a Clause to direct that such Sugars shall be lodged iu Warehouses which are contiguous to each other; and representing to the House, that the Petitioners possess or occupy Warehouses in the Port of London, which have been usually or occasionally let or employed for housing of Sugar, and which they apprehend do not come within the direct Intentions of the said Clause, and that it would be a great Hardship upon them to be restrained from letting or employing their said Premises for such Purpose, as the Value of such Premises would be reduced:

And therefore praying. That so much of the said Bill as tends to prevent the housing of Sugars in such Ware-houses, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to permit Sugars, the Produce of the British Islands in the West Indies, to be warehoused in this Kingdom, under certain Restrictions, be read a Second Time.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrafted.

And then the House adjourned till Thursiay Morning next. Ten of the Clock.

Prayers. ':

PETITION of the Owners, Commandersv and others concerned in the Commercial and Maritime Interests of this Kingdom: And also,

A Petition of the Merchants, Principa^Owners, and Mailers of Ships and Vessels in the Port of Whitehaven, and Ports adjacent;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have maturely considered a Maritime Plan, for manning the Royal Navy voluntarily, and for the better Regulation of Seamen in the Merchants Service, which was printed and published by Order of the House last Session of Parliament, and are clearly of Opinion, That it is well calculated to answer the great Purposes intended, and practicable in every Part; and the Petitioners are fully persuaded, that an ACi to form a Fellowship of all such Seamen as shall offer-to become Members, would be productive of the most beneficial Effects; that the Privileges contained in the said Plan are so considerable, and so judieiously, adapted, that every Seaman will soon.fee it his Interest do declare himself willing to serve the State, by becoming a Member of the Fellowship; and that the Royal Navy, by being always completely manned with Volunteers, will be rendered much more powerful and expeditious in all its Operations, and the Britipk Commerce, under its more effectual Protection, will greatly flourish, and increase in every Part of the Globe; and that the Petitioners, after having long felt and lamented those expensive and dangerous Delays which the naval Operations and commercial Concerns of the British Empire have often suffered by the present coercive Mode of manning the Royal Navy, are extremely happy to find that a Plan, so well calculated to prevent the like Evils in future, has so far obtained the Consideration and Sanction of the House: And therefore praying the House to resume the Consideration of the said Plan, and to order in a Bill upon the Principles thereof; and that it may, with such Alterations and Amendments as to the House shall seem meet, be paRed into a Law.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

'Although the Business of this Session has required a longer Attendance than may have been consistent with your private Convenience; yet I am persuaded that you look back with Satisfaction on the Time you have e rpployed in a faithful Discharge of your Duty to your Country, in the present arduous and critical State of Public 'Affairs.

I cannot let you . depart into your respective Countries, without afTuring you of my entire Approbation of your Conduct, and of My perfect Confidence in the Loyalty and good Affections of this Parliament.

T|jp Zeal and Ardour which you have shewn for the Honour of My Crown, your firm and Heady Support of a just Cause, and the great Efforts you have made to enable Me to surmount all the Difficulties of this extensive and complicated War, muff convince the World that the ancient Spirit of the BrUiJ/i Nation is not abated or diminished.

..In the Midst of these Difficulties, you have formed Regulations for the better Management and Improvement of the Revenue; you have, given, additional Strength and Stability to Public Credit; and your Deliberations on the Affairs of the East India Company have terminated in such Measures as will, I trust,. produce great and essential Advantages to My Kingdoms.

I have observed, with much Satisfaction, that during the Course of that important Business, your Attention was not more anxiously directed to the Benefits to be derived from the Territorial Acquisitions, than to the Happiness and Comfort of the Inhabitants of those remote Provinces.

Whatever may remain to be dpne for securing those valuable Possessions, and for restraining the Abuses to which they are peculiarly liable, you will, 1 doubt not, proceed to provide for at your next Meeting, with the same Wisdom and Temper that have goverued your late Proceedings and Inquiries.

with the Honour and Dignity of My Crown, and the permanent Interest and Security of My People.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, That this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the 13th Day of September next, to be then here holden; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the 13th Day of September next.

Among the many ill Consequences which attend the Continuation of the prteient War,' I moll sincerely regret the additional Burthens which it must unavoidably bring upon My faithful Subjects.

My Lords and Gentleman,

In the Prosecution of this great and important Contest in which We are engaged, I retain a firm Confidence in the Protection of Divine Providence, and a perfect Conviction of the Justice of My Cause j and I have no Doubt but that, by the Concurrence and Support of My Parliament, by the Valour of My Fleets end Armies, and by a vigorous, animated, and_ united Exertion of the Faculties and Resources of MyReople, I shall be enabled to restore the Blessing of a safe and honourable Peace to all My Dominions. 1

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks, of this House, for His most Gracious Speech from the Throne:

To assure His Majesty, that we fee with Concern that the War is still unhappily prolonged by that* re ft left Ambition which first excited our Enemies to commence it, and which still continues todisappoint His Majesty's earned Desire and diligent Exertion to restore the public Tranquillity:

That we are sensibly affected by His Majesty's paternal Expressions of Concern for the real Welfare of His Subjects; and we receive with the strongest Emotions of Duty and Gratitude His Majesty's gracious and endearing Declaration, that He should not answer the Trust committed to the Sovereign of a free People, nor make a suitable Return to His Subjects for their constant, zealous, and affectionate Attachment to His person, Family, and Government, if He consented to sacrifice, either to His own Desire of Peace, or to their temporary Ease and Relief, those essential Rights and permanent Interests, upon the Maintenance and Preservation of which the future Strength and Security of this Country must ever principally depend:

To declare on our Part, that we know no Means of

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where this House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that *any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

To the honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled.

The Fifth Report of the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and date, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom.

Upon the Certificate of Accounts depending in the Office of the Auditors of the Impred, next to the Pay-maders General of the Forces out of Office, dands the Name of the Right honourable Richard Rigby, the present Paymader General of the Forces. In return to our Precept, he dated to be in his Hands, upon the 28th of November lad, a Balance of Four hundred r ... 11. j|. Forty-seven thousand One hundred Fifty-three Pounds

The Act directs. That in taking an Account of the Public Money in the Hands of an Accountant, " we " shall consider what Sum may be taken out of his *0

Fifth Report of Commissionere of Public Accounts.

" Hands, to be disposed of by Parliament for the Publie Service." But in aw Office of so large a Receipt and Expenditure as that of the Pay Office, through which many Millions pass in the Year, it was not to be imagined, that a Sum in the Hands of the Paymader General upon any given Day, could possibly remain long enough in his Possession to become a Subject capable of such Discussion; he mud have ill'ued the Whole of it, long before we could, in the course of our Proceedings, have an Opportunity of examining it; and therefore we considered this Balance, not with a View to the taking any Part of that individual Sum out of his Hands, but to compare the Quantum of that Balance with the Demands upon it on the Day of its Date, and to fee whether it was not more than was necessary to answer the then exiding or approaching Claims upon the Paymader General of the.Forces, for the Services of the Army.

That we might be able to form an Opinion upon this Subject, we proceeded to enquire of what Parts this Balance was compounded, at what Time each Part was received, and for what Service intended. An Inquiry that comprehends the whole Extent of the Business in this Office.

The Public Money in the Hands of the Paymader General, is received by him, either from the Exchequer, or from the Treasury of Ireland, when Regiments are drawn out of that Kingdom, and in Part paid by Great Britain; or from Persons who, upon their Accounts being settled, are directed by the King's Warrant to pay the Balance into his Hands.

The present Paymader General has no Money in his Hands received from the Treasury of Ireland; all the Accounts of the Irish Regiments being made tip, and their whole Pay now borne by Great Britain. The Sum in his Hands, arising from Balances directed to be paid to him, was, upon the 1 ft of February lad, Eight thousand Four hundred Sixty-three Pounds Ten Shillings m and Four Pence. The Exchequer is the great Source from whence he draws his Supply.

As the extensive Transactions of the lad Year would probably furnish us with Indances of every Species of Receipt and Iffiie, we procured from the Treasury an Account of the several Sums issued to the Paymader Appendix. General of the Forces, from the 24 th of December 1779 j to the 25th of December 1780, and from thence to the 16th of May 1781 ,didinguishing the Times when issued, and for what particular Services.

From the Examinations of Mr. John Clerk of the Debentures in the Odice of the Auditor of the Exchequer; Richard Molefworlh, Esquire, late Deputy Paymader in North America; the Right honourable Richard Rigby, the present Paymader General; John Powell, Esquire, Cashier; and Charles Ef-

quire, Accountant in the Office of the Paymader General; we obtained the following Account of the Manner of transacting the Business in this Office, and of the Balance in Question.

The Supply for the Army is granted by Parliament to the Kiflg, and therefore no Part of this Supply can be issued from the Exchequer, without the Royal Sign Manual authorizing such Iffiie. After the Supply is granted, there comes from the Treasury to the Pay Office the King's Sign Manual, directing the Lords of the Treasury to issue unto the Paymader General a certain Part of that Supply (in Time of War usually a Million) by way of Impred, and upon Account, according to such Warrants and Orders as either are or shall be signed by the King. This Sign Manual, with the Treasury Warrant, and Order of the Auditor of the Exchequer made in pursuance of the Sign Manual, after being entered in the Pay Office, are lodged at the Exchequer, and give the Paymader G eneral aCredit there for the Sum mentioned in those Indruments. To obtain any Part of this Credit, the Paymader General presentsa Memorial to the Treasury, specify ing t lie Sum he requires,

and for what Service. the Treasury, by Letter, direct the Auditor of the Exchequer to issue that Sum to the Pay-master General, upon the unsatisfied Order above mentioned. This Letter being produced, and passing through the Forms of Office, he obtains from them the Sum he wants. When the Sum in this Sign Manual is exhausted, another Sign Manual, with the consequential Warrant and Order, is obtained, and in like Manner from Time to Time renewed, until there is Occasion for the last Sum, which completes the whole Army Supply of the Year; when, instead of a Sign Manual, there comes a Privy Seal, directing the Issue of that remaining Sum, and including, authorizing, confirming, and covering, the whole Supply of that Year.

It was usual formerly for the Paymaster General to apply to the Treasury every Four Months, each Time for about a Third Part of the Sum voted for the Services of the Army, under the general Head of Subsistence and Pay of the Forces at Home and Abroad; but since the Year 1759, the Practice has been to a!k of the Treasury, from Time to Time, for the Sums voted under distinct Heads of Service, and not until the Time when the Demands for the Services are near approaching.

The Services are ranged under Two general Heads, the Ordinary and the Extraordinary; the Ordinary, are those for which specific Sufns are annually voted by Parliament; the Extraordinary, are those, which, though not provided for by Parliament are nevertheless considered as necessary, and therefore paid, in Confidence of their being provided for in the succeeding Session.

As the Service is distinguished, so is the Application for it to the Treasury. Sums for the Ordinary Services are obtained upon the Application of the Paymaster General himself; those for the Extraordinary, are directed into his Hands, upon the Application of others.

After the Supply for the Pay of the Army is voted by Parliament, the Secretary at. War fends to the Pay Office the Four F.stabliftimenls for the Year; which are, The Guards, Garrisons, and Land Forced; The Forces in the Plantations, and the Garrisons in North Amei'ica and the West Indies; The Forces in Minorca and Garrison of Gibraltar; and, . The Militia; with the several Regulations of the Subsistence. The Establishment contains the Distribution of the whole Sum voted, among!! the several Regiments, Corps, Garrisons, Officers and private Men, by the Day, and by the Year, and the grofsSum allowed for each Regiment, Corps, and Garrison. To each Establishment are annexed Two Warrants, the one directing the Paymaster General to make a Deduction of Twelve Pence in the Pound out of all he shall issue, called the Poundage, and specifying to what Services it shall be applied; the other, directing a Deduction of One Day's Pay? out of the Payments in the Establishment, for the Use of ChelJ'ea Hospital.

In general the gross Sum allowed for a Regiment, or Corps, is divided, in the Establishment, into Five Parts, under the Description of The Full Pay of each Officer and private Man; the Allowance to Widows; The Allowance to the Colonel, and for Clothing loft by Deserters; The Allowance to the Captain for recruiting, Sic.; and, The Allowance to the Agent. But in the Pay Office this gross Sum undergoes a different Division, consisting of The Subsistence, The Poundage, The Hospital, The Allowance to Widows, The Nett Off-reckonings, The Clearings, and sometimes Refpits.

It is in Consequence of these Deductions fropt, and Divisions of, the gross Sums allotted to different Corps, and of distinct Sums being provided by Parliament for certain Services, That the Application by the Paymaster General to the Treasury for Money, is made under distinct Heads of Service. These Services may, for the Vol. 38.

Purpose of our Inquiry, be distinguished under Three Fifth Report

Heads; filST

First. Those Services for which the whole Sum re- public Ac-ceived by the Paymaster General, at the Exchequer, is counts, issued by him soon after he receives it.

Secondly. Those, for which the Sum he receives, belonging to particular Persons, remains in his Posses* fion upon Account of the Persons entitled* until they, or their Agents, apply to him for Payment.

Thirdly. Those, for which a Part only of the Sum he receives, is issued by him soon after he receives it, and the Remainder continues in his Hands for any indefinite Time.

Of the First Class, where he soon issues all he receives, arc, The returned Poundage; Chelsea Hospital, and the Out Pensioners; The Subsistence of the Forces in Jamaica and the East Indies, and of the Non-commis-

fioned Officers and private Men in Africa; the Subsistence and Clothing of the Militia and Invalids;

The Subsistence issued upon Account; The Stoppages of the Officers; Subsistence in the West Indies, North America, and Garrisons of Gibraltar and Minorca; The General and Staff Officers and Garrisons in Great tain; The Net Off-reckonings; The Allowances to the Colonel, Captain, and Agent: The Clearings;

Foreign Subsidies; Arrears of the Foreign Troops;

Levy Money; and all the F.xtraordinaries, Under the Head of Subsistence of the Forces at Hpme, so much of the Sum received, as the Subsistence actually amounts to, is issued to the Agents as soon as be receives it.

Of the Second Class, are. The reduced Officers, and, under the several Heads of the Garrisons Abroad, the General and Staff Officers, and Hospital Abroad: So much of the Sums voted for these Services, as is contained in each Warrant for the Pay of the Officers named in the Certificate, remains in his Hands until those Officers or their Agents apply for it

Of the Third Class, where he issues a Part only of the Sums he receives, are. The Subsistence of the Forces at Home; The Subsistence of the Non-commissioned Officers and private Men of the British Forces in the West Indies and North America, and of the Foreign Troops; The Garrisons Abroad; and The General and Staff Officers and Hospital Abroad. Besides these, there are some other Heads of Service, to satisfy which, he does not expressly apply to the Treasury for Money, but pays the Demands for them out of what lie has received under other Heads of Service: These are. The Allowance to Widows; Some Services to which the Poundage is made subject by the King's Warrant and Contingencies.

Having thus procured the Knowledge of the Services, and of the Mode'of receiving from the Exchequer, and of issuing Money for each Service; it remained, in order to find out the component Parts of this Balance, to compare the Sums received for these Services, with the Sums issued, and fee what remained in the Hands of the Paymaster General under each Head: But the Manner in which the Accounts in this Office are now, and have been kept from Time immemorial, rendered such an Invelligation hardly practicable.

When the Paymaster General passes an Account before the Auditor of the Imprest, he charges himself therein, with the Money he has received out of the Exchequer, during the Period of that Account, in one gross Sum; he verifies the Charge by the Imprest Roll, which specifies the Sums he has received in each Memorial, and the Termkin w'hich he received them, but not for what Services; all that is required of him is, to render an Account for what Services he has expended the Sum imprested to him: To do this confidently with Order and Method, his Payments must be arranged under distinfit Heads of Service; but there is no Necessity for making the like Arrangements of his Receipts, it

would

would only occasion the Entry of a Variety of Articles Iri his Charge, in (lead of One, which One* answers full fis well all the Purposes of passing his Accounts. With a View to this, is formed the Plan upon which his Books are kept; the Accounts of his Payments are under separate and distinct Heads of Service, but he has only One Calli Account; though in One Memorial to the Treasury, he often alks for several Sums, under various distinct Heads of Service, yet he enters the Re-fceipt in his Calli Book, as One entire Sum received that Day at the Exchequer, and carries it as One Sum to the King's.Account current in his Ledger: To have found out, therefore, the Savings in his Hands, under any One Head of Service, he mult have examined every Memorial presented by him to the Treasury for the Thirteen Years he. has been in Office, and have extracted from thence, and collected together, all the Sums he has received for that Service, in order to compare them with the IAues. And here too arose another Difficulty: — In tins Office, a Payment for any Service, made in a subsequent Year, is entered in the Account of that Year in which the Sum was voted for that Service, unless such Account is made up, and then it is entered in the next Open Year's Account; hence these Accounts are usually kept open, until they are ready to be passed by the Auditors of the Imprest; which Time not being yet come for the Accounts of the Paymaster General in Office, not one of his Ledgers are yet made up; he could not therefore have given us the IAues for any One Service, without making up the Account of that Service in every Year's Ledger, since he has been in Office.

Thinking ourselves by no Means warranted to take up the Time, and perhaps impede the current Business of this Office, at so busy and important a Period, by employing them in so laborious, and, unless for this particular Purpose, so useless a Talk; we had Recourse to such other Circumstances in Evidence before us, as might lead us to a Decision upon the Point we are pursuing.

From the Arrangement we have made of the Sums received by the Paymaster General from the Exchequer, it appears, that the Balance in his Hands cannot consist of any Sums comprehended in the First Class; because of them he very soon ifiues all he receives: Nor is it probable, that Sums in the Second Class can constitute any very considerable Part of it.; because it is not to be presumed, that Officers of any Denomination willfuffer their Pay to continue long without applying for it, either by themselves or their Agents.

A continual Receipt and Blue, implies a Balance continually in Hand; there must be the like continual Balance where there are Intervals between the Receipt and Blue, and a freili Supply always comes in before the Blue, as in the same of every Bank: Butour Inquiry is after a Sum more permanent; a Sum that remains long unapplied to any Service, and which, if otherwise disposed of, would occasion no Interruption in the regular Course of paying the Army Services; for such a Balance, in the Hands of the Paymaster General, we must look amongst the Sums for the Services named in the Third Class, where he ifiues less than he receives.

Under the Denomination of Subsistence for the Forces at Home, he receives more than that Subsistence amounts to, with an Intent of procuring thereby a Fund for certain Payments not specifically applied for by him, and therefore otherwise unprovided for: He receives Subsistence upon the full Establishment of the Non-commissioned Officers and private Men of Forces in

North America and Part of the West , and of the Foreign Troops; but as these Regiments must be incomplete, and the Deputy Paymasters there issue Subsistence according to the Strength only of the Regiment he does not remit to them the whole he receives but so much only as, from the last Accounts they fend him

Jt. 1781.

of the State of the Balances in their Hands, he judges will be sufficient to enable them to carry on (lie Public Service. This uniffued Subsistence of the British forces in the West Indies and North America continues in his

Hands till the Accounts of the several Regiments are made up, when it falls into the Clearings, and is issued to the Agents; but this is not till Fifteen or Sixteen Months after they become due. The uniftued Subsistence of the Foreign Troops remains with him till their Arrears are paid to the Agents -, which Time seems, from the Account of the IAues received from the Treasury, . generally to be about Two Years after they are due.

He reefeives the whole Sums voted for Garritbns, Staff, and Hospital Abroad; but the Officers in these Departments, named in the Certificates from the War Office, do not exhaust the whole Sum voted.

Hence arises a Fund composed of these Savings, out of which he ifiues for certain Services, and defrays certain Expences, without making any specific Application for them to the Treasury; these are. The Allowance to Widows; Some of the Payments to which the Poundage is made applicable by the King's Warrants; and.

The miscellaneous Head of Contingences.

To Demands for these Services, and to no other that we can discover (except such Claims for the Pay of the General and Stats Officers, and Officers of the Garrisons and Hospitals Abroad, and of the reduced Officers, as remained unsatisfied) was this Balance liable on the Day of its Date. What then was the Amount of these Demands at that Time PNothinghad been issued for the Allowance to Widows in the Year 1780; for enough remained of former Receipts, in the Hands of the Paymaster of the Widows Pennons to carry on that Service; and therefore this Balance was not liable to be reduced by any Blue under the Head of Allowance to Widows.
