Fifth Report Balance of a Paymaster General whilfthe is in Office, it of Com- js equally expedient, that he should retain his Balance as of Public ffiort a Time as possible after his Resignation; that he Account*. should pay it over to his Successor, and the subsequent Business be carried on by him, at least as much of it as can be transacted by him without causing Consulion or Delay. According to the present course of Business of this Office, upon the Resignation of a Paymaster 4th Report. General, his Accounts of the Year's Establishment are N° 3. carried on to the 24th of June, or 24th of,

preceding or subsequent to his Resignation, as is most convenient to the Public Service; when it is subsequent, he receives from the Exchequer, though out of Office, his Proportion of the Supply of the Year to that Time, and applies it in Discharge of the Demands upon the Service, which accrued down to that Period; but of these Demands, some do not come in a course of Payment, others are not applied for till feme Time after they are due; neither the Nett Off-reckonings nor the Clearings, which are the last Payments on Account of a Regiment, are discharged till Fifteen or Sixteen Months after they become due; the General, Staff, and Reduced Officers, do not all apply immediately for their Pay; Warrants for Contingencies are frequently not produced until several Months after they are payable; and the Pay-master General has Deputies in various Parts of the World, whose Accounts he mull have Time to adjust; it is therefore convenient, and prevents Trouble to the Office, that his Business should be carried on, and so much of the Public Money, as is necessary for that Purpose, continue in his Hands for some short Time afterwards; and if the Balance be confined within its proper Bounds, whilst he is in Office, the Interest of the Public will not be materially affected by the Detention of a moderate Balance, for a few Months after his Resignation.

If Claimants for Sums directed, but not applied for, in the Time of the Predecessor, must, according to the present Forms of Office, have Recourse to the Treasury for new Warrants, those Forms are inconvenient, and should be altered; the Successor should be empowered to pay such Demands, under the Authority given to the Predecessor, without putting Claimants to the Trouble and Expence of a Second Application.

Was the Paymaster General to retain his Balance until his Accounts are finally adjusted, the Public would be kept out of their Money to a very distant and uncertain Period. It is Sixteen Years since Lord Holland resigned, and his Accounts are Hill in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest unsettled; the present Paymaster General has been in Office Thirteen Years, and the first Three Years and a Half only of his Accounts are sent into that Office, and in their First Stage. The Public have a Right to be informed how their Money has been expended, and as speedily as possible after the Expenditure: The Evils attending Delay are many and obvious, both to the Perl'on accounting, and to those entitled to call for the Account. Being accustomed to go in one Track, and long Inattention to this Point, in the Departments both of the Paymaster General and of the Auditors of the Imprest, added to a great Increase of Business, have produced long Arrears; it requires, and there ought to be, an extraordinary Exettion in both Offices, to bring the Accounts forward, and to introduce and establish that Order and Regularity in making them up, and keeping them, which should be strictly adhered to in every Office of Account., To obtain and preserve an accurate and competent Knowledge of the ' State they are in, they should be made up and balanced Once a Year, to a certain Hated Time, and as soon as may be after that stated Time is elapfod. But the Time it takes to complete the Payment of certain Services, and the Manner of carrying on some Branches of the Business in this Office, are Impediments to such a Regulation, and seem not well calculated either for Perspicuity or Expedition. There are certain Services,

for which no specific Sums are appropriated, either W the Vote of Parliament, or by the Distribution in lUe Establishment; but they are paid out of Funds compounded of a great Variety and Number of Articles, fubt rafted from variousdifferentgrofsSums, either voted or allotted for certain Purposes: These Services are, Chelsea Hospital, The Allowance to Widows, The Cloathing of the Regulars, Exchequer Fees, and Salaries to certain Officers. One of these Funds is the Poundage, which consists of various Deductions of Twelve Pence in the Pound uponalmost every individual Sum (except the Half Pay, of which the Deduction is only Six Pence in the Pound) voted, or allotted by the Distributions in the Establishments, for the Army Services: Out of this Fund are paid, 1ft. The returned Poundage; that is, this very Deduction, thus made, is paid back to certainCorps; so that this Part of it seems.to lie deducted for no other Purpose but that of returning it back again, adly. A Part of this Poundage is applied towards the Expences of Chelsea Hospital. 3dly. The Remainder pays the Exchequer Fees, and the Salaries of the Paymaster General, and of other Officers.

The Expences attending Chelsea Hospital are paid out of Two Funds, blended together; the one is Part of the Poundage above-mentioned; the other is formed . of the Deductions of One Day's Pay of every Person named in some of the Establishments, and of some of the Persons named in other'of the Mtablishments: To form this Fund, and that of the Poundage, and to make these several Deductions, is the Business of the Pay Office.

The Allowance to Widows, consists of the Pay of Two Private Men a Company, and is a Part of the Establishment in every Regiment; this comes from the War Office, but the several Articles are collected together from the Regimental Distributions, and formed into a Fund, in the Pay Office.

The Fund for the Cloathing is called the Nett Offreckonings; and is composed of Deductions made in the Pay Office, out of the Sums allotted in the Establishment for the Full Pay of the Non-commissioned Officers and Private Men, in most of the Regiments and Corps.

One Effect of these Operations is, that in making up the State of every Regiment in the Pay Office, the Sum allotted for its Pay in the Establishment mull conlift of Six Parts; The Poundage, The Hospital, The Subsistence, The Allowance to Widows, The Off-reckonings, and The Clearings, and sometimes Refpits. This State, besides the Business it Creates in the Pay Office, must be examined, computed, and signed, by the Agent; for he receives the Clearings, which is the Balance due to the Regiment; the Truth of which Balance depends upon the Justness of the Calculation of the other Divisions: It must be examined too, and computed, by the Auditor of the Imprest; for the Paymaster General taking Credit in his Account for the whole Pay of each Regiment, and surcharging himself with the total Amount of the Deductions of the Poundage, Hospital, and Widows, in every Year, the Auditor cannot knqw the Accuracy of the Surcharge, without an Examination of each Article that composes it.

To Persons accustomed to the Course of Office, these Computations are easy and familiar; but they certainly must take up Time; an Object, considering the present State of the Army Accounts, worth attending to If, instead of these Deductions, certain specific distinct Sums were estimated and set apart for these Services in the Establishment; if distinct Accounts were kept of the Receipts and Payments, under each Head of Service; if the Cloathing of the Regulars was voted like the Cloathing of the Militia, separate from the Establishment; if the Sum allotted to a Regiment should be the actual Pay, and the Whole of it be distributed amongst the Officers and Private Men, and paid to them without Deduction, at such Times and in such Proportions as

fli3U

£ 2 Geo. III. 2 8° Novetnhris*

shall be deemed bed for the Service; if every distinct Service had its didin6t Appropriation, which can be easily estimated by the Experience of preceding Years; it should seem as if this Branch of the Pay of the Army might be carried on in a more simple, expeditious, and intelligible Manner.

In Public Truds, the Possibility of a Loss should be guarded against, as much as the Nature of the Trulls will admit, without any Respect to Persons, or placing any more Confidence in any Man than can be helped. The Sums that appear to have been intruded to Pay-maders General, are of a Magnitude that implies Danger to the Public; for who can give, or find Security for the Payment of them ? At the Head of this Class of Accountants, dands an Indance of an actual Loss; the lad Account that was passed of Lord Lincoln's was to the 2 4th of December 1719, between which, and the 2 5th of June 1720, Four hundred Seventy-three thousand One hundred Twenty-seven Pounds, were issued to him from the Exchequer; of this Sum it does not appear that any Account was ever given, nor have we been able to trace, either in the Pay Office, or in that of the Auditors of the Impred, the Expenditure of any Part of it; neither Book nor Paper, relative to this Account, is to be found in either of those Offices. It has been the Practice of the Paymaders General, when they went out of Office, to take with them the Books and Papers that relate to their Accounts, as their own private Property; but as the Paymaster General is an Officer appointed to a Public Trud, his Office created for the Use of, and supported by, the Public, and his Books contain Accounts of the Receipt and Expenditure of Public Money j we are of Opinion, that all these Official Books and Papers are, and should be considered as the Property of the Public, and as such, left and deposited in the Pay Office, for the Use and Information of Poderity.

The Regulations hitherto fuggeded, are upon aSup-pofitiorrthat the Conditution of this Office continues in its present Form; but there is a Modification, which, if it can be adopted, will effectually remove the Power, and therefore the Possibility, of Loss or Abuse; that is, by taking away from the Paymader General of the Forces, the Cudody of the Public Calli, and placing it in the Bank of England; this Treasury will then be converted into an Office of mere Account, and the Paymader General, instead of being the Banker of the Army, will be the Instrument only, through whom the Army Services are paid, without having the Power of applying the Public Money to any other Purposes whatever. Some Judgment may be formed how far this Plan is practicable, by comparing the Alteration it will make in the great Outlines of the Business of this Office, The Receipt, The 1 flue. The keeping the Accounts, and The Accounting, with the Forms now in Vfe. The Impred mud be to the Bank the Bank

571

mud make the Payments, by Means of Checque Drafts drawn by the Paymader General, specifying the Warrant, and the Service: The Paymader General mud keep the Account of these Receipts and Payments, and the Bank a Duplicate; both mud join in passing the Accounts, the one producing the Warrants discharged by his Drafts, the other producing the Drafts discharged by Payment. Under the present Conditution of this Office, the Paymader General keeps his Cash at the Bank; the Bank receives it at the Exchequer on his Account; he never pays in Cash, but by his Cashiers Drafts on the Bank: He keeps the Account of all these Receipts and Payments, as if they were transa&ed in Cash: The Warrant indorsed, or the Warrant and Receipt, or the Warrant and Regimental Pay Book, signed by the Agent, and Receipt for the Off-reckonings, are his Vouchers: His Deputies pay, when they can, by Drafts upon the Agent to the Remitter, who is the Bank Abroad, and accountable to the Public.

Such is the Similitude between the Mode proposed and the Mode in Use; and thus far this Regulation carries with it all the Appearance of being reducible to Practice.

W7e are well aware of the Difficulties that mud for ever attend the introducing Novelty of Form into ancient Offices, framed by the Wisdom of our Ancedors, and established by the Experience of Ages; they are considered as incapable of Improvement , the Officers educated in, and accudomed to the Forms in Use, are insensible of their Defeats, or, if they feel them, have no leisure, often no Ability, seldomany Inclination, to correct them; alarmed at the Idea of Innovation, they refid the Proposal of a Regulation, because it is a Change, though from a perplexed and intricate^ to a more simple and intelligible Sydem.

To trace this Alteration through every Branch of the Business, to mark all its Effects, that it does not in any wise didurb the Pay of the Army, perplex the Accounts, or throw Difficulties or Delay in the passing them; to point out the Steps by which it ought gradually and methodically to be introduced, is a Work of long serious Attention and accurate Examination; but the Appearance this Plan carries with it of being prao* ticable, and the Advantage it holds out to the Public, in an Office, that certainly dands in Need of some Reform, fiford us sufficient Reason for submitting the Consideration of it to the Wisdom of the Legidature.

The Examination of Mr John Hughfon\ taken upon Oath, the 12th'of June 1781-

This Examinant foith, That he is Clerk of the Debentures, in the Office of the Auditor of the Exchequer; and has been near Twenty-five Years in the Office.

The first Knowledge the Auditor of the Exchequer fcas of the Grants of Parliament for the Service of the Army, is by the Votes of the House of Commons; he is bound to take Notice of these Grants, and not to issue more than the Sums granted.

The King's Sign Manual, the Treasury Warrant, and the Order from the Auditor, gives the Paymaster a Credit in the Exchequer for the Sum mentioned in the Order; this Sum is issued to him, either in the Whole or in Parts, in pursuance of-Letters from a Secretary of the Treasury until the whole is exhausted. These Sums are entered upon the Order, as they are paid, which is one Mode of keeping the Accounts of these Payments in the Auditor's Office: The Sums mentioned in these Orders are usually round Sums, without Fractions; and when there remains in the Exchequer a Fraction only of the entire Sum voted for the Service of the Army for that Year, or whenever the last Issue is to be made, instead of a Sign Manual for that Remainder, a Privy Seal is sent to the Auditor for the Payment of it to the Paymaster, taking Notice of the Sum Total that had been directed to be issued by the former Signs Manual and Warrants, and that fticfti Sum Total, together with the Sum remaining, will satisfy the whole Sum granted by Parliament that Year for the said Services.

After an Order is completed, it is indorsed by the Paymaster or his Deputy, and remains with that Teller who pays the last Sum, as a Voucher for the Payments.

The Auditor is bound to direct the Tellers to pay the Sums mentioned in the Warrants, provided they do not exceed the Sums granted by Parliament.

John Hughfon.

Guy Carlefon,

T. Angujh,

A. Pigott,

Richard Neave,

Samuel Beachcrofl,

Geo. Drummond.

n*3.

The Examination of Richard Molesworth, Esquire, taken upon Oath, the 1 ith of June 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he was Deputy Paymaster in North America, during the Years 1776, 1777, and 1778, the greatest Part of which Time he was in Rhode Island. Whenever he apprehended that he should want Money for the Service of the Troops, he applied to the Commanding Officer of the Corps, and settled with him the Sum that would probably be wanted, and in consequence of his Approbation, he required that Sum from the Agent of the Remitters, who ftipplied him with it in Cash.

It is the Duty of the Deputy Paymaster, not to issue any of this Money, but by Warrant of the Commander in Chief, or Commanding Officer of a detached Corps; the Person entitled to receive any Sum for the Service of the Army, brings this Warrant to the Deputy Paymaster, directed to him, and specifying the Sum to be paid, to whom, and for what Service, or upon Account; upon Payment of this Sum, the Person receiving it in-dorfes the Warrant, and leaves it with the Deputy Paymaster, and gives him also Three Receipts for the Money, of the same Tenor and Date, least any of them should be loft;the Warrant so indorsed, or the Warrant and a Receipt, are the Vouchers for this Payment. One of these Receipts he transmits to the Paymaster General, with an Account of his Receipts and Payments, signed by himself; he keeps the Warrant in his Possession, if it be for an Extraordinary Service, until it is called for, upon passing the Accounts before the Auditor of the Imprest; if it be for the Pay of a Regiment, it becomes useless, after the Account of that Regiment is settled.

He himself always paid these Warrants in Cash, and not by Drafts; but if he had been in the same Place . with the Agent to the Remitters, he could have paid them, and, in his Opinion, with more Convenience, by Drafts upon the Agent.

R,{ Molesworth.

T. Angvish,

A. Piggott,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond.

The Examination of the Right honourable Richard Right), Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, 27th June 1781.

This Examinant faith, The Sum of Four hundred forty-seven thousand One hundred fifty-three Pounds Eleven Shillings and Three Pence Three Farthings, mentioned in the Return made by him to this Board, on the 28th of November last, is, to the best of his Knowledge and Belief, the whole Balance of Public Money then remaining in Ins Hands as Paymalier General of the Forces. This Balance does not include the Money in the Hands of the Deputy Paymasters Abroad; it does include the Balances in the Hands of the Cashier of Half Pay, and the Deputy Treasurer of C helfea Hospital. This Balance is liable, in his Hands, to every Army Service whatever. He is of Opinion, the whole Sum voted every Year for the Service of the Army, mud necessarily go through the Paymalier General's Hands.

He does not recoiled! any Instance where the Treasury have made any Objection to his Applications to them for Money, nor has he ever been called upon officially by them to give them a State of the Balance in his Hands.

He considers the Books of the Office, as the private Property of the Paymaster, who may if he phases, on his Resignation, take them froip the Office; it has been, as he is informed, the general Practice'of his Predecessors to take them away as soon as their Accounts were made up.

Richd Right/,

Guy Carleton,

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Ric/A Neave,

Geo. Drummond.

The Examination of John , Esquire, Cashier

in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 26th and 29th of June, and x ith of July, 1781.

Th is Examinant faith. That when it wastheUfage of the Office for the Paymaster to ask of the Treasury for a certain Portion of the Year's Supply, it was generally applied for by him under the Head of Sobfiiience ami Pay of the Forces at Home and Abroad. Since the Year 1759, the Sums have generally been asked of the Treasury under some special Head of Service.

The Paymaster receives Money from Sub-Account-^ants, in consequence of their Accounts having been settled by the Auditor, and Balances appearing to be due from them; these Sub-Accountants bring to the Pay Office the King's Warrant, directing them to pay the Sum therein mentioned to the Paymaster General; who, upon receiving it, carries the Amount to the Credit of the Public in the King's Account Current.

When the Paymaster is to receive Money at the Exchequer, he does not receive it either in Caih or Bills; but, as he keeps his Calli in the Bank, the Bank Clerk, who attends there, receives it, and gives the Paymaster Credit for it.

The Custom has been, ever since he has been in the Office, for the Paymaster to make all his Payments by Drafts on his Banker, signed by his Cashier, very rarely by himself, and then only in the Absence of his Cashier.

The Savings voted in Aid of the Supply for the Year . S780, arising from Stoppages for Provisions, the Charge , ol New Levies, Pensions of Officers Widows, and Subsistence of an Augmentation to sundry Regiments, were never directed into the Hands of the Paymaster , - Yol. 38.

General, out of the Exchequer, for those Services; but Fifth Report directed, received, and ifftied, for other Services. The ^nwT'of1*' Sum of Ten thousand Pounds out of the Savings of the pv, bijC Half Pay of reduced Officers, voted in Aid of the same Account?. Supply, was Money actually in the Hands of the Paymaster General, received for that Service.

The Secretary at W'ar requires every Year, from the Paymaster General, an Account of the Savings arising by Deathifand Promotions of Half Pay Officers, Part of which Savings is applied to Payment of Persons on the Compassionate Lift, who are the Widow's of Officers on Half Pay, and the Children of Officers.

No Account can be produced of the Heads of which the Balance in the Hands of the Paymaster General consists, without comparing the Vote of Parliament every Year, for every Head of Service, with the Application; which has never be n thought necessary to be done, and would employ many Clerks fora long Time.

'Fhe Accountant is the Officer to make up the Accounts of the Paymaster General; the only Account he himself has been principally engaged in making up, is that of Lord Holland's, which is not yet completed.

When One Year of an Account is sett led, the Balance is carried over to the succeeding Year; and upon settling the final Account, is paid either to the Paymaster General for the Time being, or into the Exchequer, as the King shall direct.

He does not believe that there remains in the Hands of the Pa matter General any Money upon Account of *

the Pay of the Irish Regiments; their Accounts being all settled and adj lifted to the 24th of December 1778.

The Pay Office has been examined, in consequence of his Directions, and no Books or Papers, relative to the Accounts of Henry F.arl of Lincoln, late Paymaster General of the Forces, are to be found there.

Those Regiments, which used to be paid in Part by the Treasury of Ireland, have, ever since December 1778, been voted and paid by Great Britain.

No Sum was issued from the Pay Office to th®

Paymaster of the Widows Pensions, during the Year 1780, as he had sufficient in his Hands to carry on that

Service. Guy Carleton, T. Anguish, A. Piggott, Rich4 Neave, Sam1 Beachcroft, Geo. Drummond. J/19 Pozvell.

as it has never been thought hecessary to keep separate and distinct Accounts of the Receipts, it would be very difficult at any Time to give an Account of what Parts the Balance in the Hands of the Paymaster General Consists, and to what. Services each Part is liable; that cannot be done, without making up all the Accounts of the Paymaster General, from the Time he entered into Office to the Date of the Balance, which mull nccelfarily take up much Time, and be attended with great Trouble.

it has been the constant Practice of the Office, ever since lie knew it, to consider the Cadi as One entire Sum, under whatever Heads of Service the Parts it consists of may have been asked. There is only One Calli Account of all the Money received.

All the Payments, of every Kind, made by the Paymaster General, are in consequence of Warrants under the Sign Manual, and countersigned either by the Lords of the Treasury, or Secretary at War: And, where the Warrant is for the Payment of Contingencies* which exceed the Sum voted, it is countersigned by both. Salaries that have a Continuance, are paid by virtue of a permanent Warrant, entered at the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest: In this Cafe, the Receipt for the Salary is the Voucher for the Paymaster General. In general, the Warrant, indorsed by the Person receiving it, is the Voucher. Where many Persons receive under the same Warrant, the separate Receipt of each, with the Warrant, are the Vouchers. For the Payment of Exchequer Fees, the Voucher is a Certificate from the Exchequer of the Sum paid. *

When a Regiment is cleared, the King's Warrant is obtained for the full Pay of that Regiment, unless there is any Respite; this Pay Warrant, indorsed by the Agent, together with the Regimental Account Book, signed by him, and the Receipts for the Off-reckonings, signed by the Person having the Assignment, are the Paymaster General's Vouchers for the Pay of that Regiment. The Voucher for the Payment of an Extraordinary Abroad, is the Warrant of the Commander in Chief, indorsed by the Person to whom the Sum is paid, or his Receipt for it, together with the King's Warrant, covering all such Payments made in One or more Years.

In the Ordinary Services, a Payment made in a Year subsequent to that in which it was voted, is carried to the Account of Payments made in the Year it belougs to, unless the Account of that Year is made up.

A Respite, is a Sum directed by the King's Warrant, countersigned by the Secretary at War, to be deduced out of the whole Pay of a Regiment; in consequence of this Warrant, which is sent to the Pay Oflice, that Sum is not applied for by the Paymaster General, but remains in the Exchequer.

A Warrant for Levy Money is made out by the Secretary at War, who signifies from Time to Time, to the Paymaster General, what Part of it is wanted; upon which, he applies for that Sum to the Treasury, and when received, issues the Whole of it to the Agents of the Regiments.

Distinct Accounts are kept of the Exchequer Fees paid, and also of the Deduction of Twelve Pence in the Pound, Hospital, and Allowance to Widows; it has not been thought necessary to poll up and settle these Accounts, until the Time the Account of the Year is made up in the Auditor's Office. , Adiftinct Account is also kept of the Sum issued upon Imprest to the Paymaster of the Widows Pensions, and of the Payments out of the Deduction of Twelve Pence in the Pound, and One Day's Pay.

The Sums received by the Paymaster General, are either from the Exchequer/ or the Treasury of Ireland,

Vol. 38.

or from Persons whose Accounts have been settled, and who have been directed to pay their Balances into his <;oners of Office. Sums received by him, under this Head, have Public from Time to Time been applied by him in Aid either Account*, of the Army Supplies, or of the Extfaordinaries; and the Balance now remaining in his Hands, on this Account, is Eight thousand Four hundred Sixty-three PoundsTen Shillings and Four Pence.

The Yearly Accounts of the Paymaster General are contained in Two Ledgers, the Full Pay and Half Pay Ledgers; all these Ledgers are kept open until the Paymaster General settles his final Account.

The Accounts of the' Paymaster General, when first sent to the Office of the Auditor of the Imprest, gene-tally contain Payments only, with their Vouchers; they remain there until the Auditor has examined them, and fends his Queries to the Pay Office. The Accounts of the first Three Years and a Half of the present Paymaster General, were sent into the Auditor's Office before Christmas last: No Queries, relative to any of

them, have as yet been received at the Pay Office.

In every Account sent to the Auditor's Office, it is usual for the Paymaster General to charge himself with the Money received by him from the Exchequer, during the Period of that Account, in one gross Sum, authenticated by the Imprest Roll, made out at the Exchequer; and to charge himself with the Money from the Treasury of Ireland, and with the several Sums received from other People; and to futcharge himself with the Gain by Exchange, and with the Poundage, Hospital, and Allowance to Widows. He discharges himself, by Vouchers for all his Payments, ranged under their several Heads of Services.

He is of Opinion, that it would not be expedient for the Paymaster General, upon the Resignation of his Office, to pay over the Balance then in his Hands to his Successor; and that the subsequent Business of the Office should be carried on by him, for the following Reasons:

First. The Paymaster General has his Deputies in various Parts of the World, who are in the constant Receipt of large Sums of Money on his Account j sufficient Time- must be allowed them to adjust and settle their Accounts.

Secondly. The Sums voted for the Army, are issued to the Paymaster General at different Times, and under various Heads of Service; if he was not permitted, after his Resignation, to complete these Services to the Period of the Year his Accounts are carried on; but that Part of those Services is to be paid by him, and Part by his Successor; it would multiply Accounts, and tend to Confusion, and the Army Accounts, at present very intricate, would be more perplexed, and the making out and passing them retarded.

Thirdly. Great Confusion would be occasioned in the Accounts, if Warrants for the Pay of the Garrisons at Home and Abroad, of the General and Staff Officers, and Officers of the Hospital, at Home and Abroad, voted in the Time of One Paymaster, were to be paid by his Successors; and the same would be the Effect respecting the Half Pay voted for the Reduced Officers.

Cha' Bembridge.

Guy Carle ton,

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Rickd Neave,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond.

Mr. Perceval accordingly delivered the Report in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty's mbit dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, return Your Majesty the Thanks of this House, for Your most Gracious Speech from the Throne.

We assure Your Majesty, that we fee with Concern, that the War is (till unhappily prolonged by that restless Ambition which first excited our Enemies to commence it; and which (till continues to disappotnt Your Majesty's earned Desire and diligent Exertion tdreliore the Public Tranquillity.

We are sensibly assessed by Your Majesty's Paterrial -Expressions of Concern for the real Welfore of Your Subjects; and we receive with 'the strongest'Emotions of Duty and Gratitude Your Majesty's gracious "and endearing Declaration, that You should not answer the Trust committed to the'Sovereign of a (Vee People, -l»or make a suitabie Return to Your Subjects (br1 their ' constant, ‘zealous, and affectionate Attachment to Yoar Person, Family, and Government, if You consented to 'sacrifice, either to 'Your own *Ddfire of 'Peace,1 or to their temporary Ease and Relief, those'eflferitHd Rights ;and permanent Interests, upoir the Maintenance and -Preservation of which the future Strength and'Secbrity of this Country must ever principally depend.

We declare on our Part, that we know no Means of making to Your Majesty-any Return so suitabie and so just, and of answering the great Trust committed to us by those whom We represent, as bygiving Your Majesty this 'firm Afiarance, that we are resolved to assist and support -Your Majesty to the utmost of our Power, in- maintaining and preserving the essential Rights and povma-Tient Interests of Your Crown- and People.

'The favourable Appearance of Affairs in Indies, and the safe and prosperous Arrival of the numerous Commercial Fleets of Yotir Kingdoms, have given "ua great'Satisfaction :Bot We fmcerdy regret that Your: Majesty's assiduous Endeavours to guard Your extehfiVe Dominions, have hot in all Places been attended wtftfh Success; and we learn with the deepest Concern, that , the Events of War have been very ‘unfortunate to Your Majesty's Arms in Virginia, and have ended in the' LofS of Your Forces in that Province.

We are fully persuaded, that the principal View of the Confederacy of our Enemies, was to foment and ‘maintain the Rebellion in; and, tinder

the specious Delusion of the Establishment of an independent Empire,' to render Your Majesty's Colonies subservient to the Power and Influence of the Crown of France: But Your Majesty may Tely on our steady Assistance to second Your Majesty's Endeavours to defeat the dangerous Designs of our Enemies, equally

Vol. 38.

prejudicial to the real Interests of America and to those of Great Britain.

We will not fail to resume the great and momentous Consideration of the State and Condition of the Dominions and Revenues which this Country possesses in the East Indies; and we trust that, in our Deliberations on those important Matters, we shall proceed with the same Spirit and Temper in which they were begun, and with the same Care and Anxiety to consider how those remote Provinces may be held and governed with the greateftSecurity and Advantage to this Nation, anti by what Means the Happiness of the Native Inhabitants may be belt promoted.

In this arduous Conjuncture, we consider it as onr First Duty to our Country, to grant Your Majesty such Supplies as the Circumstances of Affairs shall be found to require. We cannot but feel that the War 'is burthensome and expensive; but we are convinced, at the same Time, that it is just and necessary; and nothing on our Parts shall be wanting, to give Efficacy and Success to the Valour of Your Majesty's Fleets and Armies; and we dill have a firm Confidence that, by a vigorous, animated, and united Exertion of the Resources and Faculties of the Nation, and of the Spirit of a free People, Your Majesty will be enabled, under the Protection of Divine Providence, to restate the Blessing of a safe and honourable Peace to all Your. Dominions.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and others, of the Counties of Hereford and Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Roads leading from the Willerjley Turnpike Road near Parfoti, in the County of Here-yford, to Monkland Mill, in the said County, and from the Turnpike Road on Fair Mile Field, in the Parish of Stoke Prior, in the said County, to Broad Heath, near Stamford, in the County of Worcester, from the Ford's Bridge to Stockton, and from Kyre Common to the Turnpike Road at Grendon Green, in the County of Hereford, are in a ruinous Condition, narrow, and incommodious for Travellers and Carriages, and cannot be effectually amended, widened, and kept in good Repair, by the ordinary CourseofLaw: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for amending and widening the said Roads, and for keeping the same in Repair, in such Manner, and by such Ways and Means, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Alderman Harley, Mr. Ord, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Venerts, 30° die Novembris \

Anno ii* Georgii IIIlii Regis, 1781.

Prayers.

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His, Majesty Yesterday with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most Gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return you My cordial Thanks for this very loyal, dutiful, and affectionate Address. It breathes the Spirit and Firmness of the Representatives of a brave and free People. Nothing could afford Me so much Satisfaction, or tend so effeAnally to the Public. Safety and Welfare in the present Conjuncture.

Memorandum:

By an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act for establishing an Agreement with the United Company of Merchants of England, " trading to the East Indies, Sc. He."

The East India Company are required to pay a certain Sum of Money, which is specified in the said Act, in Proportion to the Number of Troops lent, or to be sent, to the East Indies, on the Requisition of the said Company: This Sum the said Company claim, under the Words of the Act, a Right of paying in the East Indies only. And as it will be necessary to advance Subsistence for Six Months to the Troops now going to the East Indies, and to provide for the Subsistence of the Recruiting Companies remaining in Great Britain, there will be wanting at present for these Purposes the Sum of £. 36,280. tot. $d. which it will be necessary to vote on Account of the said Estimate.

William Tioopeny, Junior, being examined, said, That

the Trustees have proceeded in the Execution of the said Act, and have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money upon the Credit of the said Act, which has been expended according to the Directions thereof: That the Sum of fi. 3,500 now remains due; which Money

To prove the Allegations of the said last mentioned Petition, the said Act of the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty was read: And,

The said William Tioopenybeing further examined, said. That there is a very steep high Hill, called Hill, in the said Road between and

and that it would be of great Benefit and Safety to Travellers if the Course of the fai l Road was altered, so as to avoid the said Hill; but that the Tolls arising by virtue of the said last mentioned Act, are not sufficient to defray the Expence of making such Alteration, and of carrying the Act into Execution.

And the Witness further said. That if the Course of the Road at Boxley Hill was altered as before-mentioned, many Personstravelling between London and Maidstone might be induced to pass through who at

present do not chuse to travel that Road on account of Boxley Hill; whereby the Tolls collected upon the Road between Rochester and Chalk would be increased.

That the Trustees acting under the last mentioned Act, have made Application to the Trustees acting under the first-mentioned Act, and represented to them the great public Utility of altering the Course of the Road as aforesaid, and the Benefit that might arise to the Road under their Care by such Alteration; alleging, at the same Time, that they were unable to defray the Expence attending that Work. And the Witness added. The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great for the Ser-

vice of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-two;

Ordered, That it be au Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause of Credit!

Ordered, That it bean InfiruClion to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause to make good the Deficiency of the Land Tax of the Year 1780, out of the Supplies granted for the Year 1-782.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Ord took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker refuined the Chair.

Mr. Ord reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

The other Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for continuing and granting to His Majesty certain Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-two j

Ordered, That it be an Inflru6iion to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause of Credit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they have Power to receive a Clause to direct that the Deficiency, which shall be on the 251b Day of March 1782, of the Incomesof the Duties on Malt granted for the Year 1780, to satisfy Principal and interest charged thereupon, be made good out of the Supplies for the Y'ear 1782.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Ord took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Ord reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock,

A Petition of Chai'les Baof in the Parish of Minsterworth, in the County of

Esquire, Lord of the Manor of Minsterivorlh aforesaid, and Owner offeveral considerable Estates there, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That within the said Parish and Manor there is a Common Meadow, called Minjierworth Ham, confiding of upwards of Three Hundred Acres, over which the Owners of several Estates in the said Parish and Manor have a Eight of Common yearly, from the 14th Day of to the 13th Day of February ensuing (when the said Meadow is hained up) in certain known Proportions, ascertained at the Time when the said Commons were originally apportioned and granted out; and that there are certain other Common Rights upon the said Meadow, belonging to younger Children of Copyholders within the said Manor, called Birthrights, and others belonging to all the Owners of the Copyhold Estates there, which are called Suits; and that the said Meadow is bounded on the South by a large Reen Ditch, and on the East by the River Severn, which sometimes in Summer, in high Tides, overflows the fame, to the great Detriment of the Patture, particularly by leaving great Part of the Middle thereof, which lies lowed, very wet and swampy; and that the said Meadow is liable to great Encroachments, from beingbounded on the North and West Parts thereof by several inclosed Pasture Grounds, which have Communication therewith, and from whence, as well as from the Right of taking ©ut and exchanging Cattle, Horses, ayd Sheep, and the Gates being obliged to be open, the said Meadow is liable to be surcharged, and other Inconveniences happen; and that the Petitioner has frequently drove the said Meadow, and as frequently found it overstocked; and that, in hopes of (topping such illegal Practices, he has been engaged in divers expensive Suits at Law, and other disagreeableCircumstances have arisen therefrom; and he now finds it utterly impossible, from the Situation of the said Meadow, and from Want of knowing the Number of the Commons that are let, and the Persons to whom the same are let, totally to prevent its being furchaged; and that the Petitioner hath, at his own Expence, caused Sea Walls to be made, to prevent, in some Measure, the said Meadow being overflowed; and also permitted a large Drain to be made through some of his Lands, whereby the Value of the said Common Rights has been greatly enhanced; and that the Petitioner has Reason to believe, that the Vol. 38.

Number of Bead Pastures upon the said Meadow have, since the first Allotment thereof, been very considerably encreased, arising, as he apprehends, from some of the Estates in the Parish having been divided, and Supernumerary Commons granted, or referred, upon such Divisions and Subdivisions, which it is not in the Power of the Lord of the Manor to prevent, by reason the Freeholds are conveyed without his Privity; and that, from the great Number of Cattle turned upon the said Meadow, the Banks thereof, next the River, are greatly trod down, and the Meadow frequently overflowed, to the great Loss of the Petitioner, and others entitled to Common Rights: And that the Petitioner, exclusive of his Manerial Right, has One Half of the legal Commou Rights upon the said Meadow, which; for the Reasons before dated, he cannot always find Tenants for; and that the Property in Common Rights of much the greater Part of the other Proprietors, is too small to admit of a general Allotment and Inclosure of the said Meadow; but the Petitioner apprehends, that if au Allotment therefrom was made to him, in due Proportion to his Right, anew and very useful and fubftautial Drain might be made, and the interior Parts of the Meadow, now the most liable to be overflowed from the Severn, might be drained and improved, and all fraudulent Surcharges and Impositions in great Measure prevented,- and, by lessening so large a Proportion of Common Rights, be more easily discovered; and that the Petitioner, or Persons in Trust for him, being seised of more than Three Parts in Four of the several Copyhold Estates in the said Parish, is willing to relinquish all Personal Rights, called Birthrights, which can accrue therefrom, for the Benefit of the Commoners at large; and that the greatest Part of the Lands in the said Parish consist of very small Inclosures, and Pieces of Land very remarkably intermixed, and it would be of great Utility and Convenience, if the Proprietors thereof were enabled, when they think proper, to make Exchanges of their respective Properties therein, which at present, from the different Tenures of their Estates, some of them are unable to do: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making an Allotment to him from the said Meadow in Manner aforesaid, and for effecting the other useful Purposes above mentioned.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that the Earl of Surrey, Mr. Elwes, and Sir Codring-

ton, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of several principal Merchants, Importers Seizure of of Foreign Spirits, of the City of London, whose Names SmuggM are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and-read; Setting forth. That for the more effectual Suppression of Smuggling, the Legislature has hitherto indulged the Revenue Officers with One Half of the Grofe Produce of all Contraband Goods seized by them, and condemned in His Majesty'sCourt of Exchequer, without subjecting them to the Duties payable on the Importation of such ' Goods; and that this Regulation, salutary in the Beginning, and wifely calculated to give Efficacy to the Revenue Laws, the Petitioners now find, from the Duties exceeding very considerably the first Colt of the Goods, is productive of contrary Effects, fervingas an Encouragement and Protection to the illicit Trader, while it operates as a Clog, and is a severe Grievance imposed on. the fair and regular Merchant; and that the gradual In- . crease of Duties, particularly on Foreign Spirits, has been such, that they now amount to Four Times the real Va-. lue to the Importer, and thus the Officer has a strong and too frequently an irresistible Temptation to harass the fair Trader by unjust Seizures, because the Value of the Object gives him the Means of using corrupt Influ-. ence to delay Redress, if not to obtain Condemnation, fd that the injured Proprietor may be obliged to submit to an expensive and shameful Compromise rather than contest his Rights on unequal Grounds, the Officer fereening himself under the Name of the Crown from all Expence and Risque, should a Prosecution follow, while at the same Time the Temptation isnoless strong, and has an evident Tendency to producecollufive Bargains between the Revenue Officer and the Contraband Trader, who can thus carry on his Business with Certainty and Profit at the Expence of the Revenue, and with every Advantage over the regular Merchant that corrupt Officers, by Prostitution of their Powers, can give to protest the one, and distress the other; and that the easy and obvious Remedy for this Grievance is to pass a Law, fub-jeding all Spirits seized and condemned in the Court of Exchequer to be font into the King's Stores as the sole Property of His Majesty, and Ten jier Cent, to be paid to the Officer on the estimated Value, which would be sufficient to induce those who aft uprightly to discharge

From the House of Commons, the 20th December 1781.

SIR,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to acquaint you, That you are, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same, to attend their Service in Parliament on Monday the 21st Day of January next; and you are to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what yon have done thereon, upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure of the said House.

I am. Sir,

Your humble Servant,

C. W. Cornwall, Speaker.

From the House of Comtnons, the 20th December 1781.

My Lord,

I am commanded by the House of Commons to desire your Lordship, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Members of Parliament for the Cinque Ports, to attend their Service in Parliament on Monday the 21 ft Day of January next; your Lordship will also be pleased to give me an Account of the Re ceipt of this, and what you have done thereon.

I am, with the utmost Respect,

My Lord,

Your Lordship's Mod humble and obedient Servant,

C.IV. Cornwall, Speaker, To the Right honourable Frederick Lord North, Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports.

A Petition,

22 Geo. III. ao* Decembris — 21 629

rtition of A Petit ion, purporting to be the Representation arid Hcnry Prayer of Henry Laurens, a Native of South Carolina,

.aurens. forne Time recognized by the Commissioners in America by the Style and Title of " His Excellency " Henry Laurens, President of Congress," now a close JPrisoner in the Tower of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Representer, for many Years, at the Peril of his Life and Fortune, ardently laboured toprelerve and lirengthen the ancient Friendship between Great Britain and the Colonies, and

that in no Instance he ever excited, on either Side, the Hilfentions which separated them; that the Commencement of the present War was a Subject of great Grief to him, in as much as he foresaw and foretold, in Letters now extant, the Distrefies which both Count lies experience at this Day , that, in the Rife and Progress of the War, he extended every Act of Kindness in his Power to Persons called Loyalists and Quietills, as well as to British Prisoners of War, very ample Proofs of which he can produce; that he was captured on the American Coast, first landed upon American Ground, where he saw Exchanges of british and American Prisoners in a Course of Negotiation, and that such Exchanges and Enlargements upon Parole ave mutually and daily practised in America ;that he was committed to the Tower on the 6th October 1780, being then dangerously ill; that in the mean Time he has in many Respects, particularly by being deprived (with very little Exception) of the Visits and Confutations of his Children, and other Relations and Friends, suffered under a Degree of Rigour almost, if not altogether, unexampled in in modern British History*, that, from Jong Confinement, the Want of proper Exercise, and other obvious Causes, his bodily Health is greatly impaired, and that he is now in a languifhingState: And therefore praying, That the House will condefceiid to take his same into Consideration, and, under proper Conditions and Restrictions, grant him Enlargement, or such other Relief as to the Wisdom and Benignity of the House shall seem fitting.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

And then the House adjourned till Monday the 21 ft Day of January next. Ten of the Clock in the Morning.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, Over-seers, and Inhabitants of fVoodbridge, in the County of Suffolk, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the present Workhouse in the said Town, on Account of the late grfeat Increase of Poor, is not large enough to enable the Petitioners to maintain and provide for the Poor with that Comfort and Wholesomeness which is reqnifite, and stands in so confined a Site that the same Cannot be enlarged so as to make a Workhouse suitable to contain the Poor of the said Parish; and that there are fevtetal Houses belonging to the said Parish, wherein Paupers have been permitted to dwell Rent free, which are in a very ruinous and decayed State; and that the Petitioners are desirous, but not able, to build a suitable Workhouse for their Poor, unless they are permitted 16 borrow on the Security of the Poor Rates within the said Parish, a Sum not exceeding Two thousand Pounds, as also to dispose of the present Workhouse, and the Houses wherein the Paupers are permitted to dwell as aforesaid, and to apply the Money arising therefrom towards building such suitable Workhouse; and that the Petitioners, being willing to improve the said Town of Wood are desirous that the same may be lighted at thegeueral Expence of the Occupiers of Houses within the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Ceave may be given to bring in a Bill to incorporate the said Parish of Woodbridge by the Stile of " The (-Juardiaos of the Parish of " bridge, in the County of Suffolk $" and that there may

and to erect a suitable Workhouse and proper Out-Buildings and Offices thereon, and for that Purpose to borrow, on the Security of the Poor Rates within the said Parish, a Sum of Money, not exceeding Two thousand Pounds, at any Rate of Interest not exceeding Five* Pounds per Centum per Annum, or other legal Rate of Interest, and to sell and dispose of the present Workhouse, and such other Houses with the Appurtenances belonging to the Parish of Woodbridge, as in the said Bill shall be particularly mentioned, and to apply the Money arising therefrom towards building a suitable Workhouse, and proper Out-Buildings and Offices thereto, for the Use of the Parish of Woodbridge, and with such other Clauses and Regulations as the House shall think meet; and that there may be inserted in such Bill one or more Clauses to enable the said Guardians to light up the said Town of Woodbridge with Lamps, to be affixed on the Houses or other convenient Places within the said Parish; and that the Charge thereof may be raised by Rate, to be made by the said Guardians on the Occupiers of Houses in the said Parish, or otherwise, as the House shall think fit and proper.

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, in Common Council assembled, Fiihm, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That by an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the better Support and Establishment of the Greenland and Whale Fishery, the former Bount ies, granted by an Act: of Parliament for the Encouragement of the Greenland or Whale Fishery, were declared to cease, and to be no longer paid or allowed, except in such Cases only where special Provision was made for the same by the then present Act; and that the Petitioners cannot conceal their Apprellensions, that if a less Bounty than Forty Shillings per Ton be granted, it would render ineffectual the Views of the Legislature, in making those salutary Provisions for the Encouragement of the Whale Fishery, and, as a necessary Consequence, would greatly prejudice so important and ufefuJ a Branch of Trade, the Petit ioners having Cause to fear that, on Account of the Rupture between Great Britain and the Belligerent Powers, the Navigation to the Greenland Seas and Davis's Streights will be attended with more Peril than

heretofore, and will consequently require a Bounty of Forty Shillings /«?rTon: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant such Relief as the Nature of the same may require.

A Petit ion of the Guild or Brotherhood of Masters pb, and Pilots, Seamen of the Trinity House of Kingston upon Hull, under their Common Seal, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That for the Support and Establishment of the Greenland and Whale Fishery, a Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton upon the Shipping employed in that Trade was granted by an Act passed in the Eleventh \rear of Mis present Majesty's Reign; and that, through the Operation of the said salutary Law, the Whale Fishery has been brought to a very flourishing State, great Quantities of Oil and Bone have been brought into these Kingdoms, and many Hundred Seamen have been bred and trained; but, by the Provisions of the said Act, the aforesaid Bounty in the Year 17)6 became reduced to Thirty Shillings, and is now no more than Twenty Shillings, per Ton; and that the Petitioners conceive, the principal Object of the Legislature, in parting the said Law, was the Increase of Shipping, and the Training of Seamen; and they trust that, at a Time like t he present, ‘ the House will fee the Expediency of giving every due Encouragement to such Considerations as these, and not suffer such a Branch of beneficial Commerce, and the Nursery for Seamen attendant thereupon, to cease, which from the Knowledge the Petitioners have of Maritime Matters, and the great Discouragements the Owners of Ships employed in the said Fisheries at this critical Juncture labour under from the Advance of Seamen's Wages and Insurances, they are but too well convinced will be the Cafe, unless revived and supported by the Aid of a sufficient Bounty: And therefore praying the House to take this Matter into their serious Consideration, and to pass a Law, that the aforesaid Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton upon Shipping using the Whale Fishery to Greenland, Davis's Streights, and the Seas adjacent, may be again granted for a limited Time, or to give such Relief in the Premises as the Nature of the same may require, and to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders of the Port of Liverpool, in Behalf of themselves and others,

especially ofthofe who are imtnediately interested in the Wliale Fishery to GreenlandDavis's and the

That the former Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton may be again granted for a limited Time upon Shipping employed in the Whale Fishery to Greenland, and the Seas adjacent, or that such other adequate Relief may be granted as the House shall judge meet.

Whale A Petition of the Merchants, Ship Owners, and Khery. Traders, of the Port of Kingston upon on Behalf of

themselves and others, particularly those who are immediately interested in the Whale Fishery, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton, granted by Parliament Upon Shipping employed in the Fisheries to Greenland, Davis's Streights, and the Seas adjacent, was the Means of bringing that Trade to a very flourishing State at the said Port of Kingston upon Hull, where several large Ships have been fitted out for those Seas, and great Quantities of Oil and Whalebone imported, and which has afforded a considerable Nursery for Seamen; and that the Petitioners hare teen with Concern, that the Reduction of the said Bounty, which took place in the Year 1777, lessened the Number of Ships employed in those Fisheries, and they are but too well convinced, that without a Parliamentary Aid and Encouragement the said Fisheries will entirely cease, and an End be put to a Trade of no lets Importance to the Nation in general than advantageous to the Individuals that are concerned therein; and that, ifthe Establishment and Support of the said Trade merited the Attention of the Le-giftature m Time of Peace, the Petitioners conceive, tint at such a Crifisas the present, when feme Branches of the Maritime Trade are entirely loft to these Kingdoms, others rapidity decreasing, and the above-mentioned Fisheries carried on at a much greater Expence than of late, on account of the prodigious Advance in Seamens Wages and Inferences, and particularly when the Exigencies of the State demand a constant Supply of Seamen, no Object is more deserving of a National Bounty than the Whale Fisheries: And therefore praying the House to take this important Matter into their serious Consideration, and to pass a Law, that the aforesaid Bounty of Forty Shillings per Ton upon Shipping employed in the Whale Fishery to Greenland, Davis's Streights, and the Seas adjacent, may be again granted for a limited Time, or to give such other Relief in the Premises as the Nature of the same may require, and to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Support and Efta-f. blifiiiueut of the Greenland and Whale Fishery."

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Mer- Turkey chants of England trading into The Levant Seas, being Company, offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read}

Setting forth. That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has for a long Series of Years been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that in Order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protest His Majesty'sSubjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary, that an Ambassador should be sent from England to reside at Conj and that Consuls, Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, should be established in the other Parts of Turkey where Brit iff Subjects reside, and where the English Merchants carry on Trade, the whole Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company, which, together with many other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on of this Trade, has of late Years amounted to about Nine thousand Pounds per Annum-, and that the Trade to and from Turkey, once so flourishi ng, is now, from many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance granted to the Petitioners in the last Session of Parliament has enabled them to support their Expences for the past Year, but the Petitioners are sensible they should not discharge the Duty incumbent on them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public (for whom they1 consider themselves as Trustees) if they did not, in the present Situation of the Trade, declare their Inability to support their necessary Expences unlessrelieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as may be thought necessary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That your Petitioners are impelled by the dangerous Situation to which this Kingdon is reduced by the imprudent Administration of Public Affuirk, to apply to this honourable House, to remedy those Evils which they feel and apprehend in common with the other Branches of the British Empire: The rapid Decline of our Manufactures, and the Annihilation of a very large Proportion of our Commerce, afford your Petitioners just Reason to dread, that if a Conduct similar to that by which they have been deprived of these Advantages be (till pursued, the ftnall Portion left them will not long be retained: Deeply interested as Your Petitioners are in the Welfare and Safety of those of His Majesty's Colonies which still continue to be Members of the British Dominions* they tremble for the dangerous Situation in which they stand, as in their Separation from His Majesty's Government would be involved the total Ruin of the only important Branch of Commerce now remaining to them: In this debilitated State, prested by the accumulated Weight of the Public Expence, they cannot avoid anticipating the additional Burthens which a Continuation of the present fatal and ruinous System must unavoidably bring upon them: Your Petitioners, therefore, humbly request this honourable House would adopt such Measures as its Wisdom may suggest, for enabling His Majesty to put an End to the unnatural, unfortunate, and expensive War in America, and for producing a radical Alteration in the Management of the Public Adairs, by which alone the Evils impending over us and our Posterity can be averted.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut or Canal from ham to BUftone, and from thence to Autherley, there to communicate with the Canal now making between the Rivers Severn'and Tren; and for making Colla-

tcifel Cuts tip^tro several Coal Mines:" And also,

An Act, passed in the Ninth Year of His said Majesty, to rectify a Mistake in the lait-mentioned Act, and to explain and amend the fame; were read. And, John Meredith, Esquire, Clerk to the said Company of Proprietors, being examined, said. That in pursuance of the Powers granted by the said Acts, the Proprietors have completed the said Navigation; and in the Execution thereof, passed through various large Coal Mines and Limestone Quarries, and have since discovered, that there are several other Tracts of Land Dear to the said Canal and Collateral Cuts, in which Vol. 38;

there are large and valuable Mines of Coal and Lime-stone, but to which the said Proprietors cannot, by their present Powers, extend the said Canal or Collate* ral Cuts.

That it would tend greatly to the Interest of the several Land Owners where such last mentioned Mines and Quarries lie, and be of great Benefit to the Town of Birmingham, and of public Uiility, if the Proprietors Were empowered to extend the said Canal from that Part of ofte of the said Collateral Cuts leading to Wednesbury Holloway, which lies near to a certain House called The Brick House, situate in the Parish of West Bromwich, in the said County of Stafford, by or near a certain Messuage called Willingsworth Hall, and from thence to or near a certain Fire Engin,e called zca/er Engine, with Six small Collateral Cuts from the same, to communicate with the Lands in which such new Mines and Quarries lie.

And the Witness further said. That the said Proprietors are desirous, at their own Expence, to make and execute such Collateral Branches, upon being allowed the same Tonnage, pro rata, for the Distance of such Extension, and upon being granted the same *

Powers and Authorities as were allowed them in respect of the said Canal and Collateral Cuts, already made.

And he added. That some of the Powers granted by the said Acts have been found insufficient for the Purposes intended, there not being a Power adequate for the Punishment of small Offences.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Proprietors of the Birmingham Canal Navigation to make and maintain an Extension of Canal from the Parish of West Bromwich to Broadwater Fire Engine, and to make Six small Collateral Cuts from the lame, to lead to several Coal Mines: And that Sir Robert Lawley, Sir George Shuckburgh, and the Lord Lewi/ham, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

settle^ as a Merchant in the Island of Saint Eufiatius, Euftai"H where he resided, with few and short Intervals of Ab« fence, ever since the Year 1756,) and that he carried on a reputable and extensive Trade until, on the Surrender of that Island, without Resistance, to Sir George Rodney and General Vaughan, he came under the Protection of His Majesty's Government; and that, after haying delivered in an Inventory of his Effects, in Obedience to the Proclamation published by the Commanders in Chief, on a Sudden, without any Crime on his Part, either charged, or (as he is since informed) even suspected, he received Notice, without One Day's Delay to quit the Island, where he had been settled Twenty-five Years, where his whole Substance was (edged, and

and {hat the Petitioner has no other Resource in his Misfortunes, than to lay a State of them before the House of Commons, and is confident, that the Humanity of the House will not be turned alide from attending to his great and unmerited Sufferings, on a Supposition that the Laws are open to him, and that if he is injured, he may pursue his Remedy in the ordinary Course of Justice; and that the Petitioner, unacquainted as he is with the Laws, a Foreigner, and unable to procure Advice, is much in Doubt whether the Laws apply to his Cafe, which he apprehends to be uncommon, and of a complicated Nature; and lie moll Imfinbly implores the House to recoiled, that he is despoiled <5f all he had, that therefore, if he Were willing, he is totally destitute of the Means to procure himself Justice; and that the Petitioner is therefore confident, that his Sufferings will not tie aggravated by being sent to a Remedy which he wants the Means of obtaining; and that in their great Goodness they will reflect, that if he had the ordinary legal Means, or Money to purchase them, yet the Process must be long, and it would be hard to condemn him to 1‘pend the Remainder of his declining and dispirited Age in a vain Struggle with Sir George Rodney and General Vaughan, who, by One Ad of Injustice and Oppression, have, in One Hour, acquired his whole Substance, and are enabled to defend their Wrong by the Consequence'of the Wrong itself; Mr. Cornelius Arep being then examined, said, That he is a Sadler, and lives in the Haymarlcel; that he has dealt with Mrs. Wharctm for her Patent Stirrups, and thinks the Invention very tifefu! to the Public. And the Witness further said, That he believes if the making of the Stirrups was to come into the Hands of the common Smiths, they could not be depended upon so well as they are at present.; and he farther added, that lie has heard of Persons being preferred from Danger by Means of the Stirrup.

Mr. David Polock being examined, said, That he is a Sadler, and lives in Piccadilly; he is in Partnership with Mr. Vaughan, Sadler to the Prince of Wales — That lie is acquainted with the Invention of the Patent Saddle Stirrup* made by Mrs. Wharam — That it is esteemed very useful, and he knows several Persons have been preferred from the Danger arising from the Foot hanging in the Stirrnp, by the Means of the Use of them — That he knows particularly of One Instance of the Utility of them, which is, of his Grace the Duke of Buccleugh, who having had the Misfortune to be thrown from his Horse, and his Foot hanging in the Stirrup, he was preserved from the Danger, by Means of Mrs-; Wharam s Stirrup, which disengaged him from the Saddle.

S«rem A Petition of the Fishermen in the Town and Neigh-Filbcryj bourhood of Upton upon Severn, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of an Act, passed in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act forlhe " better Preservation of Fish, and regulating the Fisheries, " in the Rivers Severn and Vcrnieu and Setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, for the Preservation of Spawn and Fry of Fish, the Meihes of Nets used in the River Severn are required to be Two Inches and an Half wide; and that by another Act, pafl'ed in the Twentieth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for Preservation of Fish in the River Severn, the Size of the Mefliesas limited by the said Act of the First of Queen Elizabeth, is confirmed, and Provision made against fishing with Nets in the River Severn below Gloucester Bridge of more than Sixty Yards in Length, and above Gloucester Bridge, of more than Fifty Yards in Length, to Ripple Jjock Stake, near Upton upon Severn, in the County of Worcester, and from thence up the River, of Twenty Yards in Length; and that after reciting in the Preamble of the said Act of the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, " that before the Navigation of the said River below Gloucester Bridge w as " increased to the Degree it now is, there were many " Weares in the said River, whereby the Passage of " Fish up the said River was confined, and Nets of " the limited Length were then sufficient for the Purpose of taking Fish; and that the said River was in many Places below Gloucester Bridge then greatly " widened, and continued Yearly widening by frequent " Floods and by violent Tides, which washed away the u Banks of both Sides of the said River, and were " liable so to do at different and uncertain Places; and *4 that Nets of a greater Length were absolutely necef-Me fary for the taking of Fish in the said River," so much of the said Acts of the First of Elizabeth and Thirtieth of Charles the Second, as relates to the Size of Melli and the Length of Net, is repealed; and by the same Act, Nets are allowed below Gloucester of Twice Vol. 38.

the Breadth of the River, and above Gloucester Nets of different Lengths, viz. from Gloucester to Ripple Loch Stake Seventy-five Yards, and above Ripple Lock Stake, where there are no Shoals, Forty Yards, and where there are Shoals, Twenty Yards only; and the Meihes of such Nets, in the Months of February, March,

April, and May, are required to be One Inch and Three Eighths wide only, and in the Months of November,

December, January, June, and July, Two Inches and an Half wide, and all other Nets are prohibited; and, by the said Act, all Manner of Fishing, except Angling, is prohibited in the Months of AlignJl, September, and October; and that by the same Act, no Person is allowed to fish or use any Nets in the Fords, Streams, and Shallows of the said River, between the Tenth Day of March and the Twentieth Day of May, nor any Person above Ripple Lock Stake to fish in the Night, viz. after Sun-Setting and before Sun-Rising; which said several Regulations the Petitioners conceive to be injurious to them and the County of Worcester in general: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that so much of the said Iaft-mentioned Act as relates to the Length of Net and Size of Mefli, and prohibiting fishing with Nets in the River Severn in the Months of August, September, and October, and the fishing on Fords, Streams, and Shallows of the said River between the Tenth Day of March and the Twentieth Day of May, may be repealed; and if it shall be thought necessary to prohibit the catching of Salmon in Worcestershire in any Part of the Year, that the Time of such Prohibition may be shortened from Three Months to One Month; and that free Liberty may be restored to the Petitioners, and all other Persons, to fish at all Seasons of the Year in the said River Severn, without incuring any Penalty, except as Possessors of Salmon during the Prohibition; and that a more equal Provision may be made for regulating the Length of Nets to be used in the said River, and which the Petitioners conceive should be somewhat more than the Breadth of the River where the same are respectively to be used, and that the Mefli of such Nets may not be less than Three Inches; and that all Persons below Ripple Lock St.ake, as well as those above, may be prohibited fishing in the Night Time, or that all Persons above as well as those below Ripple Lock Stake may be permitted to fish in the Night Time; and that the Petitioners may have such further Relief in the Premises, as the House shall think just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr Foley, Mr. Lygon, &c:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Mr. Walter Churchey being examined, said. That the

Trustees under the said Act have regularly put the same in Execution, and have made a considerable Progress in repairing the said Roads; in doing which, the Tolls, together with a large Sum of Money borrowed on the Credit thereof, have been duly expended:

That the Trustees have always, br virtue of the Powers for that Purpose in the said Act contained, considered and managed the said Roads as fepaiate and dif-tinct Districts; that they have accordingly borrowed Money on each respectively, independent of the other; that the Whole being under One Set of Trustees, Dif-putes have from Time to Time arisen about the apportioning of the Income, and Difficulties have often occurred in the Execution of the Act, from the Whole of the Roads being under One Set of Trustees and having only One Clerk; for which Reasons it is expedient that each District should be under a separate Act of Parliament:

That the Money borrowed as aforesaid is Hill due, to the Amount of£.1,800 on the Breconshire District, and £.2,100 on that of Herefordshire and that the same cannot be paid off, and the Roads effectually amended and kept in Repair, without the further Alftftance of Parliament, as the Act will expire at the End of the present Session.

Hugh Bold, Esquire, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence; and added. That it is the Willi of the Creditors of the Brecon/hir District, to have those Roads repaired by a separate Act of Parliament.
