A Petition of Richard Arkwright, of Cromford, in the County of Derby, Cotton M anpfacturer, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner, after many Years intense Study and painful Application, and after a great Variety of repeated Experiments, invented, about the Year 1768, a Machine, or Machines, for making Cotton into Yarn in a more expeditious as well as in a very different Manner from any Invention that had preceded it, and in the Prosecution of his Experiments expended considerableSums of Money, and in the Year 1769 obtained a Patent for his said Invention; and that the Petitioner conceiving that his said Invention was capable of considerable Improvements, did, after several Years further Study and Alfiduity, improve the Principles of his said Invention, and, after a large additional Expence inenrred therein, brought the same to a greater Degree of Perfection, and also invented Machines for preparing the Cotton for Spinning, by a much less expensive and much more expeditious Method than had been before pursued, for which Improvements and further Invention, he also obtained a Patent in the Year 1775; and that the Petitioner has, with his Partners, in Consequence of the said Patents, expended the Sum of £. 30,000 and upwards, in Buildings and other necessary Works, in order to carry the said Manufactory into complete Execution, over and above the Labour and Expence of instructing and training up many Thousand poor Persons, of different Ages as well as Sex, in a Knowledge of the said Manufactory; and that by the Introduction of the said Machines, the Cotton is prepared, and made into Yam, with great Facility and Expedition, and the Twill or Thread is of a superior Nature and Excellency to any that was ever before produced; hence the Manufacturer is enabled to fell in Foreign Markets, the Calicoe Business, which pronaifes to be of the greatest Importance to this Kingdom, has been introduced, many Thousand Persons are now (who were not before) employed in this Manufactory, and earn a comfortable Maintenance, and great and essential Benefit has of Consequence resulted to the Public; and that the Petitioner has, together with his Partners, in the Course of carrying on and establi firing his laid Manufactory, fullered Lpfles V*t. 38.

to the Amount of Four Or Five thousand Pounds, by the Violence of riotous and ill-disposed Persons, who have burnt anddestroyed his Buildings and other Works erected for the Purpose of carrying on the said Manufactory; and representing to the House, that the Legislature has, in many Instances, granted to Persons, for a considerable Number of Years beyond the Terra of their Letters Patent, an exclusive Right of exercising their Inventions, which, the Petitioner submits, have been of much less Public Utility and Advantage than the Inventions which he has produced, and therefore he has presumed to apply to the House, trusting, that the Merit and Importance of his Inventions will be proved to be of such National Concern and Advantage as to entitle him to the Assistance and Support of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to extend the Term granted by the First Patent in the Year 1769, so as to make the same expire with the Term granted by the Patent in the Year 1775, as some Recompense or Satisfaction for what, he hum-hly conceives, he may call his Public Services and Sufferings, or that he may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Lord John Cavendish, the Earl of Surrey, See.: And they are to meetTo-morrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Part of the Common called Ensham Heath, in the said Parish of Ensham; to which last Proposal a great Number of Proprietors of Lands within the said Parish contented, and signed their Consents to the said Bill; and that after the Petitioners had consented to the Bill, several Amendments were made thereto, and a Clause inserted therein, to exonerate certain inclosed Lands within the said Parish, belonging to particular Persons, from all Right of Common whatever, on Payment of a small Annual Sum; and certain inclosed Lands of the Petitioners, and other Proprietors, were left still subject to a Right of Common by all the other Proprietors of Lands within the said Parish; the Purport of which Clauses had been totally rejetted by the Proprietors, on the previous Proposals made to them by the said Robert Langford; and the said Bill, with such Clause therein, was afterwards passed into a Law, and without the Knowledge, Assent, or Consent, of the Petitioners: and it was, at the Time the Bill was passing, represented to the Agent for the Petitioners, who resided in the Country, that the said Bill was passing with such Alterations only as the Petitioners Agent had made therein; and the said Clause, so inserted as aforesaid, was concealed from the Petitioners Agent; and that the Petitioners find themselves very much injured by the Clause inserted in the said Bill, for exonerating the said Lands from all Right of Common, and to which the Petitioners expressly objected, previous to the said Bill being brought in, and they have no Doubt but that, if they had not been prevented by the Means aforesaid, they should have given sufficient Evidence of the Un-reasonableness of such Clause, which they were total Strangers to till after the said Bill had passed into a Law: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to alter and repeal so much of the said Att to which the Petitioners were, by the Meaus aforesaid, total Strangers, and by which they conceive themselves aggrieved; or that the House will grant them such Relief as the Nature of their. same requires.

Petitioner, after repeated Experiments, and a very great Expence in providing and construCiing the necessary Buildings and Implements, established his said Manufactory at Maidjhme, where he has, till lately, made

The said Report is as followeth; viz.

1

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled.

The Sixth Report of the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and date, the Public Accounts ' of the Kingdom.

In pursuance of the Directions of the Act by which we are appointed, our Attention has hitherto been engaged, principally, in marking the Delay, which affects the Public Money in its Passage, either from the Pocket of the Subject into the Exchequer, or from the Exchequer, back again into the Possession of the' Person who becomes entitled to it; but of dill greater Importance to the Public, is the Diminution, it fuffors in its Progress.

Intent upon the Object pointed out to 11s by the Ad as the First for our Consideration, namely, that the Public might avail themselves, as soon as possible, of the Balances in the Hands of Accountants, we have, in the Offices that have as yet come under our Examination, applied ourselves chiefly to the Investigation of these Balances, and reported upon them with as much Expedition as we were able; adding only such Suggestions of immediate Regulation as arofc out of the Subject, and occurred to us in the Course of that Investigation, but deferring, as a Matter separate and distinct, the Execution of that Part of the Act which directs us " to report an exact State of the Fees or Gratuities paid or given in collecting, issuing, expending, and accounting for, the Public Monies, and the Authority under which such Fees and Gratuities are " paid or received."

In the Course of our Examination into the Office of 81

the Paymaster General of the Forces, we observed, in the Account of the Payments made by him out of the Deductions of Twelve Pence in the Pound, and One Day's Pay, for the Year 1778, annexed to our lad Report N* 7, a Charge of "Thirty-two thousand Five £ jmi?: hundred and Fifty-seven Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence paid for Fees at the Exchequer. So large a Sum of Fees paid by One Officer, to One Office, in One Year, demanded our Attention, and leu us to require, from this Office, the Sum Total of the Fee# paid at the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer, by the Paymaster General of the Forces, during the Year 1780; the Accounts of that Year being then under our Consideration.

iBy the Return made to that Requisition it appears, Apperaj that these Fees, in the Year 1780, amounted to Thirty- \*, nine thousand One hundred and Ninety-eight Pounds £.5;,4. Six Shillings and Ten Pence; and I hat they consistedof a Poundage on the Money issued.

As the Annual Supplies, laftYear, exceeded that of all former Years, and may increase, and all Poundage Fees on those Supplies will increase in proportion, we thought it incumbent upon us to proceed to an immediate Examination into the Article of Fees, and of the Principles upon which they are founded; to the Intent, that, should they be deemed a Subject worthy the Interpofttion of the Legislature, the Public may not remain without the Benefit of a speedy Remedy for a pressing and increasing Evil.

We have had under our Examination Two Offices of large Public Expenditure; the Pay Office of the Navy, and the Pay Office of the Army: To each of these we issued our Precepts for an exa-A State of the Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities, received by the respective Officers and Clerks in those Offices, from the 24th of December 1779 to the 25th of December 1780, with the Amount thereof received by each Officer and Clerk during the said Period.

To the several Branches of the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer, that is to say, to the Auditor, the Clerk of the Pells, the Tellers, the Chamberlains, the Usher, and the Paymasters of Exchequer Bills, we issued the like Precepts; and Returns were made to us from all these Offices.

We have thought it expedient, in the Course of this Inquiry, where the Office is not executed by the Principal Officer, but by his Deputy or First Clerk, to examine the latter only, as probably bell qualified to give us the Information we wanted; we have omitted likewise, as more minute than necessary, to examine those inferior Officers and Clerks, who receive small Salaries only, or inconsiderable Fees.

As our Account of the Emoluments of these Offices is taken in a Year of the moll expensive W'ar, we have required, and dated where we have been able to obtain it, the net Produce of each Office in Time of Peace.

At the Close of our Examination into each Office, we have Hated, and inserted in the Appendix, an Account of the Salaries, Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities, distinguished under their several Heads, and the Total Amount thereof received by each Officer and Clerk in that Office, with the Sums paid for Taxes and other Disbursements, and the net Produce to each Officer and Clerk during the Year 1780; and dist, as far as appeared to us, without entering into too long an Examination, to what Amount each Office is a Charge upon the Public, the Civil List, and Individuals; but we mud at the same Time remark, that most of the Sums for Fees and Gratuities dated by us as paid by Individuals, are ultimately paid by, and a Charge upon, either the Civil List or the Public; this latter Distinfction we have made, not considering the Interest of the Crown as separate from the Interest of the Public, but because the Savings, if such there llionld be, will in' the one same foil into the Fund appropriated for the

We have distingniflied the Taxes paid by the Officers, that is, the Land Tax, and the One Shilling and Sixpenny Duties, from their other Disbursements; because the Charge of the Public in supporting these Offices is lessened by as much of these Taxes as get back again into the Exchequer; but not being able easily to discover what Diminution they suffer in their Progress, we have only dated the Amount of them, without deducting them from the Expence of the Public. r° 2. From the Return of the Pay Office of the Navy, and

f° g. from the Examinations of the Right Honourable

[° 4. Ellis, Treasurer of the Navy; Andrew , Esqu ire,

f° 5. his Paymaster; John Slade, Esquire, First Clerk in the 1° 6. Cashier's Branch; Adam Esquire, FirllClerk in ! 7. the Pay Branch; George , Esquire, Cashier;

8, Mr. John Fennell, Chief Clerk, and Mr. Robert,

Second Clerk in the Victualling Branch; we obtained the following Information relative to the Profits accruing to the Officers and Clerks in this Office.

The Business in the Pay Office of the Navy is trans-aCled by the Treasurer, the Paymaster, and Thirty-five Officers and Clerks, Nine of which are in the Cashier's Branch, Twenty in the Pay Branch, and Six in the Victualling Branch.

The Profits of these Officers coufift of Six Heads: — Salaries; Allowances for extra Service, and for telling Money at the Bank; Perquisites of odd Pence; for casting Defalcations; and for entering Probates and other Instruments.

The Treasurer and his Paymaster are paid by Salaries only, and have no other Fee or Gratuity whatever; the Officers and Clerks receive Salaries, and also the Allowances and Perquisites above mentioned.

The Treasurer is appointed by the Crown, and holds if. a,coo. his Office during Pleasure; he receives a Salary of Two thousand Pounds a Year, reduced, by the Payment of £ j,8jo. the One Shilling and Six-penny Duties, to Eighteen hundred and Fifty-Pounds: he appoints the Paymaster, and all the other Officers and Clerks in the Office.

£. 500. The Paymaster has a Salary of Five hundred Pounds

£ 46a, io. a Year, reduced by the same Duties to Four Hundred and Sixty-two Pounds Ten Shillings; he executes also the Offices of Cashier and Accountant, for which he receives no additional Salary or Emolument whatever.

The Salaries of the other Officers and Clerks are from Forty to Eighty Pounds a Year, according to their several Employments; besides which they have the Allowances and Perquisites following:

An Allowance for extra Service, which is made to those Clerks who attend the Payment of Wages and the Yards, and who complete, what are called the Full Books for Payment of the Ships and Yards; this Allowance is intended to defray their travellingExpences, and as a Recompence for their extra Trouble; the Rate at which it is paid is Seven Shillings a Day for the Number of Days in which each Clerk is so employed.

An Allowance for telling Money at the Bank is a Poundage, at the Rate of Five Shillings for every Thousand Pounds, allowed by the Navy Board to those Clerks who receive Money at the Bank for the Payment of the Ships and Yards; inConsequence of which Allowance, each Clerk is accountable for any Deficiency there may be either in the Weight or Tale of the Money he receives.

The odd Pence is a Perquisite to those Officers and Clerks who are employed in making Payments; those whole Business it is to pay Perfect Bills, the Navy Course, and Bills drawn by the Navy and Sick and 1 lurt Boards, pay the even Money only upon these Bills, and retain to themselves the odd Pence under a Shilling; those who are employed in the Payment of the Officers, Seamen, and Artificers in the Dock Yards, retain the odd Pence under Six Pence; ill Consideration ' VOL. .38.

of which they are all bound to make good any Mistakes they may make in their Payments.

The Perquisite for casting Defalcations is a Gratuity, nfually at the Rate of One Guinea by the hundred Pounds, paid by the Chaplains, Surgeons, and Pnrfers of the Navy, to the Officer who calls and Pays to them their several Shares of the Deductions made from the Seamen's Wages.

The Perquisite for entering Probates of Wills, Letters of Administration, and Warrants of Attorney, is a Fee of Two Shillings and Six Pence each Entry, paid to the Clerk in whose Department it lies to register these Instruments.

The Salaries and Allowances for extra Service, and for telling Money at the Bank, are paid, for the most Part, Quarterly, by Bills assigned by the Navy or Victualling Boards upon the Treasurer, out of Money received by him, either to pay Salaries, or from old Stores, or under some other Head of Service specified in the Assignments; and consequently all these are paid by the Public.

The Perquisites are either detained out of Sums due to particular Persons, or paid by those who apply to have their Business transa&ed at the Office; and therefore do not come out of the Public Purse, but from the Pockets of Individuals.

The Authority upon which the Receipt of the several Profits of this Office is grounded) is either an Order of the Privy Council, or Usage.

By an Order of the Privy Council, dated the 25th of May 1699, the Salary of the Treasurer of the Navy is settled at Two thousand Pounds a Year; that of his Paymaster, at Five hundred Pounds; that of his Accountant, at Four hundred Pounds; and the Salaries of '1 hirteen Clerks, Seven at Eighty Pounds each, and Six at Forty Pounds each; and in the ordinary Estimate of the Navy, voted by Parliament every Year, are inserted Allowances, to the Treasurer of the Navy Two thousand Pounds; to his Paymaster and Cashier Five hundred Pounds; to Twenty-two Clerks, Six of them Eighty Pounds, Nine Fifty Pounds, and Seven Forty Pounds each: But an Increase of the Business in this Office for these late Years, has rendered it necessary to increase the Clerks to the present Number, Thirty-five; and to every Increase the Consent of the Navy Board is necessary.

The Allowances and Perquisites are such as have been usually paid and taken by the Officers and Clerks in their several Departments, as far back as the Memory of the oldest Officers now employed in this Office reaches.

From the Account set forth in the Appendix it appears, that the Gross Amount of the Emoluments received in the Pay Office of the Navy was Eight thousand One hundred and Fifty PoundsTen Shillings and a Halfpenny; of which the Salaries, Allowances for extra Service, and for telling Money at the Bank, amounting to Six thousand Five hundred and Forty-five Pounds Four Shillings and Eight Pence, was paid by the Public; and the Residue, being One thousand Six hundred and Five Pounds Five Shillings ancf Four Pence Halfpenny, by Individuals; the Nett Receipt of this Office was Seven thousand Nine hundred Thirty-eight Pounds and a Halfpenny.

This Office consists of the Paymaster General, his Deputy, a Cashier, an Accountant, a Ledger Keeper, a Computer of Off-reckonings, a Cashier of HalfPay, and an Entering Clerk with Eight inferior Clerks, an Office Keeper, a House Keeper, and Two Messengers; and Nine Deputy Paymasters abroad.

The Paymaster General appoints his Deputies, and all the Officers and Clerks employed in his Office: They are all paid by Salaries or Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities.

The Paymaster General, his Deputy, the inferior Officers and Clerks, and Deputy Paymasters Abroad, have certain Salaries or Allowances only; the Six Officers who are next to the Deputy Paymaster receive Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities.

The Paymaster General, is appointed by Letters Patent under the Great Seal, during Pleasure; he receives Four Annual Allowances as Paymaster General of the Forces, and One as Treasurer of Chelsea Hospita): The Four are, Three thousand Pounds as the particular Salary belonging to his Office, One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty Pounds for the Payment of Clerks, Six hundred Pounds for the contingent Expences of His Office, and Twenty Shillings a Day as one of the Staff upon the Establishment; the other Allowance is Twenty Shillings a Day as Treasurer of Chelsea Hospital. The Amount of these Allowances is Six thousand and Ninety-two Pounds: Out of which he paid for himself and Officers, in Taxes, Nine hundred Sixty-two Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Nine Pence; to Clerks, One thousand Seven hundred and Seven Pounds; and for the contingent Disbursements of his Office, Three hundred and Sixty Pounds Seven Shillings and Eight Pence; making together Three thousand and Thirty Pounds Seven Shillings and Five Pence, which reduced his clear Receipt to Three thousand and Sixty-one Pounds Twelve Shillings and Seven Pence.

The Fees received by these Officers are as various as the Business they execute; each has Fees peculiar to his Branch: They consist, ibme of them, of a Poundage upon the Sums contained in Warrants brought for Payment, and in Receipts; others, of certain Sums per Regiment, paid either annually or upon transacting particular Branches of the Regimental Business; others of them are certain Sums for Reports, Certificates,

Receipts, Entries, or other Articles of official Business.

The Gratuities are voluntary Donations upon the Payment of Warrants, or for creating some i'rouble to the Office, and are given to the Officers of the Department where the Business is t ran fatted.

In the Exchequer, Six Offices came under our Examination; namely, the Auditor of the Receipt, the Clerk of the Pells, the Tellers, the Chamberlains, the Usher, and the Paymasters of Exchequer Bills. There are some Circumstances common to them all; Salaries or Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities, are the Heads under which may be ranged the Profits of all the Officers and Clerks.

The Gratuities are usual voluntary Donations, either from Public Offices or Individuals: The Yearly Accounts are made up to Michaelmas Eve; and therefore the Accounts of the Receipts and Payments of the Year 1780, which is the Year we are inquiring into, are made up to the Michaelmas of that Year.

In the First Five of these Offices, the Principal appoints the Deputy and Clerks. The First Four of them have Tables hung up in each Office, by which their Fees are regulated; these Fees consist either of a Poundage, or of certain Payments for particular Articles of Business transacted in each Office, and are paid by the Persons either paying in, or receiving Money out of, the Exchequer, or applying for their particular Business.

The Foundation of these Allowances and Fees, and the Authority under which they are claimed and paid, are as follows:

Upon the King's Accession aCertificate is transmitted from the Auditor's Ofiiee to the Treasury, pursuant to their Requisition, consisting of Two Lifts; one containing the several Fees, Salaries, and Allowances that have by ancient Custom, Letters Patent, Constitutions, or other Authorities, been paid to the Officers and Ministers of the Exchequer, either in Right of their Offices and Employments, or in Reward for their Services; the other containing the Fees, Salaries, or Allowances, that have been settled and allowed them for their Labour and Expence in managing and performing the Business of the Annuities payable at the Exchequer. This Certificate isfentback to the Exchequer, annexed to a Warrant directed to the Auditor, authorizing him to draw Orders or pass Debentures for paying from Time to Time, in the usual Manner, and at the accustomed Times, to the Officers, the Sums in the Certificate mentioned; the First Lift, amounting to One thousand Eight hundred and One Pounds Nine Shillings, out of the Money applicable to his Majesty's Civil Government; the other, amounting to Five thousand Nine hundred Pounds, out of the respective Funds applicable to the Payment of the Annuities.

This Warrant dates the Authority, under which the Treasury issued it, to be, as to the First Lift, either the Letters Patent, Constitutions, or Authorities, whereby the Officers hold their Employments, or the General Letters Patent dormaut (by which the King empowers them to make Variety of Payments therein described out of the Civil List); and as to the Second Lift, either the Powers given to them by the respective Acts of Parliament relative to the Annuities, or any other Power in them being.

In this Certificate are contained the Eleven Allowances paid to the Auditor: The Two first of them, amounting to Four hundred and Sixty Pounds Three Shillings and Four Pence, are in the First Lift, and paid to him in Eight of his Office: The other Nine,

makingThree thousand Three hundred and Five Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Eight Pence, are in the Second Lift, apd paid to him as a Recompence for his Trouble in the Business of the Annuities, by virtue of the Power vested in the Treasury by the several Acts, to provide for the Charges of Management.

The Fees upon the Iffiie are, A Poundage upon Money issued for certain Services, not for all Services:

In the Year 1780, the Sum on which the Poundage Fees were paid was near Eight Millions: Upwards of i.ocopn Twenty-two Millions more were issued in that Year, for £.»vwv*. which neither the Auditor, nor his Clerks, received any Fees whatever. The other Fees are, certain Payments for transacting particular Kinds of Business. All these Fees are regulated by a Table, specifying, both for the X*. 33. Auditor and his Clerks, the Rate, where it is a Poundage, otherwise the Quantum, of each Fee: This Table is for the most Part grounded upon Usage, recognized as ancient by the Barons of the Exchequer in the Year 1692, as to those Fees the subject Matter of which existed at that Time: and acquieljped in, as to those Fees the Subject Matter of which is of a Date subsequent to that Year.

By an Act, passed in the Third Year of William and Mary, the Officers of the Exchequer were prohibited from taking any other Fees, for the receiving or issuing the Supplies granted by that or any other Act of that Parliament, except such ancient and legal Fees as should be allowed to be so by the Barons of the Court of Exchequer; who were required to present to both Lloufes of Parliament, at the next Sessions, a Table of Fees, to be by them allowed as ancient and legal: The Barons, in pursuance of this Power, made a Report, containing the Table required: This Report is inrolled in the Office of the King's Remembrancer; a Copy of it is inserted in the Appendix: It comprehends the N* 34, Fees to be taken upon the Receipt and Issue of Money in the Offices of the Auditor, the Clerk of the Pells, the Tellers, and the Tally Court; and is the Rule, though the Act is long since expired, by which they are governed at this Day, except in some few Instances, where Usage, since that Report, has introduced Variations; one of which is, by the Barons Report the Whole of the Fees paid to the Officers of the Exchequer, upon the Issue of Money for the Army Services in general, was Three Halfpence in the Pound; but ever since the Year 1744, a Difference has been made between the Issue for the Ordinary and the Extraordinary Services; the Fees for the first continue at Three Halfpence; those for the latter are reduced to One Penny only in the Pound.

These Payments come out of different Funds; the Two first Allowances to the Auditor, the Treasury Allowance for the Tallies of Loan, the Wardrobe Fee, and the Allowance to the First Clerk, which is included in the First Lift of the Exchequer Certificate, are paid out of the Civil List; the other Nine Allowances are paid out of the Funds created by the several Acts, and therefore out of Public Money. U flier.

As whatever is wanted for Public Use should bepur-

chafed at the First Hand, and at as cheap a Rate as may be, we think it necessary for the Public Interestthat the Office of the Usher of the Exchequer should bedifcontinued, as expensive and unnecessary; and that every principal Officer should procureall Articles requisitefor his own Department, and for that Purpose be paid by the Public an annual Allowance proportioned to the Wants of his Office; a Method now practised in the

Paymaster General's, and in various other Offices.

The Teller's is One Office, at the Head of which are placed Four Officers, independent of each other, each presiding over his own distinct Division, but none of

them contributing to the Execution of any Part of the

Business. It is expedient, that in an Office of this Importance, some Person of Rank and Responsibility should preiide, to superintend, direct, and control the Execution, with an Appointment adequate to his Consequence and Station in the official Scale, leaving to subordinate Officers and Ministers the laborious Detail of the Execution; but no Advantage is derived to the Public from placing Four inoperative Officers at the

Head of this One Office.

Judging then as we muff do, solely by the Rule of

Public Frugality, and supposing the Nation to Hand in need of every practicable Retrenchment, and consequently to require the Reduction of every useless and expensive Office, we are led neeeffarily to conclude, that, as the Public Service receives no Assistance or Advantage from the Labours of the Tellers, and the Public Treasure will find a considerable Increase from

their Emoluments, the Public Interest requires their Number should be reduced.

Whatever Reasons there may be for continuing the se, and other Offices mentioned above; whether drawn from Policy or Expedience; as a Resource for the Reward of Services, in Preference to Pensions; or from Justice, for continuing them during the Lives of the present Possessors only, in Favour of the Rights of private Property; or whether it would be proper to change ' them again from Offices for Life to Offices during Plea-

sure; nil these are Topicks not within the Limits of our Commission, but for the Discussion of the Legislature; whose Deliberations comprehend Arguments drawn from every Source. — But, in whatever Shape they may be permitted to continue, every Reason of Prudence demands the Reduction of their Emoluments, from an Excess to a reasonable limited Standard.

There are likewise in this Office of the Tellers Four Officers, under the Denomination of Second Clerks, who are merely nominal, without Attendance, without Business, Care, or Trouble; but they have Fees, and to no inconsiderable Amount: In the Year 1780, the Total <£ s ns.* 4. of them was Five thousand Five hundred and Eighteen

Pounds Eight Shillings and Four Pence, and were either paid to, or to the Use of the Persons named to these Offices, or increased the Profits of the Tellers themselves. Whatever Pretensions a superior Officer may have to an Exemption from Duty and Service, a Sinecure is repugnant to the Idea of the Condition of a Clerk in Office, and therefore we are of Opinion, that common Sense requires the Suppression of the Offices of the Second Clerks to the Tellers.

We have ranged the Emoluments of these Offices, under the Heads of Salaries,‘Fees, and Gratuities.

From our Examination into the State of the Salaries, many of them appear to be made up of a Vaiiety, and sometimes of very small Payments, arising out of different Funds; of the inferior Clerks, several pay over, either the Whole, or Portions of their Salaries, or Fees, to increase the Profits of other Clerks; all which is contrary to that Simplicity and Regularity that ought to be observed in every Office, and may be easily corrected by a Regulation we shall hereafter propose.

The Fees are either Sums paid for transacting particular Kinds of official Business, or a Poundage: The First Sort of Fees fall, in many Cafes, very heavy upon Individuals; in some Cafes they fall upon the Public:

It would be much for the Benefit of both, as well as for the Honour of Government, that all Persons employed in the Public Service, and who mufl of Necessity have llecourse to Offices for Instructions, Instruments, and other official Business essential to the Execution of their Employments, should be furnished with all necessary Materials, and have their Business done in every Office without Fee or Reward: The Regulation herein after suggested, will, if adopted, be attended with this good Effect.

The Poundage is the most fruitful Source of Fees to 1

mod of the superior, and to some of the inferior Officers; it is a Payment, after some certain Rate in the Pound, upon the Sum received, or issued, or contained in some official Instrument made out in the Office and delivered to the Person applying.

In ancient Times, when the Transaction was an actual Delivery of Money, and that Money confiiled of Coin of various Denominations and Value, and possibly dipt, i

or of doubtful Weight, the Trouble and Attention of the Person employed in the Receipt or Payment increased with the Sum; and therefore the Poundage was a Mode of Reward that bore a Proportion to the Labour: But in these Times, when all Money Transactions are carried on, not by the Medium of Cash, not by the Tale or Weight of current Coin, but by the Substitution of Paper, by Calli Notes, Drafts, or Bills to any Amount; since the clear and cor.cife Method of the Debtor and Creditor Account has been so universally introduced to Practice, an Increase in the Magnitude of the Sums, though to a vast Amount, is the Addition of a few Figures, or of a few Entries, only; and the Increase of Trouble arising from it is too inconsiderable to be estimated. The Examination of Mr. Cow per, who attends daily at the Exchequer on the Part of the Bauk, thews us with what Ease, Perspicuity, and Exactneis, the various and most extensive Receipts and Payments of the Public Revenue are transacted there, by the Intervention of the Bank, with whom the principal Offices of Receipt, and several of the greater Accountants, keep their Cash: The Transactions there, of each Day, are carried on, not in Coin told or weighed by the Tellers, but by the Interchange of Cash Notes, or by the bare Entries of the Sums received and paid; and that Account being made up when the Traufuctions of the Day are finiflted, the Balance only is either taken out of, or deposited in, the Teller's Chests, in Exchequer Bills, or labelled Bags of Caff), according as that Balance turns out in Favour of, or against the Bank.

Besides this Facility in conducting Money Transactions, a Course of Years has introduced, and very rapidly within these few Years, another Alteration, raoli

Since then, on the one Hand, the Improvements of the Age have taken away the Foundation upon which this Species of Reward was built, it is but reafotiable the Superftru&ure should fall with it; and, on the other Haud the Exigencies of the Age having converted what was designed to be the Reward of Industry, into the Means of rendering some Offices lucrative to Excess, and of supporting others that are useless to the Public,

the Subject has a Right to be relieved of that Burthen; and therefore we are of Opinion, that all Poundage Fees,

of every Kind soever, should be suppressed and totally abolished: And of this Opinion was the Privy Council; who, by their Order in the Year 169.5, above alluded to,

- shewed their Scnfe of a Poundage, by directing it, in Instances therein mentioned, to be suppressed in the Office of the Treasuror of the Navy.

The remaining Head is that of Gratuities; a Species . of Emolument very liable to Abuse: It may be a Re-1 ward for Civility, Favour, or extra Service; it may be all'o the Purchase of undue Preference, Expedition, and, in some Cafes, of Procrastination; flowing, at first, from the Liberality of Opulence, the (Mentation of Vanity, or the Design of Cunning, it very soon assumes the . Name of Custom, and becomes a Claim, submitted to, to avoid the Imputation of Meanness, and frequently to the great Inconvenience of contracted Circumstances: Nor is it confined to Individuals only; the Public pay

- their Share: In the Payments out of the Deductions of . Twelve Pence in the Pound, there are Two Articles,

r 6 ia 8. tnaking Six hundred Fifty-three Pounds Twelve Shillings and Eight Pence, distributed by the Paymaster General of the Forces in Gratuities: The Public Voice unites with that of individuals, in demanding a Suppression of a Species of Emolument so easily perverted to Purposes injurious to the interest of both.

But there is One other Sort of Gratuity that requires particular Observation; that is, what is paid to the Officers and Clerks in the Pay Office of the Navy and Army, for carrying on and making up the Accounts of the Treasurer and Paymaster General after their Re-iignation. How much then does it behove them that this Evil should be corrected !. an Evil that furnishes another weighty Reason, in Addition to those urged in our former Reports, for proceeding immediately to bring forward the long Arrears in the Accounts of these Offices, in order for their speedy Completion.

Having'thusr Rated the Mischiefs attending the present Establishment, both to the Public and Individuals, and the Reasons for abolishing the multifarious Emoluments, by which these Offices are now supported, it remains for us to propose such a Regulation as appears best calculated to avoid the like Mischiefs, and most beneficial to the Public Service.

We areof Opinion, that in the Place of all these Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities, there should be substituted and annexed to each of these Offices, of whatever Rank or Denomination, One certain Salary, paid to the Officer by the Public Quarterly, and free of all Deductions; this Salary should be an ample Corapensation for the Service required; and the Quantum estimated by the various Qualifications and Circumstances necessary for the Execution, and which together form the Title to Reward.

By this Regulation, the Officer will know hislncome, the Public will know their Expence; and Uniformity and Equality will be introduced in the Provisions for Officers of equal Rank and Station in similar Offices. The Industry of some Persons requires the Spur of Profits continually flowing in, or the Hopes of Increase others prefer the Certainty of a known, sure Income, paid at Rated Times: No Arrangement can salt the Dif-positions or Occasions of all Men; but Time and Usage ' will soon reconcile ore reasonable Rule, extended through these Departments of Government.

Notwithstanding this Regulation throws upon the Public the whole Expence of these Offices, which are at present supported in Part by Individuals, yet, by adopting it, that whole Expence will become less than the Sum it now costs the Public; for that Sum is so great, as to afford every liberal Salary, and yet leave no inconsiderable Saving: Not that this is the only Saving pro--posed by the Regulation; the Public at present bear a much greater Share of the Burthen than is obvious at the First View: Besides Fees and Gratuities paid by Public Offices, and refunded to them out of Public Money, many Payments, though made by Individuals, are charged by them ultimately to the Account of the Public. For InRance, the Contractor, when he calculates the Terms upon which he may safely engage with Government, must eRimate every Article of Profit and Loss, consequential to his Bargain; to the Account of the latter, he places all his Charges, and amongR them, the long Catalogue of Fees, certain and uncertain; the first he knows, the last he will calculate not to his own Disadvantage; and if, by them, he can procure Credit, or Preference, or Expedition, he will charge them to Government at their full Price; If this Head of various Expences was blotted out of his Column of Charges, by so much would the Terms of his Contraft be more favourable to the Public.

But, besides this, so very various and extensive are the Operations of Government, that the Number of Persons employed in their Service constitute a very considerable Body of the People; and their Relief is a Pub* lie Concern. If, by discharging an Office, at present paid by a Salary from those Fees and Deductions to which it is now subject, that Salary should become greater than the Office ought in Reason to have annexed to it, it may easily be regulated and reduced to its proper Standard.

We have said, the Salary should be paid free of alt U

Deductions; that is, as far as is confident with the Laws in being. The Salaries and Fees of Office are at present subject, by Three Acts of Parliament, to the Land Tax, the Sixpenny, and the One Shilling Duties; whoever takes a View of the above State of the official Profits, will not wonder they should he deemed by the Legislature a fit Subject of Taxation; and, under the Syften* then in Use, no other Mode of Taxation could well be contrived but that adopted in those Acts, though attended with Inequality, and, in many Cafes, with Hardship; had One known Salary been at. that Time the Pay of Office, and the Neeeflities of the State required the Aid of every Subject, in Proportion to his Faculties, it is possible a Diminution of the Salary, before it issued, might have appeared a more eligible, more equal, and less expensive Mode of Taxation, than paying it entire out of the Exchequer, and then bringing back again a Part of it, delayed and defalcated by a Variety of Deductions in its Circuit; but, as it is, the Sums at present aflVfled upon these Offices mufi continue to be paid -r because, otherwise, in the Land Tax, it will occasion a Deficiency in the Sum to be raised by that Division in which the Office is assessed; and in the other Duties, it will diminish the Funds created by those Acts, and conseqpently, the Security of the Creditors upon those Funds. The Land Tax and Duties are now paid by the Officers, at stated Times, to the Collectors and Receivers: If the Mode of Payment by a clear Salary is adopted, the Total Sum, now assessed upon all the Officers in One Office, tnay Rill continue to be paid as One Sum, in like Manner, out of the same Fund with, the Salaries themselves.

We have said, the Salaries should be annexed to the Office; it ought to be a full and competent Recorn pence for the Execution, and no more; the Whole of it ought to be paid to the Person who executes, independent of the Officer who presides, but who should Rill retain the same Power of Appointment, and the same Control, that he now exercises over the inferior Officer. Where the Profits exceed what the Officer is in Reason entitled to, the Overplus should be abolished, and the Public reap the Benefit, not a Person who earns no Part of it.

In the Pay Office of the Army, some of the Offices of the Deputy Paymasters Abroad are Sinecures: Though Deputies themselves, they execute these Offices by their Deputies; being themselves engaged in very different Employments under Government.

Inffances are not wanting, in all these Offices, to warrant this Regulation of Payment by a Salary: The Treasurer of the Navy, and his Paymaster, the Paymaster General of the Forces, the Paymasters of Exchequer Bills, and their Officers, are all paid by Salaries only; and why the same Rule may not be extended to the rest no sufficient Reason has hitherto occurred to us. It might seem too sanguine, to iuggeft how far this Rule may be applied to other Offices, without a previous Examination into* their peculiar Circumstances; and yet the Advantage it holds out to the Public, its Simplicity, and Aptitude to be accommodated to all Offices, however distinguished, afford great Reason to believe it may be applied to every Department of Government.

The Principle of Economy, by which we have been guided, has led us to the Conclusions we have formed, and the Regulations we have submitted to the Wisdom of Parliament; Conclusions ftri6Hy deduced from that, Principle; and Regulations made necessary by the pressing Exigencies of the Times.

PAYMASTER'S BRANCH.

There are no Fees or Gratuities authorized or demanded; but, for want of Copper, it has for Time immemorial been customary, in paying the Wages of Officers and Seamen, and of Artificers in His Majesty's Dock Yards, to retain the Pence under Six Pence; and in respect of the latter, particularly the Notes which the Clerk of the Cheque gives to the Workmen, to specify the Amount of their respective Wages, always leave out such Pence. This has ever been considered as a Fund for making good Over-payments, and other Mistakes that - Vol. 38. 8 U must

7 16 i'i ° . 1782.

Sixth Report must unavoidably happen, where Business is carried on in the extreme Hurry in which these Payments are usually tnade; the Consequences of which always fall on the Clerks who make them; and also in discharging the Expences Public attending the Payments of the Yards. When the Sums to be paid are very small, instead of taking the odd Accounts. Pence, they are generally increased to Six Pence in favour of the Party.

It has likewise, for Time immemorial, been usual for Chaplains, Surgeons, and Pursers, or their Agents, to make a small Compliment or Acknowledgment to the Clerks, who at their Risk, and at extra Hours, adjust their respective Four Pences, Two Pences, and Venereal Cures, and Tobacco-Money; this Perquisite is entirely at the Option of the Officer, and has for many Years past been reduced to about Half of what was originally given.

The Allowance of Extra, is for attending Payments, and making up Ships and Yard Books; and that under the Head of Telling Money, is on Account of doing that Business at the Bank, in which there is always a Riik both in Tale and Weight.

The Examination of the Right ljonourable Wclbore Ellis, Treasurer of the Navy; taken upon Oath, 2 ot h November 1781.

This Examinant faith, That the Treasurer of the Navy is appointed by Letters Patent under the Great Seal, during Pleasure; he is paid au Annual Salary of Two thousand Pounds, voted by Parliament, on the Or-dinary Estimateof the Navy, subject to the Deductions of the One Shilling and Sixpenny Duties, which reduce it to the clear Sum of One thoulan'd Eight hundred and Fifty Pounds; which Sum is paid to him Quarterly, by Bill assigned by the Navy Board upon the Treasurer for Payment, out of the Money received from the Exchequer to pay Salaries. He does not receive for the Execution of the Office of Treasurer of the Navy, any other Salary, Fee, or Gratuity whatever, except the Salary above-mentioned.

The Treasurer appoints all the Officers and Clerks in his Office; he cannot increase the Number voted on the Ordinary Estimate of the Navy, without the Approbation of the Navy Beard; an Increase of the Business in the Office this Year, has made an Increase in the Number of Clerks necessary.

IV. Ellis.

N* 6.

The Examination of Adam Jellicoe, Esquire, First Clerk in the Office of the Paymaster to the Treasurer of the Navy; taken upon Oath, the 23d and 28th of August 1781.

This Examinant faith, That hisSalaiy, as First Clerk in the Office of the Paymaster to the Treasurer of the Navy, is Eighty Pounds a Year, subject to the Deduction of Six Pence in the Pound: He has, besides his Salary, an extra Allowance, at the Rate of Seven Shillings a Day, for attending Payments of Wages and the Yards, which has been an usual Allowance before, as he has been informed, and ever since he has been in the Office; he has also a Perquisite under the Description of Odd Pence; it has always been customary for all the Clerks employed in the Payment of the Officers, Seamen, and Artificers in the Dock Yard, to retain for their own Use the odd Pence, under Six Pence, in every Payment; in Consideration of which, each Clerk is bound to make good any Mistakes made by him in the Payments; such Mistakes do sometimes happen in the Hurry of Payment: But where the Payments are small, and the Person appears to be an Object, the odd Pence are not deduced, but increased in his Favour to even Money. He has another Perquisite, which is a Gratuity paid by the Chaplains, Surgeons, and Pursers, for calling and paying their several Shares of the Deductions made out of the Seamen's Wages; this Gratuity is usually at the Rate of One Guinea per Cent. The Sum of Three hundred and Five Pounds Five Shillings and Ten Pence is the whole Amount of the Profits for executing the Duties of his Office, received by him between the 24th of December 1779 and the 25th of December 1780. The Lift of the Salaries, Allowances, and other Emoluments, received by the Clerks in the Paymaster's Branch, dated the 6th of August last, signed by him, and transmitted to this Office, contains, as he believes, the Names, Salaries, Allowances, and Emolu. ments, of all the Clerks in that Branch, he having received from every Clerk therein mentioned the Account of the several Sums set against their Names, which Accounts he believes to be true.

Since he came into the Office, above Forty Years ago, the Business having greatly increased, the Number of Clerks in this Branch has been also increased, from Eight to Sixteen, besides a temporary Assistant Clerk; the greatest Number was added in the Year 17 58, when Mr. Grenville's Act passed. The afore mentioned Fees have been long customary, and most of them have been paid at the Paymaster General's Office, to the certain Knowledge of some of his Officers, for more than Forty Years; and will, on a Peace Establishment, be all of them very considerably reduced, except the Half Pay.

The Paymaster General's Office, respecting the Trail reposed in the Officers belonging to it, may be considered as one of the First in the Kingdom. The Under Clerks serve many Years at very small Salaries, without a Fee Kind, in Expectation of being rewarded for their long Services, when Vacancies happen in the upper Seats,

where Fees are allowed to be taken. The Attendance at without keeping Holidays, or having any Adjournment,

Pay-Office, Horse Guards, 17th August 1781.

The other Salary is paid to him without Deduction, out of the Money aiding by the Deductions from the Pay of the Army, by virtue of His lilajefiy's Warrant, dated the 18th of March 1774, to commence from the lotli of October 1771, and to be paid him during his Continuance in the same Office; and (luting, that the then Emoluments of the Office did not produce a sufficientand adequate Compensation and Reward for his Trouble, Care, Diligence, and Fidelity, in the Execution of the Business committed to his Charge. I Iis immediate Predecessors in this Office had other Appointments under the Crown; lie himself having no other Appointment, the Salary of Five hundred Pounds, subject to the Duties above-mentioned, conli-dering the Bank and Trnfl of the Office, was not deemed a sufficient Compensation. He receives for the Execution of this Office no Fee, Gratuity, or Reward whatever, other than the Salaries above-mentioned.

N* 15.

The Examination of John Powell, Esquire, Cashier in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 29th, 30th, and 31st of August, 17 th October, id and 6th November 1781.

Th is Examinant faith. That as Cashier to the Pay-master General of the Forces, he receives a Salary of Two hundred Pounds a Year (subject to the Duty of One Shilling in the Pound) paid to him by the Pay-master General, out of the Sum of One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty Pounds, allowed to him for under Officers and Clerks, out of the Deductions of Twelve Pence in the Pound, and One Day's Pay. This Salary has been allowed the Cashier ever since he has been acquainted with the Office, which is upwards of'Thirty-five Years. He also receives an additional Allowance of Two hundred and Seventy Pounds a Year, without Dedufci ions, for his Trouble. Care, Dil igence, and Fidelity, in the Execution of the Business committed to his Charge; this Allowance is made pursuant to the King's Warrant, dated 10th of July 1765, and paid out of the Deductions of Twelve Pence in the Pound and One Day's Pay, and he has received it ever since that Period. Besides this Salary and Allowance, he also considers himself as entitled by Custom to receive the following Fees and Gratuities: — From the Remitters to North America, Ten Shillings and Six Pence per Thousand Pounds, for all the Sums paid to them to be remitted for the Extraordinary Services of the Army, and an Annual Payment of Five Guineas each Regiment for remitting their Subsistence; from the Contractors for Victualling, Half Cent, on Victualling Warrants; from the Agents, Five Shillings per Cent, on Warrants lor Freight, Armament of Ships, Hire of Extra Seamen, Bread, Wood, Straw, and other Stores, sent to America for the Use of the Army; from the Persons to whom the Warrants are made payable. Two Guineas per Thousand Pounds on the Warrants for Prefects to Indians; from the Regimental Agents, Six Vol. 38.

Guineas for every Regiment, upon issuing the Clearings. Sixth geport To the best ofliis Knowledge and Belief, all the Fees of Contain! Gratuities above mentioned, have been allowed to mriioners of his Predecessors in Office. Sometimes Persons, upon receiving Warrants, leave the Cashier a final! Gratuity, the W hole amounting in the Year to an inconsiderable Sum. He receives no Salary, Allowance, Fee, or Gratuity whatever, for the Execution of the Office of Cashier to the Paymaster General of the Forces, except what are above mentioned, and these Fees and Gratuities are not always paid to him. The Sum Total of the Salaries, Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities, received by him in the Year 1780, as Cashier to the Paymaster General of the Forces, amounted to the Sum of Seven thousand One hundred and Seventy-five Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Six Pence; Part of this Sum* hut what Part he cannot tell, consists of Fees that became due to him in that Year, but how much thereof still remains due, or how much he received under each Head , of Fees, he is not able to ascertain. Since February 1780, he has received no Fees from the Remitters, for Remittances paid to them since that Time: All the Warrants for which the above Fees and Gratuities are paid, are for Extraordinaries, except the Warrants for Clearings, and the Remittances for Subsistence; upon Production of these Warrants to the Paymaster General or his Cashier, and Indorsement by the Person to whom they are made payable, or their Assigns, the Cashier takes and enters the Warrants into the Cadi Book, and gives Drafts upon the Bank for the Sums therein mentioned, or One Draft only for the Sum Total of all the Warrants paid to the same Person at the same Time.

This Examinant further faith, That in Time of Peace (provided the same Number of Troops should be kept on Foot as were put upon the Establishment at the Conclusion of the last War) the whole Emoluments, as near as he can conjecture, will be from One thousand Pounds to One thousand Five hundred Pounds per Annum; the Difference of those Sums will arise and depend on the Places where the great Body of His Majesty's Troops shall be stationed; if at Home, the Post of Cashier will not exceed One thousand Pounds; if Abroad, it may amount to One thousand Five hundred Pounds a Year.

Jn° Powell.

Guy Carleton,

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

liichd Ncave,

Sami Beachcroft,

Geo. Drummond.

The Examination of Charles , Esquire*

Accountant in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 10th and nth of October 1781.

This Examinant faith. That as Accountant to the Paymaster General of the Forces, he receives from him a Salary of One hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year, paid out of the Allowance made to him for the Salaries of his Officers; he pays out of this Salary the Duty of One Shilling in the Pound; this has been the usual Salary paid to the Accountant, and depends upon the Will of the Paymaster General. He receives also the following Fees and Gratuities; — from the Contractors, Ten Shillings and Six Pence per Thousand Pounds, on the Remittances to North America, for the Extraordinary Services of the Army there; from the Regimental Agents, Four Guineas for settling and Hating the Accounts of each British and Foreign Regiment; from the Agents to the Ga rrifons, for adjusting their Accounts, most of them Two Guineas, some One

The Sum Total of the Profits of his Office, received by him for One Year, ending the 24th of December 1780, exchifive of the Salary above* mentioned, amounted to Thirteen hundred Fifty-eight Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Nine Pence, and no more. N* 17.

The Examination of John Adam Frederick UeJJe, Esquire, Ledger Keeper in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 12th of October 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he is Ledger Keeper in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces; that he receives from the Paymaster General a Salary of One hundred Pounds a Year; he also receives from the Computer of Off-reckonings Eighty Pounds a Year, and from the Cashier of Half Pay One hundred Pounds a Year. The First of these Salaries has been usually paid the Ledger Keeper, ever since he knew the Office, which is about Forty Years; the Two latter were first paid to Mr. Nichols, when he was appointed Ledger Keeper; he succeeded Mr. Nichols in that Office, and the same Payments have been continued to him.

He receives from the Agents a Fee of Two Guineas a Year, for adjusting and giving a Certificate of the Accounts of each British and Foreign Regiment, at the Time of their Clearings; and from some of the Persons who apply, either for Certificates, or Receipts on dormant Warrants, Fees to a small Amount. He pays Taxes for his Office, amounting to Fifteen Pounds a Year, which being deducted from the Sum of Six hundred Seventy-four Pounds Sixteen Shillings, leaves the Sum of Six hundred Fifty-nine Pounds Sixteen Shillings, which was the Total Sum received by him for the Profits of this Office, for the Year 1780.

He was appointed Ledger Keeper by Mr. Charles Townshend, who gave him Leave, by Reason of his infirm State of Health, to execute this Office by Deputy, which he has done ever since; his daily Attendance for many Years in the Office had impaired his Eye-fight, and disqualified him from Writing. lie pays to his Deputy Eighty Pounds a Year, and to another Assistant, Fifty Pounds a Year.

John A. F. Urge.

Guy Carle!on.

T. Angnish,

Ce:\ Drummond.

N* 18.

The Examination of Thomas Bangham, Esquire, Computer of Off-reckonings in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 30th of August, 1781.

This Examinant faith, That his Office is the Com-puterof theOff-reckonings in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces: That for this Office he receives from the Paymaster General a Salary of Eighty Pounds a Year, without Deduction; but he has always, since he has been in this Department, which is about Six Years, paid the Whole of this Salary to the Ledger Keeper, finding it had been the U fual Practice of his Predecessors, as far back as Lord Holland'sTime; the Reason of which,

as he apprehends, is, because otherwise the Profits of the Office of Ledger Keeper would not be equivalent to the Troiible attending it. The real Profits of his Office arise from the following Fees and Gratuities: — Five Shillings and Three Pence per Cent, for settling, and adjusting, and making out Receipts for the Half-yearly Issues of Off-reckonings; this is paid him by the Clothier at the Time of the Issue. Seven Shillings for the Entry of each Assignment, Thirteen Shillings and Six Pence for the Entry of each Warrant; these are paid him by the Clothiers at the Time of the Entry. One Pound One Shilling for every Certificate of the Sum that has been paid upon any Assignment; this is paid him by the Person applying. An Annual Payment from the Agents of Regiments, of Three Pounds Three Shillings for each of those Regiments serving Abroad, for which Stoppage Receipts are issued. These Fees or Gratuities are paid by the Usage of this Office, and have continued the same ever since he has been acquainted with the Business. He has no other Profits whatever for the Discharge of his Office, except what are above mentioned; the Sum Total of which, for the Year 1780, amounted to One thousand and Thirty-eight Pounds Five Shillings and Six Pence, and no more. To the bell of his Knowledge aind Belief, in Time of Peace, the Profits of his Office, upon an Average, do not exceed Four hundred Pounds a Year.

Tho* Bangham.

Guy Carle ton,

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Rich* Neave,

Geo. Drummond.

The Examination of Robert , Esquire,

Cashier of Half Pay in the Office of the Pay-maficr General of the Forces; taken upon Oath, the 17th of October 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he has been in the Office of the Paymaster General of the Forces above Forty-two Years, and has been Cashier and Paymaster of the Half Pay ever since May 1753. All the Profits of his Office arise from a Salary and Fees; the Salary is Eighty Pounds a Year, paid to him, without Deduction, by the Paymaster General; his Fees arise from the Business done. He receives from each Officer Two Shillings for himself, and Six Pence for his Clerk, for every Half Yearly Payment; and Three Shillings and Six Pence for receiving and entering every Warrant placing the Officer or Officers, if more than One, on the Half Pay Lift; and from the Person producing them, Three Shillings and Six Pence for the Entry of every Power of Attorney and Probate of a Will. These are the usual customary Fees which have been paid to the Cashi.'T of Half Pay ever since he has known the Office. The Sum Total received by him for the Profit* of this Office, in the Year 17S0, amounted to Six

The Examination of Edward Wilford, Esquire, First Clerk in the Office of the Auditor of the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer; taken upon Oath, 31st OStob ill, 7th, and 30th November 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he executes the Office of First Clerk to the Auditor of the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer: He was appointed in Writing by ihe Auditor, the Duke of Newc; and was approved of and sworn in by the Comthiffibners of the Treasury, tiurfiiant to the Act of Parliament. He has been in the Offich of the Auditor about Forty Years.

The Duke of Netocastleis appointed Auditor for Life

by a Constitution Under the Hands and Seals of the Commissioners of the Treasury; he executes this Office himself, and not by Deputy: It is his Bufinef3 to super-intend all Matters relative to the Office; to sign all Exchequer Bills, Orders, Debentures, and Patents; dhd all other Instruments which pass this Office. He does hot. himself receive from the Individuals any of the Profits; they are received by his First; Clerk, and accounted for to him every Month.

The Business of this Office'is to keep a daily Account of all the Money received into and issued out of the Exchequer, under the various Heads of Duties; to make up every Week an Account of the Receipts, Issues, and Remains, of every Duty, and to transmit a Copy of it to the Treasury; and to make up and send to the Treasury an Half Yearly Declaration, containing an Account of all the Receipts and Issues during that Half Year, with the Remains. The- Auditor has a Clerk constantly attending in the Tally Court, who takes an Account daily of the Receipts, and brings it to the First; Clerk. No Issue can be made but by Warrant, Order, Debenture, or Bill; all of which pass through the Hands of the First Clerk, and give him Knowledge of the Issues. Other Branches of the Business of this Office, are, to enter all Instruments authorizing the Issue of Money; to take Care that no Money is issued without a proper Authority; to examine the Caffi in the Tellers Che^.s every Twenty-eight Days, or oftener, and to fee it hgrees with the Accounts; to examine all the Tellers Vouchers; to make out general and particular Imprest Rolls, and all Exchequer Bills; and to manage the Business of the Annuities payable at the Exchequer. It is usual to make up the Accounts in the Exchequer Twice a Year, on and to Easier Eve and Michaelmas Eve. This Office consists of the Auditor and Twenty-three fixed Clerks, and other Assistants upon extraordinary Occasions. The Profits of the Auditor arise ftoffi Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities.

Upon the King's Accession, a Certificate is sent from the Office of the Auditor to the Commissioners of the Treasury, pursuant to their RequisitiOu, containing an Account of several Fees, Salaries, and Allowances that have been usually paid to the Officers and Ministers of the Receipt Of the Exchequer; in cohfequfence of this Certificate, a dormant Warrant, with the Certificate 'annexed, is sent to the Auditor, authorizing him to draft Orders, and pass Debentures, for the Payment of the Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities contained ill the Lift, in the accustomed Manner; this Lift contains, amongst ( others, certain Fees and Allowances payable to the Auditor, amounting to Three thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-six Pounds One Shilling, Two of which, being the Sums of Two hundred and Sixty Pounds Three Shillings and Four Pence, and Two hundred Pounds, are paid out of the Civil List, the others out of the Funds created for the Payment of the several Annuities; these Allowances are paid, some Annually, some Half Yearly, some Quarterly; the Two hundred Pounds a Year by Order, the rest by Debentures. The Auditor and his Clerks are entitled to One Fourth Part of the Fees arif-Vol. 38.

73*

ing in the Tally Court, of which the Share belonging to Sixth Report the Auditor, in the last Year, was One hundred Pounds and Six Pence; his Share of the Allowance made by the Treasury for the Tallies of Loan, amounted to Seventy Accounts* Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Three Pence; he isalfo entitled to Fees upon Money issued for certain Services; an ancient Table of these Fees taken by the Auditor and his Clerks, is hung up in the Office, and he receives the Fees due to the Auditor and his Clerks, from the Person receiving Money, according to that Table. The gross Sum received by the Auditor for these Fees, during the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, amounted toTwelve thousand Five hundred and Fifty-four Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence: These Fees arose from the Issue of Seven Million Nine hundred and Eighty thousand Three hundred and Forty Pounds; of which the Money issued to the Army, and to the Master of the Mint, and the Sum of Eighty-three thousand Three hundred and Eighty Pounds Nine Shillings and Five Pence Farthing, Part of the Sum of Three hundred Sixty-one thousand and Sixty-two Pobnds, issued for Services on account, SCc. and One thousand Two hundred Pounds, Part of the Sum of One hundred Fifty thousand Seven hundred Thirty-eight Pounds, issued for Pensions, Annuities, Hie. was Public Money, the rest was out of the Civil List. The Auditor isalfo entitled to Fees for entering Patents, and on Imprest Rolls, amounting in that Year, to Thirty-nine Pounds Five Shillings, and to a Fee from the Great Wardrobe, of Four Pounds Seventeen Shillings for Vestures: He received New Years Gifts from sundry public Offices, amounting to Three hundred Forty-five Pounds Seven Shillings. The . gross Amount of all these Profits for One Year, ending at Michaelmas 178d,wasSixteen thousand Eight hundred and Eighty Pounds Six Shillings and Three Pence:

Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Eight hundred and Seventy-two Pounds Twelve Shillings; to Clerks, One thousand Six hundred and Sixty-two Pounds Ten Shillings; and for other incidental Expences, Three hundred and Twenty-nine Pounds and Two Pence; making together Two thousand Eight hundred and Sixty-four Pounds Two Shillings and Two PenCe; which being deducted from the gross Receipt, leaves the Nett Sum of Fourteen thousand and Sixteen Pounds Four Shillings and One Penny; which, to the best of his Knowledge and Belief, was the whole Sum received by the Duke of Newcastle, as Auditor of the Exchequer, for the Profits of that Office, during the Period above-mentioned. He believes, in Time of Peace the whole Profits of this Office do not exceed Seven thousand Pounds a Year.

This Examinant further faith, lhat as First Clerk to the Auditor of the Exchequer, he receives an ancient Allowance of One hundred Pounds a Year, included in the Certificate of Fees and Allowances above-mentioned.

In the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, he received the Clerks Fees, amounting to Three thousand and One Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Eight Pence; and for New Years Gifts and odd Pence, One hundred and Forty-two Pounds Seventeen Shillings; amounting together to Three thousand Two'hundred and Forty-four Pounds 'lliirteen Shillings and Eight Pence: Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Fifty-two Pounds Ten Shillings; for Incidents, Five Pounds Five Shillings; and to Clerks, Four hundred and Thirty-four Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Two Pence; together. Four hundred and Ninety-two PoundsTen Shillings and Two Pence; which reduced his Nett Receipt during the Period above-mentioned, toTwo t housand Seven hundred and Fifty-two Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence.

He believes the clear Profits of his Office in Time of Peace, will not exceed, OneYear with another, Nine hundred Pounds.

The Clerks are appointed by the Auditor, and paid by him and his First Clerk, out of the Clerks Fees and the Profits of the Auditor's Allowances, from Forty Pounds to Two hundred Tounds a Year, according to

He hath taken an Account of the Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities received by all the Clerks in this Office, and to the belt of his Knowledge and Belief, the Lift of the said Clerks, dated the 20th of November Instant, transmitted by him to this Board, contains a true Account of all the Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities received by each of them for One Year, ending at Michaelmas 1780.

It appears by the Books in the Office, that upwards of Twenty-two Millions were issued last Year from the Exchequer; for the issuing and keeping the Accounts of which, neither the Auditor nor his Clerks took any Fees whatever.

Edward Wilford.

N* 28.

The Examination of Mr. William Jones, Tally Writer to the Auditor of the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer 5 taken upon Oath, 8th November 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he executes the Office of Tally Writer to the Auditor of the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer; it is his Business constantly to attend

in the Tally Court, to take Cognizance of all the Sums received by the Four Tellers, from the Bills thrown down by them into the Tally Court, and to enter them into the Certificate Book, and every Day to transmit an Account of them to the Auditor's Office; every Week he examines the Receipts of the WTeek with the Clerk of the Pells.

The Profits of this Office coniift of Two Allowances, and Fees; one of the Allowances, as he believes, is One hundred and Twenty Pounds a Year, paid by the Auditor; the other an ancient Allowance of Thirty-five Pounds Two Shillings a Year, paid to him by Debenture. The Fees arise from the Tallies: He every Week receives from the Deputy Chamberlain, the Fourth Part of those Fees that belongs to the Auditor and his Clerk; and every Quarter pays the Auditor's Share of those Fees to his First Clerk.

He has been in this Seat only since the 5th of April last, and cannot therefore tell what is the Amount of the Year's Profits; but he believes in Time of War, the gross Produce may amount to about Four hundred and Ninety Pounds a Year; out of which must be deducted, Nineteen Pounds Eighteen Shillings for Taxes, and One hundred and Ten Pounds a Year for Clerks. In Time of Peace he believes the Nett Profits of this Office will not amount to Two hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year.

Wm Jones.

After our hearty Commendations, By virtue of His Majesty's General Letters Patent dormant bearing Date 4»tli November 1760: It appearing unto us, by your Certificate, bearing Date the 2d Day of December 1760, and which is hereunto annexed, that the several Fees, Salaries, and Allowances thercinmentioned, and amounting in the Whole to the Yearly Sum of One thousand Eight hundred and One Pounds Nine Shillings, have, as well by ancient Custom and by virtue of Letters Patent, Constitutions, or other Authorities, been paid to the several Officers and Ministers of the Receipt of the Exchequer therein described, either in Right of their respective Offices and Employments, or in Reward for #sundry Services in the said Certificate specified: Now, to the Intent that Payment may be made to the said Officers and Ministers, of all such Sums of Money as remained due to them on the said Fees, Salaries, and Allowances, on the Day of the Demise of his late Majesty King George the Second, and that they may continue to receive the said Fees, Salaries, and Allowances, as the same shall become due and payable unto them, for any Time from and after the said Day; These are, by virtue of the Letters Patent, Constitutions, or Authorities, whereby the said Officers and Ministers re-lpeftively held, or now do or shall hold, the said Offices and Employments, or of His Majesty's general Letters Patent dormant, bearing Date the 6th Day of November 1760, as the same may respectively relate to the Payments to be made in pursuance hereof, to pray and require your Lordship to make and pais Debentures, or draw Orders (as may be requisite) for paying unto the Officers and Mininers afore-mentioned, all such Sum and Sums of Money as remained due to them on or for any Time before the 25th October 1760, being the Day of the said Demise, for or upon any of the Fees, Salaries, or Allowances afore-mentioned, and «lfo for so paying from Time to Time hereafter, in the ufnal Manner, and at the accustomed Terms and Days of Payment, to such Officers and Ministers, all such Sum and Sums of Money as shall grow or have become due and payable to them, for any Time or Times from and after the said 25th 1760, on the said

Fees, Salaries, and Allowances: and let the Debentures to be made, or Orders to be drawn as aforesaid, for the Monies payable on the said several Fees, Salaries, and Allowances, for any Time before and for the said 25th Udober 1760, be satisfied out of any Monies in the said Receipt of the Revenues, which were applicable to the Uses of his said late Majesty's Civil Government; and let the Debentures to be made, and Orders to be drawn in pursuance hereof, for the Monies that shall become payable on the said Fees, Salaries, and Allowances, for any Time from and after the said 25th October 1760, be satisfied out of any Monies which shall from Time to Time remain in the said Receipt, appli-18

cable to the Uses of His present Majesty's Civil Government. And whereas it appears by the said Certificate, that there is also several Fees, Salaried, or Allowances (otherthan those above ment ioned) settled and allowed to the Officers of the said Receipt, in respect to the Labour, Pains, Charge, and Expence they are at in managing and performing the Business of Annuities payable there; which said (aft-mentioned Fees, Salaries, and Allowances together, according to the Particulars expressed in the said Certificate, amount to the Yearly Sum of Five thousand Nine hundred Pounds; These are, by virtue and in pursuance, as well of the Powers given unto us in this Behalf, by the several Aft# of Parliament passed concerning the said Annuities, or concerning the respective Funds appointed for orcharged with the Payment of the fame, as of any other Power# in us being, to pray and require your Lordship to make and pass Debentures, or draw Orders, as may be requisite for paying unto the said last mentioned Officers of the said Receipt, as well as all such Sums of Money as remain due to them in respect of the said last mentioned Fees, Salaries, or Allowances, on or for any Time before the said 25th of October 1760; as also for paying to such Officers, from Time to Time hereafter, in the usual Manner, and at the accustomed Terms or Days of Payment, all such Sum and Sums of Money as shall grow or have become due and payable to them for any Time or Times from and after the said 25th Day of October 1760, on the same Fees, Salaries, or Allowances; which said several Debentures or Orders are to be satisfied out of the Monies of the said respective Funds arisen or to arise in the said Receipt, and applicable to the Payment of the said Annuities, according to the Directions and true Intent and Meaning of the said respective Acts: And for so doing this shall be your Lordfiiip's Warrant.

Whitehall, Treasury Chambers, the Third Day of January 1760.

Hollis

B. Legge,

To Henry Earl of Lincoln, James Oswald.
