The Examination of Edward Roberts, Esquire, Deputy Clerk of the Pells; taken upon Oath, the 23d, 25th, 30th and 6th of

November, 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he executes the Office of Deputy and Fir (I Clerk to Sir Edward Walpole, Clerk of the Pells; it has not been usual, as he believes,' everfince the Beginning of this Century, for the Clerk of the Pells himself to transact any Part of the Business of this Office; it is now, and has been as long as he remembers, carried on solely by the Deputy. This Office confiiis of the Clerk of the Pells, his Deputy and First Clerk, and Fourteen under Clerks, One of which (the Clerk of the Introitus) has Fees, but no Salary; Thirteen of them have Salaries at his Pleasure; and to the Clerk of the Declarations he allows a Portion of his own Fees, for entering, examining, and signing Imprest Rolls.

It is the Business of this Office to enter and record all Money paid into or issued out of the Exchequer; to record all Instrumenls that relate to the ilfuing of Money; and to take Care that no Money is issued without a proper Authority. He has in his Custody a Key to , the Tellers Chelts, and attends Daily the opening the fame, whenever the Tellers receive or pay Money; he examines into the State of the Calli, and every Week makes up an Account of the Receipts, I flues, and Remains, on every particular Head of Revenue, of which there are now above Two hundred and [Seventy, and transmits it to ihe Treasury. Every Half Year he makes a Declaration, engrossed upon Parchment, of all the Receipts and Issues during that Half Yalf, of which One Copy is kept in the Office, and One transmitted to the Treasury: Helikewife, Twice a Year, examines, enters, and ligns the General Imprest Roll of all Persons who have received Money upon Account; likewise the particular Imprest Roll for every Accountant who applies for it.

The Emoluments, accruing to the Clerk of the Pells from this Office, comfift of Allowances and Fees, and some small Gratuities; all of which arc received by the Deputy, and accounted for to the Principal. The Allowances are certain Payments; some, for the Management of Annuities created by various Acts of Parliament, and paid out of the Funds applicable to the Payment of those Annuities; others;by Constitution or ancient Usage, and paid out of the Civil List: All of these are paid to him by Order or Debenture, made out, some Annually, some Half Yearly, some Quarterly, by virtue of the General Letters Patent dormant. The Sum Total received by the Clerk of the Pells, under this Head of Allowance, from Michaelmas 1779 to Michaelmas 1780, amounted to One thousand Six hundred and Three Pounds Eleven Pence; out of which were deducted for the Duties of One Shilling and of:; Vol. 38.

Six Pence in the Pound, One hundred and Twenty Pounds Eight Shillings and Eleven Pence; which reduced it to One thousand Four hundred and Eighty-two Pounds Twelve Shillings. He is entitled to Fees, either upon the Receipt or the Issue of Money; those upon the Receipt-arise from the levying of Tallies, are receiver I in the Tally Court, and consist of nearly One Fourth Part of the whole Receipt in that Court: The Total of these Fees amounted, in the Period above-mentioned, to One hundred and Ninety-four Pounds Five Shillings and Ten Pence Halfpenny. The Fees accruing to him from the Issue are at various Rates on, the various Services for which Money is issued: They are either according to the Rates Rated in the Barons Report, or, in some Instances, at a lower Rate, and are paid by the Persons receiving, OHt of the Sums they receive. There are also some other certain small ancient Fees, paid by. the Persons who apply for the Entry or Inrollment of various particular Initruments relating to the Issue of Money. The Amount of all these Fees was, in the Time above mentioned, Seven thousand Seven hundred Pounds Two Shillings and Eight Pence. There are likewise some small Gratuities received Annually by the Clerk of the Pells, at the Option of the Persons who give them, amounting to Fifty-five Pounds One Shilling. The Sum Total of all these Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities, received by the Clerk of the Pells, for One Year, ending at Michaelmas 1780, was Nine thousand Four hundred and Thirty-two Pounds One Shilling and Six Pence Halfpenny; out of which he paid for One Year's Land Tax, One hundred and Sixty Pojunds; for the One Shilling Duty, One hundred and Thirty-five Pounds; for Salaries to his Deputy and Clerks, One thousand Two hundred and Sixty Pounds; and for other incidental Expences, Two hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Nine Shillings and Six Pence; making together One thousand Eight hundred and Thirty-four Pounds Nine Shillings and Six Pence; w'hich reduced the Nett Income of his Office for that Year, to Seven thousand Five hundred and Ninety-seven PoundsTwelve Shillings and a Halfpenny: Which Sum, he verily believes, was all the Money received by the Clerk of the Pells for the whole Profits of his Office during that Year. He believes, in Time of Peace the Nett Profits of this Office do not exceed Three thousand Three hundred Pounds a Year.

This Examinant further faith. That he is appointed to the Office of Deputy, by Deed under the Hand and Seal of the Clerk of the Pells;.he is constituted his First Clerk, by a separate Instrument under his Hand, and approved of, and sworn into that Office, by the Commissioners of the Treasury.

The Profits of his Office arise from a Salary, Fees, and Gratuities. His Salary is Four hundred aml Twenty Pounds a Year, paid him Quarterly by his Principal out of his Gross Receipts. This has been the usual Salary

paid.

aid to the Deputy and First Clerk ever since he has nown the Office, and depends on the Will and Pleasure of the Principal. His Fees consist of a Rate of Two Shillings and Six Pence Cent, upon One certain Issue, according to the Barons Report; and Ten Shillings a Skin for inrolling and signing Patents, and such like Instruments; and One Pound One Shilling for every Constat of Seizures; and a small Annual Allowance from the great Wardrobe, in lieu of Liveries. The Gratuities are received by him on New Year's Day, from various Offices, at their Option. The Sum Total of these Emoluments is Seven hundred and Three Pounds Six Shillings and One Penny; out of which was paid Twenty-two Pounds for Taxes, which reduces the clear Receipt of this Office for One Year, ending at Michaelmas 1780, to Six hundred and Eighty-one Pound Six Shillings and One Penny.

N*38.

The Examination of Mr. Henry Thomas, Clerk of the Introitus, in the Office of the Clerk of the Pells; taken upon Oath, lft November 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he is Clerk of the Introitus, in the Office of the Clerk of the Pells, and appointed by him. It is his Business to attend constantly in the Tally Court; to take an Account of and enter the Sums received by the Tellers from the Bills thrown down by them into that Court; te write " Recorded" upon each Bill; to charge the Tellers with the Sums they receive; to examine and compare with the Entry the Tallies when read by the Chamberlains, to see that they agree; to enter these Receipts in a Book kept for that Purpose, and afterwards to inroll them.

There is hung up in the Tally Court, a Table of the

Fees due to the Officers and Clerks; the Clerk of the Pells, and his Clerk in the Tally Court, sire entitled to One Fourth Part of those Fees; except in the Article of Sheriffs Proffers, and some other trifling Exceptions, in which there is some Variance from that Rule of One Fourth. All these Fees arise from the levying of Tallies, and are paid by the Persons applying for them. He and his Clerk are also entitled to One Fourth Pirt of the Allowance made by the Treasury to the Officers of the Tally Court, for Tallies of all Loans levied without Fees.

The Tally Court Fees are received by the Junior Deputy Chamberlain, and divided by. him frequently. The Clerk of the Introitus receives from the Deputy Chamberlain the Fourth belonging to the Office of the Pells, and accounts with the Deputy Clerk of the Pell* for the tJfe of his Principal, for Four Pence each Tally. He keeps the Remainder himself, which has always been considered as belonging to the Clerk. The Treasury Allowance is received from the Teller by the Deputy Clerk of the Pells, who pays to the Clerk of the Introitus One Third as his Share: He is also entitled to some small Fees for Tallies of Pro or Assignments and Constat^ and to Two small ancient Allowances of Five Pound* each, and receives some small Annual Gratuities from some public Offices.

The Sum Total of all these Profit* received by him, from Michaelmas 1779 to Michaelmas 1780, amounted to Three hundred Forty-eight Pounds Nine Shillings, and Nine Pence Halfpenny; out of which he paid, frw Taxes Nine Pounds Seven Shillings, which reduced hi* clear Receipt to Three hundred and Thirty-nine PouftH* Two Shillings and Nine Pence Halfpenny: He receivM no other Profit whatever for the Execution of this Office. He believes, in Time of Peace the Income will hot exceed Three hundred Pounds a Year.

Henry

Guy Carleton,

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Richd Neave,

Sam1 Beachcroft,

Geo. Drutnmotid.

To the Commissioners of Publio Accounts, Gentlemen,

In Obedience to your Precept, bearing Date on the 14th of Jubf 1781, we the Deputy Tellers of the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer, transmit to you the following Account; being an exact State of the Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities received by each of the Four Tellers of the Receipt of Exchequer, and the Officers and Clerks in their Offices, with the Total Amount thereof received by each of the said Officers and Clerks during the Year 1780.

First, A State of the Salaries.

There are also many other Annuities granted for hives and Terms of Years, viz1. 14 per Cent. Excise 1693, 4 Tonnage 1694, 9 per Cent. 1709, Life Annuities in 17.45, *746, 1757, Lives and Survivorship in 176$, and Lives ,1778 and 1779; which are paid at the Exchequer to a very considerable Amount, for which the fellers and Clerks have bo Allowances whatever.

The First and Second Clerks have no Salaries, but have Fees and Gratuities as herein after mentioned.

The Under Clerks, being at present Three in each Office, receive Salaries from the Tellers in such Proportions as their respective Principals think proper to allow them. These Salaries are often varied, according to the Merit and Service of each Clerk; and these Clerls have no Establishment in the Office, and receive no other Emolument than their Salaries from their Tellers, and same faiall Gratuities, which will bestated in the following Account.

Secondly, A State of tire Fees.

The Authority under which Fees are claimed by the Tellers, and their Clerks, is ancient Usage.

In order to explain the Manner and the Proportion in which these Fees arc taken, it will be necessary for us to refer you to the following Fable of Fees, extracted verbatim from the Report of the Barons of the Exchequer, presented by them to the Lords and Commons in Parliament assembled, pursuant to an Act of the Fourth Year of King William and Queen Mary, and to make some Observations upon the present Practice of the Office, in Cafes where we deviate from the Rates set forth in the Barons Report.

Here follows so much of the Barons Report as relates to the Tellers Office.

We mull observe, that these Fees are paid by the Persons who receive the Monies, and are not carried to the Account of the Public: And we mull add an old Table of Fees, taken by the Clerks for receiving Monies, to which the Barons seem to refer in their Report. This Table contains several Heads, not mentioned by the Barons, which consist chiefly of Branches of the old Revenues of the Crown, which did not come under the COnsideration of the Barons of the Exchequer, because their Report related to the Aids and Supplies granted and to be granted by the Parliament then lilting. These Fees form a very inconsiderable Part of the Sum dated ' in this Account, as the Amount of the Fees taken for receiving Money, called Bill Money.

The Table of Fees allowed by the Barons of the Exchequer for issuing Money, is the Rule of our present Practice; except in the following In (lances, where Fees are either abated by old Agreements, or abolished by Acts of Parliament.

First, The Fee allowed by the Barons, for Monies issued to the Land Forces, is now taken only for such as are issued for the voted Services; and, by an Agreement, made in the Year 1744, the Officers of the Exchequer, in Consideration of the Iocrease of the Army Services, and of their Fees thereupon, tonfented to remit One Third Part upon the Extraordinary Services of the Army, which reduces the Tellers Fee to^*-. 9 per Cent, and the Clerks to is. z\d. per Cent.

Secondly, For Monies issued for Pensions to the Pay-master of the Pensions (an Office created in the Year 1702, since the Barons made their Report) the Tellers and their Clerks have, by Agreement, abated th< ir Fees, and have always taken the same Fee as the Queeu's Treasurer formerly paid.

Thirdly, AH Monies issued to the Queen's Treasurer. Prince's Cofferer, or to any of the Royal Family, are exempted from Fees, and all other Charges, by Acts of Parliament.

Fourthly, The Commissioners and Officers of the Treasury, and many others, are excused from paying Fees, by Courtefv; and Fees are frequently remitted in the Whole or in Part, upon Sums issued for charitable Uses.

State of the Gratuities.

The Tellers pay New Year's Gifts to the Amount of 22. 17-r. each* to the Lords and other Officers of the Treasury, but receive no Gratuities whatever for theiu-selves.

Their First Clerics receive New Year's Gifts in the following Proportions:

From the Bank - £.21 ----- --To each First Clerk.

From the South Sea

Company - - 21 ----- --To D*

From the Paymaster of the Army - 4 4 — To D*

46 4 — To each First Clerk.

The Gratuities to the Under Clerks are so inconsiderable, that no regular Account is kept of them. By the bell Information which we can get, they do not amount to Four Score Pounds a Year to the Four Offices.

The Bank give Annually Two Guineas each to Eleven Under Clerks; and Four Guineas to the Junior Clerk in Mr. Pratt's Office, for his daily Attendance at locking up the Office where their Cash is kept.

The South Sea Company distribute Annually Twenty Guineas amoftg the Twelve Under Clerks.

The Million Bank give a Guinea and a Half to the Clerks in Mr. Pratt's Office, and Half a G uinea to those in Lord Northington's; in which Offices their Annuities are paid, for their Trouble In entering their Accounts, and taking Care of their Orders.

The Receiver of the Sixpenny Duty, and the Receiver of the Land Tax upon Offices assessed in West~ ininjier, give each of them Ten Guineas Annually to be distrilmted among the Under Clerks, for their Trouble in deducting those Duties upon Payments in the Exchequer. The Receiver of the Tax upon Places and Pensions has sometimes given them a small Gratuity for their Assistance in the same Kind of Service.

There are no Fees taken by any of them for expediting Business, dr demanded upon any Pretence; and what they receive from the Companies and Persons above mentioned, are merely voluntary Gifts for any extraordinary Trouble.

Memim: The Account here stated, gives the Gross Amount of the Profits of the above-mentioned Offices: which are subject to the several Taxes annually paid by all the Officers under the Crown, and to the Payment of the Twelve Under Clerks.

It is to be observed, that the Tellers give Security to the Crown for all Losses and Deficiencies 5 and that the First Clerks (for whose Appointment the Approbation of the Lords of the Treasury is neoeffiuy} in like Manner give Security to their respective Tellers, to indemnify them from the very great Hazards uttending the Execution of Offices, which are charged with the Receipts and Issues of Monies to so considerable an Amount.

We the underwritten Deputy Tellers of the Exchequer, deliver the foregoing Account, as an exact State of the Salaries, Fees, and Gratuities received by each of the Four Tellers of the Receipt of the Exchequer, and the Officers and Clerks in their Office, with the Total Amount thereof received by each of them, and by each of the said Officers and Clerks, during the Year 1780.

The Examination of Daniel Esquire, Deput)'-and First Clerk to the Earl of One of the Tellers of the Exchequer; token upon Oath, the iith, 13th, and 15th November 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy and First Clerk to the Earl of Hardwicke, the Senior of the Four Tellers of the Exchequer: He was appointed by Deputation, dated the 7th of October 1745; and, as First Clerk, was approved of and sworn into his Office by the Commi (boners of the Treasury, according to the Act of Parliament.

The Teller is appointed by the King, by Letters Patent, for the Term of his Life; and gives, as he is informed and believes, Security to the Crown, if of Age, himself in Three thousand Pounds, and Two Sureties in Two thoustmd Pounds each. The Office of Teller was granted to the prefect Pofteflbi's in Rever-fion, and during tlteir Miuonity. The Teller is empowered by his Patent to make a Deputy, which Deputy transacts all the Bufeness of the Office; the Teller himself does not, nor has it Ireen usual for him to execute any Part of it whatever. The Deputy gives Security to the Teller as Deputy and First Clerk, by Bond, himself in Five thousand Pounds, and Two Sureties in Two thousand Five hundred Pounds each.

It is the Business of this Office, to receive, keep, and pay the Money 1 belonging to the Public; every Person who jwys Money into the Exchequer, enters in the Wade Book, the Name of the Person who is to pay it, the Sum, and upon what Account; the Deputy Tc4ier transcribes this Entry in the Walle Book in Latin, upon a Piece of Parchment, called a Bill, signs it, and trans-niits it through a Pipe into the Tally Court.

I'pon Production of an Order or Debenture directed by the Auditoiyaud recorded by the Clerk of die Pells, the Deputy Teller pays to the Person applying, the Sum therein mentioned, taking his Receipt; these Receipts and Payments are all entered in various Books every Day, the Receipts are agreed with the Clerk of the Pells, and the Payments with the Examiner of the Teller's Vouchers: the Teller agrees the weekly Certificate which is transenilted to the Treasury, with the Auditor and Clerk of the PeHs; the Half Yearly Certificate is agreed in like Manner. The Public Money is kept in Obefts, to which there are Three Keys, One kept by the Teller, One by the Clerk of the Pells, and One by the Chamberlain; these Three attend whenever it is neccftary to open the Chests.

Thts Office consists of the Teller, the Deputy, and First Clerk, the Second Clerk, and Three 'Under Clerks, all of whom are appointed by the Teller. The Emoluments received by the Officers in this Office, conSIt of a Salary, Allowances, Fees, and Gratuities. The Tellers have each lan ancient Salary or animal Fee, the Senior Thirty-tiiree Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence, and the Three Juniors Thirty-one Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence, paid to them by Debenture Half Yearly: Each Teller has also a Fourth Part of certain annual Allowances, for the Payment of Clerks, madetothem by the Commissioners of the Treasury, by virtue of several Acts of Parliament, as a ilcoonipenoe for the Trouble which the Management oft he Annuities created by those Acts, give to the Office; -which Fourth Part amounts to the Sum of Three (hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds Fourteen Shillings and One 'Penny Farthing; these Allowances are paid -Quarterly fey Debenture. The Teller has no Fee upon the Receipt of Money; his Fees arise from the Issue, and are grounded upon ancient U'sage; they are paid to him by the Perfotis receiving, according to a Table of Fees inferred initlie Barons Report, with the following Variations; for Money issued to the Army, the Rate in the Barons Table is Five Shillings

and Seven Pence Two Tenths p which is the Rate now used for the voted Services; hut for the Extraordinaries, the Fee taken for the Teller, is Three Shillings and Nine Penceper Cent, only; for Annuities, Rewards, Sfc\ in the Barons Report, in which Pensions are urfderstood to be included, the Rate is Two Pounds Ten Sh illings per Cent,; but the Fees taken by the Teller for the Payments made to the Paymaster of the Pensions, is only Three Shillings and Four Pence per Cent, being the Rate for the Queen's Treasurer in the Barons Report. Money issued to the Queen's Treasurer and the Prince's Cofferer, though included in the Barons Report, are now exempt from Fees by Acts of Parliament, as is likewise Money issued to the Royal Family. The Fees arising from these Ifl'ues, are divided equally amongst the Four Tellers every Quarter; One Fourth Part of which amounted, in the Year ending Michaelmas 1780, to Seven thousand and Thirty-eight Pounds Fifteen Shillings and One Halfpenny. The Salary, Allowances, and Foes amounted together, to Severn thousand Four hundred and Eleven Pounds-Fifteen Shillings and Nine Pence Three Farthings, and are the only Emoluments to which the First Teller was entitled in that Year. The Earl of did not

receive the Whole of the Salary of Thirty-three Pounds Six Shillings and Eight Pence; Mr. 'Cozen/kend, the then Senior Teller, dying within that Year, his Executors became entitled to a final 1 Part of the Difference between the Salary of the Senior and a Junior Teller. The Deputy Teller receives all the Profits to winch the Teller is entitled, and accounts for them with his Principal every Quarter; there are several Services, for which Sums amounting to above FourteenMillions were i(Tiled, upon which no Fees were taken in the Tellers Office, being exempt either by Acts of Parliament, Usage, or Courtesy.

The Taxes paid in the last Year by Lord for his Office, amounted to Three hundred and Twenty-eight Pounds Twelve Shillings and Threepence; he also paid for Clerks and other Expences, Three hundred and Eighty-four Pounds Thirteen Shillings and One Penny Farthing, amounting together to Seven bundled and Thirteen Pounds Five Shillings -and Four Pence Farthing: which reduced the Nett Profits of the Office of the First Teller for the Year above-mentioned, to Six thousand Six hundred and Ninety-six Pounds Eleveu Shillings and Nine Pence Halfpenny. To the heft of his Knowledge and Belief the Earl of Hardzvicke received no other Fee, Gratuity, or Emolument whatever, for the Profits of his Office during the said Time, except as above-mentioned.

Upon the Payment of Money, the Deputy dedufits all the Fees due to the Tellers and Clerks: he detains also the Laud Tax, and the Shilling and Sixpenny Duties. The Fees are divided every Quarter equally among the Four Offices; the Taxes are paid to the several Receivers, upon their Application.

The Fees paid at this Time by the Pa vmaster General of the Forces, for all the Officers of the Exchequer, for the voted Services, is One Penny Halfpenny in the Pound; and for the Extraordinaries, One Penny in the Pound. The Fee of One Penny Halfpenny is grounded upon the Barons Report which authorizes the same Fee for all Money issued for Army Services: Bnt he has heard, that fence the Year 1744, a Fee of One Penny only has been taken for the Extraordinaries of the Army, in Consequence of some Agreement entered into at that Time between the Treasury and the Officers of the Exchequer.

The Profits of the First Clerk and Second Clerk arise from Fees and Gratuities; the Deputy has no Emolument as such, but only the Fees and Gratuities belonging to the Ollice of First Clerk. L'pon the Receipt, the Fees due to him are called Bill Money, and are in Consideration of his writing the Bills; they are received of the Persons who pay in Money, either at

a certain Rate per Bill, or at the Rate of Sixteen Pence

per Thousand Pounds, according to an ancient Table of Fees used in the Office. These Fees belong to the Four First Clerks only, and are equally divided amongst them: The Share of each Clerk amounted in the Year endingat Michaelmas 1780, to One hundred and Eighty-m two Pounds Nine Shillings. Upon the Issue, the Fees due to the Clerks are a certain Rate per Cent, similar to those due to the Teller, according to the Services for which the Money is issued, as inserted in the Barons Report, with the like Variations and Exemptions.

These Fees are received from the Persons to whom Money is paid; and are divided in equal Shares amongst the Four First and the Four Second Clerks. These Fees amounted, in the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, to Eleven thousand and Thirty-six Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Eight Pence; One Eighth Part of which to each Clerk, was One thousand Three hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny. Each First Clerk has also an Annual Gratuity from some of the Public Offices, amounting to Forty-six Pounds Four Shillings a Year: These Fees and Gratuities received by him, as First Clerk to Lord Hardwicke in the Time above-mentioned, amounted to One thousand Six hundred and Eight Pounds Five Shillings and One Penny; he also received from his Principal, Three hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds Fourteen Shillings, which was the Allowance received by him for the Payment of Clerks; in consideration of which he pays the Three Under Clerks; the Second Clerk, likewise, by Direction of the Teller, allowed out of his Share of his Fees to him as First Clerk, Two hundred and Thirty Pounds, to make up the Deficiency of the Salaries paid by him to the Under Clerks, and as an additional Recompence for his Care and Trouble in the Execution of his Office. The Total of these Sums is Two thousand One hundred and Seventy-seven Pounds Nineteen Shillings and One Penny: Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Fifty-six Pounds; and to the Three Under Clerks, Four hundred Pounds; and to Porters [One Pound One Shilling; which reduced his clear Receipt to One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty Pounds Eighteen Shillings and One Penny; the Whole of which Sum was received by him for his own Use, and was the Total Sum received by him for the Execution of this Office, during the Period above-mentioned.

This Examinant further faith, That ever since he has been in the Office, which is upwards of Thirty-six Years, the Second Clerk has never attended or done any Business in the Office; he always paid to the Person, nominated by the Teller as the Second Clerk, the Share of the Fees belonging to that Office, retaining to his own Use the Sum directed by the Teller, except during a Vacancy, when he paid it to the Teller himself.

The Second Clerk's Fees amounted in the last Year to One thousand Three hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny; which was reduced by the Payment of Forty-two Pounds Ten Shillings for Taxes, and Two hundred and Thirty Pounds Allowance for the First Clerk, and Five Shillings to the Porter, to One thousand One hundred and Six Pounds Seventeen Shillings and One Penny; which Sum he paid to the Father of Mr. Joseph who is

the Second Clerk, and under Age.

Daniel Wray.

The Examination of William , Esquite, Deputy and First Clerk to the Ear!

One of the Tellers of the Exchequer; taken upon Oath, the 16th of November 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy and First Clerk to the Earl of Northing ton. One of the Tellers of the Exchequer, and receives for him all the Emoluments which he is entitled to as Teller. For the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, he received for Lord Northington, his Patent Fee of Thirty-one Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Four Pence; his Proportion of Fees being Seven thousand and Thirty-eight Pounds Fifteen Shillings and One Halfpenny; his Share of the Allowances, paid pursuant to the Annuity Acts, Three hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds Fourteen Shillings and . One Penny Farthing; and for the Rent of the Houflb belonging to him as Teller, Forty Pounds; making togetherSeven thousand Four hundred and Fifty Pounds Two Shillings and Five Pence Three Farthings: Out of which he paid for Taxes, Three hundred and Thirty-seven Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Six Pence; and for Salaries to Three Under Clerks, Three hundred and Niuety Pounds; and for Gratuities and incidental Expences, Forty-four Pounds Nineteen Shillings; amounting together to Seven hundred and Seventy-two Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Six Pence; which reduced his Profits, as Teller, for that Year, to the Sum of Six thousand Six hundred and Seventy-seven Pounds Five Shillings and Eleven Pence Three Farthings; all of which he has either paid to or received for the Use of Lord Northington; and, to the belt of his Knowledge

and Belief, is the Total Amount of the Profits of his Office, as Teller, for that Year.

He further faith. That as First Clerk in this Office, he received, during the same Period, One thousand Three hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny, as his Share of the Fees; and One hundred and Eighty-two Pounds Nine Shillings, as his Share of the Bill Money; and Forty-six Pounds Four Shillings, for Gratuities; making together One thousand Six hundred and Eight Pounds Five Shillings and One Penny: Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Forty-seven Pounds Ten Shillings; and other Expences, Four Pounds Four Shillings; together, Fifty-one Pounds Fourteen Shillings; which reduced the Whole Profits received by him from his Office for that Year, to One thousand Five hundred and Fifty-six Pounds Eleven Shillings and One Penny; the Whole of which he received to his own Use.

The Second Clerk is appointed by the Teller, under his Hand and Seal. The Fees of the Second Clerk are received by the First Clerk, and amounted, for the Time above-mentioned, to One thousand Three hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny: Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Forty-two Pounds Ten Shillings, and Five Shillings for Expences; which reduced the clear Amount to One thousand Three hundred and Thirty-six Pounds Seventeen Shillings and One Penny; which Sum he paid to Woodcock,

Esquire, as Second Clerk in this Office, who was appointed in 1763; but has not, that he knows of, attended or done any Business in the Office since his Appointment.

Price.

The Examination of Charles Townshend, Esquire, Deputy and First Clerk to the honourable John Jeffreys Pratt, Fourth Teller of the Exchequer; taken upon Oath, the 19th November 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he is Deputy and First Clerk to Earl Temple, the Third Teller of the Exchequer, and receives for him all the Proftts of his Office: That during the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, the Gross Profits of this Office amounted to Seven thousand Four hundred and Fifty Pounds Two Shillings and Five Pence Three Farthings: Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Three hundred and Thirty-seven Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Six Pence; for Three Under Clerks, Three hundred and Sixty Pounds; for other Expences, Forty-four Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Six Pence; making in all Seven hundred and Forty-two Pounds Seventeen Shillings; which reduced his clear Receipt, as Teller, to Six thousand Seven hundred and Seven Pounds Five Shillings and Five Pence Three Farthings; which Sum he paid to Lord Temple.

He further faith. That the Fees as First Clerk, were One thousand Three hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny; the Share of the Bill Money, One hundred and Eighty-two Pounds Nine Shillings; and the Gratuities, Forty-six Pounds Four Shillings; together, One thousand Six hundred and Eight Pounds Five Shillings and One Penny: Out of which he paid. Taxes, Forty-seven Pounds Ten Shillings; Expences, Five Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Six Pence; making together. Fifty-three Pounds Five Siblings and Six Pence; which reduce the Profits of the Office of First Clerk to One thousand Five hundred and Fifty-four PoundsNineteen Shillings and Seven Pence; out of which he retained to his own Use, Four hundred Pounds, being the Allowance made to him by Lord Temple for the Execution of this Office, and the Gratuities of Forty-six Pounds Four Shillings: He received no other Fee, Gratuity, or Reward whatever, for the Execution of this Office, during the said Period; for the Remainder, being One thousand One hundred and Eight Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Seven Pence, he paid to Lord Temple.

Ever since he has been in the Teller's Office, which is upwards of Twenty-six Years, the Second Clerk has never to his Knowledge attended or done any Business in the Office; and ever since 1773, when he was appointed Deputy Teller, he has received the Fees of the Second Clerk, and remitted them to Lord Temple. During the last Year, the Second Clerk's Fees amounted to One thousand Three hundred and Seventy-nine Pounds Twelve Shillings and One Penny; out of which was paid Forty-two Pounds Ten Shillings for Taxes; the Residue, being One thousand Three hundred and Thirty-seven Pounds Two Shillings and One Penny, he remitted to Lord Temple. He did not know who was the Second Clerk until after the Precept of this Board was received at the Exchequer, when he applied to Lord Temple for the Name of the Second Clerk in this Office, who gave him the Name of his Youngest Brother.

Welles.

Guy Carle ton,

This Examinant faith. That he is Deputy and Fit ft Clerk to the honourable John Jeffreys Pratt, the Fourth Teller of the Exchequer; that he held the same Office under Mr. Townshend the late Teller, who died in May 1780.

The Gross Profits of this Office for One Year, ending at Michaelmas 1780, consisting of the Patent Fees, the Fees of IfiTue, Allowance for Clerks, and the Rent for the Teller's House, amounted to Seven thousand Five hundred and Eleven Pounds Three Shillings and Seven Pence Three Farthings: Out of which was paid, for Taxes, Three hundred and Twenty-nine Pounds Nine Shillings and Six Pence, and for Two Under Clerks, the whole Allowance received by the Teller for Clerks, beingThree hundred and Thirty-nine Pounds Fourteen Shillings and One Penny Farthing; and for incidental Expences; One hundred and One Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Five Pence Three Farthings; amountingto-gether to Seven hundred and Seventy-one Pounds One Shilling; which being deducted from the Gross Profits, leaves the Sum of Six thousand Seven hundred and Forty Pounds Two Shillings and Seven Pence Three Farthings, as the clear Profits of this Office during the said Time; which Sum he received and paid to Mr. Townshend and his Executors; and to Lord Camden, the Father of Mr. Pratt, in Proportion to the Time Mr. 7or onjhendand Mr Pratt held this Office.

Ever since he has been Deputy Teller, which is about Twenty-three Years, during the Time Mr. Townshend was Teller, the Second Clerk attended and executed Part of the Business of the Office, and received, to his own Use, all the Fees of the Second Clerk, subject to the Payment of the Taxes only; there were then but Two Under Clerks, who were paid between them the whole Allowance for Clerks, deducting the Six Penny Duty; and the Second Clerk, Mr. Jones, received all the Second Clerk's Fees that accrued in the Year above-mentioned, till the Time of Mr. Death,

which amounted to Eight hundred and One Pounds Two Shillings and One Penny, out of which he paid his Proportion of the Taxes, being Twenty-six Pounds Ten Shillings and Ten Pence, which reduced his clear Receipt to Seven hundred and Seventy-four Pounds Eleven Shillings and Seven Pence. Mr appointed

N. 51.

The Examination of Abraham , - Esquire,

Deputy to Montague Burgoyne, Esquire, one of the Chamberlains of the Exchequer j taken upon Oath, 21st and I2d November 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he is Deputy Chamberlain in the Receipt of the Exchequer to Montague -goyne, Esquire, one of the Chamberlains of the Exchequer. The Chamberlain is appointed by the Crown, by Letters Patent, to hold his Office for Life, and to exercise it by himself, or his Deputy or Deputies. Mr. Burgoyne does not execute any Part of the Business of this Office himsel£ but the whole of it by his Deputies. He has been Deputy Chamberlain ever since the Year 1735, to Three successive Chamberlains, none of whom ever executed any Part of the Business themselves.

This Office, on the Receipt Sjde, consists of Two Chamberlains and Two Deputies, and no other Officer} it is called the Tally Court, whose Ifcifiness it is, to strike Tallies for the Persons who pay Money into the Exchequer. ThiaTally is an Acquittance, and consists of Two Parts; the Tally, which is delivered to the Person who pays; and the Counterpart, called the Foil, which the Deputy Chamberlain on the Court Side takes and keeps until the Person paflesdiis Accounts; the Sum paid in being cut upon the Tally, and the Name of the Person, the Date, and the Head of Duty, being wrote on each Side by the Tally Writer; and the Tally being split into Two Parts, the Senior of the Two Deputy Chamberlains, both of whom constantly attend* reads the Tally, the other holds the Foil, and fees that it agrees with the Tally, and the Clerk of the Introitus fees that it agrees with his Entry of the Receipt. In this Office are kept the* Standard Weights and Mea-fiires; the Weights and Measures delivered to the Sub->4

jests are here sized and sealed; this happens but feldorn. The Chamberlains al'so have each a Key to the Treasury, where the Standard Pieces of Gold and Silver are kept, and attend at the Trial of the Pix, which happens once in Five or Six Years.

The Chamberlain is entitled to a Salary of Fifty-two Pounds Three Shillings and Four Pence a Year, paid him Half Yearly by Debenture, by virtue of the Dormant W arrant; which Salary is reduced, by the I and Tax and Six Penny Duty, to Forty-six Pounds Seventeen Shillings; this Sum the Deputy receives, and pays to the Chamberlain.

He further faith. The Deputy is appointed by Deed, under the Hand and Seal of the Chamberlain: He is entitled, as Senior Deputy, to Four ancient Salaries of Ten Pounds, Forty Pounds, Seven Pounds, and Forty Pounds a Year, making together Ninety-seven Pounds, paid to him by Order or Debenture. He is also entitled as Deputy in general, to One Eighth, and in a very lew Instances to a greater Share of the Fees paid by the Persons paying Money into the Exchequer for firiking their Tallies, which Fees are estimated, in feme Cafes, by the Tally, and in others by the Sum paid in, according to an ancient Table of Fees hung up in the Tally Office. When the Tallies are taken from the Office, which is frequently many Days after the Payment in, the Person applying pays the Fees, which Fees are divided generally Twice a Week into Four Parts, One for the Auditor and his Clerk, One for the Clerk of the Pells and his Clerk, One for the Tally Cutter, and One for the Two Deputy Chamberlains, in equal Shares j in One or Two trifling Cafes this Division is not adhered to: This has been the Usageever since he has been in the Office. His Share of these Fees for the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, amounted to One hundred and Ninety' Three Pounds Seventeen Shilling? and Five Pence.

The Fees arising from the Tallies Itruck on the Contributions to Annuities and the Lottery, and for some other small Payments, are allowed by the Treasury, and amounted in that Year to Seventy Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Three Pence; he also received a Gratuity of Three Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Six Pence; which several Sums amounted to Three hundred and Sixty-five Pounds Four Shillings and Two Pence: Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Eighteen Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Six Pence, which reduced his clear Receipt to Three hundred and Forty-six Pounds Five Shillings and Eight Pence, out of which he paid to his Principal Seventy Pounds, being the Sum he pays to him annually by Agreement, out of the Profits of his Office; the Remainder, beingTwo hundred and Seventy-six Pounds Five Shillings and Eight Pence, he kept for his own Use. and received no other Salary, Fee, or Gratuity whatever; for the Execution of this Office, during the said Time. He further faith. That the One Shilling and Six Penny Duties are deduced in the Teller's Office, and the Land Tax is paid to the Collector.

As Senior Deputy Chamberlain he keeps One of the Keys to the Tellers Chests, and attends whenever they are opened, for which Service, he receives One of the Salaries of Forty Pounds a Year above mentioned,

Farley.

The Examination of Mr. William Deputy to the honourable Frederick , one of the Chamberlains of the Exchequer; taken upon Oath, 26th November 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he is Deputy Chamberlain in the Receipt of the Exchequer to the honourable Frederick North, One of the Chamberlains of the Exchequer; he was before Deputy to Sir Simeon who never executed, nor does the present Chamberlain execute, any Part of the Businessof the Office. He receives as Deputy; the like Salaries and Fees as are received by the Senior Deputy, except tfieSalary of Forty Pounds a Year for locking up the Treasure. These Salaries and Fees amounted in the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, to Three hundred apd Twenty-five Pounds Four Shillings and Two Pence; out of which he paid for Taxes Eighteen Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Six Pence, which reduced the Nett Receipt to Three hundred and Six Pounds Eight Shillings and Eight Pence. He does not receive this Sum to his own Use, but accounts for the Whole of it (except the Gratuity of Three Pounds Thirteen Shillings and Six Pence from the Paymaster General of the Forces, and another small Sum of about Ten or Fifteen Shillings) to his Principal; and receives from him a Salary of Fifty Pounds a Year, and no more, for the Execution of this Office; which is the Salary that has been paid to him ever since he has been Deputy.

W. Hammond.

Guy Carletoni

1 r

derick North, one of the Chamberlains of the Exche- Sixth Report quer: He is appointed Deputy by Deed, and exebutes the Business of this Office; the Principal executes no guyic Part of it. . Account*.

This Office on the Court Side consists of the Two Chamberlains, Two Deputies, and a Clerk $ and the Business is to receive from the Tally Court, and keep the Foils, until an Account is brought to bejuliified, at which Time the Tallies for the Sums paid into the Exchequer are produced with the Account, and left with the Deputy Chamberlain, who compares the Tallies with the Foils, and if they agree, a peculiar Mark is made on each, by an Inilrument kept for that Purpose, by which Mark the Officers of the Pipe know that the Tallies have been examined and approved in this Office.

The Deputy certifies upon the Account., that the Tallies are received and joined ',an Entry of them is made in a Book, the Account is delivered back, and the Tab lies kept till called for by, and delivered to, the Clerk of the Pipe. The Foils continue in the Office. Unless the Tally is produced, the Account never is, and cannot be, passed in this Office.

The Chamberlain is entitled to an ancient Salary of Fifty-two Pounds Three Shillings and Four Pence, paid by Debenture, and subject to Taxes, amounting to Five Pounds Six Shillings and Four Pence; he is also entitled to Thirteen Pounds Six Shillings and Six Pence, in lieu of Veftures, subject to One Pound Six Shillings and Eight Pence for Fees: The clear Sum arising from these Two Payments, is Fifty-eight Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Ten Pence; which Sum he receives and pays to the Use of Mr. North.

He receives, as Deputy, an ancient Salary of Five Pounds a Year, payable by Debenture and Fees from the Accountants or their Agents, for joing Tallies, according to an ancient Tablehungup in the Office. The Fees oh the Loans are paid by Order of the Treasury at the Exchequer; all the Fees are equally divided between the Two Deputies.

The Salary and Fees received by him in the Year endingat Michaelmas 1780, amounted to Three hundred and Fifty-two Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence: Out of which he paid, for" Taxes Sixteen Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence, and to the Clerk Twelve PoundsTen Shillings; which reduced the clear Receipt* during that Year, to Three hundred and Twenty-four Pounds Six {Shillings and Ten Pence; this Sum be paid,

Part to the Representatives of Sir Simeon , and

Part to the Use of Mr. Norths who was appointed Chamberlain during that Year, deducing therefrom Fifty Pounds, being the annual Salary allowed to hirp> both by Sir Simeon Stewurt and Mr. North, for the Execution of this Office; besides which he received no other Fee or Gratuity whatever.

It is not necessary that both the Deputies should always attend, in general the Business may be done by,

One; but for greater Expedition, the Attendance of both is sometimes necessary. The Clerk is paid a Salary of Twenty-five Pounds a Year,

James Galloway.

Guy Carletoni T. Anguish,

The Examination of Mr. Charles Alexander, Deputy Tally Cutter in the Receipt of His Majesty's Exchequer; taken upon Oath, 29th November 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy Tally Cutter to Thomas Lamb, Esquire, who holds the Office of Tally Cutter, under an Appointment from the Lords of the Treasury, during Plea lure; he has been Deputy about Seven Years, and has executed the whole Buli-nefsofthis Office himself, with occasional Affiliance Mr. Lambhas not executed, nor has it, as he believes, been usual for the Principal to execute any Part of it.

This Office consists of Two Persons only, the Tally Cutter and his Deputy y the Business is to take from the Tellers Bills the Sums received, and to prepare the Tallies by squaring them and cutting upon them the Sums in Notches, after which he delivers them to the Tally Writer. The Profits of this Office to the Principal consists of Two Payments, of Five Pounds Ten Shillings a Year, payable by Order and Debenture, and of an Allowance for cutting Tallies on Contributions, payable by Warrant from the Treasury; this Sum varies as the Loans vary, and amounted in the Year ending at Michaelmas 1780, to One hundred and Forty-one Pounds Six Shillings and Six Pence; these Sums are paid out of the Civil List; He is affo entitled to One Fourth Part of the Sums paid for Tallies (with a few Exceptions) received by the Deputy Chamberlains in the Tally Court from the Persons taking out their Tallies; this Fourth Part amounted in the same Year to Three hundred and Sixty-six Pounds Seven Shillings and Ten Pence: These Sums together amount to Five hundred and Thirteen Pounds Four Shillings and Four Pence; out of which he paid, for Land Tax Fourteen Pounds Ten Shillings, the Sixpenny Duty on the Salary Two Shillings and Nine Pence, and Allowances to his Deputy, Fifty-seven Pounds One Shilling and Three Pence, which reduced his clear Receipt for that Year to Four hundred and Forty-one Pounds Ten Shillings and Four Pence; which Sum he received for, and paid to Mr. Lamb. The Deputy has a small Annual Payment of One Pound Ten Shillings from the Uiher for grinding Tools, and some small Gratuities, amounting to One Pound Three Shillings and Six Pence; he was allowed by his Principal a Salary of Fifty Pounds a Year, and Five per Cent, on the Treasury Allowance, all which amounted in that Year to Fifty-nine Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Nine Pence.

Ch* Alexander*

Guy Carletoriy T. Anguijhy

A. Piggott, )

The Examination of Charles , Esquire,

Deputy to the honourable Horace Ulher of the Exchequer taken upon Oath, the 3d, 5th,_and6th December 1781.

This Examinant faith, That he is Deputy Ulher of the Receipt of the Exchequer to the honourable Horace Walpole, the Ulher; he was appointed by Deed, under the Hand and Seal of the Ulher, and has been Deputy Seven Years. The Ulher is appointed by Letter* Patent for Life, to exercise his Office by himself, or his Deputy or Deputies. He believes it has always been usual for the Ulher to execute his Office by Deputy; the present Ulher transacts no Part of the Bufinefc himself, it is all done by the Deputy.

The Office consists of the Ulher, his Deputy, and a Clerk, who is now also Yeoman Ulher; the Ulher appoints them all.

It is the Business of this Office to supply the Treasury and Exchequer with all Kinds of Stationary Ware, Tables, Delks, and Turnery Ware, and the Exchequer with Coals; to keep the Keys of the Doors of the Exchequer, and to employ the Persons who do Repairs to the Exchequer, and the Inside of the Treasury. The Advantages to the Ulher arise either from certain small Half Yearly Payments, or from the Profits he makes by his supplying the Treasury and Exchequer with these Articles, at a Rate according to an ancient Table of allowed Prices, kept in the Offices of the Ulher and Auditor. He has a Profit of Forty per Cent, upon extraordinary Articles not included in the Table, and Three Shillings and Six Pence in the Pound on Bills for Repairs. He delivers nothing to any Office without a Note, specifying the Article wanted; and every Half Year he makes out an Account for each Office of every Article he has served to that Office, which Accounts

12 Geo. III. i \° Februarii. 77 r

counts are both compared with the Notes, and signed by the Deputies or First Clerks in each Office, and are the Uther's Vouchers: Two Liberates are then made out, one for the old, the other for the new Offices; these Liberates contain all the Articles in those Vouchers, with the Prices; they are carried with the Vouchers to the Auditor; they are there examined and signed by him, then signed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, after which they are paid, by Orders under the General Letters Patent dormant. All these l ees and Profits, that accrued to the Uhl ter during the Year ending at Michaclmns 1780, amounted to Five thousand Two hundred and Ninety-three PblmdsSixSliillings and One Farthing: Out of which he paid, for Taxes, Four hundred and Seventy-six Pounds and Five Pence Farthing; for Fees at the Tivafury and the Exchequer, Forty-six Pounds Eighteen Shillings; for incidental Exper.cts, One hundred and Five Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Ten Pence; to his Deputy, a Salary of One hundred and Forty-four Pounds, and One Third of the Poundage on the Bills for Repairs, Two hundred and Thirty-four Pounds Four Shillings and Six Pence, to the Clerk, a Salary of Fifty Pounds, and as Yeoman Ullier, Thirty-six Pounds Eight Shillings and Three Pence; amounting together to One thousand and Ninety-three Pounds Six Shillings and One Farthing; which reduced his clear Receipt for that Year to Four thousand Two hundred Pounds; whicirSuin he paid to Mr. Walpole. The Stuns contained in t he Four Liberates for t hat Ye.lr, amounted to Fourteen thousand Four hundred and Forty Pounds Three Shillings and Six Pence.

Me further faith, That as Deputy Ulher, be received from his Principal A Salary ot One hundred kind Forty-four Pounds, and a Third Part of the Poundage on the Bills for Repairs, Two hundred and Thirty-four Pounds Four Shillings and Six Pence; end Fees from the Stationer and others, Onfe hundred and Forty-five

Pounds Five Shillings and Eleven Pence; making together Five hundred and Twenty-three Pounds Ten Shillings and Five Pence, reduced, by Four Pounds paid for Taxes, to Five hundred and Nineteen Pounds Ten Shillings and Five Pence; which was the whole Nett Profits of this Office for that Year. That he hath been informed by the Clerk, and believes it to be true, that he is paid by the Usher, a Salary of Fifty Pounds a Year, and he received in Gratuities, Seventy-six Pounds, One Shilling, making together One hundred and Twenty-six Pounds One. Shilling; as Yeoman Usher he received from the Usher a Salary of Ten Pounds, for Incidents, Twenty-six Pounds Light Shillings and Three Pence, and in Gratuities from others. Twenty-three Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence; together. Fifty-nine Pounds Ten Shillings and Nine Pence.

The Two Liberates for the old Offices amounted in the Year 1780 to Twelve thousand Three hundred and Thirteen Pounds Nine Shillings and Five Pence Halfpenny; of which, Three thousand Four hundred and Eighty-seven Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Seven Pence, was for Repairs, and Ninety-lix Pounds for Coals: These Liberates are paid out of the Civil List. The Two Liberates for the new Offices amounted to Two thousand One hundred and Twenty-six Pounds Fourteen Shillings and One Halfpenny, of which, Five hundred and Twenty-eight Pounds Six Shillings and Eleven Pence, was for Repairs, and Eighty-five P winds Ten Shillings for Co&Is: These Two are paid out of other Funds.

N* 64.

The Examination of Nathaniel Barwell, Esquire, one of the Paymasters of Exchequer Bills; taken upon Oath, 4th December 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he is One of the Pay-masters of Exchequer Bills: He is appointed by a Constitution under the Hands and Seals of the Commissioners of the Treasury, during Pleasure.

This Office consists of Three Paymasters, a Comptroller, an Accountant, a Cashier, Two Clerks, a Housekeeper, and Messenger; and at the Time the Public Bills are paying, as many Assistant Clerks as are wanted. The Paymasters appoint all the Officers and Clerks, except the Comptroller and Housekeeper, who are appointed by Constitution by the Commissioners of the Treasury.

The Business of this Office is to pay off and discharge the Principal and Interest due upon all Exchequer Bills.

When Public Bills are to be paid off, in consequence of a Letter from the Secretary of the Treasury, a Computation is made of the Principal and Interest due Vol. 38.

upon the Bills therein mentioned, from the Days they Report were severally issued to a given Day, of which public of

Notice is given by Advertisements; this Computation pubiic being sent to the Treasury, a Warrant and Order are Account*, obtained for the Payment of the computed Sum to the Paymasters of Exchequer Bills, which Sum is paid by the Tellers to the Bank, on the Account of those Pay-rnafters, and is drawn for from Time to Time by any Two of them, either payable to the Exchequer Bill Holders, or to their Cashier, to enable him to discharge Sums not exceedirigFive hundred Pounds.

The Bills taken by the Bank are some of them in h daily Course of being discharged by the Receipt of the Aids and Duties upon the Credit of which they ere . issued, and the Account of them usually settled every Week with the Bank: and others of them are discharged in consequence of Acts of Parliament for that Purpose, in like Manner as the Public Bills are paid.

The Exchequer Bills, when discharged, are cancelled, and kept in the Office, until sent to the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, where the Accounts are passed every Year.

The Paymasters, and all the Officers and Clerks, are paid by certain, annual Salaries, which have been the same ever since the Year 1736: The Three Paymasters have Eight hundred and Fifty Pounds a Year equally divided between them; the Comptroller has Three hundred and Fifty Pounds; the Accountant, One hundred and Fifty Pounds; the Cashier, Eighty Pounds; the First Clerk, Sixty Pounds; the Second Clerk, Fifty Pounds; the Housekeeper and Messenger, Forty Pounds, each: The Sum to pay these Salaries is craved annually of the Treasury by Two Memorials. One thousand Four hundred Pounds, Part of it, is paid out of the Duties arising from the Malt, and the Remainder out of some other Public Fund, by virtue of the Authority vested in the Commissioners of the Treasury by the several Acts of Parliament.

The Paymasters, out of their Salary of Eight hundred and Fifty Pounds, pay Sixty Pounds for the Land Tax, and Forty-two Pounds Ten Shillings for the One Shilling Duty, for themselves and their Clerks, which, reduce their Salaries to Seven hundred and Forty-seven Pounds Ten Shillings. The Comptroller's Salary of Three hundred and Fifty Pounds is reduced, by the Payment of Forty-one Pounds Ten Shillings for Taxes, to Three hundred and Eight Pounds Ten Shillings.

No Fees or Gratuities whatever are taken by any of the Officers or Clerks in this Office, except a Sum of Two Pounds Seven Shillings a Year, allowed to the Accountant, for making up his Annual Account. The contingent Expences of this Office for the Year 1780 (except what, as he believes, was furnished by the Ulher of the Exchequer) including the Fees for passing the Accounts, amounted to One hundred and Sixty-nine Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Seven Pence, and no more.

Nath1 Barwell.

Guy Carleton,

T. Anguish,

A. Piggott,

Sam1 Beachcrqft,

Geo. Drummond.

N* 76.

'This Examination of Mr. Cmopets One of the Clerks of the Bank; taken upon Oath, the 22(1 November 1781.

This Examinant faith. That he is a Clerk in the flank, and appointed by the Directors to attend the Exchequer; which he does every Day, Holidays excepted, at the Teller's Office, with Two more of the Bank Clerks, in order to take an Account of the Principal SumsYeceived into, and paid by, the Exchequer* When a Person brings a Sum to be paid into the Exchequer, after he has entered it in a Teller's Book; the Sum is either brought or sent to the Bank Clerk, from that 'feller's Office; it is usually in Bank Notes, and seldom in Calli; the Bank Clerk examines the Notes, keeps them, arid gives Credit for them to the Teller from whence they come.

Where the Person who is to pay in Money keeps Calli with the Bank, he directs the Chief Cashier to pay it into the Exchequer; the Cashier gives the same Directions to the Bank Clerk: When the Bank has received the Public Loans, the Cashier gives the like Directions; and the Bank Clerk, when he comes to the Exchequer, makes the Entry into the respective Tellers Book, and gives them Credit for these Sums.

Where Money is paid by the Exchequer, the Teller gives the Bank Clerk Directions to pay such a Sum to such a Person; the Bank Clerk pays it usually in Bank Note's, and debits that Teller for the Sum: Where the Person receiving keeps Calli at the Bank, the Bank Clerk generally carries it to his Account. AH the Receipts and Payments at the Exchequer, where the Bank is concerned, are transacted in this Manner, unless where the Sums are small, in which same the Tellers pay or receive themselves.

After One o‘Clock, the Bank Clerk agrees and settles the Accounts with the several Tellers, and either pays to or receives from each Teller the Balance; if a large Sum, in Exchequer Bills of One thousand Pounds each, and the Remainder in Calli; otherwise in Calli, in Bags, labelled with the Sum therein contained, and the Initials of the Name of the Bank Clerk who delivered it; where the Balance is under One hundred Pounds, it is paid or received in loose Calli. The Customs, Excise, Stamp Office, Poll Office, Salt Office, and several of the Receivers of the Land Tax, the Paymaster General of the Forces, the Treasurer of the Navy, and Treasurer of the Ordnance, all keep Calli with the Bank.

A. Cowpert

Guy Carleton,

T. AnguiOi,

A. Piggott,

Rich dNeave,

Sam^ Beachcro/t,

Geo. Drummond.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury.

The Memorial of John Esquire, Acting

Executor of the Right honourable Lord

Holland, deceased, late Paymaster General of H is Majesty's Land Forces, in Behalf of his Lordship's Deputy, of himself as Cashier, the Accountant, Clerks, and under Officers, employed in drawing out and settling his Lordship's Accounts with the Auditors of the Impreli.

May it please your Lordships,

I have the Honour to acquaint your Lordships, That his late Majesty was moll graciously pleased to appoint the Right honourable Henry Lord Holland, deceased, to be Paymaster General of his Land Forces, On the 15th of July 1757; and that he continued iii that Employment to the 1 ith of June 1765, being very near Eight Years.

That ,the Accounts of the Receipts and Paymetits of Henry Lord Holland, deceased, are made up and laid before His Majesty's Auditors of the Imprest, and his Lordship's final Account is near being closed.

Wherefore, I tnuft beg Leave to observe to your Lordships, That the very great Augmentation of the Army during the last War, and the extensive Operations thereof in all Parts of the World, naturally made the Accounts of the late Henry Lord Holland more intricate and voluminous than the Accounts of any of his Predecessors were; yet, by the Diligence and Attention of the Persons employed therein, the Accounts of his Lordship, amounting to the Sum of £.45,907,697. i6j. 4 were made up without any Expence to the Public for additional Assistance or Allowance.

In Consideration whgreof, and that Allowances have always been pnade to the Deputy, Cashier, Accountant; Clerks, and under Officers employed in this Business, I most humbly pray Your Lordships to move His Majesty for a Warrant, to authorize the Right honourable Lord Sondes, One of the Auditors of the Imprest, to pass and allow, on the final Account of Henry Lord

Holland, deceased, late Paymaster General of His Majesty's Forces, the Sums mentioned in the annexed Particulars, being for Pay or Allowances of the Officers, whose Names are therein set down, and likewise for the incidental Charges and Expences attending the fame, and for Allowances paid, and to be paid, for passing the Accounts through the several Offices.

Which is most humbly fubtnitted to your Lordships*

ition from A Petition of the Merchants, Tradesmen, and In-itolagainlt habitants of the City of was presented to the

Was. House, and read; Setting forth. That your Petitioners are compelled, by the dangerous Situation to which this Kingdom is reduced, by the imprudent Administration of Public Affairs, to apply to this honourable House for a Remedy of those Evils, which they not only apprehend, but so sensibly feel in common with the other Branches of the British Empire: The rapid Decline of our Manufactures, and the Annihilation of a very large Proportion of our Commerce (manifested by a Diminution of more than One Half of the Arrivals of Vessels to this Port) afford your Petitioners just Reason to dread, that if a Conduct similar to that which brought on these Misfortunes be ftiil pursued, the small Portion of Trade which is now left them, will not long be retainer!: Deeply interested as your Petitioners are in the Welfare and Safety of those His Majesty's Colonies which ftiil continue to be Members of the British Dominions, they tremble for the dangerous Situation in which such Colonies now Hand, as in their Separation from His Majesty's Government, would be involved the total Ruin of the only important Branch of Commerce now remaining to your Petitioners: In this debilitated State, pressed by the accumulated Weight of the public Expence, they cannot avoid anticipating the additional Burthens which a Continuation of the present fatal and ruinous Syftero must unavoidably bring upon them: Your Petitioners, therefore, humbly requestthishonourable House will adopt such Measures as its Wisdom may suggest, for enabling His Majesty to put an End to the unnatural, unfortunate, and expensive War in America, and for producing a radical Alteration in the Management of public Affairs, by which alone the Evils impending over us, and our Posterity, can be averted.

Ordered, Tliatthe said Petition do lie upon the Table.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Consideration jjoniton the Petition of Alexander Macleod, Esquire; and Election, also the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed. Inhabitants of the Borough of Honiton, in the County of Devon, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Anns was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and One hundred and Seven Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glafies, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Fifteen Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of William Adam, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioners, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Four other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of William Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Thirty other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Thirteen other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House; One, on account of his being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, which he had before verified upon Oath; Five, on account of their then serving on Select Committees; and Seven, on account of their having already, in this Session of Parliament, served on Select Committees.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being / complete, Lists of the said Names were delivered by the Clerk to the said Counsel.

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides withdrew.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Edward Inge informed your Committee, That the said City and County is very large and populous^ and very extensive Trades and Manufactures are carried on therein, which employ great Numbers of Persons; many of whom frequently contract Small Debts to a great Annual Amount; and although such Persons are well able, yet they often refuse to pay such Debts, presuming on the Difficulties their Creditors lie under in suing for and recovering the same — That if a more easy and speedy Method of recovering Small Debts within the said City and County and Liberties was provided, the same would greatly contribute to promote Industry, and encourage useful Cred it, and would be of great Advantage to all Persons redding and trading within the said City.

John'*, Mr. Fox reported from the Committee, to whom the &e. Petition of the Owners of Estates and Houses, and of Pavi'n^ Jnhab'tants in those Parts of the Parish of Saint John av, ng' the Evangelist, in the City of which are ex-

eluded from the Provisions and Benefit of the several Acts for paving and regulating the City of Westminster, and of several Owners of Estates and Inhabitants in certain Parts of the Parish of Saint Margaret, Westminster, lying intermixed with, or contiguous to, the said Parish of Saint John, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had di-rested him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to amend and render more effectual several Acts made relating to paving, cleansing, and lighting the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, was read; wherein it is declared, That for the Purposes thereof, the Parishes of Saint Margaret and Saint John the Evangelistshall in all Respects be considered as One Parish only; and also, that as there are several Streets and Places in the said United Parishes, where the Inhabitants are not of Ability to raise Money sufficient to defray the Expence of new paving or repairing, cleansing, and lighting such Streets and Places under the Regulations of that Act, it should not be lawful for the Paving commissioners to order any of the Streets or Places within the said United Parishes to be new paved or repaired, cleansed, or lighted, except the several Streets and Places in the said Act mentioned; but that whenever the Commissioners should be of Opinion that the Streets and Places so left out of the said Act should be so advanced in Rent that the Inhabitants should be of Ability to contribute to the Paving, the same should be subject to be paved, cleansed, and lighted under the Act. And,

Mr. John Bradley being examined, said, That the Commissioners always understood that the Streets not enumerated in the Paving Acts were left out of the last Act, hecaufeat that Time the Inhabitants w ere deemed utterly incapable of pay ing their Quota of the Expence of Paving and Lighting, and of Course the same would have become a heavy Burthen on the rest of the United Parishes — That the Consequences of the Exclusion has been fatal to that Part of the Parish of John, the Houses therein having ever fmee been going to De-VOL. 38.

cay — That the Streets are so wretchedly paved and lighted, and are so offensive from Nuisances and Annoyances, that People in decent Circumstances can never be expected to reside in them, and of Course the Parishes are so far from being now, or having any Prospect of becoming in future entitled to be admitted to partake of the Advantages of the said Paving Act, that they are in an incomparably worse State than they were at the passing of that Act, and are daily growing worse.

That the Sitting of Parliament compels Carriages to go near a Mile round — That the Track they are obliged to take is in general very narrow', and in some Places so narrow that Two Carriages cannot pass each other; of Course the Wear has been very great, and the Pavement so bad as to be highly detrimental to Carriages and Cattle, several of which have been maimed or killed by Reason thereof. — And the Witness further' said, That the Junction of the Bowling Alley, Peter Street, Tuflon Street, and Wood Street, is particularly dangerous.

That the Streets in general lie so flat, and in such uneven Directions, that for Want of proper Drains and Levels they cannot be effectually kept clean.

That the Value of Estates in the said Places is most grievously reduced, many Parrs thereof not being habitable — That it would be advantageous to the Land and House Owners, to the Parish, and to the Public, if Power was given by Parliament to repair and level the Pavements, and light the Streets, and to remove Nuisances and Annoyances, as eft'cftually as they may be able; as, under the Regulation of the present Paving Acts, the Parish cannot, nor are ever likely to be able to bear the Expence of paving and lighting the Parish a the other Parishes in Westminster.

That it would be a Means of raising the Value of Estates in the said Parts of the said Parishes, and of public Utility, if the Highway or Road leading from the End of Market Street to the Westminster commonly called The Horse Ferry Road, was properly amended and kept in Repair, and Nuisances and Annoyances in or near the same removed, and prevented in future.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending and repairing the Pavement in, and for lighting such of, the several Streets, Lanes, Ways, and other Places in the United Parishes of Margaret and Saint John the Evangelist in Westminster, as are at present excluded from the Provisions of an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty, intituled,

" An Act to amend, and render more effectual, several " Acts made relating to paving, cleansing, and lighting " the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places within " the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent;" and for preventing Nuisances and Annoyances in or near the fame: And that Mr. Fox, Mr. Byng, and Mr. Marsham, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were by the Clerk taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glasses, and were then drawn by the Clerk in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Three Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of John Parry, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Petitioner, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Six other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Thomas Dimfdale, Esquire, being drawn, he required to be excused from serving on the said Select Committee, on Account of his being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards; and having at the Table verified the same upon Oath, he was excused accordingly.

And the Names of Thirty-five other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of Thomas Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee by the Counsel for the Sitting Member, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Five other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Seventeen other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Three, on Account of their being Sixty Years of Age or upwards, which they had before verified upon Oath; Eight, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees; Five, on Account of their having already in this Session of Parliament served on Select Committees;
