Mr. Byng reported from the Committee, to whom the Stepney and Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are there-unto subscribed, being Owners of Estates, Merchants, Record. Manufacturers, Dealers, Tradesmen, and others, residing within the Mauors of Stepney and Hackney, in the County of Middlesex, the Hamlets and Liberties of the fame, and of the Parts adjacent, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, passed in the Twenty-first Year of His present Majesty, for diminishing the Fees payable, and altering the Mode of Proceeding in the Court of Record within the Manors of Stepney and Hackney, in the County of MiddleJ'cx, the Hamlets and Liberties of the fame, was read: And,

Charles Beck, Esquire, being examined, said. That the Provisions and Regulations made and prescribed by the said Act, hath been found of very essential Benefit to the District to which it extends, but that some of its Powers have been found inefleftual to fulfil the good Intentions of the Legislature in passing the fame; and that in order to render the same completely useful to the trading Part of the Inhabitants within the Jurisdiction of the Court, by promoting necessary Credit, and obviating the Contrivances and Evasions of fraudulent Debtors, some further and other Powers are necessary.

That the very easy and humane Mode prescribed by the said Act, for the Discharge of Debts by' Weekly Payments, has been found a great Relief to the poor Inhabitants within the Jurisdiction, and so serviceable to the Creditor, that it is unanimously wished that some Enlargement of the Sum to be recovered on an Action may be had.

That it hath become a Matter of Doubt, what is the Extent of the Jurisdiction of the said Court; by which Means the Business thereof is liable to frequent luter-fuptions and Embarrassments — That it would be for the Ease and Convenience of the Persons fitting as Judges, and serving as Jurymen therein, to have the Limits thereof exactly ascertained.

Tliatthe Inhabitants of several Parts intermixed with, or immediately adjoining to, the Places within the Jurisdiction of the said Court, although not actually within the same, being sensible of the Advantage of suing for their Debts therein, frequently apply to the said Court, or submit to its Process; but in order to render the same completely beneficial to such Places, it is expedient that the same should for the Purposes of the said Act be declared to be within the Limits and Jurisdiction of the said Court of Record; which many of the Inhabitants and Tradesmen are very desirous of.

Your Committee then examined John Mors Ellis, 1 Esquire, the Steward of the said Court, as to the Parts of the said Act which have by Experience been found to be defective; who said. The first Defect is the Want of a sufficient compulsory Power in the Court to oblige the Defendant, when able, to pay the Debt; as at present, a Man can be imprisoned but a Fortnight for a Debt of Filly-nine Shillings, and this in a Prison where there is every Accommodation, and where the Prisoner is allowed to work at his Trade for his Maintenance.

At present, the Operation of the Law is unequal in the very same District; as in the Court of Requelis, in this Jurisdiction, they imprison Six Weeks for the smallell Sum possible, perhaps for a Shilling, and that Imprisonment is in the common Gaol in Clerkemoell,

amongst

18° Februarii 1782.

amongst Felons, and where they are not permitted to Work at their Trades, and where the Fees on Discharge are very high.

From the Provisions in the said Act, there is no Ne-ceftity for any Man's going into Confinement, as the Court directs the Mode of Payment suitable to the Circumstances, Family, and Abilities of the Defendant; that there mud always be an Execution against the Effects in the first Place, and it is only in the same of a Deficiency thereof that the Person of the Defendarit can be taken.

That of Course, none but the most profligate and abandoned do go into Confinement, whereby, and by having removed their Effects out of the Jurisdiction, or made a Bill of Sale of them to some Relation, for the Purpose of protecting them, they injure their Creditors, and abuse the Lenity of the Act.

That in order to remedy this Evil, it is conceived there should be an Extension of the Time of Imprisonment.

That another Defect is, the Want of Power in the Court to follow the Defendant's Goods, after Execution on Judgment, when fraudulently removed by him. The Reasons for it are obvious, and the Necessity of such a Clause in inferior Courts was seen and allowed upon solemn Argument, and a Remedy provided in the Act for preventing frivolous and vexatious Arrests. But this Court cannot have the Benefit of that Law under the Powers of the present Act, because, independent of the great Expence, incompatible with the Spirit of the present Law, it makes no Provision for the Removal of summary Proceedings into the superior Courts, which would indeed be impossible.

From the Necessity of such a Power being allowed prior to the passing of the present Act, there is a much stronger Reason for asking it now, because, from the humane, and benevolent Spirit of the Act, tending to preserve a Family in a settled State, and to avoid any Occasion for its Flight and Removal, and allowing a partial Payment of the Debt weekly, in very small Sums, proportioned to the Wages received, and the Family to be maintained out of it, a Confidence is placed both by the Court and the Creditor in the Debtor, that those Payments should be regularly made, and their Humanity shall not be imposed on for the Purpose of gaining Time for a Removal of the Effects out of the Jurisdiction of the Court; for which Reason, a Clause suited to the Spirit of the said Act is necessary for the Purpose of following the Goods at a small Expence, that the Creditor may have the Benefit of his Judgment.

That the Act is also defective in not settling the local Jurisdiction of the Court; that Doubts have arisen, concerning the Meaning of the Words " Liberties of the fameand it is conceived that the several Parishes, Dilti ifts, and Liberties through which the Process of the Court has usually gone, and been acquiesced in, except in only One or Two very late Inllances, should be declared to be its Jurisdiction, and especially as the Inhabitants of those Places are desirous of receiving the Benefit of the Act.

That the general Credit given within this Jurisdiction is, from the Poverty of the Inhabitants, under /. io; that there is no other Method but that of applying to the said Court, for attempting a Recovery of such a Debt without the Ruin of the Defendants, who generally fly from their Habitations, and leave their Families a Burthen to the Parish, which is also often ruinous to the Plaintiff, who is not only injured by the Loss of his Debt, but his Diilrefles are increast'd, by lhe F.x-pence he has incurred in endeavouring to recover his Demand — That as the Arrest by Mesne Process, for Ids than/. 10, is taken aw'ay by the late Act of Parlia-liament, a speedy Mode of Recovery is necessary, and it is conceived, an Extension of the Sum to be sued for jti this Court is necessary.

That no Provision is made, that the Officer receiving the Suitor's Money should give Security for the due Payment of it over, and that a Clause for that Purpose* is absolutely necessary.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for explaining, amending, and rendering more effectual, an Act, passed in the Twenty-firit Year or His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for diminishing the Fees " payable, and altering the Mode of Proceeding, in the Court of Record within the Manors of and

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, it appeared to your Committee, by an Inspexi-raus of the Fourteenth Year of King Charles the Second, That, by Letters Patent of the 23d of April, in the Fourth Year of the Reign of King Edward the Sixth, Power was given to the Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens of the City of London, to hold all and all Manner of Contraftaand Demands whatsoever, within the Town and Borough of happening and

growing, by like Actions, Bills, Plaints, Process, Arrests. Judgments, Executions, and other Things whatsoever, in such Manner and Forms as such happening in the City of London had been, Time out of Mind, taken, held, levied, prosecuted, and executed, before Voi. 38.

the Mayor and Aldermen anct Sheriffs of the said City, or in any of them had been sued in the said City, and that the Inhabitants of the said Town and Borough, and the Parishes and Precinfrs therein, might be impleaded and plead in Form aforesaid; and by the same Letters Patent, Powers were also given to the said Mayor and Commonalty and Citizens, for impannel-ing of Juries for the Trial of such Issues: Then,

Mr. John Tozonfend, Prothonotary of the Borough

Court of Record, being examined, said. That by virtue of the said Letters Patent, the said Court has been usually held on Monday in every Week, whenever there was Business to proceed on, at the Town Hall of the said Borough — that when any Cause is at Issue, the Judge of the Court is acquainted therewith, the Jury are summoned, and he attends, to decide; that the Witness never knew him neglect attending — that Canfes are very often stayed till there are a sufficient Number to make it worth while for Counsel to attend — that the Court is not an open Court for Attornies — that, there are Three Attornies belonging to the Court, befidt s a Bailiff, Gaoler, and Six or Seven Officers — that the Bailiff summonses the Jury, who are the moil respectable Men in the Borough — that Causes are tried upon Debts from Forty Shillings to any Sum, and that many Actions are brought for Debts above Ten Pounds — that the Mode of Proceeding in the said Court for the Recovery of Debts between Forty Shillings and Ten Pounds, is very dilatory, and the Expences attending the same are very bnrthenfome to the Suitors, by Means whereof many Persons now submit to the Loss of their just Debts.

And he produced to your Committee, several Bills of Charges in Proceedings against Debtors; whereby it appeared, that the Expences of suing for Debts frequently exceed the Debt — that in One Cause the Debt amounted to £.2. 10s. and the Costs were£.5. 15s. id.i and in another Cause where the Debt was only .3. 3 the Costs amounted to £. 6. 6r.

Mr. James Bullock being examined, said, That if the Regulations now prayed for by the said Petition were granted, it would be of great Advantage to all Persons residing within the said Borough, and also be of great public Utility.

Then, to prove the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition, Mr. William Mason being examined, said.

That the Eastern Half of the Hundred of Brixton, is a Place of extensive Trade and Commerce, and Debts between 40$. and £.10 are frequently contrafted between Persons resident therein and the Tradesmen and Inhabitants of the Borough — that the Mode of Recovering the said Debts is very dilatory; and it would be of great Benefit and Advantage to Persons resident within the said Eastern Half of the Hundred of ton, as well as the Inhabitants of the Borough, if the Powers and Jurisdiction of the said Court of Record, under the Regulations prayed for by the present Application, were to be extended to the several Parishes, Precincts, and Liberties within the said Eastern Half of the Hundred of Brixton.

was read: And,

George Dance, Esquire, Surveyor to the City of London, being examined, said. That the Gaol of Newgate being in a great Measure burnt and demolished during the Riots and Insurrections in the Month of June 1780, the Sum of £. 10,000 was granted by Parliament towards building the fame.

That the said Gaol being under the immediate Care and Di rest ion of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of Lond, they have proceeded, with all the Dispatch in their Power, to lay out the Money so granted by Parliament, in repairing and rebuilding the said.Gaol, and particularly in providing different Apartments for the Reception of Prisoners.

That the Middle Quadrangle, with the Chapel and I-odge, is now completed, and it is intended to remove the Prisoners into the Middle Quadrangle at the present Se (lions.

That a spacious Infirmary has been built, the Cells for condemned Prisoners repaired, the Press Yard paved, and the Passage to convey the Prisoners to the Sessions House is nearly finished.

That the Bills for the Works already done, amount to the Sum of £.11,871. 4$. 4 of which the Sum of £.2,194, \s. 4 {d.now remains due.

That the Estimate for completing the Works necessary to be done to the said Gaol, amounts to £,19,000. if. id. which, with the Money already expended, makes the Sum of £.31,398. of 10 including the Sum of £.526. 15. 5 advanced for Fees and Disbursements in obtaining the Grant of the said Money.

That the Excess of £. 871. 5f. 5 above the Estimate delivered to the Committee of this honourable House, in the last Session, was occasioned by the Committee for building the Gaol finding it necessary, in the Prosecution of the Works, to have some intire new cross Walls built in the Centre Quadrangle of the Gaol; some Stone Cells erected for refractory Prisoners, with other additional Works.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Hammond was examined; who said, That he had known Cohham Bridge Twenty Years; that it is ! a very narrow Bridge, and Two Carriages cannot pass each other; that it is locked up with a Bar in the Day Time, which is taken down at Night, but that he never knew any Toll paid for passing over the Bridge. Then, Mr. Joseph Pic/stone informed your Committee, That the said Bridge is private Property, One Halfof it being the Property cf Thomas Page, Esquire, and the other Half the Property of t heRevercnd Dr. Richard Palmer, and Thomas Hurst, Esquire; that the said Parties have been applied to, and consent to give up their Property in the said Bridge, upon its being made a public County Bridge, and supported by the County at large; that they have also agreed to give the Sum of Four hundred Pounds/, together with the old Materials, and likewise to give Libert}' to dig Brick Earth and Sand, and to cut Fuel, for the Purpose of rebuilding the Bridge. And, Mr. John Smith produced a Record of Conviction upon a Trial at the Assizes, whereby it appeared, that Cobham Bridge is private Propert}-, and liable to be shut up;and that the Proprietors are not obliged to open it either by Night or Day, except in 'pme of Floods. Then,

Several Members present gave the following Information; viz. One Member said. That he had met with great Difficulty and Danger in parting over the lliver in the N ight, when the Bar was up; — another, That he was irt great Danger from the Water coining into his Chaise, when he was parting the Ford atthe Time the Bar Was up; — another, That he was very near being drowned in parting over the River, and that it is highly necessary the Bridge should be opened , — and another Member tfoitl, That lie lives in the Neighbourhood, and it is the Desire of all the Inhabitants that the Bridge should be an Vet. 38.

open Bridge; and that it is at present the moll dan* gerous Place in the County.

'Sir.Hammond being again called, was examined with respect to the State of Godalming Bridge, and said, That it is a very narrow Bridge, and always locked up, except in Time of Floods; that it is upon the great Road from London to Portsmouth, and is the Property of Miss Ma-

ly neut, who repairs it by the Tenure of her Estate. And,

William Man God/J/ur//, Esquire, informetl vour Committee, That Miss Molyneux has consented to give up her Property in the said Bridge* together with the old Materials, and Liberty to dig Brick Earth upon the Waste of her Manor, upon its being made a public County Bridge, and supported by the County at large. Then,

Several Members present said, Thnt they have voluntarily given Money for passing over Godalming Bridge, but that no Toll was demanded; that the Passage through the Water, when the Bridge is locked, is at all Times very dangerous to Persons not well acquainted with the Place, and that there were numberless 1 nltances of Accidents having happened.

Mr. David May being examined as to the State of leather head Bridge, said. That it is a very narrow Bridge, and the Parapet Wall so low, that lie has seen Sheep jump over it, and has heard of many Accidents happening to Persons in parting the Bridge; that it is not an open Bridge, except when the Water is high, being (lopped up by a Bar at each End, but that no Toll is demanded for parting over; that the Inhabitants think they have a Right to keep the Bar up, except in Time of Floods, and then the Churchwardens give Orders for opening it; that it is the Property of the Parishes of Leatherhead and Fetcham; that there is a

PieceofLand at Lcptherhead appropriated to the Repair of this Bridge, which is let for Eighteen Shillings a Year, and he has heard there was Land at Fetcham for the same Purpose; that there was a Rate at Fetcham last Year for repairing the Bridge; that several Sums of Money are paid Yearly for Carriages parting the Bridge, and having the Bar always tak-n down for them; that the Portsmouth Coach pays Two Guineas a Year, and he believes the Guildford Coach pays the fame; that the Land Frigate from , pays

Two Guineas a Year, and a Mr. Clayton used to pay Five Shillings a Year; that he never knew any Rate at Leatherhead for repairing the Bridge, but it has been done by the Rent of the Piece of Land, and Money given by Persons for parting over. Then,

Mr. Thomas Withall,(Churchwarden of the Parish of

Fetcham) was examined; who said, That the Parish are willing to give up their Property in the Bridge, upon its being made an open Bridge; that they had a Rate of Three Halfpence in the Pound, about Two Years ago, for repairing the Bridge; that he has heard of Accidents happening to Carriages passing, and there are several Instances of Horses going over the Parapet Wall ;and that lie saw the Ports mouth Coach overturned, about Two Years ago, near the Entrance to the Bridge, which is very dangerous.

Being asked, If there had not been Lands within the said Parish, the Rents of which were appropriated to the Repairs of this Bridge? lie said, There is such a Tradition; but he had enquired of the old eft People in the Parish, who knew nothing about it, nor where the Land laid.

Mr. Aaron Wickham (Churchwarden of the Parish of Leatherhead) informed your Committee.That at a Vef-try lately held, the Parish were willing to give up their Property in the Bridge, upon its being marie an open Bridge, but that they were not willing to give up a Piece of Land (about Two Acres and a Half, lying in the Common Field) which has been appropriated for the Repair of the Bridge, and is now in the Occupation of Mr. Clair, and let for Eighteen Shillings a Year.

:lofure. the County of Oxford, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That in the last Session of Parliament, the Petitioner applied to the House for a Bill for inclosing certain Lands in the Parish of Ensham, and for setting out and regulating Part thereof as a Common Paftnre; and that while the Bill was before a Committee of the whole House, a Clause was received for exonerating certain inclosed Lands, situate within the said Parish, from a Right of Common at a particular Time in every Year, and for establishing certain annual Payments chargeable thereon, in lieu of such Right; and that the Petitioner finds a Petition of several Persons, who were entitled to such Right of Common as aforesaid, has been presented to the House, alledging, that the said Clause was inserted in the Bill without their Knowledge or Consent, and that the same was injurious to them; and the Petitioner finds that he, or his Attorney, is charged with having procured that Clause to be inserted in the said Bill; and that the Petitioner is much surprized to find himself, or his Attorney, charged with any improper Conduct relative to the Clause in Question, as the Substance of that Clause was communicated to a great Number of the Parties who attended a Public Meeting at Ensham, which was called for that Purpose about the End of April last, and they then expressed their Approbation thereof; and that the Petitioner believes the said Clause not any wife injurious to the Parties interested, as it establishes certain Payments which had subsisted for several Years, and that the Payments fb established are equal to the Value of the Right of Common extinguished by the Bill: And therefore praying. That he may be heard, by his Counsel, before the Committee to whom the said Petition is referred, against the said Charge, and also touching the several Matters contained in the said Petition.

And the said Petition was readSetting forth, That the Petitioners, in the present State of Public Affairs, moved by every Sentiment that can impress the Human Mind with Regard for the Common Welfare of this Kingdom and its Dependencies, are impelled to implore this honourable House to interpose, in such Manner as to their Wisdom shall seem most effectual, for preventing the Continuance of the unfortunate War with America.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That it is the Opinion of this House, that, the further Prosecution of offensive War on the Continent of North America, for the Purpose of reducing the revolted Colonies to Obedience by Force, will be the Means of weakening the Efforts of this Country against her European Enemies; tends, "under the present Circumstances, dangerously to increase the mutual Enmity so fatal to the Interests both of Great Britain and America; and, by preventing an happy Reconciliation with that Country, to frustrate the earned Desire graciously expressed by his Majesty to restore the Blessings of Public Tranquillity;

And a Debate arising in the House thereupon;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the Debate be adjourned till this Day Fortnight;

The House divided.

Mr. Speaker,

crefl on A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are k Debt, thereunto subscribed, being Manufacturers and Traders within the Borough of Preston, in the County of Lancaster, and in the Neighbourhood thereof, waspresented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are in formed. That Petit ions have been preferited to the House from the Manufacturers and Traders in London and Westminster, and other Places, dating the many Hardships they labour under from the long Credit they are often obliged to give to their Employers, and that it would tend very much to reduce the Price of Labour, and of Goods and Articles in Trade, if Look Debts were pennitted to bear Interest, after the Rate of Five Pounds per Centum per Annum, after the Expiration of a certain limited Credit; and that the Petitioners have experienced many of the Hard ships and Inconveniencies which arise from giving long Credit in the Course of Trade, without any Allowance for the fame, and are fully sensible of the Truth of the Allegations contained in such Petitions, and submit to the House, that if Book Debts were, alter a limited Credit, permitted to carry Interest, many of the Grievances which the Petitioners and other Traders labour under from long Credit being given would be removed, and it would be attended with salutary Effects as well to the Petitioners, and all other Traders and Manufacturers, as to the Public in general And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Answer to Address.

Address of Thanks for the Answer.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty on Friday last with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this Most Gracious Answer:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

There are no Objects nearer to My Heart, than the Ease, Happiness, and Prosperity of My People.

You may be allured, that in pursuance of your Advice, I shall take such Measures as shall appear to Me to be most conducive to the Restoration of Harmony between Great Britain and the revolted Colonies, so essential to the Prosperity of both; and that My Efforts shall be directed in the most effectual Manner against our European Enemies, until such a Peace can be obtained as shall consist with the Interests and permanent Welfare of My Kingdoms.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His Most Gracious Answer to their Address, presented to His Majesty on Friday last; and for the Afl'u ranees His Majesty has most graciously been pleased to give them of His Intention, in pursuance of the Advice of this House, to take such Measures as shall appear most conducive to the Restoration of Harmony between Great Britain and the revolted Colonies; and that His Efforts shall be directed in the most effectual Manner against our European Enemies, until such a Peace can be obtained as shall consist with the permanent Welfare and Prosperity of His Kingdoms. This House being convinced that nothing can, in the present Circumstances of this Country, so essentially promote those great Objects of His Majesty‘s paternal Care for His People, as the Measures which His faithful Commons have most humbly but earnefty recommended to His Majesty.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty, by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty's Most honourable Privy Council.

At the Committee on the East India Judicature;

Ordered, That the Chairman do write to Mr. Barwell the following Letter:

Sir,

The India Judicature Committee having arrived at

a Period of their Enquiry in which your Name fre-qently occurs, and on which you may possibly be able to aftord Information to the Committee, or wish to give Explanation relative to your Sentiments and Conduct whilst a Member of the Council General of Bengal, the Committee have directed me to give you this Notice, and to request your Attendance at Twelve on day Morning.

Jovis, 28° Februarii, 1782.

At the Committee on the East India Judicature.

Richard Smith, Esquire, in the Chair;

Richard Barwell, Esquire, a Member of the House, attending,

Mr. Francis's Letter, of 12th 1780, from the

former Report, was read to Mr. Barwell: And,

He was then asked,

What Rule was laid down in the Act of Parliament of 1773, to regulate the Conduct of the Council General of Bengal I

As this Question goes to M&er of Fast, I can only answer it by a Reference to the Act of 1773.

20

Then the said Act was read.

Mr. Barwell was then asked.

Whether some Orders did not arrive from the Court of Directors whilst you was a Member of the Council General, relative to the Term for which Contrafts were to be made ?

I muftobserve upon the Letter which I) have received from the Chairman of the Committee, that I come to« tally unprepared to answer to the present Question, in the Idea that the Enquiry proposed on the present Occasion, was confined to the Objectexpressed in the Infli-tution of the Committee, " th Judicature Committee." If my Conduct, in any Respect, is criminated, and any Object to which the Committee chuse to esquire, 1 shall, with much Pleasure, give the Committee all the Satisfaction in my Power; but I must desire thatthofe Points be precisely stated, that I may at Once go to their Object without encroaching upon their Time. The present Question is loaded with an Imputation, the End of which I can form no Judgment of, and is not to the Purpose for which I suppose myself required to attend on this Day.

The Letter to Mr. Bariovll being then read;

And the Powers of the Committee being nlfo read;

As Mr. Barwell has mentioned that bo is come totally unprepared to answerthe present Question, the Committee inform him, that they will port pone Ins Examination to any future Time that is convenient to him.

To which Mr. Barwell said,

I am both ready and willing to give the most full and unreserved Information to the declared Purpose for which the Committee was instituted; but if, by what I have heard stated in Conversation, it is ex-pefted that I ath to Hand before the Committee to be examined to any Points of Mr. s Charges, as

I understand brought forward against the Governor General and the Court of Directors, I hope the Committee will difpehfe with my entering into such a Contest. I have no Purpose to' continue here the Difientions that, have prevailed abroad. But if I can give any Information which will tend to the Welfare of the Foreign Settlements of the East India Company, I shall be very happy to be informed of the Object of the Committee, and will deliberately state what, from a Knowledge and Experience of Twenty-three Years constant residence in that Country, and Ten Years in the Government of it, may enable me to do.

The present immediate Object of Enquiry isDifobe-dience of Orders: Are you wilting to answer all Questions relative to that Object ?

I must refer to the Two AnfVers Ihave already given to the Committee: If the Difolu dience of Orders respectsany other Objects than what relates to the Judicature of Bengal, or any Regulations for the interior Controul and Regulation of that Country, so far as the Happiness of the Natives are connected or dependent Upon those Breach of Orders, I mil ft decline to answer, becauseit can establish no other Point than the Merits of the Question, how far certain Parties in the Government Abroad have been right in refilling the Objects of another Party in that Government.

The Committee then proposing to deliberate, and the Room being cleared, and Mr. Banoell infilling upon his Privilege as a Member of the House, of being present during the Debate, the Committee observed to Mr. Barwell, that the Matter proposed to be debated concerned the Method to he pursued by the Committee upon the Answers before given by him; and that Mr. Barwell being the Party concerned in that Debate, they thought he had no Right to be present during the Debate: And Mr. Barwellftill persisting in his Right to be present during the Debate, Two of the Members of the Committee attended the Speaker for his Opinion thereupon; who being returned, reported to the Committee, That the Opinion of the Speaker was, that Mr.

[niniftrution Barwell, had no Right to infill upon being present dura Bengal. r'no Debate; whereupon Mr. withdrew.

And Mr. Barwell being afterwards called in, was asked,

The Committee not being able to collect from your Answers, whether you consent to be examined by them or not, on such Points as they may consider within their Inllructions, and not tending to criminate yourself, they desire from you a clear and decisive Answer in the Negative or Affirmative ?

I observe, That if I answer in the Negative to to this Queliion, from the Manner in which it is worded, it may be inferred that I decline (which I mean not to do) to enter into the Merits of Tranfa&ious to which a De- gree of Criminality is suggested. I have already" been de-

nied, as I have this Moment understood from the Speaker, that Civility, which as a Member of Parliament, if I do not misinterpret it, I was entitled to, in being rsquested to withdraw when the Committee withed to debate thr Point involved, in my Two Answers to the Two First Questions. fflriraainlv with to answerto every Matterthat can possibly ned>rought forward here or in any other Place, that may at all queliion my Conduct in my Situation of Counselior of the Government General of Bengal, or a Servant of the Company. But if wo precise Matter is brought forward, arid nothing is Hated, I will not Hand before the Committee in any other Capacity than as a Member of the House, willing to give them every Light in mv Power of what may be beneficial to the State in the Regulation of their Indian Poireflions: I will not appear as answering to, whether this or that Man did right or wrong in the Government of that Country; nor do I conceive that to bean Object to which the Powers of this Committee go, under the Instructions of Parliament: If they do, even in that Cafe, every Matter shoutd be precisely stated, and the Examination go to the Proof of such Matter; not to examine with a View to find Matter which may in its Nature be charged to Individuals, and cannot benefit the State.

A Petition of Sir David Carnegie, of Southejk, Baronet, was delivered in at the Table, and read; Setting forth, That, upon the Death of William Earl of Pan-mure in the Kingdom of Ireland, late Member for the County of Forfar, the Petitioner offered himself a Candidate to represent the said County, and that the ho^ notirabie Archibald Douglas likewise offered himself a Candidate to represent the said County; but the said Archibald Douglas having in his Person the Right and Title to the Earldom of Angus, in Scotland, the Petitioner was and is advised, that the said Archibald Douglas was incapable of being elected a Member to serve in Parliament; and the Petitioner did, at the Meeting for Election, upon the i ith Day of February last, in the Presence and Hearing of the Electors, object to the Eligibility of the said Archibald Douglas, in respect of his being a Peer of Scotland; and the Petitioner at the same Time produced, and read to the Freeholders then met for the Purpose of Election, a Copy, certified under the Hand of the Clerk of Parliament, of a Petition presented to His Majesty on Behalf of the said Archibald Douglas, afierting his Right to the said Peerage; and that, notwithstanding such Intimation, a Majority of the Freeholders then met were prevailed upon, by the Practices of the said Archibald Douglas, to vote for him, in Opposition to the Petitioner; whereby, and by Means of other undue Practices of him the said Archibald Douglas and his Agents, he the said Archibald Douglas has illegally procured himself to be returned Member for the said County, in prejudice to the Petitioner, who was the only Candidate capable of being elected, and who was duly elected, and ought to have been returned: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and t® grant him such Relief as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 16th Day of April next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the ioth and 1 ith Years of His present Majesty's Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in former Cafes, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Coun-fel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Surridge informed your Committee, That the said Street called Queen Street, which is not included in any Paving Act, adjoihs to that Part of the Parish of Saint Anne, Limehouse, where, by the Bill now depending, a new Street is to be formed, and leads from thence into Broad Street, near Ratcliffe Cross, through Pump Yard, where an opening for Carriages is already made. The Witness further said, That the said Street called London Street is not included in any Paving Act. and is the di-rest Way from Queen Street to Mile End Road', and will become a very great Thoroughfare when the said Opening and new Streot are completed; that the said Two Streets are very much annoyed by Nuisances and Obstructions, and the Pavement thereof very irregular, and not calculated to bear the heavy Carriages which, after the aforesaid Opening and Street are completed, will pass thereon. And he added, That the Communication between the Hamlets of Limehouse and Ratcliffe, through Queen Street, and from thence into Mile End Road, will be incomplete, unless those Two Streets are properly paved and regulated.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of Parliament of the Fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne was read; whereby it appeared, That all Persons not free of the Corporation of Great Yarmouth are authorized, upon Payment of certain Duties or Sums of Money therein mentioned to the Mayor, Aldermen,

Burgesses, and Commonalty of the said Borough, to import Coals, Culm, and Cinders into the said Port, and to sell the same in like Manner as Burgesses or Freemen of the said Corporation are authorized to do. And,

Mr. Thomas Smith, Assistant Water Bailiff* of the said Borough being examined, said, That it frequently happens that Coals, Culm, and Cinders are imported into the said Port in Ships or Vessels which belong, in separate Shares, as well to the Burgesses or Freemen as to Persons who are not free of the said Corporation, and that the Loading in such Ships or Vessels is the separate Property of such Persons; and that in order to evade Payment of the Duties or Sums of Money which ought to be paid by Persons who are not free of the Corporation, for such Coals, Culm, and Cinders, false Lifts or Accounts of such Ships or Vessels, and of the Loading thereof, are frequently made cut and delivered by Ship Mailers and others; and that by Means of such Practice the said Mayor, Aldermen, Burgesses, and Commonalty, are deprived of great Part of the Duties or Sums of Money to which they are entitled by virtue of the said Ach And he produced to your Committee

That in same such Bill passes into a Law, the same will be extremely burthensome and injurious to the Petitioners, by fub-jectfngthem to a very enorroousTax; and that they conceive there is no Colour of Reason why the said Bridges should be deemed County Bridges, but on the contrary, as they are at present, and have been ever since the Building thereof, understood to be private Property, and to be kept in Repair at the Expence of certain particular Persons, by reason, or on account of the Tenure of their respective Estates, or other Contingencies, together with the VartlhesofLeatherhead and Felcham, such particular Persons and Parishes ought to continue subject to the Repair of such Bridges, from Time to Time, when necessary; and that the Petitioners reside many Miles from the said Bridges, and can derive little or no Benefit therefrom; and if the said Bridges are declared to be County Bridges, the Expences of rebuilding and repairing the same will of Course be paid out of the County Rates, which are very partially and unequally laid, and will make the Burthen particularly grievous on the Petitioners; for the Quota of the County Rate made upon each Parish and Place is paid out of the Poor's Bate, which in the Hundred of Tandridge, by having the said additional Tax laid upon it, will be an Expence not to be borne without the greateftDifficulty; and that the Petitioners beg Leave further to submit to the House, whether, in case it shall be determined to rebuild the said Bridges for the Accommodation of the Public, it w ill not be reasonable that the Expence of rebuilding or repairing the same be paid by a Toll on Cattle and Carriages passing thereon, together with some Contribution from the Persons and Estates now liable to the Repair thereof; or if the Expences must be borne out of the County'

Rate, that such Rate should be equal throughout the.

County: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill, or such Parts thereof as may affect them, and have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall fecui meet.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, every Owner of any Barge, Lighter, Trow, Keel, or other Craft, forearming Goods, Wares, Merchandize, or Passengers above Twelve in Number, shall yield and pay Annually unto His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, the Sum of Two Shillings and Six Pence for a Licence to navigate or pass such Barge, Lighter, Trow, Keel, or other Craft, upon any River or Canal Navigation within the Kingdom of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be charged a Duty of One Farthing per Ton on the Tonnage of every Barge, Lighter, Trow, Keel, and other Craft carrying Goods, Wares, Merchandize, or Passengers above Twelve in Number, for every Mile Gich Barge, Lighter, Trow, Keel, or other Craft, shall navigate or pass on any River or Canal Navigation within the Kingdom of Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be charged a Duty of Three Pence Ton on the Tonnage of every Ship, or Vessel, employed in the Coasting Trade, from one Part of the Kingdom of Great Britain to another, where such Ship or Vessel shall pass by open Sea, except Ships laden wholly with Coals, Lime, Limestones, Chalk, Marl, or Dung.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said several Duties shall be under the Direction of the Commissioners for managing His Majesty's Duties on stamped Vellum, Parchment, and Paper.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Person who shall keep any Office or Place for buying, felling, fegiftering, disposing, or otherwise dealing in, any Tickets or Parts thereof, in aqy Lottery whatsoever, or shall, by Writing or Printing, publish the setting up or using such Office or Place, shall first take out a Licence for that Purpose.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there shall be raised, levied, and paid, unto His Majesty, His Heirs and Successors, the Sum of Fifty Pounds for every such Licence.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Monies to arise by the said Duties shall be applied towards defraying the Expences attending the Commission to be made forth for managing, directing, and drawing such Lottery.

by Means of which Manufactory, the Importation of printed Callicoes for the Company's Account, hath been increased to a very alarming Degree, and the Goods they have lately imported being framed on the Improvements in the Printing Trade made in this Country, are, as the Petitioners apprehend, not on any Account to be considered as within the Meaning of the Act of Parliament of the Eleventh and Twelfth of William the Third, under Colour of which they are now imported; for at the Time of passing that ACI, the Species of Goods which hath lately been imported to the Detriment of the Printing Trade in these Kingdoms, was not known in th eEqfi Indies, but only fuel) Goods as were the original Invention and Manufacture of the Natives of the Country from whence the same were exported and brought here by the East India Company; and that the several Laws made from Time to Time, for preventing the Emigration of Artists and Workmen, and the Exportation of Utensils employed in different Branches of the Trade and Manufactures of these Kingdoms, do not extend to prevent the like Evils happening to the Trade and Business of Printing; and that the Increase in the Importation of printed Callicoes from the East Indies for Exportation, hath already most materially injured the Export Trade of printed Callicoes, Cottons, Muslins, and Linens, from these Kingdoms, and, in Process of Tiape, the Whole of that Trade must be irretrievably loft, to the manifest Injury and Detriment of Individuals and the Public, and the grievous Distressof many Thousand Artificers and poor Persons now employed in that Business; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that by Means of the late Alterations made in the Manufactory of printed Goods in India, in Imitation of the Briti/modern Improvements, the Practice of smuggling EajIndia printed Goods into this Cdnntry will be greatly increased, and the Revenue of the Kingdom much hurt, as it is become extremely difficult, if not impossible, to distinguisti the Gobds printed in India from Goods printed in Great Britain: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and relieve them from their present Dilirefs and Apprehension of a total DestruClion of their Trade, by laying such Duties on the Importation of pointed Goods from the East Indies, not to be drawn buck on Exportation, as may put themanufactured Goods on an equal Footing with them at the foreign Market; and by making fuel) Regulations as may be necessary for preventing the Emigration of Artificers, and Exportation of Machines, Plates, and Utensils, employed and used in the Printing Trade, or by such other Means as to the House, on considering the Circumstances of the Petitioners Cafe, shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Cotton and Callicoe ManufactureVs of the Town and Neighbourhood of Chorley, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting iorth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Richard Arkwright, of Crom-ford, in the County of Derby, Cotton Manufacturer, hath presented a Petition to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill to give him the exclusive Use, for a Term to be therein mentioned, of certain Machines for the preparing and spinning of Cotton Wool into Yarn; and that the Petitioners submit to the House, that all Grants of exclusive Privileges aftefting great and extensive Manufactures, are extremely prejudicial, and ought not to be countenanced or encouragedin a Commercial Country; and that the Cotton Manufacture is carried on in the County of Lancaster, and the adjacent Counties, to a very great Extent, whereby many Thousands of industrious poor People are usefully employed; and that the fair! Richard Arkwright hath not, by his Petition, let forth such Grounds as ought to entitle him to the extraordinary Aid and Abidance of Parliament to prolong the Duration of the Patent mentioned in his Petition to be first granted to him, which is near expiring, or of giving Efficacy to the Patent mentioned in the Petition to be lait granted to him, which upon a solemn Trial at Law has been determined to be void; and that the p fling a Law for the Purpose desired by the said Richard Arkwright, will be very injurious to the Peti-

tioners and others concerned in the said Cotton Manufacture: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Petition and Bill, in case Leave should be given to bringa Bill into the House according to the Prayer of the said Petition, and that same may no* pass into a Law.

Ordered That the said Petition do lie Upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom toe Petition of Richard Arkwright, of Cromford, in the County of Derby, Cotton Manufacturer, is referred.

the Petitioner, and by admitting several illegal Votes ini Favour of the said Percy Charles Wyndham, gave a Majority of Votes upon the Poll for the said Percy Charles Wyndham, and returned him inllead of the Petitioner; and that several Persons were restrained from giving their Votes in Favour of the Petitioner by Threats and other undue Influence; and that the Con-dust of the Returning Officer was throughout the Whole of the said Election partial and unjustifiable And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to' grant him such' Relief as to the House shall feerri meet.

A Petition of the Owners and Mailers of Ships belonging to the Ports of Neioca Sunderland, Shields, Whitby, Scarborough, Lynn Regis, and Yarmouth, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Bebalfof themselves and many others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that, by an Order of the House, made early in this present Session of Parliament, the Time for presenting Petitions for Leave to bring in Bills, is limited to the Seventh Day of February last; and that the Petitioners did notdifeover the same till after the Time mentioned in the said Order had expired, and the Petitioners had prepared a Petition in order to be presented to the House, for Leave to bring in a Bill to revive an Act of the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to regulate the loading of Ships with " Coals, in the Ports of Newcastle and ,"

and which expired at the End of the last Session of Parliament; and that the said Act was of great public Importance, not only to the Coal Trade of Newcastle and Sunderland, but to the great Nursery of Seamen arising therefrom: And therefore praying. That the House will so far dispense with their Order as to permit the Petitioners, at this Period of the Session, to present their Petition, for Leave to bring in a Bill to revive the said Act, with the like Powers, Regulations, and Provisions, as are contained therein.

Ordered, That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present a Petition as desired by the said Owners and Mailers of Ships belonging to the Ports of Neio-cafile, Sunderland, Shields, Whitby, Scarborough, Lynn Regis, and Yarmouth.

Then a Petition of the Owners and Matters of Ships belonging to the Ports of Newcastle, Sunderland, Shields, Whitby, Scarborough, Lynn, xnd Yarmouth,w\\o{*i Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and many others, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Act mentioned in the last preceding Petition; and setting forth. That the said Act being now expired, and having had for its Objects not only the Increase of Seamen, who upon all Exigencies have been incorporated with the Royal Navy, but also the Advancement of the Property of the Petitioners, who are largely concerned in Ships chiefly employed in the Coal Trade at Nciocastle, Shields, and Sunderland, and the said Act having been found, by Experience, in othei Respects highly beneficial to the Coal Trade of the said Ports, by excluding all undue Preference in the Loading of Coals at such Ports, and by establishing a Rule which obliges Persons, employed as Fitters in the said Ports, to load all Ships as they are entered in their Turn, whereby the Public in general, and the Market in particular, are constantly and regularly supplied with Coals on easy Terms, to the great Advantage of the industrious Poor, and the Manufacturers of this Country; and that if the said Act was again revived, it would be attended with all the Advantages stated by the Petitioners, and which they have so happily expc-rienced during the Time the said Act was in Force, ami moreespeciallyas it has been found, sincetheExpirat ion thereof, that Coals have been greatly advanced in Price at London, and the different Ports, owing to the Want of such a Law: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration; and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for reviving the said Act, with the like Powers, Regulations, and Provisions as are contained therein; and that the same may be extended to the Term of Twenty-one Years, or to such other Term as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. John Child being examined, said. That a considerable Progress hath been made in amending the said consolidated District of Road; in doing which, the Tolls, together with a large Sum of Money borrowed on the Credit thereof, have been duly applied — That by Reason of a Canal made by an Act of Parliament of the Sixteenth Year of His present Majesty, from the Navigation on the South Side of in the County of Stafford, to Frogall, and the Railway from thence to certain Limestone Quarries in Caldon, in the said County, very large Quantities of Lime and Limestone are conveyed upon the said Navigation to the Neighbourhood, which used to be supplied with Lime by Land Carriage upon the said Turnpike Roads, by which, and by Means of divers Exemptions, the Tolls have been so much reduced, that the Income acifing therefrom is become insufficient to pay the Interest of the Money borrowed, and to keep the said Roads in tolerable Repair: And he concluded with saying. That unless some Relief is granted by Parliament, the Roads must go to Ruin, and the Debt now owing cannot be paid off.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Cotton and Callicoe Manufacturers, and Cal-licoe and Linen Printers, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, and the Counties adjacent, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth. That the Manufacture and Printing of Cottons and Linens are justly estimated amongst the most valuable Branches of Trade in these Kingdoms, and within a few Years past have been brought to a great Degree of Perfection, not only for Home Consumption, whereby His Majesty's Revenue is greatly increased, but also for Exportation to Foreign Markets, where great Quantities have been fold; and that the Patterns and Method of Printing used in this Country have, within a few Years last past, been made known and imitated in The East Indies with such Exact-ness, that it is difficult, if not impossible, to distinguish Callicoes printed there from those printed in Great Britain; and that the Proprietors of the East India Company having oflato Years imported Callicoes printed in The East. Indies for Exportation, upon Payment of a very small Duty, where the British Patterns and Method of Printing have been introduced, have increased their Imports of Printed Callicoes to an enormous Amount, and through the low Price of Wages in The East Indies, and other Causes, are enabled to export and fell them at Foreign Markets much cheaper than the l ike Species and Quality of Goods of the Manufacture and Printing of this Country can be afforded, whereby the Export Trade of Cottons, Callicoes, and Linens, printed in Great Britain, has already been very greatly injured, and is in Danger of being entirely loft; and representing to the House, that the Similitude in the Patterns printed in India and Great Britain will be a great Inducement to the Practice of smuggling into this Country the Callicoes printed in India, to the great Injury of Iits Majesty's Revenue, and the Manufacture and Printing of Cottons and Linens in Great Britain, for Home Consumption, upon which many Thousands of His Majesty's Subjects depend for Employment and Support: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to lay such a Duty upon the Importation into this Kingdom of Callicoes, printed in The East Indies, not to be drawn back upon Exportation, as is necessary, and shall be sufficient to regulate and equalize the Price at Foreign Markets with Cottons, Callicoes, and Linens printed in Great Britain, or to grant the Petitioners such other Relief as to the House shall seem expedient and just.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Secretary Fox acquainted the House, That he tiad a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, being concerned to find that Discontents and Jealousies are prevailing among His Loyal Subjects in Ireland, upon Matters of great Weight and Importance, earnestly recommends to this House, to take the same into their most serious Consideration, in order to such a final Adjustment as may give mutual Satisfaction to both Kingdoms.

G. R.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most Gracious Message; and toaffure His Majesty, that this House, feeling with His Majesty the deepest Concern that Discontents and Jealousies should have arisen among His Majesty's Loyal Subjects in Ireland, will, without Delay, take the same into their most serious Consideration, in order to such a final Adjustment as may give mutual Satisfaction to both Kingdoms.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty's most honourable Privy Council.

THE Lord Trentham reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses of the Borough of Newcastle under Lyme, in the County of Stafford, under their Common Seal, and of the Freeholders and other principal Inhabitants of the Borough and Pvarish of Newcastle under Lyme aforesaid, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Bills of Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Sparrow being examined, said. That within the said Borough there is a certain Parcel of Waste Ground, called The Marsh, containing about Twenty-three Statute Acres (exclusive of the Public Roads and Highways over the fame) on which the Freeholders; Owners, and Occupiers of Messuages, Lands, and Tenements within the said Borough, have Right of Common, and the Soil thereof belongs to the said Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, as Lords of the Manor; that the said Waste Ground is at present in a very neglected State, and of little Value to the Inhabitants and Persons interested therein, by Reason of the great Spoil and Waste committed, and the Heaps of Rubbish and other Nuisances placed, upon the fame, by Means whereof the same is become very obnoxious to the Inhabitants and the Public; that if the above Nuisances were removed; and the said Waste Ground was inclosed and leased out for Terms of Years, and the Rents and Profits thereby arising applied in Aid of the Poor's Rates of the said Borough, which are now very burthensome, it would be of great Advantage to all the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and of great Public Utility. And he added, That there have been several Meetings had, when great Numbers of the Parties interested attended, and it was understood the Town were unanimous for the Application.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for inclosing and leafing a Piece of Waste Land, called The Marsh, within the Borough of Newcastle under Lyme, in the County of Stafford, and applying the Profits thereof in Aid of the Poor's Rates of the said Borough: And that the Lord Trentham and Mr, Gilbert do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Byng reported from the Committee, to whom the Hanover Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and Vestrymen, Square of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, in the City Paving,

and Liberty of Westminster, and County of was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of the Eleventh of His present Majesty was read; whereby it appeared, that Powers are vested in the Commissioners and Parochial Committees jointly, for the Purpose of paving, cleansing, and lighting the several Streets, Squares, and Places within the City and Liberty of Westminster: And,

Mr. Edward Waters, Inspector to the Parochial Committeeof the said Parish of Saint George, Hanover , being examined, said, That the Whole of the said Parish

(except

Militia Pay and Clothing.

022 150 Ap A, 1781.

(except certain Places which are under the Di rest ion of particular Acts of Parliament, and also except a few inconsiderable Streets and Mewfes, the Inhabitants whereof being poor, are not desirous of having them paved, and which are all lighted) hath been paved according to the Directions of the several Acts made for that Purpose.

Mr. John Aujlin, Clerk to the Parochial Committee, then produced a State of the Debt incurred for the Purposes aforesaid, amounting to the Sum of£. 41,000 and upwards, besides what is owing upon certain optional Streets: And added, That the Interference of the said Commissioners within the said Parish, is now become altogether unnecessary, the Work being almost completed.

Thomas Wiggins, Esquire, one of the Parochial Committee, being next examined, informed your Committee, That great Delays are occasioned by the Parochial . Committee being obliged, on many Occasions, to wait upon the Commissioners; and particularly in order to obtain previous Leave to advertise to make Contrafts, and afterwards to get them approved and confirmed, although no one Contraft of this Parish has ever been objected to by the Commissioners since the passing of the said Act — That it has happened, that when these Applications for Leave to advertise to make Contrafts have been lent down to the Commissioners, they have been so long detained before they were returned to the Committee, that the fubflfting Contrafts have expired Two Days before they were received. He further said, That it will be a very great Saving to the parochial Committee, and the Business will be much more ad van-tageously conducted, if the Interference of the Commissioners were taken away, as the several Officers appointed by them have been paid at sundry Times, upon an Average, from 180 to £.130 per which,

in the Course of Ten Years, has amounted to £.1,480; and that the whole of the Rates levied and collected in the said Parish, after paying the Interest of the £.41,000 /borrowed, do not amount to more than£. 800 for the Repairs of the Payment of the whole Parish under the Committee, out of which is first deducted the Amount of the above Salaries. And the Witness is of Opinion, That placing the whole Power in the Vellry, would not only be a great Saving, but would also very much expedite the Business of paving and lighting the said Parish.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for better paving, cleansing, and lighting Part of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, in the County of

Middlesex; and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein: And that Mr. Byng and Mr. Secretary Fox do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Secretary Fox acquainted the House, That he Miflagefrom had aMeflagefrom His Majesty to this House, ligned the King, re-by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the jj* g^pendi-House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Mem- ture. bers of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, taking into Consideration the Supplies which have been given with so much Liberality, and supported with such uncommon Firmness and Fortitude by His People, in the present extensive War, recommends to His faithful Commons the Consideration of aneffe£tual Plan of Economy through all the Branches of the Public Expenditure; towards which important Object, His Majesty has taken into His actual Confide-pation, a Reform and Regulation in His Civil Establishment, which He will shortly cause to be laid before-this House, desiring their Assistance towards carrying the same more fully into Execution. His Majesty has no Reserves with His People; on whose Affections He rests with a sure Reliance, as the bed Support of the true Honour and Dignity of His Crown and Government; and as they have hitherto been His best Resource upon every Emergency, so He regards them as the most solid and liable Security for an honourable Provision for His Person and Family.

G. R.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That an humble Addrefr to Address be presented to His Majesty, to express to His the King* Majesty, that His truly paternal Regard for the Wel-fareof His People, meets a just Return in the Gratitude produced in the Breads of His faithful Commons, by His Majesty's most Gracious Message to this House:

To allure His Majesty, that His favourable Acceptance of the Zeal and Fidelity of His Subjects, manifested through the whole course of this arduous War, will animate them to the utmost Exertions for the Glory and Happiness of a Prince, who fetsa just Value on the Services, and is touched with an affectionate Sympathy in the Sufferiugs, of His People:

That His faithful Commons, deeply affected with His Majesty's noble and generous Procedure, and encouraged by a Recommendation at once glorious to His Majesty, and perfectly consonant to our Delires and Duties, will, as soon as His Majesty shall be pleased to communicate more particularly the Reformations and Regulations He is pleased to adopt, apply ourselves, with all Speed and Diligence, to give a full Efted to His Majesty's most gracious Intentions:

That His faithful Commons consider the unreserved Confidence which His Majesty reposes in this House, as a full Compensation for their earned and dutiful Endeavours to deserve that invaluable Testimony of His Royal Favour, a Confidence by which His Majesty will reign in the Hearts of His People, and in which he never can be deceived with regard to His Crown, His Person, and His Family: AKing of Great Britain cannot have so perfect or so honourable a Security for every thing which can make a King truly great and truly happy, as in the genuine and natural Support of an uninfluenced and independent House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for better securing the Duties payable by virtue of an Act of the Fifth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, on the Importation of Coals, Culm, and Cinders, into the Port of Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk; without any Amendment: And also.

Hanover A PETITION of the principal Inhabitants of Old Square and Nero Bond Street, in the Parish of Saint George,

Paving. Hanover Square, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented, for taking the present Power of paving, cleansing, and lighting the said Parish o Hanover Square, out of the Hands of the Commissioners appointed for that Purpose by several Acts of Parliament, and vesting the same in the Rector, Churchwardens, and Vestrymen of the said Parish; and alleging, that Old and New Bond Street were paved under the Direction of the said Commissioners, by virtue of VOL. 38.

an optional Clause in an Act fnade in the Fiflh Yenr of His present Majesty, ever since which they have been at a very great Expence in paving and repairing the said Street, and have incurred a Debt of 6;oooo, and are now rated at Three Shillings in the Pound for the Purposes aforesaid; and that the Petitioners apprehend the said Streets might be paved, cleansed, and lighted, at a more moderate Expence, under the Direction of the said Rector, Churchwardens, and Vestrymen, than under the Management of the said Commissioners: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill lor the Purposes aforesaid, and that the same may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for better paving, cleansing, and lighting Part of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, in the County of Middlesex, and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein, be read a Second Time.

A Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Exe- Hanover cution the several Acts of Parliament for paving, Square cleansing, and lighting the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Paving, other Places within the City and Liberty of and other Places therein mentioned, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for better paving, cleansing, and lighting Part of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, in the County of Middlesex, and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein; and Setting forth, That the Petitioners have fecn the Evidence upon which the said Bill is founded, and deny some of the Facts therein stated; and beg Leave to represent to the House, some Reasons why they presume, upon the general Idea of Benefit arising to the several Parishes and Places comprized in the general Paving Commission, that no Parish should be suffered to separate itself from the others, more particularly the Parish of George,

Hanover Square, that being one of the fargest and most opulent, and having paid the least Regard to the Terms and Directions of the general Paving Acts, over which the Petitioners preside; that, if the said Bill pafles, the Petitioners Power, as Trustees for the Streets called Optional Streets, ceases, and they will beunderno other Care but that of a Parish Committee, and of course the Securities of the Mortgages will be weakened; that the Committee established by the Paving Act of the Eleventh of His present Majesty, for the said Parish, have been continually negligent of their Duty, and the Petitioners are frequently obliged to call upon them to mend the Pavements, cleanse, and other Matters which are most shamefully neglected until they are so called upon; that the said Committee have neglected, though often called upon by the Petitioners, to lay before them their Accounts of Money rated, collected, and in Arrear, in the Parish, as the Act directs; that the Accounts of the Committee are kept in a very imperfect and confused State, and the Petitioners doubt not to prove, that Sums of public Money have been misapplied; that the Committee have made the Rates to the Amount of £.50,000, and borrowed upwards of £. 41,000 on the Credit of the Rates, or Part of them, and have never given the Petitioners an Account thereof, in Manner directed by the said Act of the Eleventh of His present Majesty; and that the ciif-uniting the said Parish lrom the general Commission mull throw a great additional Expence upon the other Parishes and Places under the < etitiouers Care; and that the Poor's Rates in the said Parish, by wuich the Paving Rates are regulateu, are made in a very fallacious and unfair Manner, many Houses not being rated at more than One-half, and a great many at not more than One fourth Part of their Rent; and the Petitioners beg Leave to observe that if other Parishes and Places had taken the Example shewed them by the Parish of

Saint George, no Parish could have been properly paved

94^ *4° -4

and regulated, and tins has been one great Cause why the Parish of Saint George has not been paved in so proper a Manner, and with such good Materials, as it ought to have been, and also why it is not yet completed; and that the Petitioners for the said Bill have stated, in their Petition, that they have borrowed £.40,000 and upwards, and the Evidence on the Petition for the Bill dates, that they have borrowed £.41,000 and upwards, for the Purpose of paving and regulating their Parish, whereas the Certificate signed by the Committee for that Parish, to the Petitioners, to Lady Day 1782, dates the whole Sum to be only £.38,375; and that the Petitioners rely on the Justice of Parliament, that, as they are legal Trustees for all the Parishes and Places included in the General Paving AA of the Eleventh of His present Majesty, and Parties to all Contracts, as well as Trustees for the several Creditors who have lent Money on the Rates, particularly the Optional Streets, the House will not permit the said Paridi of Saint George, Hanover Square, to be separated and taken from the Petitioners Controul, until the Committee have fairly accounted with the Petitioners for all the Monies they have borrowed and raised by Rates or otherwise, and shewing how much is in Arrear, and in every other RespeA proved to the Petitioners and the Public, that they have acted fairly and equitably in the Trud reposed in them: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, and be permitted to produce Evidence to shew why the same ought not to pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then beard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Mr. Byng reported from the Committee, to whom Sr the Petition of the ReAor, Churchwardens, Overseers Workhousc. of the Poor, Vestrymen, and principal Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint Luke, in the County of Middlesex, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Richard Jennings, Vestry Clerk, being examined, said.

That there was a Lease taken by the Parish, of a House and Ground in Old Street Road, of one Mr. James Brown, for a Poor House; it expired at Midsummer 1779 — That it is in bad Condition, and cannot be put into Repair for the proper Reception of the Poor, without a considerable Sum of Money being expended on it — That the Parish are only Tenants on Sufferance, and have had Notice to quit next Michaelmas — That they have offered Terms to Mr. William Robinson, who would not accept them, but demanded Two hundred Guineas for a Fine, and Eighty Guineas a Year Rent, clear of all Taxes.

And being further examined, he said, That the Poor of the said Parish are numerous, amounting at present to near Three-hundred and Fifty; and that it would be for the Advantage of the Parish to ereA a proper Workhouse; but that a sufficient Sum for that Purpose cannot be raised without the Aid of Parliament.

Mr. James Carr, a Surveyor, being examined, said.

He had surveyed the present House, and made an Estimateof the Expence of the necessary Repairs for Twenty-one Years, which would cost Eight Hundred and Sixty-seven Pounds, or thereabouts; which Term of Twenty-one Years is the Extent of what Mr. Robinson can grant.

Mr. Thomas Mutter, a Surveyor, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of the lait Witness; and both concurred in saying. That a commodious House for the Reception of the Poor, might be built for Four thousand Pounds, in a better Situation, and on all Accounts preferable to that now in Use.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill more effectually to enable the Inhabitants of the Parish, oiSaint Luke, in the County of Middlesex, to purchase, hire, or ereA a Workhouse, within or near the said Parish for the better Reception and Employment of the Poor of the said Parish: And that Mr. Byng, Mr. Alderman Wilkes, and Mr. Whitbread, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Expence of the Coinage of Gold in this Kingdom is borne by the Public.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Expence of the Coinage of Gold in tMs Kingdom ought not henceforth to be borne by the Public, but that a Dedo&ion ought to be made for the future out of the Gold coined at the Mint, to defray the Whole, or a considerable Part of the Espenoe of such Coinage.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the State of the Coinage of Gold in this Kingdom defefves the immediate and ferrous Consideration of Parliament.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Expence of the Coinage of Silver in this Kingdom is borne by the Public.

Rejbboed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Expence of the Coinage of Silver in this Kingdom ought not henoeforth to be borne by the Public; and that a greater Deduction ought to be made for the future, out of the Silver coined at the Miht Jhan out of the Gold coined at the Mint, to defray the Expence of Coinage.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the State of the Coinage of Silver in this Kingdom doth also-deserve the ferrous Consideration of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Chairman do move the House, That Leave he given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend the Laws now in being relative to the Gold Coin of this Kingdom, and the Exportation of Gold.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That in a Period of Twelve Years, from the Year 1767 to the Year *779, inclusive, the Surplus Nett Revenues of the East India Company, under the Presidency of Fort Saint George, above the Civil and Military Charges, and the Expences of Buildings and Fortifications, have never, except in One Year, been equal to the Purchasii of the Iuveftment for Europe.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That in the Two first and Two last Years of the said Period of Twelve Years, within the former of which the First War with Hyder Ally happened, and within the latter the Expeditions to Pondicherry and Mahe, ft* Charges and Expences exceeded the Nett Revenues in £. 941,781 upon the whole Four Years.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the1 Average Nett Surplus Revenues under the Presidency of Fort Saint George, for each of the Eight Years, from the Year 1769 to the Year 1777, during which the Company was at no Expence on Account of War, was not equal fto the Purchase of One Half of the Investment for Europe, calculated upon an Average of the Seven Years from 1771 to 1778.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That upon the whole Period from 176710 1779, including the Four Years of War above-mentioned, the Revenues under the Presidency of Fort Saint George, exclusive of their commercial Receipts, have exceeded the Charges In no more than £. 51,961.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Balances due by the Zemindars, and by the Reuters of the Company's Lands in the NorthernCircars, have very much increased of late; and that the Zemindars are in general much distressed, and involved in large Debts.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That besides the Tribute payable to the Company, it has been the Practice for the Chiefs of the subordinate Settlements to receive from the Zemindars certain large Sums of Money, under the Name of Nazir, or Free Gift.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That these Nazirs, or Free Gifts, which are arbitrary, and bear no certain Proportion to the Tribute, have not, since the Acquisitions of the Circars, been accounted for to the Company, but have been taken by the Chiefs, as a Perquisite of their Station.
