Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the said Sir Thomas Rumbold, on the 27th of June 1777, John Whit chilly Esquire, on the 12th of June 1777, and Peter Perring, Esquire, on the 2d of June ly'jj, did respectively enter into Covenants with the East India Company, binding and obliging themselves not to carry on any Traffic or Commerce for their own Benefit, excepting in the Disposal of such Goods as they might have remaining on Hand, and the collecting and getting in of such Debts as might be owing to them in respect of Trade carried on antecedent to their entering upon their several Offices; and that they should, respectively, within Thirty Days thereafter, deliver in to the Council of the Presidency at the Council Board, a full and just Specification, upon Oath, of the Debts due to them respectively, in the Course of Trade or Commerce theretofore carried on, and of the Wares and Merchandize on Hand, and to dispose of them within the Space of Nine Months; and that they should not lend Money to any of the Country Powers, by way of Mortgage on Land or Crops; and also, that they should, respectively, within Thirty Days next after their taking upon them their respective Offices, deliver to the Council, on Oath, a specific Account of all such Loans, if any, as at that Time they should respectively be concerned in; and that the said Sir Thumas Rumbold covenanted to accept of 40,000 Pagodas pei' Ammmy the Use of the Fort House and Hate, and the Commis-Tion on Coral, in Consideration of his being appointed Governor and President; and that John Whitehill and Peter Perringy Esquires, respectively, covenanted to accept of 16,000 Pagodas per Annum, each, in confe-queuce of their Appointments as Counsellors.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Records of the East India Company, transmitted from Fort Saint George, do not contain any Specification by Sir Thomas Rumbold of Goods on Hand, Debts due, or Loans made, before his taking upon him the Offices of Governor and President.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That in April 1775, the Court of Directors of the East Indict Company lent out written Orders to the Presidency of Fort Saint George, to appoint a Committee of Five Members of their Council (tfhich then coniifted of Nineteen) to be a Committee for the Purpose of invef-tigating upon the Spot many essential Points respecting' the Five Northern Circars, and the Jaghire Lands contiguous to Madras; which would tend to furniffi the East India Company at Home, and their Servants Abroad, with a Knowledge of the most important Fads on which the Settlement of the Tribute to be paid by the Zemindars, and the Rent to be paid by the Renters of the Company's Demesne Land, ought to be adjusted; and also for the better Regulation of the Police and Government of those Districts, with a particular View to preventing Extortion and the Oppression of the Jowei CJafies of the Native Inhabitants.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That in Conformity to the Orders of the Court of Directors, a Committee of Five Members of Council was appointed, but were prevented from proceeding in the Discharge of their Duty by the Cor.fusions which took place during the Government of Lord Pigot; and that at the Conclusion of his Government, in the Month of August 1776, the succeeding Governor and Council deviating from the Letter of the Company's Orders, by reason of the Reduction of the Number of Coun-fellors, preserved the Spirit of them, and appointed Three of the Company's Servants near to the Rank of Counsellors, in Conjunction with Two Members of the Board, to fulfil the Company's Orders, and gave them written Instructions, in exact Conformity to the Company's Orders of the 12th of April 1775.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That a Letter was written by the Governor and Council of Fort Saint George, dated the 21st of September 1776, acquainting the Court of Directors with the necessary Deviations from the Letter of their Orders, which was read before the Board of Directors on the 2d of April 1777, whilftSir Thomas Rumbold was a Member of that Board; and that such Deviation was not then, or at any subsequent Time, objected to.

Resolved, That it appearsto this Committee, That in January 1777, a competent Number of the Committee of Circuit began to carry the Company's Orders into Execution; and that in December following, notwithstaud-ingfome Impediments which had arisen, the Presidency determined on the vigorous Prosecution of that Business, and proceeded to fill up the Vacancies which had happened in the Committee, from among the Servants of the Company inferior to the Council: which became necessary from the State of the Council at that Period; and that the Committee, so constituted, continued their Investigations until soon after the Arrival of Sir Thomas Rumbold Tit Madras, on the 8th of February 1778.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Sir Thomas Rumbold, having arrived at Madras on the 8th of February 1778, did, on the 24th of March, move the Council to discontinue the Committee of Circuit, and to order the Zemindars of the Northern Circars to repair to Madras, and there to settle their Annual Tribute; Madras being situated at the Distance of about 550 Miles from Vizagapatam, a Place nearly in the Centre of the Circars, and Ganjam, the Northern Extremity, being distant about 720 Miles; and that the Measure of abolishing the Committee of Circuit was inilantly acceded to by the Council, without substituting any other Mode of executing the Company's Orders in its Place, although Messieurs Whitehill, Smith, Johnson, and Perring had in December preceding ex-

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Thomas Rumbold and the Council of Fort Saint George, ill dilfolving the Committee of Circuit of the Jaghire Lands and Northern Circars, disregarded the Spirit of the Orders of the East India Company, and acted in direct Opposition to some of its most valuable and essential Interests; that the declared Object of the Company's Instructions still remains unattained* and the East India Company still unpoflefled of the desired Information; and that such Miscondull is chiefly to be imputed to the Influence of Sir Thomas Rumbold.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the calling down of the Zemindars to Madras, was remonstrated against from the East India Company^k Three subordinate Councils of Mafutipatam, Ganjam, and Vizagapatam; who stated, as their Objections to the Measure, that it would impede the Collection of the Company's Revenues, already much in Arrear, and would distress the Zemindars, who were both averse to the Journey, and ill able to suppoi t the Expence of it; iut that notwithstanding this. Sir Thomas Rumbold, and the Majority of his Council, persevered in the Measure, and, by repeating their Orders, inforced Obedience to them; and that notwithstanding these ltemonftrances, accompanied with Complaints from the Zemindars themselves, several of them were brought down and detained at Madras lor many Months $ and that Vifieram Rauze in particular was detained till the Month of December 1778, and that Silteram Rauze remained there from November 1777 to December 1778.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That whilst the Zemindars were at the Presidency, the Treaties for their respective Cowles (or Leases) were carried on by Sir Thomas Rumbold only; and that the Grounds of such Treaties were in no Instance laid before the Council or Select Committee collectively, so that the East India Company might have the Means of forming a Judgment upon them, with respect to their Duration, or the Propriety of the Tribute or Rents reserved.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Governor and Majority of the Council of Fort Saint George did, by Menaces and harfti Treatment, compel Vifieram Rauze, the Rajah of Vijianagrum, to employ Silteram Rauze as the Duan or Manager of his Zemiudary, in the room of Juggernaut, a Man of Probity and good Cli iracter; and did also compel him to a Reconciliation with the said Sit ter am Rauze, who appears, by the former Proceedings on the Records of the Settlement, to have been a Man of bad Reputation, and difaflVCted to the Company's Interests; and that -Sir Thomas Rumbold was the chief Promoter and Adviserof the harfti and unmerited Treatment of the Rajah, and that he wassupported in it by Mr. Whitehi.il and Mr. Perring.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the compullive Menaces made use of towards the Rajah Vifieram Rauze, and the gross ill Treatment which he received at the Presidency, were humiliating, tmjuft, and cruel in themselves, and highly derogatory to the Interests of the East India Company, and to the Honour of the British Nation.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That about a Month after the Arrival of Sir Thomas Rumbold, the Chief and Council of Vizagapatam represented, by Letter of the nth of March 1778, which was read at the Board on the 10th of April following, that they were possessed of undeniable Proof, that 130,000 Rupees had been remitted to Silteram Rauze, then at Madras; that a further Sum of 70,000 Rupees was negociating ©n his Account; and that great Oppression of the Inhabitants of this District had been used in order to raise the Sums above-mentioned.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Silteram Rauze contracted by Bond to pay Mr, Redhead, then private Secretary to Sir Thomas Rumbold, One Lack of Rupees; the Consideration of which was, That Nlv. RedheadQiou\<\ use his Influence in obtaining for him the Duanship of Vifianagrum, a Reconciliation with his Brother, a Confirmation of the Adopt ion of his Son by Vifieram Rauze, the Possession of the Zemindary of Ancapilly, and the Restoration of the Fort of Vifianagrum; all of whichl were obtained from the Governor and Council; and that notwithstanding the Discovery of this Corruption, by Means of a judicial Appeal to themselves, the Governor and Council did hot take any Notice of it in their Correspondence with the Court of Directors.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, from a Codicil annexed to Mr. Redhead's Will, That Omeirul-Omrah had an Order from his Father to pay him the Sum of One Lack of Rupees.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Anthony Sadlier, Esquire, late Chief of Mafulipatam^ and now one of the Council of Fort Saint George, did> by Letter to Sir Thomas Rumbold, dated the 5th o(May 1778, inform him of various Gratuities, amounting to very large Sums, stipulated for and in Part received by Three of the Company's Servants, namely, Mr. White-hill, Mr. Floyer, and Mr. Craufurd, who had preceded Mr. Sadlier in the Chiefship of Mafulipatam, and in Proof thereof, inclosed the Translation of a written Account of the Particulars, the Original of which had been delivered to Mr. Sadlier on his succeeding to the Chiefship, by the Company s Dubash or chief Interpreter; and that Sir Thomas Rumbold did not, in his Anl'wer to an accompanying Letter of the same Date, take any Notice whatsoever of the Dubafti's Account, nor did he, as far as appears by the Evidence before this Committee, ever communicate the same to the Council at Fort Saint George, or the Court of Directors.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Thomas Rumbold, in thus suppressing Mr. Sadlier's Information of the Peculation of the East India Company's Servants at Mafulipatam, both from the Council of Madras, and from the Court of Directors, greatly failed in his Duty as President and Governor of Fort Saint George; and also acted in direct Breach of that Part of his written Covenants with the East India Company, by which he expressly engaged, with all convenient Speed, to give Notice to the Court of Directors of all Deceits, Abuses, and Breaches of Orders, which he should know, hear of, or suspect, with the Names of the offending Parties; and that, by such Suppression and Concealment, he the said Sir Thomas Rumbold was guilty of a great Breach of the Trust reposed in him.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That by a Letter of Instruction, dated the 12th of April 1775, which ordered the Establishment of a Committee of Circuit of the Jaghire Lands and Northern Circars, the Court of Directors expressed their Sense of the good Consequences which would refillt from taking the Jaghire Lands into the Company's immediate Possession, and that the Nabob should in no same rent them without agreeingto such Arrangements as the Company should deem neceft'aryj to which Order it was added, That the Governor and Council might agree with the Nabob for a Lease of One Year only.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That by a Revenue Letter from Fort Saint George to the Court of Directors, dated the 5th of February 1778, beingonlyThree Days previous to Sir Thomas Rumboid's Arrival at Madras, the then President and Council of Fort Saint George informed the Company of their having continued the Lease of the Jaghire Lands, in Conformity to their repeated instructions, for the current Year only; but apologized for the Measure, as doubting whether the Company might not expect to 11 M have

George the 20th of July :177s, observed, that this valuable Possession of the Company was shamefully neglected and oppressed by those employed by the Nabob in his Collections; and added a Recommendation to advertise the letting of them from Three to Five Years, to avoid the destruc-i.tive System of letting them from Year to Year; that they were accordingly advertised for Three, Five, and Ten Years, on the 4th of September 1778, and that various Proposals were sent by private Persons to the Board.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That in consequence of a Letter from the Nabob of Arcot to Sir Thomas Rumbold, dated the 9th of September 1778, the Select Committee on the 5th of October came to a Resolution, which was strongly recommended by Sir Thomas Rumbold, to grant to the Nabob a Lease of the Jaghire Roads for a Period of Three Years.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, thus granting a Lease of the Jaghire Lands to the Nabob for Three Years, was in direct Disobedience to the repeated positive Orders of the East India Company, and contrary to the Practice which before the Administration of Sir Thomas Rumbold had uniformly prevailed at Madras, in consequence of those Orders; and that this Disobedience is highly aggravated by the cogent Reasons of Convenience to the Company, and of public Policy, which were known to be the chief Grounds of retraining the Lease of those Lands to the Ylabob to OneYear only; and that Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, as the principal Adviser and Promoter of this Measure, and John Whitehill, Charles Smith, Samuel Johnson, and Peter Paring, Esquires, who concurred in it, are severally guilty of a great Breach of Trust, and of a high Crime and Misdemeanor.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That by several Treaties entered into by the East India Company with the Nizam of the Decant in 1766 and 1768, it was expressly ilipulated, as a Condition of his confirming t he Cession of the Northern Circars, that the Guntoor Circar should continue to be podefied by Bazalet Jung during his Life, or until it were his Highness's Pleasure that the Company diould take Possession of it.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That in the Month of April 1779, a Treaty was entered into by Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, with Bazalet Jung, (or the immediate Possession of the Guntoor Circar, without the Consent or Knowledge of the Nizam; and that in consequence of such Treaty, a military Force, under the Command of Colonel Harpur, was ordered to attempt a March to Adoni, the Capital of Bazalet Jungs other Territories, through a Part of the Dominions of Ilyder Ally Caivn, without his Permission.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That on the 22d of February 1779, the Governor and Council of Fort Saint George acquainted Mr. Holland, their Ministerat the Nizam's Court, with the Steps they had taken respecting the Guntoor Circar; who, by Letter dated the 17th of May, informed Sir Thomas Rumbold, that the Nizam was thereby offended in a very high Degree; but that such Letter was never entered on the Company's Records at Fort Saint George, although Sir Tho?Jias Rumbold acknowledged the Receipt of it on the 10th of June 1779.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That on the 4th of October 1779, Sir Thomas Rumbold laid before the Select Committee of Fort Saint George, a Letter from the Nabob of Arcot, bearing date the 19th of , September preceding, requesting to have a Lease of the Guntoor Circar for the Space of Ten Years; which was 20

carried by the Votes of Sir Thomas Rumbold, Sir Hector Munro, and Mr. Whitehill, although Mr. Smith desired Time only till the next Committee should assemble, in order to form his Judgment upon a Point of such Magnitude and Importance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet* in treating with Bazalet Jung without the Participation of the Nizam, in marching Troops into the Country of Hyder Ally Cawn, without having obtained his Consent, and in granting a Ten Years I-ease of the Guntoor Circar to the Nabob of Arcot, di(regarded the true Interests of the Company, by a gross Breach of Solemn Treaties with the Nizam, stained the National Honour, and was thereby guilty of a high Crime and Misdemeanor.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That on the 12th of June 1780, the Supreme Council pofi-tively ordered the immediate Restoration of the Guntoor Circar to Bazalet Jung; but that such Restoration was by Mr. Whitehill, then Governor, and the Select Committee o(Fort Saint George, deferred on frivolous Pretences till the 23d of September, subsequentto the Irruption of Hyder Ally Cawn, which occasioned the Suspen-fion of Mr. Whitehill from the Government, by Authority of the Supreme Council.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That John Whitehill, Esquire, in Two several Minutes, entered by him of Record the 7th and 8th of November 1780, on the Sub j eft of his Suspension, difpmed the Authority of the Supreme Council, derived from an Act of the Legislature, and otherwise conducted himself with great Disregard to legal Suboidination; and that he declared, in a Minute adrireffed to Sir Eyre Coote, that should he be disinclined to submit, and Force were used to drive him from his honourable Station, it would be a Subversion of Government, and that it would depend on his Prudence and Discretion, if he should not give Birth to the Horrors of Civil War in the Settlement, in a Moment when Unanimity and Cooperation were essentially necessary to the Preservation of the Carnatic, and the Safety of Madras.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Whitehill, Esquire, by not paying immediate and implicit Obedience to the Orders of the Supreme Council, and by his intemperate and contumacious Conduct on the 7th and 8th of November 1780, held out an alarming Example of Disobedience to the Orders of his lawful Superiors, and of Difrespect to the Acts of the British Legislature; and was thereby guilty of a high Crime and Misdemeanor, aggravated by his repre-fenting it as an Act ol Forbearance in himself, if he should not involve the Settlement in the Horrors of a Civil War.

ReJ'olved, That it appears to this Committee, That according to the express Terms of the Treaty of 1768, between the Nizam of the Decan and the East India Company, confirming the Cession of the Five Northern Circars, a Tribute of Five Lacks of Rupees was payable to the Nizam of the Dccan.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That by a Letter written by the Select Committee of Fort Saint George to the Government General, dated the 7th of February 1779, acquainting them with Mr. Hollands Million to the Court of the Nizam, they expressed a strong Conviction of the hostile Inclinations of that Prince towards the British Interests; and that in their Instructions to Mr. Hollond, they enjoin him to conciliate the Nizam's Mind, and to removeany Doubts respecting the future regular Payment of the Tributeor Pefhcufli payable to him, and to communicate every necessary Intelligence as early as possible to the Supreme Council as well as to themselves.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That on the iothof June 1779, when Sir Thomas Rumbold had been informed of the Nizam's Resentment again!! the Government of Fort Saint George, on account of the

Rejblvedy That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Attempt made to withhold the Tribute due to the Nizam, at a Time when Sir Thomas Rumbold was personally apprized of that Prince's particular Resentment in consequence of the Tran faction respecting the Guntoor Circar, by Mr. Hollands unrecorded Letter of the 1 7th of May, and when the Council in general was aware of his unfriendly Disposition towards the Company's Interests, was unjust and impolitic, greatly inflamed the Nizam's Resentments, tended to extinguish his Confidence in British Honour, and to impress ilie Powers of India with a Dillruft of the good Faith of the Nation; and that Sir Thomas Rumbold was thereby guilty of a high Crime and Misdemeanor.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Governor General and Council deemed it expedient, on the 14th of February 1780, to appoint Mr. Holiond their Resident at the Nizam's Court, as the Person most proper to recover the Good-will of that Prince; and that they applied to the President and Select Committee of Fort Saint George, for their Permission that he might remain there in that Capacity, which was refused; and that Mr. Holiond was suspended from his Rank in the Company's Service at the Recommendation of Sir Thomas Rmnbold, on the Eve of his Departure from Fort Saint George; and that this Recommendation was carried into Execution by John White hilly Esquire, and the Council; and that Mr. Holland's official Communication with the Supreme Council of Bengal w as a principal Ground relied on by Sir Thomas Rumbold for such Recommendation, although Mr. Holland had been expressly enjoined by his Instructions to be punctual and early in such Communication.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Refusal of the Select Committee of Fort Saint George to permit Mr. Holiond to continue as Resident from the Supreme Council at Hydrabad, >vas derogatory

A PETITION of the Owners and Commanders of Supplying Ships residing in the Cities of London and West- Seamen5 minster, and others concerned in the Commercial Interests of this Kingdom, was prefenled to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Petitioners have maturely con-lidered the Bill more effectually to supply with Seamen His Majesty's Ships of War when Occasion shall require, and to encourage Men, under certain Regulations and Bounties, voluntarily to engage themselves for that Service whepeveer they shall be duly called for; which at the Closeof the last Session was printed by Order of the House; and are clearly of Opinion that it is well calculated to answer ihe Purposes intended, and pradicable in every Part; and that the Petitioners, after having long felt and lamented those expensive and dangerous Delays which the Naval Operations and Commercial Concerns of the British Empire have often suffered by the present Mode of impressing Seamen, are extremely happy to find that a Bill, so well suited to prevent the like Evils in future, has so far obtained the Consideratipri and Sandion of the House: And therefore praying the House to resume the Consideration of the said Bill, and that it may, with such Alterations and Amendments as to the House shall seem meet, be passed into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Portland.

I have it in Command from His Majesty, to inform this House, That His Majesty being concerned to find that Di fcon tents and J ealoufies are prevailing among His loyal Subjects of this Country, upon Matters of great Weight and Importance, His Majesty recommends to this House to take the same into their moil serious Consideration, in Order to such a final Adjustment as may give mutual Satisfaction to His Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland.

Copy of a Resolution of the House of Lords in Ireland, Mercurii, 170 die Apr ilis 1782.

Die Mercurii, 170 Aprilis 1782.

Resolved, By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal in Parliament assembled, Nemine dissentiente, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return Him our Thanks for the most gracious Message sent to this House by His Majesty's Command, through the Medium of hisGrace the Lord Lieutenant; and to assure Him of our most unftiaken Loyalty and Attachment to His Majesty's Person and Government, and of the lively Sense we entertain of His paternal Care of His People of Ireland, in thus enquiring into the Discontents and Jealousies that subsist amongst them, in order to such final Adjustment as may give mutual Satisfaction to His Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland:

That, thus encouraged by His Royal Interpofltion, we shall beg Leave, with all Duty and Affection, to lay before His Majesty the causesof such Discontents and Jealousies:

Affairs.

To represent to His Majesty, That His Subjects of Ireland are entitled to a free Constitution; that the Imperial Crown of Ireland is inseparably annexed to the Crown of Great Britain, on which Connection the Ilap-piaefs of both Nations essentially depends; but that the Kingdom of Ireland is a distinct Dominion, having a Parliament of her own, the foie Legislature thereof:

That there is no Power whatsoever competent to make Laws to bind this Nation, except the King, Ixtrds, and Commons of Irelan; upon which exclusive Right -of Legidation we eonfider the very Essence of our Liberties to depend, a Right which we claim as the Birthright of the People of , and which we

are determined, in every Situation of Life, to assert and maintain:

To represent to His Majesty, That we have seen ' with Concern certain Claims, both of Legislature and Judicature, asserted by the Parliament of Great,

in an Act passed in Great Britain in the Sixth Year of George the First, intituled, "An Act for the better securing the Dependency of upon the Crown

u of Great Britain

That we conceive the said Act, and the Powers thereby claimed, to be the great and principal Causes of the Discontents and Jealousies that subsist in this Kingdom:

To allure His Majesty, That this House considers it as a Matter of conliitutional Right and Protection, that all Bills which become Law should receive the Approbation of His Majesty, under the Seal of Great Britain; but we consider the Practice of suppressing our Bills in the Council of Ireland, or altering them any where, to be a Matter which calls for Redress:

To represent to His Majesty, That an Act, intituled,

" An Act for the better Accommodation of His Majesty's Forces," being unlimited in Duration, but which, from the particular CircUmstancesof the Times', passed into a Law, has been the Cause of much Jealously and Discontent in this Kingdom:

That we have thought it our Duty to lay before His Majesty these, the*principal Causes of the Discontents awl'Jealousies fubfiliing in this Kingdom:

That we have tlffe greatest Reliance on His Majesty's Wisdom, the moll sanguine Expectations from His virtuous Choice of a. Chief Governor, and the greatest Confidence in the wife and conliitutional Council His Majesty has adopted:

That we have moreover a high Sense and Veneration for the British CharaCler; and do therefore conceive,

that the'Proceedings of* this Country, founded as they are in Right, and'supported by Conliitutional Liberty, mull' have' excited the Approbation and Elteem of the British'Nation; That we are the more confirmed in this Hope, inasmuch as the People of this Kingdom have never expressed a Desire to share the Freedom oi Great Britain, without at the same Time declaring their Determination to share her Fate, Handing or felling with the British Nation.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Leeds and Mr. Pepys:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for providing Quarters for certain Foreign Troops, lately employed in His Majesty's Service in the Defence of the Island of Minorca, and expected to arrive soon in this Kingdom, for a limited Time; without any Amendment: And also,

I-ord John Cavendish acquainted the House, That he Civil lilt! had a Message from fiis Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty: and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty has found, with Ooncern, that notwithstanding the Two several Payments of the Civil List Debt, and the subsequent Increase of the Civil List Revenue, a considerable Debt is since incurred: His Majesty, therefore, desires the Advice and Aid of the House of Commons, as to the Mode of discharging that Debt, and preventing the like in future, without laying any new Burthen on His People, whom it is ever His Wnh, as much as possible, to relieve.

For these Purposes His Majesty lays before the House, the Plan of Reform which He has judged proper

to make in HisEftabliflimeptf, to be perfected by the Wisdom of Parliament, for the Honour of the Crown and the Public Benefit.

G. R.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicmte, That an humble Addrefioi Address be presented to His Majesty, to allure His Mef&gc, Majesty, that this House, affected with the most grateful Sense of His Majesty's Goodness, in desiring the Advice of this House with regard to the Discharge of the Debt affecting His Civil List Revenue, and for preventing the like in future, without any new Burthen on His People, will take into immediate Confutation His Majesty's most Gracious Message; and that His faithful Commons will apply themselves without Delay, to find the bell Means of providing for the Discharge of the Debt on the Civil List, and will life their best Endeavours to give Stability and Effect to the Reform which His Majesty has been graciously pleased to make in His Establishments, for the Honour of the Crown and the Public Benefit; and that this House, in Imitation of such an Example, will hold themselves particularly bound to make every Exertion in their Power to establish a strict Economy in all the Brauches of the Public Expenditure.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty's most honourable Privy Council.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to take His Majesty's said most Gracious Message into Consideration.

And the Resolutions of the Committee were read $ and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is the Duty of the Chairman and Directors of the East India Company to transmit, with all convenient Speed, and by all fitting Ways and Means, to India, all Acts of Parliament relative to the Company's Affairs, and the ordering and governing their Servants within the Limits of their Charter; and to take such Steps as may be most conducive towards effecting the Purposes of the Legislature for the Relief of the Natives.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Lawrence Sulivan, Esquire, Chairman of the East India Company, did cause to be made an Entry in the

Vol. 38.

Minutes of the Court of Directors, containing an untrue Account of a Conference held with certain Members of the House on the 27 th Day of June last; by Means whereof the Provision, *- hich according to an Engagement entered into by him on his own Part, and on Behalf of the Court of Directors, for the Relief of certain Natives confined in the Common Gaol of Calcutta, appears to have been unnecessarily and dangerously delayed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said LawrenceSulivan, Esquire, did not do what he might and ought to have done towards the early and effectual Transmission of an Act of Parliament of the last Session, intituled, "An Act to explain and amend " so much of an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of " the Reign of I Iis present Majesty, intituled, "An " Act for establishing certain Regulations for the better " Management of the Affairs of the East India Company, as well in India as in Europef as relates to the st Administration of Justice in Bengal; and for the " Relief of certain Persons imprisoned at Calcutta in " Bengal, under a Judgment of the Supreme Court of " Judicature; and also for indemnifying the Governor " General and Council of Bengal, and all Officers who " have acted under their Orders or Authority, in the " undue Resistance made to the Process of the Supreme <c Court," to India; by which Delay the good Purposes of the said Act, in regulating the Judicature in Bengal,

and

Administrt-tion of Justice inBengal, &c.

794 2° Mali.j4. 1782,

and in providing Relief to individual Natives, as well as to the People at large, may be frustrated.

Refulved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the giving and enforcing Oaths of Secrecy, without Authority of Law, and without any Exception to the same of Examination by a competent legal Authority, is an Offence, and tends to the Destruction of all judicial Proceeding and parliamentary Enquiry.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Lawrence Sulivan, Esquire, did enforce the Observance

of an Oath of Secrecy of the Nature and Effect mentioned in the last Resolution, upon Mr. one of the Secretaries or Clerks of the East India Company, specially restraining him from giving Information to a Select Committee of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the holding, by any Judge of the Supreme Court at Fort William in Bengal, an Office granted by, and tenable at the Pleasureot, the Servants of the East India Company, is against the good Purposes and Policy of an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of His Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for establishing certain " Regulations for the better Management of the Affairs " of the East India Company, as well in India as in " Europe," and tends to create a Dependance in the said Supreme Court upon those over whose Actions that Court was intended as a Controul.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Appointments of Offices of the aforesaid Description, to any Judge of the Supreme Court, ought to be held null and void, and that the Directors of the East India Company should order the same to be in Fast annulled and vacated accordingly.

Resolved, That Warren H Esquire, Governor General of Bengal, and Sir Elijah Impey, Knight, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of William in Bengal, appear to this Committee to have been concerned, the one in giving, the other in receiving, an Office not agreeable to the true Intent aind Meaning of the Act of the Thirteenth Year of His present Majesty, intituled,

" An Act for establishing certain Regulations for the " better Management of the Affairs of the East India " Company, as well in India as in Europe which tin-justifiable Transaction between them was attended with Circumstances of evil Tendency and Example.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Powers given to the Governor General and Council of Bengal, by an Act, made in the Thirteenth Year of His Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act for " establishing certain Regulations for the better Management of the Affairs of the East India Company,

" as well in India as in Europe," ought to be more distiuftly ascertained.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it will be proper to reduce into one Act the leve-ral Acts of Parliament made to regulate the East India Company, and further to explain and amend the fame, and also to make new Regulations and Provisions to the same End.

Mr. Strahan accord ingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; Where the same was read; and is as follow-eth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

James Buck informed your Committee, That Port-man Square hath lately been new paved, and a considerable Part thereof hath been inclosed with Iron Rails, and set apart, in order to be laid out as a Garden or Pleasure Ground for the Use of the Inhabitants; but that no Improvement has yet been made to the Ground so inclosed — That there is not at present a Fund sufficient for defraying the Expence already incurred on account of making the said Inclosure, or for watering the said Square; and that the said Square is subject to Nuisances and Annoyances of various Kinds.

And the Witness further said, That if the said Inclo-sure was laid out with proper Walks, and otherwise embellished as a Garden or Pleasure Ground; and if Powers were given for watering, fvveeping, and cleansing the said Square, by a Rate to be laid for those Purposes; and if Provision was made for effectually preventing all Nuisances and Annoyances therein, it would N

be of great Benefit and Convenience to the Inhabitants.

A Member present confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the Improvement of Portman Square, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. Strahan and Mr. Greville do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Bill of Pains A Petition of SiY Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, was sTain^S^1^ Pre^ente(^to ^ie H°u^e> and read; Setting forth, That TTJfcumbold, the Petitioner, finding himself much aggrieved by a Bill Itc. depending in the House, for retraining the Petitioner

and Peter Perring, Esquire, from going out of this Kingdom for the Space of One Year, and until the End of the then next Session of Pari iament, and for discovering the Estate and Effects of the Petitioner and Peter Perring, Esquire, and for preventing the Transporting or alienating of the fame, humbly entreats the Attention of the House to the particular Circhmflances and Hardships of his Cafe; that the Petitioner, labouring under the Weight and Ignominy of Accusations exhibited in a Committee of this honourable House, which have been, and Hill are, the Subject of a Suit now depending in one of the Courts of Westminster Hall, and having beeh hot only precluded from the Privilege of a regular Trial in the ordinary Course of Law, but like wife hitherto unheard any where in his Defence, and it being altogether uncertain when he is to be heard, is now, by the said Bill, punished with severe Restraints and Disabilities, at a Time when the Petitioner must be presumed to be innocent, and when, as the Petitioner conceives, if any such Bill ought to pass, the Object of it cannot, upon any Principle of Law or Justice, be extended further than to render him amenable to Punishment in case of his being proved guilty; and that the Petitioner is, by the said Bill, immediately, and for a great Length of Time, deprived of the Rights of Personal Liberty, and the free Use, Enjoyment, and Disposal of his private Property, which the Petitioner is entitled to as his Birth-right in common with the lowed Subject in the Kingdom, until he has incurred a Forfeiture of them by Law; and the Petitioner is rendered absolutely incapable not only of making any Provision for an adult Family in case of Marriage, or otherwise, tyut likewise (with the Exception only of such Debts as are for necessary Subsistence) of contracting or discharging any which may accrue subsequent to the 29th of lall Month, during the Continuance of the Aid Bill, however necessarily the same may be incurred in a Variety of extensive Concerns, and even in providing the Means of Defence for himself in the Proceedings against him both here and in the Courts of Law; and that the Petitioner is likewise, as the Bill dands, compelled to a Discovery of all his Property for some Time back, under the fevered Penalties in case of Omissions or Default, which, from the Distance of some Part of that Property, and the Loss of Books of Accounts, and other Documents, on Board The General Barker, it will be impossible for him to make in the Terms and within the Time prescribed by the Bill; and that the Petitioner cannot believe that the Justice and Humanity of the House will suffer Accusation to pass for Guilt, nor Punishment to precede a Trial; and yet the only Reason assigned for the severe Penalties and Disabilities inflicted

by the said Bill is a Surmise and Suspicion of Breaches of Fruft, Crimes, and Misdemeanors, from all which the Petitioner doubts not to be able fully to vindicate himself when the House will be pleased to hear his Defence; and that the Petitioner is greatly alarmed to observe so long a Period affixed to the Continuance of the severe Restraints impoied by the said Bill, without any Provision for Mitigation or Relief in case no Proceedings should follow the Charges alledged against the Petitioner, or in case the same should be delayed, or should prove upon Examination to be ill founded; and in the mean Time the excessive Bail required to be given by the Petitioner, for which the Redraints laid on his Property render it impossible for him to give an Indemnity, mud probably operate as an immediate and necessary Imprisonment, and this too, notwithstanding that the Petitioner is possessed of a considerable Real and other Estate, any Part of which that may be thought reasonable he is willing to deposit as a Security, and notwithstanding that, by the other Provisions of the 18

said Bill to which the Petitioner does not object, all the Petitioners Property, his Honour, and his Life, (land pledged for his Appearance; and that the Petitioner 1

conceives, that no Precedent, under the Circmndances of his Cafe, could warrant a Bill of such a Nature, even if any Precedent were to be found; but the Petitioner is advised that such a Proceeding will appear totally unprecedented in the Annals of Parliament without some previous Proof or Confession of Guilt; and that, in particular, the Two redraining Bills in the Cafes of the South Sea Company and of the Charitable Corporation, which seem to have been followed as Precedents by the £

said Bill, were, besides other essential Differences between those Cafes and the present, passed after the Guilt of the Parties had been decided upon, and for the Purpose of ascertaining the Pecuniary Compensation to be made for that Guilt, the Adjudication thereof being expressfy recited and affirmed by the Bills which imposed the Redraint: And therefore pray ing the House to take his same into Consideration, and give him Leave to be heard, by himself or Gounfel, against the said Bill, or that hemay have such otherReliefin the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioner be then heard, by his Counsel, against the said Bill, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit;

A Petition of William Targett, Ranger, and T,n<ion

William Harding, Voters for Members to serve in ec lon* Parliament for the Borough o f Hindoin the County of Wilts, in Behalf of themselves and other Voters in the said Borough, was delivered in at the Tuble, and read;

Setting forth, That at the late Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of llindon, in the County of Wilts, in the room of Lloyd Kenyon,

Esquire, whose Seat was vacated by his accept ing of the Office or Place of His Majesty's Attorney General, which said Election came on on or about the 22d Day of April last, the Petitioners demanded a Poll to be taken in Favour of Sir John Lade, Baronet (he not being then present) and that other Voters of the said Borough voted for the said Lloyd Kenyon-, that the said Lloyd Kenyon, by himself or Agents, previous to and during the said Election, was guilty of gross Bribery, in corrupting the Voters; that a general System of Corruption prevailed in the said Borough, and the Voters were influenced to vote for the said Lloyd Kenyon by beneficial Promises made to them by the said Lloyd Kenyon, or his Agents; and that, after the Teste of the W rit, and on the Day of Election, the said Kenyon, or his Agents, at his own Charge and Expence, treated the Voters with Victuals and Drink, contrary to the Statute iu that same provided; and that several illegal Threats and Promises were made by the said Lloyd Kenyon, or his Agents, to influence Persons to vote for him (many of which have been performed) and that the ReturningOflicer canvafl'ed the said Borough, and acted as Agent for the said Lloyd Kenyon, and was guilty of the most illegal Partiality in Favour of him, previous to and during the said Election, by admitting Persons to vote for the said Lloyd Kenyon who had no legal Right to vote, and rejecting several Persons who had a legal Right to vote, and tendered themselves at the Poll to vote for the said Sir John Lade, and also in bargaining, or causing Bargains to be made, with many of the Voters, previous to the Election, to vote as he directed; and that by these, and various corrupt and illegal Means, a Majority of Votes was obtained on the Face of the Poll in Favour of the said Lloyd Kenyon, and he was declared duly elected, in direct Violation of the Freedom of Election, and in manifest Prejudice of the Petitioners and other Voters in the said Borough, their Franchises being materially aftected thereby: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief therein as to them shall leem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesdaythe 28th Day of this Instant May, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Retraining A Petition of Peter Perringate of Saint George,

Sir T. Rum- Madras, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; bold,&c.from Setting forth. That the Petitioner is informed a Bill Kingdom* has been brought into the House, for restraining Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, and the Petitioner, from going out of this Kingdom, for the Space of One Year, and until the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and for discovering the Estate and Effects of Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, and the Petitioner, and for preventing the transporting or alienating the fame; contaiuingProvisions, and Penalties which deeply affect the Petitioner; and that this Proceeding is founded upon mere Accusation against the Petitioner, unconvicted of any Offence, and unheard in his Defence, against such Accusation; and that the Petitioner hath been always ready to submit his Conduct to any Authority whatever, competent to an Enquiry into it, and to abide the Justice of his Country; that he does not, nor ever did, entertain the Design of withdrawing himself, or removing his Effects, from the Reach of those Laws to which he is or may be amenable; and that he apprehends, a Proceeding which takes such a Design for granted, without any previous Foundation laid before the House, or any just Cause for suspecting \ ol. 38.

ternative by which he can avoid an ignominious Imprisonment, not only previous to the Conviction of any Offence whatever, but before the Charge against the Petitioner is put into such a Shape as either calls for or permits the Petitioner's Answer to it; and that, were he differently circumstanced, to compel the Petitioner to furnish Sureties, by a Bill which compels a Discovery of all his Property, disables him from alienating any Part of it, and is universally understood to lead to a Confiscation of it, is, by the same Proceeding, directing an Act to be done by the Petitioner, and depriving him of the Means of performing it, since it leaves him without the Possibility of indemnifying any Persons who might be willing to become his Sureties; and that to require excessive Bail of any Person accused of an Offence, is, in the moll ordinary Cafe, deemed a Grievance and Opprefiion to the Subject, but the Grievance and Oppression become indeed intolerable when accompanied with an Act founded upon ex parte Evidence only, laying the Subject under a complete Restraint from the Use of his Property; and that there are several other Clauses in the said Bill equally unwarrantable in the Circumstances of the Petitioner's *

Cafe, unjustifiable upon any Principle of Justice, and subversive of those Rights of a Subject of this Realm, to which the Petitioner is entitled: And therefore praying the House to permit him to be heard, by his Counsel, against the several Clauses of the said Bill, or such of them as shall be grievous and oppressive to the Petitioner.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the1 Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for restraining Sir Thomas Rumbold,

Baronet, and Peter Perring, Esquire, from going out of this Kingdom for the Space of One Year, and until the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and for discovering the Estate and Effects of Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, Peter Perring, and John,

Esquires, and for preventing the transporting or alienating of the fame, is re-committed; and that the Petitioner be heard, by his Counsel, before the said Committee, upon his Petition, if he thinks fit.

A Petition of the Sugar Refiners of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Manufactory carried on by the Petitioners, bath fuflered exceedingly from the Events of the War; and the Loss of the Islands of Dominica, Saint Vincent, Grenada and the Grenadines, Tobago, Saint Christoper's, Nevis, and Montserrat, have so reduced the Sugar Import, that the Trade is almost at a Stand; and that Brown Raw Sugars, such as before the Commencement of Hostilities were usually from 28.9. to 30.9. per Hundred Weight; now fell for upwards of 70.?. jyer Hundred Weight; and that the Sugar Revenue falls short above £. 400,000 per Annum of its estimated and expected Product, and the Sugar Houses are /hutting up and dismantling in the several, Ports of this Kingdom; and that whilst the Petitioners suffer such Losses and Inconveniences, it is a great Hard/hip upon them to see the Prize Sugars still carried out of the Kingdom to supply Foreign Manufactories; and alledging, that the Bill now depending before the House, to admit Sugar from Saint Christopher's, Nevis, and Montfer rat, does not tend to afford the Public or the Petitioners any adequate Supply or Relief; and that the Sugars of Dominica, Grenada, and Tobago, are, by the Concessions of the French King, carried to Neutral Places, and the Planters and Merchants of Saint Christopher's, Nevis, and McntJ'crrat, can ask for no Privilege whatever, to which those of the before-named Islands have not at leaf! equal Claim; and that a Species of Supply, the Continuance of which is to depend upon Licences to be granted or re-fufedatthe Pleasure of a French Governor, or at the Will of the French King, is so precarious in its Nature, that itiholds forth no Security to the Petitioners, and they trust will, on many Accounts, be found totally unworthy the Adoption of the British Legislature; and thatas the British Planters are become unable to furnish a sufficient Quantity of Sugar for the Public Use, and the English Buyer is compelled to depend upon a Foreign Supply, the Petitioners conceive that it is the Interest of the Public in general, that they should be allowed to buy at the best Neutral Markets, and at such Markets upon the best Terms; and that a Bill which should establish a Distinction between Neutrals, would, as they conceive, infringe the Public Right, byvefting the Powers of a Monopoly in Persons who are become unable to render those Advantages in Return, on which alone the Title to such a Privilege was ever pretended to have been founded; and that the Restraints which were formerly laid on the Importation of Tobacco, Cotton, and some other Articles, have been lately removed by Acts of Parliament, and the Petitioners trust i 7 that

The Lord Advocate of Scotland presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for regulating the Execution of the Law, and for rendering the Payment of Creditors more equal and expeditious in certain Cafes of Insolvency, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland: And the same was received; and read the First Time.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and Manufacturers in the Town and County of Newcastle ufxni Tyne, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That an extensive Trade hath for many Years past fub-fifted between Scotland and the said Town, as well as moll of the commercial Cities and Towns in England, who mull therefore be greatly interested in, or affected by, every legislative Ad that shall either promote or depreciate the general Advantages of fair commercial Dealings between those Two Parts of the Kingdom; and that it is an experienced and well known Fact, that, in Cafes of Insolvency in Scotland, the Creditors there have generally, by early Applications to their local Modes of judicial Procedure, uuknown in England, gained great and injurious Preferences to the English Creditors, who, in numerous Infiances, have either been deprived of any Share of the Insolvent's Effects.or otherwise have been obliged, after pursuing tedious, dilatory, and expensive Proceedings, to content? themselves with some small and disproportionate Parts of such Effects; sind that the Bankrupt Law for Scotland, which passed in the Year 1772, and is now near expiring, removed the Grievances above dated, inrespecl of the Distribution of the Personal Effect. of Bankrupt^ in Scotland, but left their Real Estates unaffected, and as much in the Power of the Scotch Creditors to obtaiu uujufl and undue Preferences therefrom as the same were before that Law was made-, and that the Petitioners with great Pleasune find, that it is the earned and laudable Desire, not only of the Royal Boroughs iq Scotland, but of the colledive Body of the Merchants, Traders, and Manufacturers in that Country, to have the said Bankrupt Law renewed, with such Amendments as Experience has suggested to fetafide all Partiality-and Itijustice, dilatory and expensive Proceedings in Cafes of Insolvency, and that they are for that Purpose preparing a Bill, to he laid before the House, to prevent all unjust Preferences, to abolish all unueceflary Law Expences, to procure a full and fair Surrender of Info! vents' Estates and Effects upon Oath, to establish proper Rules for the Direction of Adignees on an improved Plan, and finally to, bring under the Statute the Real as well as the Personal Estates of I nfol vent Debtors, as in England; and the Petitioners are persuaded such a Bill can never be opposed by impartial Persons, or upon honourable Motives: And therefore praying. That, if such a Bill shall be permitted to be brought in, it may (after receiving such Alterations and Amendments as the House shall dictate) pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The Lord Advocate of Scotland reported from the Committee of Secrecy, appointed to enquire into the Causes of the War that now fnbiifts in the Carnatic, and of the present Condition of the British Possessions in those Parts, and to report the same to the House, with their Observations thereupon, That the said Committee had received Evidence relating to John Whitehill, Esquire, heretofore Governor and President of the Settlement of Fort Saint George, on the Coast of Coro-mandeli in the East Indies, and to Thomas Lewin, Esquire, late Secretary to the Council at Madras, having withdrawn themselves from this Kingdom; which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Your Committee undemanding, from Report, That John Whitehill, Esquire, heretofore Governor and Pre-iident of the Settlement of Fort Saint George, on the Coast of Coromandel, in the East Indies, is now out of this Kingdom, called before them the following Persons: viz.

Mr. Thomas Lewin, who, being examined, said, He

Vol. 1 8.

was acquainted with Mr. Whitehill. And being asked. Where he is now ? said. He has heard he is in Paris. And being asked, When he last saw'him in this Country ? said, " I think it was in November last — he did not remain here above Six or Eight Days — he was attacked with the Gout — this Country was so cold, that he was ndvised to go to the Continent; I think Dr. Smith advised it; 1 am not positive — I have frequently heard from him, that his Intention was to find a more settled Climate, which he has done, and means to stay some Time — he never mentioned any Thing, I believe, of the . Committee of Secrecy fitting upon his Affairs."

And being asked, Whether Mr. W/iitehill has any Reason to flay Abroad, respecting any thing that may come against him ? said, " Messrs. Gregg and Potts are his Attornies — I think he means to return here when the Weather gets better — The East India Company-have filed a Bill in Chancery against him, which is going on — his going was so sudden, and his Health in such a State, that he could not make any Arrangement of his Affairs before he went — When he was in Town, he lodged with me in Charlotte Street; he had a House in Queen Anne Street it is my House; Mr. Whitehill

had made an Agreement to purchase it, and I took it oft' his Hands; he had made no Preparation to go into it; he had made an Agreement for it before he went last to India; his Name remained on the Door about a Fortnight, or perhaps a Month, after he went away; " lie put his Name on the Door, but had no Time to arrange his Family, or Way of Life; I took the House off his Hands about Five Months ago; when he went away, it was understood between us, that I was to have the House, but the Deeds were not executed by him; it was held under a Mortgage; the Mortgagee has made it over to me, but Mr. Whitehill has not put his Name to it, because there is a Risk in fending over Deeds; General Joseph Smith is the Mortgagee."

And the Witness being asked. Why he put his Name on the Door? said, " I might perhaps like to live in it; I took it off when I advertised to let it; my Horses are in the Stable till I can let it — It is a better House than mine; it is above my Fortune — General Smith lent Mr. Whitehill the Money on the House; it was his own House; General Smith has assigned the Mortgage to me for the Value which I gave him; it was mortgaged in 1777; I gave the whole Money; the Mortgage was £. 4.500; the House cost £. 8,000."

Being asked. Whether the Mortgage was purchased by him as his own, or as for Mr. said,

" With my own Money; Mr. has been a

kind Friend to me; be wished to make me a Present of the House, if I would pay off the Mortgage, and in a Course of Time he would pay me the Money back, and give me the House." And the Witness added, " If he should die, it would be a fad Thing to me, and to many others, as his Affairs are so deranged."

And the Witness having said that the Transaction was finished between him and Mr. Whitehill, since he went Abroad; and being asked. What that Tran-action was ? he said, " His conveying the House to me; all I expect is a Transfer from him of the House, which I had his verbal Agreement for; I have nothing under his Hand, but that is not particular with him — I imagine the Payment of the Money and the Transfer of the House is to be done at the same Time.- — -Whdn he was Governor, I was Secretary to the Council; I Jived very much in a Habit of Intimacy with him."

And being asked, Who have the Knowledge of his Affairs, to settle in same of his Death? said " I have a letter of Attorney from him."

And being asked, If he has any Landed Property in England? said, " No; I fancy his Effects are in India-, lie has nothing in the Funds; the only Thing I know of, he has a Bill upon the Company, in the Hands of the Banker, about £.8,000; the Demands upon him are larger than that — -I don't know of any Schedule of his

St. Luke's A Petition of several Inhabitants of the Parish of Workhouse. Saint Luke, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill more effectually to enable the Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Luke, in the County of Middlesex, to purchase, hire, or erect a Workhouse within or near the said Parish, for the better Reception and Employment of the Poor of the said Parish; and setting forth. That the Parishioners are already poffoffed of a proper House for the Reception of the Poor of the said Parish; and the Petitioners apprehend, the building of anew House would occasion an unnecessary Expence to them, who are already burthened with heavy Taxes, the Rate for the Relief of the Poor being Four Shillings in the Pound, and, should the said Plan for building the said Workhouse be carried into Execution, the Petitioners apprehend it would amount to an additional Rate of One Shilling in the Pound for several Years, which Burthen the Petitioners would be unable to bear; and they conceive the present Workhouse might be made convenient for the Reception of the Poor at a much less Expence than would be occasioned by building a new one: and that the Vestrymen of the said Parish consist of Fifty-four Persons only, and the Petitioners conceive, that if a greater Number of Persons properly qualified were authorized to act as Vestrymen within the said Parish* Vol. 38.

the Business of the same would be conducted in a better Manner, and at a less Expence, than at present: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Provision may be made in the said Bill for the Purpose& aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the said Bill is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee, Hanover to whom the Bill for better paving, cleansing, and Square lighting Part of the Parish of Saint George, Hanover paving-Square, in the County of Middlesex, and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein, is committed, That they have Power to make Provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the Prayers of the several Petitions which were presented to the House upon the 3d and 6th Days of this Instant May, and were then eferred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

His Majesty's Proclamation, issued in purfttande of the said Address, is as followeth:

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION

for apprehending Thomas Lew in, Esquire.

GEORGE R.

Whereas on the First of this Instant May, Complaint being made to the House of Commons, that... Lewin, Esquire (late Secretary to the Council at , at

the Time John Whilchill, Esquire, was Governor of that Presidency) having been ordered by the Committee of Secrecy, appointed to enquire into the causes of the War that now subsists in the Carnatic, and of the present Condition of the British Possessions in those Parts, to attend the said Committee on the precedingDay, and also on the First Day of this Instant May, had neglected so to do; it was thereupon ordered by the' said House of Commons, that Thomas Esquire, should be

taken into Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending the said House of Commons: And whereas the said Serjeant at Arms having been called upon to give an Account of what had been done in relation to the taking the said Thoihas Leivin, Esquire, and the Messenger

who was sent in Search of him being called in and examined, and having acquainted the House that he had withdrawn himself, and was not taken; an humble Address hath been presented to Us by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, in Parliament assembled, that We , would be graciously pleased. to issue our Royal Proclamation for apprehending the said Thomas with

a Promise of a Reward for the fame; We have thought lit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council; to issue this Our Royal Proclamation, hereby requiring and commanding all Our loving Subjects whatsoever, to discover and apprehend, or cause the said to be discovered and apprehended, and to carry him before fouie of Our Justices of the Peace, or Chief Magistrates of the County, Town, or Place where he shall be apprehended, who are respectively required to securethe laid Thomas Lewin, and thereof give speedy

Notice to one of Our principal Secretaries of State; to the end he may be forthcoming to be dealt withal and proceeded against according to Law. — And for' the Prevention of an Escape of the said Thomas Lewin into Parts beyond the Seas, We do require and command all Our Officers of the Customs, and other Our Officers and Subjects of and in Our respective Ports and Maritime Towns and Places within Our Kingdom of Great Britain, that they and every of them, in their respective Places and Stations, be careful and diligent in the Examination of all Persons that shall pass or endeavour to pass beyond the Seas, and if they shall discover the said Thomas Leivin, then to cause him to be apprehended and secured, and to give Notice thereof as aforesaid: And We do hereby strictly charge and, command all Our loving Subjects, as they will answer the contrary at their Perils, that they do not any ways conceal, but do discover him the said Thomas Lewin, to the end he may be secured: And for the Encouragement of all Persons to be diligent and careful, in endeavouring to discover and apprehend the said Thomas Lewin, We do hereby further declare, that whosoever shall discover and apprehend the said Thomas Leivin, and shall bring him the said Thomas Lewin before some Justice of the Peace, or Chief Magistrate as aforesaid, shall have and receive as a Reward for the discovering, apprehending, and bringing the said Thomas Lewin before such Justice of the Peace, or Chief Magi-\ t»L. 38.

strateas aforesaid, the'Sum of Five hundred Pounds; which Our Commissioners of Our Treasury are hereby required and directed to pay accordingly.

Given at Our Court at Saint James's, the Seventeenth Day of May, One thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-two, in the Twenty-second Year of Our Reign.

God save the King.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. James Burne, an Officer belonging to the Custom House, informed your Committee, That the Port of London is now Unit in respect to the Importation of Foreign Corn and Grain.

George Middling, a CornfaClor, being examined, said, That according to the present Prices of Corn and Grain, there is no Appearance of the said Port being opened for a considerable Time to come. — Which last Evidence was confirmed by Mr. James Blatch.

Mr. James Burne being again examined, informed your Committee, That 5,066 Quarters of Wheat were imported into the Port of London, in the Months of August and September last: 10,008 Quarters and Two Bushels of Oats between the 7th of February and 27th of July 1781; and 4,561 Quarters of Peas, between the 15th of April 1779 an^ I7t*1 August 1780- And he produced the original Warrants from the Custom House, which confirmed his Evidence.

Then several Warehousekeepers were examined; by whose Evidence it appeared, that the several Quantities of Wheat, Oats, and Peas, mentioned by Mr. Burne, are now in their Custody, in certain Warehouses under the King's Locks. — And all the Witnesses said, That keeping such Corn in Warehouses is attended with a considerable Expence, and notwithstanding all the Care that can be taken, the same is daily reduced in Quantity, and growing worse in Quality.

Mr. William Anderson, aCornfactor, being examined, said, That if the above-mentioned Corn were brought to the London Market, it would not materially affect the Price of Corn there, the Quantity being so very inconsiderable.

This Evidence was confirmed by several CornfaClors

Ijrefent, who all agreed, that this Quantity would not ower the Price of Corn, in that Market, Six Pence in a Quarter.

and. Madras, Esquire, was p re fen ted to the House, and read;

Sboldr Setting forth. That the Petitioner is informed, that a fcc. ' Bill is depending in the House, for inflicting certain Pains and Penalties on the Petitioner and Sir Thomas Rumbold, Baronet, for certain Bi caches of Public Trust, and High Crimes and Misdemeanors, committed by them whilst they respectively held the Offices of Gover-nor and President, Counsellors, and Members of the Settlement of Fort Saint George, on the Coast of Coromandel, in the East Indies; and alledging, that the Petitioner is very unjultly charged with the said Breaches of Trust, High Crimes and Misdemeanors, and will be very unjustly and heavily aggrieved by such Pains and Penalties, if the said Bill should pass into a Law; and that the Petitioner is fully able to establish his Innocence; and therefore praying, That the House will take his same into their Consideration, and permit him to make his Defence, and to be fully heard, by himself or his Counsel, against the Bill, and the several Charges contained therein, and that sufficient Time wifi be allowed him for that Purpose.

Ditto. Another Petition of Peter Perring, late of Fort Saint

George, Madras, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill mentioned in the last preceding Petition; and felting forth, That the several Charges contained in the said Bill, so far as the same relate to or affect the Petitioner, are unjust and groundless, as the Petitioner doubts not to prove to the 'Satisfaction of the House; and that the Petitioner is informed, that the said Bill contains many Charges against the said Sir Thomas Rumbold, for various Offences in which the said Bill doth not and could not with Truth alledge that the Petitioner was in any Manner concerned; and that the said Bill doth not, and confidently with Truth could not, impute to the Petitioner, that he has marie, either by the Means of the Conduct charged against him in the Bill, or other wise, any undue or improper Gains or Emoluments during his Residence in India \ and that the Petitioner apprehends, that the same dated against him in the said Bill, differing so materially, both in the Number and Nature of the Offences therein laid to the Petitioner's Charge, from the same therein dated against the said Sir Thomas Rumbold, ought to have been made the Subject of a separate Bill; that the Attempt to punilli both by the same Bill will be extremely injurious to the Petitioner, as it tends to destroy the Distinction between the very different Offences Vol. 38.

Countess of

Oxford's

E:lates.

with which the said Sir Thomas Rumbold and the Petitioner are charged, to weaken the Effefl of the Evidence uliich the Petitioner hath to lay before the House in Support of his Innocence, bj confounding it with the Testimony which may be adduced by Sir Thomas Rumbold, and, that it endangers the Safety of the Petitioner, by exposing him to tlieSufpicion of more Guilt than the Bill imputes to him: And therefore praying, That the House, if it shall think fit to hear the Charges so made against the Petitioner, will either direct that the same shall be made the Subject of a separate Bill, or will, by hearing the Evidence against the Petitioner, and the Petitioner's Defence, separately and distinctfrom such Proof as shall be given against the said Sir Thomas Rum-bold, and such Defence as he shall think proper to fub-mit to the House, or in some other Manner, effectually provide, that the Petitioner shall not be prejudiced by being included in the aforesaid Bill; and that he may be heaid, by his Counsel, touching the Matters aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Planters of His Majesty's Sugar Colonies, and Merchants trading thereto, whose Names °* are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and their absent. Brethren, was presented to the House, and' read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are greatly alarmed, by observing, in the Yrotes, that the Sugar Refiners of London have again applied to Parliament, not only renewing their Prayer of the last Session of Parliament, for Leave to import Prize Sugars at Plan-

tation Duty, but extending it to the Ad million of all Sugars indiscriminately in Neutral Vessels from Neutral Places at the same Duty; and that after the full Confix deration which their Prayer underwent in the last Session of Parliament, and the Protection then given by the House to the Rights of the Petitioners, they conli*. dently trust the House will not now admit a Propofitioti which goes to Consequencesmuch more pernicious that* that which was in the last Session rejected, whilst no new Failure of Supply can be Ihevvn Efficient tojuftily such a total Overturning of the whole Svftem of Laws, upon which the Cultivation of the Sugar Colonies

depends; and that the Petitioners have most cheerfully acquiesced with the Principle of the Bill lately passed, whereby their late Fellow Subjects in Saint V*

Montfernit, and Nevis, will be hill entitled to import the Produce of their Estates at British Plantation Duty, the Conquest of those lllands will not therefore tend, as the Petitioners conceive, to dimiiiilh the Supply, whilst there is the greatest Reason to expect that the Importation from the other lllands in the present Year must be much greater than it waslall Year, because the Hurricane with which they were visited in the Month o f October 1780, had laid waste large and cultivated Parts thereof, which produced little or nothing in the Year 1781, but are now so far recovered from that Calamity, that their Produce in the Year 1782 will be very considerable; and that notwithstanding so great

A Petition of Stephen Fuller, Esquire, Agent for Jamaica, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Application mentioned in the* preceding Petition; and representing to the House, That at a Time when this Nation is involved in an unhappy Confeft with its own Subjects, and at open War with Three great Maritime Powers; when the Price of Freight and Premium of Insurance is greatly enhanced; when Lumber, Provisions, and all Plantation Ltenfilsj bear an advanced Price; when the Taxes of the Bland are exceedingly increased; when a heavy additional Duty has been laid upon the Importation of British Plantation Sugar; at a Time when so many Circum-llances united contribute to increase the Price of Sugar, and without which Increase the poor and middling Planter cannot go on, at this very Time to pull down the whole System of our Commercial Laws, erected by the Wisdom of our Ancestors, and to set up in its Stead an arbitrary and unnatural Innovation, calculated to build up a small Number of Manufacturers upon the Ruin of many (for the Planters are Manufacturers as well as the Refiners): and Hill more expressly and avowedly calculated to moderate, that is, to lower, the natural Price of a Commodity which so many Causes, not under the Controul of either Planter or Merchant, conspire to raise higher than it has been in former Wars, is nnreasonable and unjust, and, as every Thing that tends to discourage our own Sugar Colonies at the same Time naturally tends to encourage those of our Enemies, it is evidently impolitic; and alledging, that if Sugars are permitted to be imported in Neutral Vessels, and from Neutral Places, the Door is wide opened for the Sugars of the whole World, for those of our Enemies as well as those of the Neutral Powers; in confe-quer.ee of which the French Sugar, which are for the most Fart greatly superior in Strength and Colour, and eoinequently inolhulvantageoiisto the Refiner.will take Place at Market of f lic British Plantation Sugars, parti-

cularly those of Jamaica, whereby the Sure of them will he clogged and retarded, and in some Cafes totally prevented, unlessat a very inferior Price for Exportation, to the great and mauifeft Injury of the Planter,

Kingdom, will never be accotnpliftied by opening your Markets to your Enemies, and by fending ydUr Money into their Louhtry, never to return in Exchange for rival Commodities, thereby giving an unnatural Encouragement to the Production of their Colonies, nor by any other Method but that of a rational and permanent System of Encouragement to the Agriculture and Commerce of youf own Colonies, and iucreasing, byevery possible Means, the Production of aComihodity foeflential to the Commerce and the Revenue of this Kingdom; and that any other Methods of moderating the Price of Sbgars, particularly those in Question, will turn out iti the Find ruinous to the Planter, and productive of Effects totally different from those held out upon this and a former Occasion, lbr the Contemplation of the House'. It also appeared. That by an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, for establishing an Agreement between the East India Company and the Public, it was

Enacted, That the Sum of£.400,000 should be paid into the Exchequer, at the Times and in the Proportions therein mentioned, the last of which Payments was of £. 100,000, and was to have been made on 1st December 1781, for the Use of the Public; and on Failure of Payment, the Company were thereby made liable to . Damages, at the Rate of £. 15 per Centum, on the Monies unpaid, with full Colls of Suit; and it was thereby further Enacted, That from the 1 ft Day of March 1781, the clear Profits of the said Company should bedisposed of and applied as follows; The Company were first to set apart in each Year such Sum as should be equal to £.8 per Centum per Annum upon the Company's Capital Stock of £. 3,"200,000, and in case there should be a Surplus, Three-fourth Parts of such Surplus should be set apart and applied for the Use of the Public, and the remaining Fourth Part thereof should be referred and retained for the Company's Use, and that it should be lawful for the Company to apply such Money as they were to retain for themselves, and other Money in the said Act mentioned, in the Payment of Dividends to the Proprietors of the Stock of the said Company, not exceeding £.12. 10s. pe; provided that the Company's Bond Debt did not at any such Time exceed £. 1,500,000, and provided they did not increase their present Dividend of£. 8 per Centum more than at the Rate of £. 1 per Centum in each Year: And in order to ascertain the said Yearly Profit, the Company were to cause to be made up Yearly for each Year, with as much Accuracy as the Nature of the same would admit, a Statement of the Profit and Loss upon the Whole of their Trade and Revenues, together with a State of the Debts of the Company in England, from the ill of March in every Year, to the ill Day of March in each succeeding Year; which said Account was to be signed and delivered to the Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, or the High Treasurer for the Time being, as therein is mentioned.

It also appeared, by an Account produced to your Committee, That the Profit upon the Whole of the Company's Trade and Revenues, from the ill of March 1781 to the ill of March 1782, did not amount to so much as a Dividend at the Ilate of A 8 per Centum, by the Sum of £.22,023: And it further appeared, That besides the Payments in that Account, there were other Debts due from the Company, which ought to have been paid previous to the ill of March 1782, which were postponed; viz.
