It also appeared, That the 18 Ships mentioned in the Petition, in the ordinary Course ought to have arrived in Time for their Cargoes to have been fold and converted into Calli before the ill of March 1782, but that they did not arrive till 1781; by Means of

which late Arrival,- the Goods -could not be put up to Sale till after the ill o { March 1782.

It further appeared. That there are Three Species of Customs payable by the Company; One called Rated Customs, being on the Quantity of Goods imported; another, Unrated, which is paid ort the gross Amount of the Sales: The First are paid by Instalments, a Moiety in 6 Months after the Entry of the Ship at the Custom House, and the other Moiety at the Expiration of 12 Months after such Entry: The Unrated Customs are now payable within 3 Months after the Close of each Sale. The Third Species of Customs is, £. 15 per Centum on Mullins and Callicoes, payable within 20 Days after the Sale.

It also appeared, That £. 300,000, Part of the £. 400,000, has been paid to Government, agreeable to the said Act of the last Section; and that by Means of the late Arrival of the said 18 Ships, the Company were not enabled to pay the remaining £.100,000, and the Customs, at the Time they became due, and to continue the Dividend to the Proprietors at £. 8 per Centum, without borrowing Money for those Purposes; and that the Lords of the Treasury have postponed the Payment of the£. 100,000 to the ill of June next, and of the said Customs to the 21st of June.

It also appeared, That the Account directed to be made out by the said Act, by which the Dividend is to be made to the Proprietors, may not include the real Profits of the Company's Trade, and Territorial Pof-sessions, within the respective Year, if made for One Year only, but if made for Seven Years, such Account would be a fair Account of the real Profits of the Company's Trade, and Territorial Possessions, upon a Medium taken of the whole Seven Years; and that the general Balance of an Account for One Year, very much depends upon the Conduct of the Directors of the Company, as to the Quantity of Merchandize they shall put up to Sale, and the Times in which they shall stipulate to make their Payments, but such Balance could not be effected upon the Average of Seven Years.

Sir George Yonge reported from the Committee, who Members riot were appointed to draw up Reasons to be offered to the to becon-Lords, at a Conference, for disagreeing to the Amend- Con-ment made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, tractSt An Act for redraining any Person concerned in any ContraQV Commission, or Agreement, made for the Public Service, from being elected, or dtting and voting as a Member of the House of Commons, which this House hath disagreed to; That the Committee had drawn up Reasons accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To the Fird, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, and Seventh Amendments, made by your Lord blips to the Bill, intituled, An Act for redrawing any Persons concerned in any Contract, Cormtiiflion, or Agreement, made for the Public Service, from being elected or fitting and voting sts a Member of the House of Commons, the Commons do agree.

To the Sixth Amendment made by your Lorddiipsr. which is, tb insert the Words, "except fuqli Wares

and Merchandize as shall be of his own Growth, " Production, or Manufacture, and also except such " Houses, Warehouses, Lands, and Tenements, as shall cc be hired out, or contracted for, for the Service of the Public/' the Commons do disagree;

Because,

First, They cannot suggest to themselves any Reason for excluding from a Seat in the House of Commons, the Merchant, who shall furnish for the Public Service, those Wares and Commodities which the Course of his Dealings with Foreign Countries may enable him to do; which Reason is not equally applicable to the Farmer, the Grazier, the Grower of Timber, the Manufacturer, and every other Person deriving a Profit from the Rent of his Houses, Warehouses, or Lands — That undue Influence, which it is the Object of this Bill to destroy, resides equally in every Contract or Agreement that is made with the Commissioners of the Treasury, or any of the Public Boards; and therefore the Contractor under such Circumstances, of whatever Denomination he may be, ought equally to be retrained from being elected, or fitting and voting as a Member of the House of Commons.

Secondly, Another Reason, which induces the Commons to aifagree with this Amendment, is, that in their Opinion it gives great Opportunities for Fraud and Collusion, and opens a very wide Door for evading the principal Object of the Bill. — There are very many Articles furnished for the Public Service, which are of the Growth, ProduClion, and Manufacture of Great Britain, and it will be a very easy Matter for any Person furnishing these Articles, who wishes to be a Member of the House of Commons, to give them such a Colour and Appearance of their being of his own Growth, ProduClion, or Manufacture, as it will be extremely difficult, if not totally impossible to detect.

For these Reasons, the Commons hope that your Lordships, who have shewn your Approbation of the Principle of the Bill, will not insist upon an Amendment, which in their Opinion tends to render the Provisions of the Bill fruitless and nugatory.

The said Reasons being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

That every Transgression of those Orders, without evident Necessity, by any of the sevenfl British Governments in India, ha9 been highly represensible, and has tended in a chief Degree to weaken the Force and Influence, and to diminish the Resources, of the Company in those Parts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Imerference as a Party in the domestic or national Quarrels of the Country Powers, and all new Engagements with them in offensive Alliance, have been wifely and providently forbidden by the Company, in their Coirimands to their Administrations in India.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every nnnecessary or avoidable Deviation from those well-ad vised Rules, should be followed with very severe Represension and Punishment for it, as an In-hance of wilful Disobedience of Orders, and as tending to disturb and destroy that State of Tranquillity and Peace with all their Neighbours, the Preservation of which has been recommended as the First Principle of Policy to X\\e British Governments in India.

Ri'solved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Maintenance of an inviolable Character for Moderation, good Faith, and scrupulous Regard to Treaty, ought to have been the Ample Grounds on which the British Governments should have endeavoured to establish an Influence superior to that of other Europeans over the Minds of the Native Powers in India; and that the Danger and Discredit arising from the Forfeiture of this Pre-eminence, could not be compensated by the temporary Success of any Plan of Violence or Injustice.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That as any elsential Failure in the executive Conduct of the Supreme Council or Presidencies would make them justly liable to the mofl serious Ani-madveriions of their Superiors; so should any Relaxation, without sufficient Cause in these Principles of good Gov ernment, on the Part of the Directors themselves, bring upon them, in an heavier Degree, the Resentment of the Legislative Power of their Country, which alone can iutcrpole an effectual Correction to t he general Miirule.

Rtf)(red. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, T'liiit the Conduct of the Company and their Servants in India to the King and Nudjiff Caion, with respectto the Tribute payable to the one, and the Stipend to the other, and with respect to the Transfer of the Provinces of Corah and ILlahabab to the Vizier, was contrary to Policy and good Faith; and that such wife and practicable Measures should be adopted in future, as may tend to redeem the National Honour, and recover the Confidence and Attachment of the Princes of India.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That too strong a Confirmation cannot be given to the Sentiments and Resolutions of the Court of Directors, and of the Court of Proprietors of the East India Company, in Condemnation of the Rohilla War: That the Conduct of the President and Select Committee of Bengal appears, in almost every Stage of it, to have been biassed by an unreasonable and unjust Partiality to the Vizier, to transgress their own as well as the Company's positive and repeated Regulations and Orders: That the Extermination of the Rohillaswas not necessary for the Recovery of Forty Lacks of Rupees; and that, if it was expedient to make their Country a Barrier against the Maratlas, there is Reason to believe^hatthis might have been etfeCied by as easy and by a less iniquitous Interference of the Government of Bengal, which would at the same Time have preservd the Dominion to the rightful Owners, and exhibited an attentive Example of Jt'ftice as well as Policy to all India.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Company's Servants in their Presidency of Bombay, were guilty of very notorious Instances of Disobedience to the Orders of their Employers, as well in

Vol. .38.

the Proceedings against the &at>dt) of firoticti, as in the Commencement of the Maratta War* by the Seizure of the Islands of Saljette and Caranja.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee; That the Court of Directors madeufe of very strongEjcpreffions to communicate their With of acquiring those Islands, and the Fortress of Boffein; and although in the Month of April 1775, previous to the Receipt of Intelligence that Salfette was taken, they Very explicitly confined their Servants at Bombay to Measures of Nego-ciation, as the only Means they authorized for making the Acquisition; yet, after Knowledge of the Event, they do not seem to have signified any Displeasure at the Transaction, or any farther Anxiety than about the Preservation of the Conquest; and that the Court of Directors, in this Instance, gave Countenance and Sanction to the very Measure they had themselves so pointedly condemned, and are therefore so far chargeable with the Responsibility of it.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in forming an offensive Alliance with Ragoba, the Government of Bombay violated the Orders of the Company against any Connections of that Nature, and against any Interference in the Quarrels of the Native Powers; that they undertook, without a Certainty of an adequate Revenue, or a sufficient Military Force, and without proper Communication with the superior Government, upon which they were to depend for Sanction and Support, to place that Chief on the Mufnud at Poona, and thereby to involve themselves in a Wac with the ruling Ministers of the Maratta State; while Ragoba himself was not in the mean Time able to give the CompanyfecurePoffeflion of any of the Grantshe had made to them for the Purchase of their Assistance.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Measures taken by the Majority, which then consisted of Messieurs Clavering, Monson, and Francis, in the Government of Bengal, for the Restoration of Peace, \vere wife and just in their Principle, and comformable to the Spirit of the Company's Orders, notwithstanding that their Method of Interference was not afterwards approved of by the Court of Directors.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Terms of the Treaty concluded by Colonel Upton at Poorunder, in the Beginning of March 1776, were honourable and advantageous to the Company; when the Circumstances of the Rife and Progress of the War, the Want of Resources for carrying it on, the State of the contending Parties, the Inftrndions of the Superior Council, and the general Sentiments of the Company, are attended to.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That the Perseverance of the Superior Government, in directing the Execution of the Articles of Accommodation, was judicious and commendable, notwithstanding that the Presidency of Bombay protested against them as inadequate and highly injurious to the Reputation, Honour, and Interests of the Company; and that the Court of Directors, in their Letter of the 15th December 1775, which reached Calcutta on the 1 ft, July 1776, declared their Intentions of keeping all Territories and Possessions ceded to the Company by the Treaty concluded with Ragoba

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the President and Council of Bombay, in granting an Asylum to Ragoba, after the Qonclufion of the Treaty of Poorunder, did not thereby commit any direct Infringement on the Stipulations of that Treaty, provided they had taken no other offensive Measure in Support of his Cause; and it appears that this Conduct coincided with the Sentiments and Instructions of the Court of Directors, who made the personal Safety of Ragoba one of the Conditions of their Acquiescence in the Treaty of Poorunder.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Sir Eyre Coote, in his Letter of the 18th January 1779, condemned the Conduct of the Two Presidencies of Bengal aiul Bombay, and with good Reason denounced the probable bad Consequences of the Expedition to Poona, and of the March of the Detachment " which " was fenl from Bengal at an iromenfe Expence, and " could produce nothing but Distress to the Company, not to say Dishonour to the Nation, whether

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the President and Selecl Committee of Fort Saint in their Letter of 7th February 1779, with no less forcible Reason, denounced the like fatal Consequences of these Measures, and Juilly pointed out the alarming Influence which the ill-timed and unfortunate Euterprize from Bombay might have on the Minds of the Country Powers, to the Prejudice of the Interests;

that they foresaw with Justice that it might operate as an Encouragement to Hyder Ally " openly to refill the " proposed Attempt on Make that there was therein great Foundation for their Apprehensions of the unfavourable Impression which those Measures and Events might fix in the Disposition of the Nizam, already biassed against the Company; that they represented, with Truth,\ the Danger to which, in those Circum-liances, their Northern Circars would be exposed, should the Nizam be induced to venture upon Hostilities against them; that they therefore, with provident Policy, resolved to fend a Rsfident to his Durbar, who might have the bed Intelligence of his Temper and Motions.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the first ostensible Defigti of the Deputation to Hyderabad was perverted to a raoft impolitic and diflio-nourable Purpose, by the Steps taken for obtaining a Relinquishment of the Pelhcufli, and, as such, tended rather to inflame than compose the Resentment of the Nizam; which Conduct was the more unpardonable in the President and Select Committee of Fort Saint George, because they had apprehended, with such early and just Forefight, the dangerous Effects of his Diflatisfaction, and the Necessity of averting it.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Motives, as well as Success of the Nizam's Instigations, to form and animate a Confederacy of the great Country Powers against the British Possessions in India, and the calamitous Events which ensued, may be properly attributed both to the unjustifiableProceedings against the Maratta Government, and to the Conduct of the Madras Presidency, in regard to the Pelhcufli and the Guntoor Circar.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Instructions and Powers given to Colonel Goddard by the Superior Council, on 5th April 1779, fiXQd on them, from that Time, the chief Direction and Respon-fibility of the Treaty and War with the Marattas.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That whatever Backwardness was afterwards manifested by the Maratta Ministers to any Accommodation, unless upon very hard and humiliating Terms to the Company, must be ascribed as well to their too realoDable Diffidence in our Sincerity, as to their advantageous Pretensions from the Convention of , and the

well-known Discontent or Enmity which our Conduct had raised in other Powers against us.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Expences of the War, and especially of the Detachment sent to the Malabar Coast, were felt and acknowledged to be, in a very serious Degree, distressing to the Reffga/Government, and greatly over-balanced every Voi. 38,

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That immediately upon Advice of the Success of Hyder Ally in The Carnatic, the Governor General and Council gave Proof of the readiell and most important Exertions for the Assistance of the Presidency of and took

immediate Measures with a View to obtain Peace with the Marattas, and to regain the Friendship of the

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it must be reckoned amongst the many additional Mischiefs which have arisen chiefly from this improvident War with the Marattas to the Company's A flairs, that the Military Force of The Carnatic had been weakened by Reinforcements sent to the Malabar Coast; that the Bengal Government have been under the Necessity ofsupporting, on their Confines, the Army of a Fower, confederated, however involuntarily, against them; that they have been obliged to sue for the Mediation of the same Power (the Rajah of Berar) have submitted to a Refusal, and purchased at last an uncertain, because apparently an unauthorized Treaty, on most extravagant and dishonourable Conditions, with his Son Rajah Chimnajee; and finally, that, being burthened

with the Expences of a variety of distant Expeditions, while their Allies are in Distress, and their Tributaries under Oppression, there is also an alarming Deficiency in their own Resources of Revenue and Commerce, by the Accumulation of their Debt and the Reduction of their Investment.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Attempt made by the Government General, in the Month of January 1781, to form an Engagement of Alliance, offensive and defensive, with the Dutch East India Company, by the Means, and upon the Terms Hated in the Proceedings of their Council, was unwarranted, impolitic, extravagant, and unjust.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, according to the last official Dispatches from Bengal, dated 15th May 1781, the Prospect of Peace was not then propitious, because it did not seem to be wished for by the Marattas upon the Terms proposed, £nd because the Government of Bengal, not thinking it de* firable, without obtaining even additional Advantages, had reprobated the System of Defence which the Presidency of Bombay wished to have adopted; and that the Conduct of the Government General, as far as it might tend to procraflinateAccommodation with th was evidently injurious to the Interests of the Company and to the Nation.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Government General had been previously in possession of a Letter from the Duan of the Rajah of Berar, containing Overtures for Mediation for Peace, and Alliance with the Pefhwa; and that this material Information was wholly suppressed by them in their Dispatches to the Court of Directors, but a Copy of it was sent by the same Conveyance to the private Agent of Mr. Hafings; and that in thus neglecting to make immediate Communication to the Court of Directors of such important Intelligence, the Government General appear to have failed in an essential Part of their. Duty.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Court of Directors, in their latest Dispatches, have given Instructions, which, if duly obeyed by their Governments in India, may have already perfected the desirable Work of Peace; and that every Encouragement and Assistance which may be thought necessary, should be given by Parliament to expedite the Accomplishment of it: " iriiat the Principle of Pacification may be extended as soon as possible to a general Restoration of

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the Purpose of conveying entire Convifl ion to the Minds of the Native Princes, that to commence Hostilities without just Provocation against them, and to pursue Schemes of Conquest and Extent of Dominion, are Ivleaftires repugnant to the Wish, the Honour, and the Policy of this Nation; it is the Duty of the Court of Directors, in Conformity to the Sense expressed by this House, forthwith to recall such Member or Members of their principal Presidencies as appear to have been chiefly concerned in wilfully acting upon a System tending to inspire a reasonable Dilirull of the Moderation, Justice, and good Faith of the British Nation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That if any Perfotis, in Violation of the Public Faith given by the East India Company in the Year 177.5, and contrary to the true Intent and Meaning of the several Resolutions of this House of the apth of April last, have taken in Sequestratiun or otherwise the Revenues of Tanjore into the Management of the Nabob of Arcot, or of the East India Company; it is the Duty of the Court of Directors forthwith to order the said Revenues to he returned to the Administration of the King of Tanjore, agreeable to the Treaties of the Years 1762 and 1775.

Resolved, That Warren Ha fling Esquire, Governor General of Bengal, and William Hornby, Esquire, President of the Council at Bombay, having, in fundrv In-llances, acted in a Manner repugnant to the Honour and Policy of this Nation, and thereby brought great Calamities on India, and enormous Expences on the East India Company, it is the Duty of the Directors of the said Company to pursue all legal and effectual Means for the Removal of the said Governor General and Pre-fidenfc from their respective Offices, and to recall them to Great Britain.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that the Maratta Government of Poona, in the Thirteenth Article of the Treaty made by Colonel Upton, declared, that the Chout of Bengal and its Dependencies had, for Time out of Mind, been Part of the Jaghire of the Boiinfelloi they therefore could not withdraw it; hut if the said Bounfetlo, or any of his Descendants or Successors, or any other Person, should cause Disturbances, by claiming or demanding the Chout on Bengal or its Dependencies, they did engage never to affilt them themselves, or permit any Mar alt a Chief, dependant on them or the Rnjahfiiip, to give them any Assistance; and that the Governor and Council General of Bengal did not think it advi(cable to accept the Concessions made by this Article, and agreed therefore that it should be left out of the Treaty, and Colonel Upton was directed to decline any Explanation upon it; but, if that could not he avoided, to inform the Maratta Mmillers, that their Reason for omitting it was, an Apprehension that it might be underltooood to contain an Acknowledgment of a Right which did not exist, and which they concluded the Maratta Ministers themselves had ho Thoughts of infilling on when they proposed such an Article.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That Rajah Moodagee Boojlah, in a Let ter to Mr. Hajtings, Governor General of Bengal, made a speeific Demand of Fourteen Lacks of Rupees per Annum, as a Tribute due from Bengal to him; and which Tribute he declared was acquired by his Ancestors, and vested in himself by Inheritance.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, That the Governor General of Bengald\d pay to Moodagee Boojlah, Rajah of Berar, and to his Son Ghimnajce, certain Sums of Money, to the Amount of Twenty-six Lacks of Rupees, under the Denomination of Subsidy or Loan.

Resolved, That the Payment of any Sums of Money to Moodagee Boojlah, or to his Son Ghimnajce, under the Denomination of Subsidy, and Hill more if advanced as a Loan, whilst his Army was on the Frontiers of Bengal, may be considered as an actual Acknowledgment of his Claim of Tribute from the Provinces of Bengal; which Claim is not founded, and ought not, directly or indirectly, to be acknowledged.

John Murray, Esquire, being examined, said. He was well acquainted with the Navigation of the Solway Frith; understands the Limits thereof to be from Saint Fee's Head in the County of Cumberland, to Borough Head in the County of Wigton; and added, that he has

-known Coals to be carried in a Cart across the said Frith from Bolness to Annan.

Robert Wells, Esquire, being then examined, with respect to the Solway Frith, informed your Committee,

he is well acquainted with its Situation; that he considers the Boundaries of the said Frith to be from Saint Bee's Head in the County of Cumberland, to Borough Head in the County of Wigton .- — The Witness also informed Your Committee, He has forded the said Frith from Bolness to Dorneck, which, when the Tide is in, is about Two Miles in Breadth.

Captain FerguJJon being also examined, said. He was well acquainted with the Navigation of the Solway Frith; that there is not a Port in the said Frith which he has not navigated to and from; understands the Limits of the said Frith to be all within Saint Bee's Head on the South Side, and Borough Head on the North Side; that he has frequently walked across from Bol-ness to Dorneck; understands the said Frith to be navigable to Rockliffe when the Tide is in, but at low Water may be forded as low down as Bolness; that there is not a Port in the said Frith, within the Boundaries above mentioned, to wit, from Saint Bee's Head to Borough «4

Maii. 1782.

Head, into which a Vessel can fail except when the Tide is in.

George Chalmers, Esquire, being examined, said. He has been a Merchant, and often traded from Scotland to England; knows that the Trade on the Navigable or Estuary Rivers or Friths in England is not subjectedto the same Regulations, or the same high Custom House Fees, with that carried on upon the open Sea Coast: — The Witness also informed Your Committee he knows that the Officers of the Custotns of Scotland have of late Years subjected the Scotch Rivers Or Friths to the Rules and high Fees which belong only to the Open Sea Coast Trade; and that in fomelnliances they have ex-acted Duties on Coals within the Limits of Rivers where no such Duties were payable, and that they have considered the Limits of such Rivers as generally bounded by their first Bridges, except with respect to a final! Part of the upper River of Clyde -, that he refers particularly to the Friths of Forth including the Frith of Mur-

ray, tile Frith oiCiyde, and the Frith of Solway-, and that he ktiows this to have been a very considerable Prejudice to the Commerce, Manufactures, Agriculture, and Navigation of that Part of the Country.

Upon the Whole, Your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That by the Articles of the Treaty of Union, and subsequent Statutes, the Trade ofwhether carried on upon the Open Coast, or in Estuary Rivers or Friths, is subjected to the same Restrictions and Regulatious with that of England, and is entitled to the same Rights, Privileges, and Advantages which the Open Coast Trade, or the Trade on similar Rivers or Friths in England,. respectively enjoy.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Trade on the Navigable or Estuary Rivers or Friths in England is not subjected to the same Regulations, or the same high Custom House Fees, with the Trade carried on upon the open Sea Coast.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Limits to distinguish any of the Friths or Rivers in Scotland from Sea, or open Sea, have not been properly ascertained, excepting the Frith of Forth, in so far as regards the Coal Duty; and for Want of this A seer-tainment the Officers of the Customs (excepting on a small Part of the River Clyde) have of late Years subjected all the Scotch Rivers in general, as far as to their first Bridges, to the Rules and high Fees, and even in some Instances to the Duties, of the open Sea Coast Trade, contrary to Law and the Practice of England in similar Situations, and to the great Hurt of the Commerce, Manufactures, Agriculture, and Navigation of that Part of the United Kingdom.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Limits of the different Friths or Estuary Rivers in Scotland should be ascertained, to distinguish them from Sea, or open Sea; and that the Limits of the Frith of Forth ought to be fixed from the Town of Dunbar to the Promontory of Redhead, as they are ascertained by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, <c An Act for reviving,

" continuing, and appropriating certain Duties upon " several Commodities to be exported, and certain Du- ties upon Coals to be Water-born and carried Coastwise; and for granting further Duties upon Candles for Thirty-two Years; to raise Fifteen hundred thousand Pounds by Way of a Lottery, for the Service of ct the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Eleven,

" and for suppressing such unlawful Lotteries, and such " Insurance Offices as are therein mentioned;" in regard to the Duty on Coals, with this Regulation, that all Goods which pals out of the largeli Branch of this Frith called The proper Forth, into the smaller Branch thereof called The Tay, and all Goods that pass vice versi out of the Tay into the larger Branch, shal I be subject

A MESSAGE by Sir Francis Molyneux, Gentle- Royal Assent man Uftier of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty's Commission for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate Attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

The said Report is as followeth; viz.

To the Honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, in Parliament assembled.

The Seventh Report of the Commissioners appointed to examine, take, and date, the Public Accounts of the Kingdom.

The Act of the last Session of Parliament, for continuing and amending the ACtof the preceding Section, by which we were Grd appointed, having, by a particular Clause, " authorized and impowered us to examine " the several Accounts of Extraordinary Services incurred, and not provided for by Parliament, which " have been laid before the House of Commons dnee the " id of January 1776," we considered that Clause not as imperative upon us, to dop short in the Pursuit we were at that Time engaged in, under the Authority of the former Act, and to proceed immediately to the Examination of these Accounts; but rather as the Designa-tion of a Subject, selected from among the numerous Objects committed to us in general Terms by the Fird Act, as the next for our Consideration, after we should have completed the Inquiries we were then pursuing. Those Inquiries being finished, we have, in Obedience to the Intention of the LegiRature, thus iignided to us, directed our Attention to the Accounts of the Extraordinary Services incurred, and not provided for by Parliament, which have been laid before the House of Commons dnee the id of January 1776.

In this, wide Field, where the Objects are so numerous, so various, and so complicated, we have, in our Choice of the Subject, been attentive to the Public Voice, as far as we have been able to collect it, and have selected for our Inquiry, as much suspected of Abuse, that Part of the Public Money granted for the Extraordinary Services of the Army, which has been expended in North America; endeavouring to trace it from its Issue out of the Exchequer to the final Disposition of it in that Country, with a View to discover whether any Part of it has been, and by what Means, intercepted in its Passage or diverted in its Application.

We entered upon this Inquiry sensible of many obvious and discouraging Difficulties in our Way. This Money is expended in a didant Country: The Evidence of the material Circumstances of every Transaction of Expenditure is in that Country; except where, in a few Indances, we have had it in our Power to apply to an Accountant himself, who has either passed his Accounts in the Office of the Auditors of the Impred, or brought in his Hand his Vouchers, fair and regular upon the . Face of them. By what Means then are we to detefl (if such there has been) Peculation, Fraud, or Misapplication?

We admit no Charge against Persons Abroad, who have no Opportunity of being heard in their own Defence; and we are cautious that our Examination does *7

not lead to Self-accusation. Thus deditpte of the proper Evidence, and with so unpromising a Prospect before us, we fetoutin Search of such Materials as we could find, and as the Nature and Circumstances of the Subject would afford.

We extracted from the Journals, and from the Ac- Appendi; counts presented to the House of Commons, the Sums granted for the Extraordinary Services of the Army every Year, from the id of January 1776 to the 3 id of December lad; the Total of these Sums is Nineteen Millions Five hundred and Two thousand Niue hundred £ Sixty-nine Pounds Two Shillings and Eight Pence.

We obtained, by Requisition from the Office of the Pavmader General of the Forces, an Account of the '* Money issued to Mefirs.//«Wey and Drummond, pursuant to His Majesty's Warrants, for the Extraordinary Services of His Majesty's Forces serving in North America during the same Period. This Sum amounts to Ten Millions Eighty-three thousand Eight hundred Sixty-three Pounds Two Shillings and Six Pence.

We proceeded, in the next Place, to inquire by what Means this Money passed to North America Of this we received Information from Thomas Neale, Esquire, N*j. the Agent in London to Messrs. H and , who are engaged in a Contract with Government to make these Remittances for a Commission of One and a Half per Cent, clear of all Fees of Office and Expence of Transportation. All this Money passes from the Exchequer, through the Hands of the Paymader General of the Forces, to the Remitters, and from them to their Agents in North America; who pay it to the Deputy Paymader General of the Forces residing in that Country. It passes from the Exchequer to the Remitters in the following Manner:

When the Commander in Chief in North America fends to the Agents a Requisition, specifying a certain Sum to be wanted for the Extraordinary Services of the A''my for the ensuing Quarter, the Agents, in couse-quenceof this Requisition, draw Bills upon the Remitters, and transmit to them the Requisition with a Lid of the Bills annexed; upon the Receipt of which, the Remitters apply by Memorial to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury for Money to extinguish those Bills, and receive from them a Warrant upon the Paymader General of the Forces, for the Payment of a Sum upon Account, for the Use of His Majesty's Forces in North America: This Warrant being satisfied by the Issue from the Exchequerto the Paymader General, in consequence of a Treasury Letter and Order of the Auditor, the Paymader General gives to the Remitters his Draft for it upon the Bank. If the Commander in Chief makes no Requisition, the Ageuts themselves send to the Remitters an Account of what Money will be wanted, and they apply for it to the Treasury, and receive it in like Manner from the' Paymader General of the Forces.

There are Two Ways by which this Money goes from the Remitters into the Hands of their Agents:

The one is by Bills thus drawn by them upon the Remitters, which Bills they receive the Value for there, and the Remitters discharge when presented to them in London: The other is by fending oat to them, actual Caih; this is done according to special Directions given for that Purpose by the Ixirds of the Treasury to the Remitters, whenever it becomes necessary to support the Exchange by increasing the Quantity of current Calli in the Hands of the Agents.

The Commander in Chief directs Money into the planets of these Accountants, by his Warrant to the Deputy Paymaster General, requiring him to pay to the Officer named a certain Sum for the Purptofe therein specified. These Warrants are of Two Kinds; Temporary, and Final: The Temporary Warrantis for Money upon Account, and granted upon the Application of the Officer, to enable' him to carry on the Service: The K* 6. Final Warrant is for Money to reimburse the Officer Expences actually incurred, and mentions that the Vouchers are lodged with that Officer. , .

Every Qjiarter, or as soon after as the Service will admit, these Officers make an Abstract of all the Sums they have expended in their several Departments during that Quarter, digested under different Heads of Expence. Every Officer carrieshis Abstracto the Commander in Chief for his Inspection, and for the Purpose of being reimbursed the Amount of that Abstract. If, upon Examination, no Objection arises to any of the Articles, he grauts to the Officer a Final Warrant upon the Deputy Paymaster General, for the Total Sum contained in the Abstract: Upon Production of this Warrant, with the Ahftract annexed, at the Pay Office of the Army, the Officer takes up and caucels, as being of no Use, the Temporary Warrants he has received in that Quarter; and, deducting from the Sum in the Abstract the Sums contained in the Temporary Warrants, he receives the Balance, leaving both the Final Warrant and Abstract with the Deputy Paymaster General; who fends them every Quarter to the Pay Office of the Army in England, as Vouchers for the Paymaster General of the Forces, upon patting his Account before the Auditors of the Imprest.

Through these Channels is the Money, granted for the F.xtraordinary Services of the Army, conveyed into the Hands of certain Officers intruded with and responsible for the Expenditure of that Money: How this Expenditure has been conducted, was the next, and the material Subject of our Inquiry.

The Quarter Matter General, the Barrack Matter General, the Committary General, and the Chief. Engineer, are the Officers to whose Management the greatest Share of this Money is committed; and therefore to them we principally directed our Attention: We examined such of them as we could find, who either were then, or had been employed in these Departments; and collected what Information we could from the Vouchers in their Possession, orfrorn those they had delivered into the Office of the Auditors of the Im-prest; all of which were, in consequence of our Ke-quilition, submitted to our Inspection.

In purfning this Inquiry into the Methods and Forms _ by which this Expenditure has been carried Oh, we Have had in View Two principal Objects; one is, to discover whether any Fraud has in Fast been committed upon the Public m the Coxirfe of these MoneyTranfac-ttons; the other is, to observe whether the Public has been sufficiently guarded against Fraud and Imposition, in the Modes adopted for carrying on this Expenditure.

Could a single Instance of Fraud be drftjovered in any of the Accounts of these Officers, Inch a Discovery would so corrupt and vitiate that Account, as to subject the Whole oPit to a Revision and Unravelment, though adjafted and parted with' all the Solemnities of the Exchequer.

These Accountants are charged with- alHhe Sums they have received of- the Pay matter General of the Forces, by the Warrants of the Commander in Chief. They cannot discharge themselves, but by the Receipts of the Persons to whom they or their Officers have paid these Sums. The Receipts are fair upon the Face of them; each contains all the Essentials of a true Voucher; a Date, the Subject Matter, the Sum paid, the Peism of whom received, and the Person receiving. If the Transaction has not been a fair one, and Government has been defrauded of any Part of the Money, 'the Voucher, which is the Evidence of that Transeftion, must, in some Part of it, be false or fraudulent: To discover whether it be so or not, the Person, who appears to have signed it, is always a material, and, in some Cafes, the only Witness, who can tell whether the Sum specified in the Receipt to have been received, was in Fast the Sum bona, side paid; but Persons under this Description are not amenable to us, fitting in this Kingdom; they are in North America. Numberless, and in a Variety of Ways, may have been the Frauds and Impositions committed upon Government, without the Knowledge even of the Officer who palTes the Accounts, being himself not privy to the Payments, but relying, for the Truth of the Vouchers he produces in his Discharge, upon the Integrity and Fidelity of his inferior Officers.

Rumours of Imposition, and of much Wealth acquired during a ffiort Service upon flender Appointments, may create a Stifpicion of some concealed Management, and be a Ground for Inquiry by proper Authority; but they are not Proofs upon which can be supported, against any Person whatever, the heavy Charge of defrauding the Public.

Having the refore no Hopes of pursuing this Subject Vot. 38.

with Effect, we turned our Attention to the Second Seventh Object we proposed; that is, to those Openings''

Fraud, and that Possibility of Abuse, which the Modes ^bHc*" ° of conducting these Money Transaction^ have left with- Accounts. ont Fence or Guard: And we are of Opinion tlutt the Public have not been sufficiently protested irrTwo material Points: First, The Officers intrnfted with itte Expenditure of the Public Money have been permitted1 to have an Interest themselves in the Subject Mat ter oP Expence: Secondly, The Vouchers, by which the Accountants discharge themselves of the Sums intruded to tliern, are allowed without having undergone sufficient Examination. j

It is a Branch of the Business of the Quarter Matter 1 General to provide Waggons and Horses, with their' necessary Attendants and Appendages, for the Use of1 tire Army, either when in Quarters, or in'Mdtion; and, when1 there is Occasion to transport therti, or -to supply theii1 Wants by Water, their SttperintendantThPrtiflles them with Vessels, and whatever is necessary for f Carriage by Water. It is the Duty of these-Officers ' to make the Contrafts for the Articles, and to fee thofe1 Contrafts honestly and substantially performed; to take care that each Article is properly equipped; ' andadequate to the Service it is intended for; and that the Service, for which Payment is claimed, hhis bCeif,1 in Fast,'performed/; These Officers are placed, oh the Part of Government, as a Check and Controul tipon the Chntraftors, to protest the Public from Loft or tm-position. The Barrack Matter General anfd 'Chief Engineer stand upon the same Ground, in respect to the Waggons and Horses made Use of in their Departments, and not provided by the Quarter Matter General. But it has been the Usage, as far back as our Inquiry has gone, for the Officers in these Departments to be themselves the Propfietors of, or to have Shares or Interests in, a great Number of the Vessels and small '

Craft, and in almost all the Waggons and Horses, employed in these Services: These Officers have purchased or procured them upon their own Account, and let them out to Government at the fixed Prices of Hire; , the same Person, employed by and acting for the Pub-, lie, contrafts, on the Part of the Public, with himself, for the Hire of his own Property, controuls his own Actions, and' pays himself with the Public Money intrusted to his Charge: His Trust and Interest draw opposite Ways: His Trust obliges him to be frugal for the Public; to hire at the lotveft Price (lower, if he ‘ can, than the Price allowed by Government); to take _

Care that what he hires is complete and fit for Service; to employ as few Vessels and Carriages, and for as ffiort a Time, as possible: But his Interest leads him not to spare the Public Purse; to let to Government, . at the same fixed Price, all the Vessels, Carriages, and 1 Horses, he can collect, by whatever Means procured, or at however low a Price he may have purchased them; and whatever may be their Condition or Differ-. \ ence in Point of Goddness, to keep them continually i _.. in Pay, whether wanted, or employed, or not, and for > as long a Time as he can contrive; and his last Advantage may be, the fpffering them to be taken or destroyed by the Enemy, to entitle him to the Value from the Public. In such aCoqteft between Duty and Interest, it is not uncharitable to suppose the Public '

Interest will frequently be sacrificed to private Emolument. But this is not the only Mischief: Tfiis Practice has a manifest Tendency to corrupt and'endanger the Service of the Army; it weakens the military Dif-cipline; it infuses into the Soldier the Thirst for Gs^n,... amt diverts his Attention from Honour, and fys £01107; try's Service, to the Pursuit of Wealth, and thattqo by intrenching upon the Treasure of his Country. t

The Establishment was hardly ever complete, from *he conftaot Difficulty of procuring the Number of Waggons it required; as they Were therefore so scarce in that Country, and the Cattle could have been employed to more Advantage than upon the Pay of Government, it might have been advantageous to the Inhabitants to have had the Use of them for the Time the Army were in Quarters; and the Hire of them, for some Months every Year, would have been no inconsiderable Saving to the Public.

All Orders and Regulations of every Kind proceed from the Commander in Chief: His Power extends,

without Controul, over the whole Army and all its Connexions. it is limited only by his Discrelion; consequently every form of Proceeding, every Usage and Mode of Practice, mud rest either upon his Orders or his Acquiescence. That we might learn upon what Authority this Custom, for the Officers to be Contractors of this Description, was grounded, we required from-Sir William Hoice and Lord the Orders

and InllruXions issued by them in North , rela-

tive to the several Departments employed in the Expenditure of the Public Money. The Returns to these Requisitions contained the Appointment of the Super-intendant of Vessels, and the Regulation of the Payment of their Hire, in the Offices of the Departments in which they wereemployed, both above mentioned, together withother Orders made from Time to Time for different Purposes of Regulation: Rut we found at one Period only Orders relative to the Point immediately under our Consideration. These Orders were issued by Lord Cormoallis, are dated the 43d December 1780, and

contain Matter very important to the Subjex before us. Lord Cormoallis had upon several-Occasions found, that the Waggons and Horses provided for the Public Service by the Quarter Master General were in bad Condition, and neither fit nor able to perform the Services required. To remedy these Abuses, he thought ik necessary to direct, that the Quarter Master General should have no Property in either the Waggons or Horses; and to that End he issued Orders, enjoining him not to charge more for Waggons and Horses than lie had actually paid; not to charge the Hire of Waggons and Horses purchased; not to purchase them but upon Government Account; and, if he hired them, to pay the Proprietors the full Price for Hire allowed by Government. He ordered all the necessary Craft to be purchased on Government Account; and some of the Vessels to be discharged, as soon-as they came under the Direction of his Deputy Quarter Master General at Portsmokth in the Chef apeak, upon his Representation that thbywere unnecessary. He ordered likewise the Commissary General not to charge Government for the complete Ration, unless he Supplied that Ration from the Stores from England,', and to charge no more Tor frefti Provisions, Flour, or Indian Meal, than what they cost him. The Manner of conducing this last Office it is notin our Power to inquire into; the Commissaries General are dead; and their Accounts not in England.

These Orders are levelled at Abuses at that Time existing; and these Abuses all tend to the defrauding of the Public for private Emolument.

By pursuing the Rules of Computation inserted above, we are enabled to discover how much would have been saved to the Public had the Waggons and Horses been purchased at first on Account of Government. From the Lift inserted in the Appendix it appears, that the Average Number of Waggons constantly employed in the Service, from the 25th of 1776 to the

31st of March 1780, that is, Three Years and a Quarter*, was Seven hundred Thirty-nine; and the Average Number of Horses, One thousand Nine hundred Fifty-eight; and the Average Number of Drivers Seven hundred and Sixty: The Average Hire of all these Amounts 1 VOL. 38.

to One hundred and Four thousand One hundred Thirty- jr. 104,13a: two Pounds a Year; from whence deducting Sixteen thousand One hundred Eighty-one Pounds the Hire of l6>lSl-Seven hundred and Sixty Drivers, at One Shilling and Two Pence each per Day, there remains the Sum of Eighty-seven thousand Nine hundred Fifty-one Pounds. £ *7.95!. Seventy-five thousand Nine hundred and Two Pounds fop Two Years more, to the 31st of March last; that is, the Public have paid Four hundred and Seventeen 7>59*. thousand Five hundred Niilety-two Pounds for the lingle Article of the Hire of Waggons and Horses; the Whole of which might have been saved, had the Mode contained in the Orders of the 23d of December 1780 been at first adopted.

From the Circumstances thus disclosed, it can hardly be doubted that this PraXice, of letting out for Hire tb Government, has been highly lucrative to the Officers engaged in it. The Officer is a Trustee for the Public; as such, he is bound to husband the Public Money committed to hisCharge with as much Frugality as if it were his own; what he saves, or what he gains, he laves and gains not for himself, but for the Public. He ought not to be permitted, by any Management or Contrivance, -to carve out for himself an Interest in the Execution of a Public Trust: If that Interest has been pro-duXive, how far fufch Profit belongs to the Public, and whether, by Bills Of Discovery filed by the proper Officer of the Crown, or by what other Means, it may be discovered, and reclaimed for the Public, are for the Wisdom of Parliament to decide.

It is of public Concern this Evil should be speedily correXed: It flows from permitting a Trull to reside,

with an Interest, in the same Person. The Remedy is, to take away the Interest, and by that Means to restore the Trull and Controul to its full Force, that it may freely operate for the Benefit of the Public, uninfluenced, by private Considerations.

But the Remedy may be extended Hill farther: It should seem as if it would be more beneficial to the Service, if the Officers were relieved entirely from the Trouble of making the Payments. When their Military Duty calls them to the Field, they mull neglex their Duty as Paymasters, and leave that Branch to be conducted entirely by their inferior Officers and Clerks.

It seems to be a Hardship upon a Quarter Master General, to be subject to account for very large Sums, no.

Part of which he paid himself, but merely because they were paid in his Name, and at his Office, whilst lie himself was absent upon other Duty.

There is no necessary Connexion between the Mili-

tary Duty of these Officers and the Expenditure of Money for Military Services: This latter belongs properly to a Civil Department, and may beexecuted by a Civil Offi- cer. Major General William Roy, who, during the last War in Germany, was in the Departments both of the Quarter Master General and Chief Engineer, informed us, that no Public Money was issued to himjn either of these Capacities: He was no Accountant; but all the Expences incurred in these Departments were defrayed by the Deputy Paymaster General of tffe Forces, pur-

Seventh Re. ft 1 ant to the Warrauts of the Commander in Chief issued n?jflionert°m' ^or Purpose. The Quarter Mailer General and of Public Chief Engineer were considered in that Army as Checks

Account*, upon the Expenditure on Behalf of the Public: They were to see that the Articles supplied were good of the Kind, adequate to the Services they were intended for, and that there was no Waste.

We are therefore of Opinion, that the Orders of thte 23d December 1780, should be put in Force forthwith throughout the whole Army: that no Officer should be permitted to have a Property or Interest in any Article whatever, which the Duty of his Office obliges him to provide for the Service of the Army; If purchased, it should be purchased by and for the (life of Government; if hired, it should be hired of Persons unconnected witht Military Service. We are likewise of Opinion, that the Payments should be taken from the Military Officer, and thrown upon the Deputy Paymaster General of the Forces, who is the proper Cashier of the Array* to be carried on by him, in pursuance of the Warrants of the Commander in Chief.

The other Point, in which we think the Public have not been sufficiently guarded, is the Allowance of the Vouchers without Sufficient Examination: This Defect pervades every Branch of the Expenditure under our Consideration. The principal Officers in these Departments are the Persons accountable: They make up, pass, and swear to the Accounts; but, having a Variety of other material Business to transact in their several Stations, they have no Leisure to attend to the actual Payments: A Quarter Mailer General, whose Account £*0,000. ^mounted to above Six hundred thousand Pounds, wad for Five Months together upon Duty in the Field, without having been able once to attend his Office. lie is likewise obliged to pass the Account of a Sura never received by him, but issued to and expended by an Affiil-aut Deputy Quarter Mailer General, whom he neither ^*35- appointed nor knew; and the Warrant issued to this Assistant Hates, that the Sum therein directed i$ to be accounted for by the Quarter Mailer General. The Chief Engineer considers himself as liable to account for Sums, no Part of which he either receives or pays, nor are the Payments made in his Name; for, though the Sum is made payable to him by the Warrant, yet he never actually receives it; bu^he indorse* the Warrant to the Paymaster of the Works, who receives the Whole, and with it discharges Bills, either directed to him for Payment by the Chief Engineer Of the Commander in Chief, or at his own Discretion without the Intervention of either, and.takes the Receipts in his own Name.

Tltis important Business of Expenditure, that requires Attention, Circumspection, Accuracy, and Fidelity, must be entrulled to inferior Officers, Clerks, and even to Strangers. /

The Making up and Examination of the Accounts is conducted in the following Manner: — Every Quarter the Accountant collects together from his Deputies, Afirstants, and Clerks, all the Vouchers for the'Payments made by them during that Quarter: They are abstracted1, digelled under Heads, and bundled up together. The Abstract is produced to the Commander in Chief for his Inspection and Approbation, and in order to obtain a Final Warrant for the Amount of the Abstra6L The Vouchers are ready for his Inspection. if he requires it. This is the FirstCheokto which the Account is submitted. It is not to be imagined that the many important Objects, that mud continually engross the Attention of the General of an Army, will afford him either Leisure or Patience to examine voluminous Bundles of Vouchers: He may fonaetimes, upon a transient View of the Abstract, find some Article that excites his Curiosity to call for an Explanation; but lie cannot pofl#>ly enter into the Detail, or minutely examine into the Circumstances ofa complicated Receipt; and therefore, uulefsfach an Instance ocqurs for Inspee-22

lion* the Vouchers are? left unesam hied in the Hands of the Accountant, and the Commander in Chief depends upon his Honour that he has them in his Possession.

After the Final Warrant is obtained* this Abstract and the Vouchers are lent Home to be examined, that the Account may be passed in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest. It is utterly impossible the Vouchers can be sufficiently scrutinizediu this Office, for want of Evidence: The Accountant is the proper Person to give them Information; and he, very possibly, is not privy to the Payment, or to any one Cirpumftance dated in the Voucher.

Charles Harris, Esquire, One of the Deputy Auditors of the Imprest, tells us the Grounds upon which a1 Voucher, for a Payment for the Extraordinary Service Abroad, is, and of Necessity mud be, allowed in that Office: If it contains a certain Sum received, the Signature of a Person receiving, and a just Computation, and agrees with the AbstraiCT, it is deemed and admitted as a fair Voucher: For the Truth of it, they rely upon the Oath taken by the Accountant before hie BarojiS of the Exchequer, when he paflfes his Account. In Fast, in those Accounts which have been already passed in this Office, nh Inquiry seems to have been made into the Truth of the Vouchers, whitqver Questions might arise upon the Face of them. By the Form of this Oath, which We Obtained from the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest, the Acotmtant {Wears that the Account is just and true, according to the best of his Knowledge' and Belief: These latter Words mud, as we conceive, be interpreted by him so to qualify the Oath, as to enable hirrito swear with Safety to those Items of Ins Account, of tlte Iranfact ing of which he has no Other Knowledge that what the Vouchers themselves give him, aid where lie knows nothing of the Persons Who transact them, except probably their general Characters: No great Reliance, then, can be had, for the Truth of the Voucher, upon the Oath of the Accountant; because that Oath, so worded, is no additional Evidence of its Truth.

From thus tracing the Voucher, from the Pay Office of the Department in North America to the Office of its finalExamination ini England, it appears, that the Public may be defrauded in a Transaction, and yet the Voucher of that Transactk>n may pass through all its Stages of Examination unfa spefted and unimpeached, and be sworn to by the Accountant without the Violation of hiS Oath. Various are tWe Ways and Means by which the Fraud may be committed: The Agreement or Purebafe may be made by Collusion: The Subject Mattefr of the Receipt may be false in Quantity or Quality: The Service over-rated, or not performed: The Sum inserted may be more than the Suiahona^side paid: The Receipt may be obtained by Compuifion or Collusion, upon false or forged Certificates: It may have been signed hr Blank, and filled up afterwards with false Sums, or signed with a feigned Name; and yet the VoteheT may be fair'upon the Face of it; and these girofs Frauds will escape Detection.

These Suggestiorrt are not mere Snrmifes; they rest not'on bare Possibility or Imagination: They are warranted by what we have observed in the Accounts of the Quarter Masteri General, which have been passed in the Office of the Auditors of the Imprest. Certain Vouchers have been there admitted as Evidence of Payments, to Persons who never did in Fact receive, nor could be supposed likely to be entrulled with the Receipt of the Sums inserted in these Vouchers: The Receipts for the Hire of the Drivers, Waggons, and Horses (no inconsiderable Sum) are not in Truth what thtey purport to be upon the Face of them; they carry the Appearance ofi and are produced as the Receipt of, a certain Sam, by the Person whose Name or Signature is set opphfite. to that Sum; the Sum is compounded of the Hire of the Driver; Waggon, and Horses, fora certain Time; but the Man receiving, or signing, or

The Artificers and Labourers are paid by Lifts, in like Manner with the Drivers; not individually in the Office of the Department, but by the Overseers, who receive the grbfs Amount of the Lift, and, after having paid it, bring it back to the Office, with the Names of the Persons receiving set opposite to the Sums they were to receive.

Since the Drivers (and very numerous they are) are prevailed upon or induced by Custom to sign Receipts for Sams they never receive, there may be Reasons or Inducements for the tike Practice in various other Branches of the Expenditure; and in every Instancb of this Kind the Voucher is not true.

Having been informed that some Meafares had been taken by the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, for the Purpose of controtrling. the Expenditure of this Money in North America, we issued to them our Precept for Copiesof the Commissions and Instructkms given to the Commissaries of Accounts in North America, and Extracts of their Correspondence relative thereto: In consequence of this Requisiti'on, we received the Copy 37* of a Commission, dated 15th 1779, appoint-

ing Major DuncanDrummondCovcimMSary of Accounts, to examine, audit, and certify all Accounts whatsoever of Money due for Forage, Bread, and Provisions, furnished by Contract or otherwise, and delivered for the Use of the Army and Hospitals, and for all other Extraordinary Services. The same Power had been before delegated to Daniel Chamier Esquire, by Com* million dated ill of February 1777,but does not appear to have been ever executed. We find,- by Papers transmitted to us with this Commission (some of which N* 38. we have inserted in the Appendix) that in pursuance of that Commission, and of Directions and Instructions relative thereto, transmitted from Time to Time from the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury to the Commanders in Chief and Commissary of Accounts, some Progress has been made in carrying the Powers of that Commission into Execution;, bdt how far it has been effectual to the Prevention or Diminution of the Evil, it has not been in our Power to discover.

Of the Ten Millions and upwards that have been issued for these Services to North America within the laftSix Years, Accounts of a few Officers only, amount* £. 1,100,000. >ng to about One Million One hundred thou'fond Pounds, have been as yet rendered in the proper Office. £. 140*00The Accounts of about One hundred and Forty

thousand Pounds more are ready: So that the Expense. 8,760,00c; diture of Eight Millions Seven hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds Hill remain to be accounted for.

By an Account of the yearly average Number of H is Majesty's Forces serving at Nezo York and its Dependencies, from the iff of January 1776 to the 3 iff of December 1780, extracted from Returns of those Forces made to us from the War Office, pursuant to our Requisition, it appears that the Number of the Forces decreased every Year from 1778; but front the Account of the Contractors for remitting, the Issue for the Extraordinary Services of the Army greatly increased during the same Period.

In the Account of the Issues to the Officers in the Eour Departments, we find that the Warrants issued to the Quarter Mailers General fmce the 16th of July 1780, and to the Barrack Mailers General since the 29th of June 1780, and tb the Commissaries General since the 25th of May 1778, have been all temporary, for Suifts 6h Account; that no final Warrant has been granted since those several Periods-: So that these Sums have been issued without even the Ceremony of a Quarterly Abstract, and the confidential Relianoe on the Officer that his Vouchers are forthcoming.

Of tliele Ten Millions there have been issued tb Canada, between the ill of June 1776 and the 23d of October last, Two Millions Two hundred Thirty-six thousand add Twenty-nine Pounds Eleven Shillings and Seven Pence; a Province, whose Military Operations fmce the Year 1777, the Public are not made acquainted with. This Issue has been increasing every Year, and no apparent Reason for it; and upon the Expenditure in this Province there exists no Check or Controul, that we know of, whatever.

These are Circumstances of Suspicion and Alarm. The ordinary Forms of Examination and Accounting are neither comprehensive nor strong enough to embrace the various Circumstances of this Expenditure: They call for a minute, accurate, and rigid Investigation; but none such can, as we apprehend, be obtained in this Kingdom; the Evidence essentially necessary for that Purpose cannot be procured here. Should it be thought proper to subject these Accounts to such a Scrutiny, we can devise or fuggeff no Method of obtaining this End, unless the Legislature should think proper to refer all of them to ah Extfhnnraiifon to North America, by Persons intelligent in the Sdbject Matter, and unconnected with the Expenditure; wfib niay inquire into every Cirbufnftstnfce of thk Trdnfaction, and have Recourse to every Perfotf concerned in if, dnd who may be authorised aftd directed tc/etfaffitoe1 into the whole Expenditure1, aW well of the antecedent' as subsequent Iflites. The Gommahdetein Chief ntWy be enjoined to give them their Chttnffehahfce, Ptfote&idit, and Support, and not to1 grant Warrants fert* the Payment of any Article of these Expibrtees Without the Testimony of their Allowance. The DtfellbwanCe the Voucher comes too late, after Payment. By a ChCfck and Controul thus established Upon the Spbt, and by an able and conscientious Execution of such' <i Trull, the Publicmight be enabledto obtain Reffitution where they have been defrauded, and Security a'gHihft Imposition and Peculation for the future.

for remitting Money for the Use and Service of Ftis Majesty's Forces serving in North America. When a Requisition is sent by the Commander in Chief at New York to the Agents of the Remitters, expressing the Want of a certain Sum for the Extraordinary Services of the Army, for the ensuing Quarter, that Requisition is transmittefd by them to the Remitters in England, and a Duplicate is sent, as he is informed, by the Commander in Chief, to the Treasury.

The Remitters usually receive, with the Requisition, Advice of Bills drawn upon them by their Agents in consequence thereof; upon which they apply to the Treasury by Memorial, with a List of the Bills annexed, for Money to enable them to extinguish those Bills: They then receive from the Treasury a Warrant, directed to the Paymaster General of the Forces, to pay to the Remitters the Sum therein mentioned, to satisfy the Whole or a Part of the Sum mentioned in the Memorial. The Paymaster General receives the Money from the Exchequer, and gives to the Remitters a Draft upon the Bank for that Sum; who apply the same to extinguish those Bills.

Where no Bills are drawn by the Agents, and Money is to be remitted to America, in order to support the Exchange there, Money is obtained from the Paymaster General of the Forces in the same Manner, and remitted to America according to special Directions given by the Treasury. Money thus remitted thfc Agents are directed to be very careful of, and not to make Use of, unless the Money-holders should lower the Exchange upon them.

Where the Commander in Chief makes no Requisition, the Remitters receive from their Agents Information of what Money is wanted. The Agents pay the Sums they receive for the Use of the Army to the Deputy Paymasters Abroad, upon their Application.

This Examinant further faith, That the present Agreement between the Treasury and the Contractors, for remitting is One and a Half per Cent. together with all Fees of Office, and the Expence of Transportation. The Contractors would not take upon themselves the Payment of the Fees of Office, because they knew not how to draw the Line relative to the Quantum.

The Examination of Thomas Neale Esquire; taken upon Oath, the 26th of February and 6th of March 1782.

This Examinant faith, That he is Agent in London to Messrs. Harley and Drummond, the Contractors *7

Sir William Howe faith, That he was Commander in Chief of his Majesty's Forces within the Colonies laying on the Atlantic Ocean, from Nova Scotia to Wtfl Florida, from the 10th of October 1775 to the 23d of May 1778.

No Money placed in the Hands of the Deputy Paymaster General of the Forces, for the Extraordinary Services of the Army, can be issued without the Authority of the Commander in Chief; this Authority is sometimes delegated by him to General Officers commanding Corps, in Cafes of Necessity, where the Communication is either interrupted or too distant.

He, as Commander in Chief, exercised this Power, by granting either Temporary or Final Warrants to Of-

iicqs

4

22 Geo. III. i o° Junii. 1075

ficers at the Heads of those Departments employed in the Expenditure of the Public Money for the Army Services. The Temporary Warrant, is a Warrant for Money issued upon Account at the Requisition of the Officer. At the End of every Quarter, or as soon after as the Service would admit, lie, as Commander in Chief, required from the Heads of each Department an Account of the Sunv expended for the laftrimfettled Quarters: Pursuant to this Requisition, the Officer laid Before him the Quarterly Abllraft of the Money disbursed by him in his Department, distinguillied under particular Heads; he examined this' Abstract, and if any Charge was either new, or higher than lie expected, A>r wanted Explanation, he either called for the Voucher for that Article, or for the Officer to explain it; other-wife the Vouchers were left unexamined in the Possession of the Officer, to be produced by him in the Office -where his Accounts were to be finally passed. The Vouchers are so numerous, and the Duties of a Commander in Chief arc so various and extensive, that it is -almost impossible for him to give his Attention toa'minute Examination into Accounts; but he generally either enquired of the Officer whether he had the Vouchers for the different Articles, or depended upon his Honour that he had them all in his Possession. If no Objection appeared to this Abfiraet, he granted a Pinal Warrant, directed to the Deputy Paymaster General, for the Payment of the total Sum therein mentioned, with the Abstract annexed. The Officer, as he apprehends, carries this Final Warrant to the Deputy Pay mailer General, takes up from him, and cancels the Temporary Warrants, and receives the Balance, leaving with the Deputy Paymaster General the Warrant anil Abstract, as his Voucher.

The Officers to whom he, as Commander in Chief, issued Money, for which they were accountable, were, the Secretary and Paymaster to the Commander in Chief, the Paymaster General of the Provincial Troops, the Quarter Master General, the Commissary General, the Barrack Master General, the Chief Eugineer, the Su-perintendant of Indian Adairs, the Bridge Master, the Purveyors of the Hospitals, and the Commissary of Prisoners. When lie came to the Command of the Arm-y, he found that the Quarter Master General, the Commissary General, the Barrack Master General, «nd the Chief Engineer, were Officers enirufted with the Expenditure of Part of the Public Money; he continued to entrust them with so much Money as the Services of their respective Departments required. He does not consider it as absolutely necessary that these Officers should be entrusted with the Payment of Money; that Trust may be lodged in other Persons. All these Accountants were paid in the same Manner, upon producing Abstracts of their Expenditure, by-Final Warrants granted to them upon the Deputy Paymaster General: He found this to be the Mode in Use when he first took the Commasd of the Army, and continued it during his Time. Confidence is placed in the principal Officers, that they execute their several Trusts with Honesty and Fidelity, and they are subject to a future Account at Home. If these Accounts were not discharged, the Service could not go on. Lists of/these Warrants are sent Home every Quarter, or soon after every Settlement, to the Commissioners of the Treasury. in feme Cafes of inferior Officers, lie did not discharge the Accounts until they had been examined by some Officer to whom lie referred them. There was no Check upon the Officers employed in this Expenditure, except the Examination by the Commander in Chief above-mentioned.

The Regulations by whiqh the several Departments are governed, flow from the Commander in Chief, and no Alterations can be made in those Regulations but by his Orders. In forming the Regulations, he usually consulted the Officers at the Heads of the several De-

Yoi.. 38.

partments. He, as Commander in Chief, appointed all Seventh those additional Staff Officers which the Necessity of the Commission Service required, such as Deputy Quarter Matters, De- trs „f pubUe puty Barrack Matters, some Assistant Commissaries, and Accounts, other inferior Officers, and the superior Officers themselves, upon a Vacancy.

He settled what Number of Waggons, Horses, and Drivers should be employed for a Campaign; and the Distribution of them amongst the several Regiments,

Corps, and Departments. These were in general retained the whole Year; had they been discharged at -the End of the Campaign, it would have been hardly possible to have procured them when wanted; and all of them were at one Time in the Winter, whilst the Army was at Philadelphia, employed in bringing in Forage, and the regimental Waggons were constantly employed in the regimental Servioes.

He settled the Price of the Hire of the Waggons,

Horses, and Privers, and the Tonnage of the Small Craft employed. No Waggons or Horses were purchased for the Use of the Army; the hiring them was considered as the greatest Saving to the Public, because they could then be discharged at any Time without Loss. If they were loft in the Service, the Proprietors were to be paid for them.

Finding a Necessity for a Naval Officer who ftiouhl provide proper Vessels, and take Care that they were well equipped, and forth-coming when wanted, and not detained in the Service longer than was necessary — for these, and other Purposes mentioned in the Warrant, he appointed Captain David Laird to the Office -of Super-intendant of Vefl'ejs. This firanoh before belonged to the Department of the Quarter Master General, but his Buimefs grew too exlenfive for him to give l'uffieicnt Attention to it. *

Mr. Daniel Chamier received aCommission appointing him Commissary of Accounts attending the Army in North America; but he does not know or believe 'that he ever acted under that Authority.

The Examination of the Right honourable Lieutenant General Earl Cornw; taken upon Oath, 27th of February, and ift of,

1782.:

Lord Cornwallis faith. That when he was left in Command in South Carolina, in June 1780, lie received Instructions from Sir Henry Clinton, the Commander in Chief, to grant Warrants upon the Deputy Paymaster General in Charles Town, for Money applicable to the Services of the Array; in consequence of these Instructions, he issued Warrants to the several Officers employed in the Expenditure of the Public Money, particularly to the Quarter Master General, Commissary General, and Persons in other inferior Departments; most of these Warrants were, as he believes. Temporary, and upon Account, and granted upon the Application of Officers, suggesting that they were in want of Monty to carry on the Services of their several Departments.

Having found, upon several Occasions, the Waggons and Horses employed in the Public Service in bad Condition, and unable to perform the Services required, he wished to apply the most effectual Remedy to this Evil; and, as it had been customary for the Quarter Master General to provide both for the Use of the ^rmy, he thought it necessary to direct that the Quarter Master General should have no Property in either the Waggons or the Horses; and this was one Object of Orders issued

by him, and dated the 23d December 1780: The same Orders contained Directions relative to the Craft provided by the Quarter Mailer General for the use of the Army. Another Object of these Orders was the Com* miliary General: He had observed that it had been the Custom for the regimental Quarter Mailers, when they received Provisions from the Commissary General, to give him Receipts for a complete Ration, without distinguishing whether it confilted of Provisions received from Europe, or procured in that Country; whereas the latter were often got for nothing, or at a Price inferior to that of the European Ration: To remedy this Evil, he issued those Orders relative to the Commissary General. To prevent Provisions taken from the Country, and either not paid for, or paid for at a certain Price, from being charged to the Account of the Public, either at all, or at a greater Price than they were purchased at, he appointed Commissaries of Captures, who collected Provisions from the Country, and gave Receipts for them to those Persons only who were Friends; and delivered out those Provisions to the Troops without taking Receipts for them; by which Means those Receipts only given to the Proprietors of the Provisions could be brought in Charge against the Public.

That these Receipts given by the Commissaries of Captures might be paid at New , and some Indulgences promised by him to the Troops might be allowed, he delivered to the Commander in Chief at New York a Paper containing Memorandums for that Purpose, which Paper he will lay before the Board, as it fully describes the Steps he had taken relative to his Mode of supplying the Army under his Command.
