A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunder written, on Behalf of themselves and others belonging to the honourable Band of Gentlemen Pensioners, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for enabling His Majesty to discharge the Debt contracted upon His Civil List Revenues, and for preventing the same from being in Arrear for the future, by regulating the Mode of Payments out of the said Revenues, and by suppressing or regulating certain Offices therein mentioned, which are now paid out of the Revenues of the Civil List; And setting forth.

That the Petitioners are under the greatest Concern to find it proposed to be enacted by the said Bill, " That all " Commission and other Offices belonging to the Band " of Gentlemen Pensioners under the Captain of the " Band, as also the Vacancies in the Band of Gentle-.

" men Pensioners, should not be fold, but that the " Officers and Private Gentlemen of the Band of Petitioners should be filled only by Officers of the Army " or Navy upon Half Pay;" and alledging, that it has^ been customary for many Years part, to purchase the Office of a Private Gentleman of the Band of Pensioners, and to sell the same '(with the Approbation of the Captain) as Occasion offered; and, in Confidence of being permitted to fell such Office, the Petitioners have been induced to give on an Average One thousand Guineas for the fame; and that the Salary of such Oflice, after Payment of the Land Tax and other Outgoings, seldom producing more than the Net Annual Sum of Seventy-nine Pounds, and the Expence of the necessary Regimental or Uniform Dress of the Petitioners being deducted thereout, reduces the Income to about Seventy-six Pounds ])er Annum; and that many of the Petitioners being Gentlemen of small Fortunes, and having little else to depend on than this Income, and some of them being married, and having Children, will be very much distressed if they should not be permitted to fell their Offices: And therefore submitting their same to the Justice of the House, trusting, that.

On dueConsideration, they shall have such Indemnity

their being deemed the Produce ot Germany, which fiave been entered as Growth on Single Duties, which the Officers contend were liable to the Treble Duties, according to an Act of the Eighth and Ninth of William and Mary, and therefore seized the fame; and that a Bill to permit Drugs, the Product of Hungary and Germany, to be imported from the Netherlands, or any Port of Germany, on Payment of the Single Duty, and other Purposes, is now depending before the House: And therefore praying. A Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Artificers employed by His Majesty's Board of Ordnance, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Artificers employed by the said Board, being offered to be presented to the House;

Lord John Cavendish, by His Majesty's Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have been employed by the Board of Ordnance for several Years, and there is now owing to the Petitioners, for Stores delivered, and Work performed, a very large Sum of Money, for which they have received Debentures, issued by the said

.Board; Mid that the Petitioners undertake to exeente the Business of the Board of Ordnance in Expectation of being regularly paid at the End of every Twelve, but certainly not to exceed Fifteen Mbnths; and the Petitioners are now in Possession of Debentures to a very considerable Amount, many of which far exceed that Credit, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners have frequently applied to the Board of Ordnance for Payment, and for shortening the Time of Credit, and have received for Answer, That the Board were perfectly satisfied with the Reasonable-nefe of their Application, but that it was not'in their Power to give them Relief; and that the Debentures issued by the Board of Orduance bear no Interest, and the Time of Payment having of late become very uncertain, they are not negociable, except at a most enormous Discount: And therefore praying the House to take, into Consideration the very great Hurdthips the Petitioners labour under, and that all Debentures issued by the Board of Ordnance in the PosseifioD of the Artificers,. may bear Interest from the Expiration of Twelve Months from the Date thereof, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as the House shall think just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A MefTage from the Lords, by Hell:

Mr. Leeds and Mr.

others, trading to and from Bengal, in conducing their Ships and Vessels through the said Channel, and like-wife while they remain at Anchor in the Entrance of the said River Hooghly exposed to Tetnpefts and the Violence of the Tides, the Petitioner did, in the Month of May 1770* first form a ProjeCfc of exploring a new Track, or Channel, for the safe conducting of Ships of large Burthen from Sea, and also of establishing a Place, or Harbour, for them safely to ride at Anchor in, whereby the Dangers above-mentioned might be avoided, and the usual Losses saved; and accordingly the Petitioner having, as well from his own Observation as the Report of others, found that a Brandi of the said River Hooghly, called Channel Creek, might be a Channel adapted to this Purpose, did, in the Month of June 1770, make his first; Survey thereof; but as the Plan, from the Expences attending it, and the Knowledge to be acquired of the Navigation, might take much Time before it could be carried into Execution, the Petitioner did not then think it proper to lay th& same before the Public, but in the Year 1771 he made other Surveys of the said Navigation, and the Rivers and Creeks ad-joiningto and communicating with it, and having upon these Surveys found the Project to be worthy the Attention of the Public, the Petitioner soon after presented a Copy of his Survey to John Cartier, Esquire, at that Time President and Governor of Fort William, in Bengal, who approved thereof, and gave the Petitioner Encouragement to prosecute his Surveys, and the Petitioner, therefore, continued from Time to Time to examine the new Channel, and has, by great Labour and Expence, completed tnoft exaCfc Surveys of its Navigation, whereby it fully appears that great and important Advantages would refillt to the Public by bringing the said Navigation into general Use, and establishing a Refitting Station for his Majesty's Ships at a Place called New Harbour, distant from the Sea about Twenty-six Miles; and that the Petitioner did, in the Year 1775, lay the Subject of thlsBufiness before the Governor General and Council of Bengal, confiding of Warren Hajlings, Esquire, General Sir John Clavering, the honourable Colonel Monson, Richard Barwell, and Philip Francis, Esquires, who ordered Letters to be written to the Petitioner, alluring him of their Protection and Assistance in the Prosecution and Completion of the said Harbour, and on the 28th Day of June 1776, they did unanimously execute to the Petitioner a Grant for the said Harbour, bearing Date the ift Day of June 1776; and that Reports on the Harbour and Navigation to it were made by Sir John Clarke, late Commander of his Majesty'sShip Dolphin, Captain George Farmer, of the Sea Ho/je Sloop of War, but late of His Majesty's Ship Quebec, Captain John Ritchie, Marine Surveyor 1o the Fuji India Company at Bengal, Captains Savage, Brom field, Smith, Newte, Ogilvie, Arthur, Maw, Apple-garth, and several other Commanders of East India Ships, 20 ' who

To the Second Amendment made by your Lordships, in Press i. Line 24. the Commons agree.

Tti so much of the Third Amendment made by your Lordships, in Press 1. Line 26. as proposes after Kingdom" to leave out " they," the Commons agree; but to so mu'Ch of the said Amendment as proposes to insert; ". having Permission so to do from proper! Authority," instead thereof, the Commons disagree; because 4heJWords " proper Authority" are too vague and uncertain, and the Corps may be prevented from acting at all, while they are consideriUg the Propriety of the Authority.under which they are to act: But supposing the Authority to be well defined, if it is at a Difiance (which probably would be the Cafe) the Opportunity might be. loft, and this Plan defeated, one. of whole principal Excellencies is, that the Force isdiffufed every wherei and ready to act with Expedition and Effect on all, and particularly on sudden. Emergencies.

The Commons therefore think that there is no Occasion for such inconvenient Reilraints, but that the Corps may be well left to the Command of their Officers, under such Instructions and Regulations as His Majesty in HijWifdom shall think proper to give, especially when it is considered, that no such Corps will be entitled to Pay on their Marching, which may be considered as a Motive for their doing so improperly, except in the same of an actual Rebellion or Invafioti, and their Marching for the Purpose of acting against such Rebels or Invaders.

To the Fourth Amendment made by your Lordships, in Press 1. Line 32. the Commons agree.

To the Fifth Amendment made by your Lordships, in Press 1. Line 33. the Commons disagree; because it is the Plan of the Bill, that no Corps shall be subject to military Discipline, except in the same of actual voluntary Service, on the Occasions mentioned in the . Bill, and the Receipt of Pay.

These are plain Propositions, all depending on each other: nor would it be possible to extend the Power of military Discipline beyond those specific Cafes (which, as it seems, is intended to be done by this Amendment) without departing from that main Principle of the Bill, that all the Service under it must be voluntary.

To the last Amendment made by your Lordships, in Press 1. Line 36. the Commons agree.

For these Reasons the Commons hope, that your Lordships will not inlist on the Amendments proposed to be made by your Lordships to this Bill, to which the Commons have disagreed; as by that Means the passing of the Bill may be risqued, or the Effect of it may be weakened, at a Time when not only your Lordships, who have so high an Interest in providing an efficient Defence for your Country from the Perils with which it is surrounded, but every Individual in it, is called upon to Hand forward and contribute his Assistance, and when every possible Exertion is become necessary for our Preservation.

The said Reasons being severally read a SecondTime,

were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That a Conference be desired with the Lords, upon the Subject Matter of the Amendments made by their Lordships to the said Bill.

Ordered, That Mr. Secretary at War do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

Conferred aCommission of Lieutenant Colonel on William Pcacocke, Esquire, and hath also given Commissions of Major and Captains to Gentlemen, Natives of Ireland, -poriefling no Property in the County, by whom Four Vol unteer Companies have beenraised by Beat of Drum, while their Militia were serving out of the said County, and confiding chiefly of Natives of Ireland, neither raised nor attested according to the Militia Laws, but as Regulars, and exceeding Three Times the Number of the established Militia of the County of Anglesey, and that the Petitioner beipg informed that the said Commissions, and all Acts done under the fame, Were wholly illegal and void, and finding hiraself nevertheless actually superseded in the Command of the Anglesey Militia (without any Notice given him or any Court Martial) by the illegal Appointment of Officers of superior Rank, hath made several fruitless Attempts to obtain Redress by Representations to Sir Bayley,

and by Memorials delivered to the Earl of and to Lord Amherst; and that the Petitioner hath been informed, that a Court of Inquiry was hejd at Vox Heath respecting the Commissions so granted, and, notwithstanding repeated Applications, the Report and Proceedings of the said Court have been, in a Manner unprecedented, suppressed by Persons in Office; and that the Petitioner hath lately caused Application to be made to the Court of King's Bench, for a Mandamus to Sir Nicholas Bayley, to declare the Commissions of several of the Officers of the said Volunteer Companies vacant, which Mandamus the said Court, after hearing whatever could be urged on Behalf of Sir Nicholas Bayley, granted; but such Officers still continue to act, though several Gentlemen of the County, properly qualified, offered to accept the vacant Commissions; and that the Petitioner, being informed that the Redress to be obtained in a Court of Law will be inadequate, may be long delayed, and may be finally eluded, thinks it his Duty to represent to the House the present Situation of the Militia of the County of Anglesey, commanded by Officers holding Commissions indeed granted in due Form, but void by Law, and whose Orders it may therefore be neither safe to obey nor prudent to refill, and in this Dilemma the private Men are compelled to serve (contrary to all the Provisions in the Militia Laws) under Officers neither qualified by I.aw nor known in the County, nor even understanding their Language, from whom they have experienced the moil injurious and nujuft Treatment, of which they have made many Complaints to the Com-7

mander in Chief, and others having Authority to redress their Grievances; and that the Petitioner apprehends, that the Grant of these Commissions by Sir Nicholas Bayley is not less subversive of the whole System of Militia Laws than injurious to Individuals, and conceives the Object of these Laws is to form a Constitutional' Force for the internal Defence of Great Britain, by disciplining the Inhabitants of the several Counties under' Officers who have an Interest in the Country they defend, and whose Property is a Pledge to their Fellow Citizens, that they will not concur in any Design against the Public Liberty; that this Object is loft if the Restraints if these Laws may be openly violated, by raising a Military Force contrary to all the Provisions respecting the Militia of the County, and neither Officers nor Men connected with the County for which they prbtend to serve: And that the Petitioner, sensible of this Injustice, and being well advised that the present festablishment of the Anglefetj Militia is tinconiiitutional and illegal, and a Measure calculated only for private Advantage and Emolument, to procure Rank and Pay for Officers not entitled to hold Coiri-missions (as the said Volunteer Companies are exceedingly defective in their proper Complement of Men) submits the same to the House, praying, That such Relief may be granted therein as shall be judged proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

during so long a Session, bears the most honourable Testimony to your Zeal and Industry in the Service of the Public for which you have provided with the cleared Discernment of its true Interests; anxiously opening every Channel for the Return of Peace; and furnishing with no less Vigilance the Means of carrying on the War, if that Measure should be unavoidable.

The extensive Powers with which I find Myfeif invested to treat for Reconciliation and Amity with the Colonies which have taken Arms in North America, I shall continue to employ in the Manner most conducive to the Attainment of those Objects, and with an Earned-ness suitable to their Importance.

The Zeal which My Subjects in Ireland have expressed for the Public Service, ihows that the Liberality 9F your Proceeding towards them is felt there as it ought; and has engaged their Affections, equally with their Duty and Interest, in the common Cause.

The Diligence and Ardour, with which you have entered upon the Confi deration of the British Interests in the East Indies, are worthy of your Wisdom, Justice, and Humanity. — To protect the Persons and Fortunes of Millions in those distant Regions, and to combine Our Prosperity with their Happiness, are Objects which amply repay the utmost Labour and Exertion.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you My particular Thanks for the very liberal Supplies which you have granted with so much Chearfulness and Zeal for the Service of the current Year. I reflect with extreme Regret upon the heavy Expence which the Circumstances of Public Affairs unavoidably call for. It shall be My Care to husband your Means to the belt Advantage, and, as far as depends on Me, to apply that Economy which I have endeavoured to let on Foot in My Civil Establishment, to those more extensive Branches of Public Expend iture; in which llill more important Advantages may be expected.

My I^otxls and Gentlemen,

The important Successes, which, under the Favour of Divine Providence, the Valour of My Fleet in the West Indies hath obtained, promise a favourable Issue to Our Operations in that Quarter. The Events of War in the East Indies have also been prosperous. Nothing however can be more repugnant to My Feelings than die long Continuance of so complicated a War.

My ardent Desire of Peace has induced Me to take every Measure which promised the speediest Accompli fitment of My Willies; and I will continue to exert My best Endeavours for that Purpose. But if, for Want of a corresponding Disposition in Our Enemies, I should be di (appointed in the Hope I entertain of a speedy Termination of the Calamities of War, I rely on the Spirit, Affection, and Unanimity of My Parliament and People to support the Honour of My Crown, and the Interests of My Kingdoms; not doubting that the Blessing of Heaven, which I devoutly implore upon Our Arms, employed as they are in Our just and necessary Defence, will enable Me to obtain fair and reasonable Tefms of Pacification. The most triumphant Career of Victory would not excite Me to aim at more; and 1 have the Satisfaction to be able to add. that I fee 110 Reason which should induce Me to thiiiKof accept^ ng less.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty's Command, said;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure, That Parliament this Parliament be prorogued to Tuesday the 3d Day prow*®*!-of September next, to be then here holden; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday the 3d Day of September next.
